title: W01 · D1 – Sepsis-3, SOFA and SOFA-2, screening

questions.stem: According to the Sepsis-3 definitions, sepsis is best defined as:
options: Suspected infection plus ≥ 2 SIRS criteria
Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection
Infection plus serum lactate > 2 mmol/L
Suspected infection plus qSOFA ≥ 2
Infection requiring ICU admission
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, operationalised as an acute SOFA increase of ≥ 2 points. The emphasis moved from inflammation (SIRS) to organ dysfunction, which carried ~10 % hospital mortality in the derivation cohorts.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Infection plus ≥ 2 SIRS criteria is the old Sepsis-1/2 concept; SIRS is both non-specific and insensitive.
- C – Lactate > 2 mmol/L is a criterion of septic shock (together with a vasopressor requirement), not of sepsis.
- D – qSOFA ≥ 2 is a prognostic prompt outside the ICU, not part of the definition.
- E – ICU admission depends on local resources and is unrelated to the definition.

**EDIC trap:** "SIRS" or "qSOFA" in a definition question is almost always the distractor.

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. Sepsis-3. *JAMA* 2016;315:801–810.

questions.stem: Regarding septic shock according to Sepsis-3:
options: The criteria apply despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
Hospital mortality in the derivation cohorts was approximately 10 %.
Serum lactate > 4 mmol/L is required.
A vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg is required.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Both clinical criteria must persist despite adequate volume resuscitation; hypotension from uncorrected hypovolaemia does not qualify.
- B (False) – Hospital mortality with both criteria exceeded **40 %**; ~10 % is the figure for sepsis (SOFA ≥ 2).
- C (False) – The threshold is lactate **> 2 mmol/L**; > 4 mmol/L belonged to the older EGDT/SSC era.
- D (True) – A vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg is the circulatory criterion and must coexist with lactate > 2 mmol/L.

**EDIC trap:** a vasopressor without hyperlactataemia, or hyperlactataemia alone, is not septic shock.

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. Sepsis-3. *JAMA* 2016;315:801–810; Shankar-Hari M, et al. *JAMA* 2016;315:775–787.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of qSOFA?
options: Respiratory rate ≥ 22/min
Systolic blood pressure ≤ 100 mmHg
Altered mentation
Heart rate > 90/min
All of the above are qSOFA components
questions.expl:
**Why D:** qSOFA has three items, 1 point each: respiratory rate ≥ 22/min, altered mentation (GCS < 15) and systolic BP ≤ 100 mmHg. Heart rate > 90/min is a SIRS criterion and has no place in qSOFA.

**Why not the others:**

- A – RR ≥ 22/min is a qSOFA item.
- B – SBP ≤ 100 mmHg is a qSOFA item.
- C – Altered mentation (any GCS < 15) is a qSOFA item.
- E – Incorrect, because heart rate is not a qSOFA component.

**EDIC trap:** mixing qSOFA with SIRS (HR > 90/min, RR > 20/min, temperature, WBC) or with the RR > 20 threshold.

**Ref:** Seymour CW, et al. *JAMA* 2016;315:762–774; Singer M, et al. *JAMA* 2016.

questions.stem: Concerning sepsis screening in the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines:
options: NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS are recommended over qSOFA as a single screening tool.
The recommendation regarding screening tools is conditional.
Prehospital screening (e.g. in ambulances) is addressed by a strong recommendation.
qSOFA is recommended as the single preferred screening tool in hospitalised patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SSC 2026 recommends NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS over qSOFA as a single screening tool in acutely ill hospitalised patients, because qSOFA has low sensitivity (good prognostic, poor screening tool).
- B (False) – It is a **strong** recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence.
- C (False) – Prehospital screening with a standard tool is new in 2026 but only **conditional, very low certainty**.
- D (False) – qSOFA is recommended **against** as a single screening tool.

**EDIC trap:** both SSC 2021 and SSC 2026 advised against qSOFA as a single screening tool.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has a baseline SOFA of 0. Which acute change defines sepsis according to Sepsis-3?
options: SOFA increase ≥ 2
SOFA increase ≥ 3 in at least two organs
SOFA increase ≥ 1
Any SOFA increase with lactate > 2 mmol/L
SOFA ≥ 4
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Sepsis-3 operationalises organ dysfunction as an acute SOFA increase of ≥ 2 points consequent to infection. If pre-existing dysfunction is unknown, baseline SOFA is assumed to be 0, so a SOFA of ≥ 2 attributable to the pneumonia defines sepsis (~10 % hospital mortality).

**Why not the others:**

- B – There is no requirement for ≥ 3 points or for two organs; a total Δ ≥ 2 suffices.
- C – A 1-point rise is below the threshold.
- D – Lactate is not part of the sepsis definition; it is a septic shock criterion.
- E – The definition uses an acute change of ≥ 2, not an absolute value of 4.

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. Sepsis-3. *JAMA* 2016;315:801–810.

questions.stem: Regarding the SOFA-2 score (JAMA 2025):
options: It retains six organ systems.
It was externally validated in more than one million patients.
A gastrointestinal organ system was added.
Its development combined a modified Delphi consensus with data-driven analysis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SOFA-2 keeps six organ systems, renamed brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney and hemostasis.
- B (True) – External validation in ~1.24 million ICU stays in 6 cohorts, after development and internal validation in ~2.1 million (≈ 3.3 million in total).
- C (False) – GI and immune dysfunction were discussed but **not included**, owing to a lack of reliable, widely available variables.
- D (True) – A modified Delphi consensus was combined with data-driven analysis; new variables reflect modern organ support (advanced respiratory support, mechanical circulatory support, RRT).

**EDIC trap:** expect principle questions (6 systems, what was not added) rather than exact thresholds.

**Ref:** Ranzani OT, et al. SOFA-2. *JAMA* 2025;334:2090–2103.

questions.stem: Which term was abandoned by the Sepsis-3 task force?
options: Sepsis
Severe sepsis
Infection
Septic shock
Organ dysfunction
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The Sepsis-3 task force abandoned "severe sepsis" as redundant: once sepsis itself means infection-related organ dysfunction, a separate "severe" category adds nothing. Under Sepsis-1/2, sepsis = infection + SIRS and severe sepsis = sepsis + organ dysfunction.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Sepsis was redefined (dysregulated host response with organ dysfunction), not abandoned.
- C – Infection remains the prerequisite of sepsis.
- D – Septic shock was retained and redefined (vasopressor for MAP ≥ 65 mmHg + lactate > 2 mmol/L despite fluids).
- E – Organ dysfunction (Δ SOFA ≥ 2) is the core of the new definition.

**EDIC trap:** any option that uses "severe sepsis" as a current category is wrong.

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. Sepsis-3. *JAMA* 2016;315:801–810.

questions.stem: Hyperlactataemia in sepsis:
options: Is unaffected by hepatic lactate clearance.
Is one of the two clinical criteria of septic shock.
May result from β2-adrenergic stimulation of aerobic glycolysis.
Always indicates tissue hypoxia.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Reduced hepatic lactate clearance (liver hypoperfusion or dysfunction) contributes to hyperlactataemia.
- B (True) – Lactate > 2 mmol/L together with a vasopressor requirement for MAP ≥ 65 mmHg despite adequate fluids defines septic shock.
- C (True) – Endogenous and infused catecholamines stimulate β2 receptors, accelerating aerobic glycolysis and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, so lactate rises without tissue hypoxia.
- D (False) – Lactate also reflects adrenergic stimulation, reduced clearance and mitochondrial dysfunction; it is not a pure hypoxia marker, so fluids are not pushed merely to normalise it.

**EDIC trap:** "a high lactate always means hypoperfusion" – false.

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. *JAMA* 2016; Garcia-Alvarez M, et al. *Crit Care* 2014;18:503; SSC 2026.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with urosepsis is on noradrenaline 0.1 µg/kg/min for MAP 66 mmHg after 30 mL/kg crystalloid. Lactate is 1.4 mmol/L. According to Sepsis-3 he has:
options: SIRS without sepsis
Cannot be classified without qSOFA
Septic shock
Sepsis without septic shock
Severe sepsis
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Septic shock requires **both** a vasopressor to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg **and** lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids. With lactate 1.4 mmol/L only the circulatory criterion is met. He still has sepsis: noradrenaline ≤ 0.1 µg/kg/min scores 3 cardiovascular points in the original SOFA, so Δ SOFA ≥ 2.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Sepsis-3 no longer uses SIRS, and he has organ dysfunction due to infection.
- B – Classification uses SOFA; qSOFA is not needed.
- C – Lactate ≤ 2 mmol/L excludes septic shock by Sepsis-3.
- E – "Severe sepsis" was abandoned in 2016.

**EDIC trap:** hypotension on a vasopressor without hyperlactataemia is not septic shock.

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. Sepsis-3. *JAMA* 2016;315:801–810.

questions.stem: Which statements about the original SOFA score are true?
options: The neurological component uses the Glasgow Coma Scale.
Each organ system scores 0–4 points.
The renal component uses urine output or creatinine.
The respiratory component uses the PaO2/FiO2 ratio.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – The CNS component uses GCS (15 = 0 points, 13–14 = 1 … < 6 = 4); sedation makes it hard to assess.
- B (True) – Six organ systems, each scored 0–4, maximum 24.
- C (True) – Renal points come from creatinine or urine output (< 500 mL/day = 3, < 200 mL/day = 4).
- D (True) – Respiratory points come from PaO2/FiO2; 3–4 points (< 200 / < 100 mmHg) require ventilatory support.

**EDIC trap:** a K′ item with all four statements true is uncommon but legitimate; judge each statement on its own.

**Ref:** Vincent JL, et al. The SOFA score. *Intensive Care Med* 1996;22:707–710.

open.q: A ward nurse calls you about a patient with suspected pneumonia who has qSOFA 2. Explain how you would classify this patient according to Sepsis-3, and why qSOFA alone is insufficient both to diagnose sepsis and to screen for it.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
- Organ dysfunction = acute increase in SOFA ≥ 2 points due to infection (baseline assumed 0 if unknown) – SOFA, not qSOFA, must be assessed.
- qSOFA (RR ≥ 22/min, altered mentation, SBP ≤ 100 mmHg) is a prognostic tool identifying higher risk of poor outcome; it is not part of the sepsis definition.
- qSOFA has low sensitivity, so it is a poor screening tool.
- SSC 2026 recommends NEWS, NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS over qSOFA as a single screening tool (strong recommendation, moderate certainty).
- If the patient additionally needs a vasopressor for MAP ≥ 65 mmHg with lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids, he meets septic shock criteria (mortality > 40 %).

open.q: Explain why the original SOFA score needed updating and summarise the main features of SOFA-2.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Original SOFA (1996): 6 systems, 0–4 points each, max 24.
- Weaknesses: outdated vasopressor doses (dopamine as reference), no account of modern organ support (HFNO, ECMO, RRT, mechanical circulatory support), difficulty assessing GCS in sedated patients.
- SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025) developed by modified Delphi consensus plus data-driven analysis.
- Development/internal validation in ~2.1 million and external validation in ~1.2 million patients from diverse settings.
- Retains 6 systems, renamed: brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney, hemostasis; new variables and thresholds reflecting current organ support.
- GI and immune dysfunction were not included (lack of reliable, widely available variables).
- The sepsis definition (Δ ≥ 2 points) remains tied to the Sepsis-3 concept.

title: W01 · D2 – SSC 2026: screening, lactate, timing of antibiotics

questions.stem: According to SSC 2026, an adult with probable bacterial pneumonia and sepsis, but NOT in shock, should receive antimicrobials:
options: Within 6 hours, after results of procalcitonin
Within 24 hours
Within 3 hours of recognition
Only after blood cultures result
Immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition
questions.expl:
**Why E:** For **probable or definite** sepsis without shock SSC 2026 recommends antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h of recognition (strong, very low certainty) – the same window as for septic shock. The 3-h window is reserved for *possible* sepsis without shock after a time-limited rapid assessment.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Procalcitonin is not used to decide whether to start antibiotics, and 6 h is not an SSC window.
- B – 24 h is far beyond any SSC time frame.
- C – Within 3 h applies to *possible*, not probable, sepsis without shock.
- D – Cultures are taken before antibiotics only if this causes no substantial delay; results are never awaited.

**EDIC trap:** "possible" (3 h) vs "probable/definite" (1 h) is the key word in the stem.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: In the GRADE system as used by SSC:
options: Best-practice statements are ungraded.
"We recommend" denotes a strong recommendation.
"We suggest" denotes a conditional recommendation.
A strong recommendation can be made even when the certainty of evidence is very low.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Best practice statements are ungraded; they are used when benefit is unequivocal (e.g. "sepsis is a medical emergency").
- B (True) – "We recommend" = strong: most informed clinicians would act this way.
- C (True) – "We suggest" = conditional (weak): reasonable variation according to patient and context.
- D (True) – GRADE separates strength from certainty; a strong recommendation can rest on very low certainty when benefit clearly outweighs harm, e.g. antibiotics within 1 h in septic shock.

**EDIC trap:** "a strong recommendation requires high-certainty evidence" – false.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812. Guyatt GH, et al. GRADE. *BMJ* 2008;336:924–926.

questions.stem: A patient has possible sepsis without shock and the likelihood of infection is judged low. SSC 2026 suggests:
options: Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
Procalcitonin-guided initiation of antibiotics
Empirical antifungal therapy
Deferring antimicrobials while closely monitoring the patient
Antibiotics within 3 hours regardless of further findings
questions.expl:
**Why D:** New in SSC 2026: in possible sepsis without shock and with a **low likelihood of infection**, deferring antimicrobials while closely monitoring the patient is suggested (conditional, very low certainty). This reflects stewardship – unnecessary antibiotics cause resistance, C. difficile infection and toxicity, and may delay an alternative diagnosis.

**Why not the others:**

- A – The 1-h window is for shock or probable/definite sepsis.
- B – Procalcitonin should not be used to decide whether to start antibiotics.
- C – Empirical antifungals have no role when infection itself is unlikely.
- E – The 3-h window applies only if concern for infection persists after rapid assessment, not "regardless".

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Regarding lactate in SSC 2026:
options: Measuring lactate is suggested only in patients with septic shock.
Capillary refill time may be used as an adjunct to other perfusion measures.
Serial lactate measurements are suggested to guide resuscitation when lactate is elevated.
Fluids should be continued until lactate normalises.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Measuring lactate is suggested in possible, probable or definite sepsis, not only in shock (conditional, low).
- B (True) – Capillary refill time as an adjunct to other perfusion measures is suggested (conditional, low), based on ANDROMEDA-SHOCK.
- C (True) – With elevated lactate or shock, serial measurements are suggested to guide resuscitation (conditional, low).
- D (False) – Fluids should not be continued merely because lactate is not yet normal; lactate also rises with β2 stimulation and reduced clearance.

**EDIC trap:** lactate is a guide, not a target to be normalised with fluid.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812. Hernández G, et al. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK. *JAMA* 2019;321:654–664.

questions.stem: Empirical anaerobic coverage in sepsis (SSC 2026) is suggested:
options: For all patients with septic shock
Never, as anaerobes are rare in sepsis
Only in patients with specific risk factors for anaerobic infection
Only when blood cultures grow anaerobes
In all patients older than 65 years
questions.expl:
**Why C:** New SSC 2026 statement: in patients **without** risk factors for anaerobic infection use an empirical regimen without anaerobic coverage; **with** risk factors (e.g. an intra-abdominal source) include it – both conditional, very low certainty. The aim is to avoid unnecessary spectrum, which harms the gut microbiota and promotes resistance.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Shock alone is not a risk factor for anaerobic infection.
- B – Anaerobes matter in specific sources, so coverage is not "never" indicated.
- D – Empirical therapy is chosen before culture results are available.
- E – Age is not the criterion for anaerobic coverage.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Concerning the 2026 SSC guidelines as a document:
options: They contain fewer than 50 statements.
Most statements are strong recommendations.
They were published only in Critical Care Medicine.
They are a joint initiative of ESICM and SCCM.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – SSC 2026 contains **129** statements (46 new), produced by 69 experts from 23 countries.
- B (False) – About **63 %** are conditional; strong recommendations are the minority.
- C (False) – Published simultaneously in *Intensive Care Medicine* and *Critical Care Medicine*.
- D (True) – SSC is a joint initiative of ESICM and SCCM.

**EDIC trap:** most SSC recommendations are conditional – do not assume "guideline = strong".

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: In a septic patient requiring ICU care, SSC 2026 suggests admission to ICU within:
options: 1 hour
6 hours
3 hours
24 hours
12 hours
questions.expl:
**Why B:** SSC 2026 suggests that adults with sepsis or septic shock who require ICU care are admitted to the ICU **within 6 h** (conditional, low certainty), because delayed transfer from the ED/ward has been associated with worse outcomes in observational data.

**Why not the others:**

- A – 1 h is the antibiotic window for shock and probable sepsis, not the ICU-admission target.
- C – 3 h relates to antibiotics in possible sepsis and to the initial 30 mL/kg of fluid.
- D – 24 h is far longer than suggested.
- E – 12 h is not an SSC time frame.

**EDIC trap:** 6 h is also the ideal window for source control – both are conditional recommendations.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Regarding blood cultures and procalcitonin:
options: Procalcitonin should be used to decide whether to start antibiotics.
Antibiotics in septic shock may be delayed until two sets of cultures are obtained, regardless of time.
Blood cultures must be taken before antibiotics even if this substantially delays them.
Procalcitonin can support decisions about discontinuing antibiotics.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Procalcitonin plus clinical evaluation should **not** be used to decide whether to start antibiotics.
- B (False) – In septic shock antibiotics are given immediately, ideally within 1 h; cultures must not delay them.
- C (False) – Cultures are taken before antibiotics only if this does **not substantially delay** them (strong, low certainty).
- D (True) – Procalcitonin with clinical evaluation can support decisions to shorten or stop antibiotics.

**EDIC trap:** PCT helps with stopping, never with starting.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why SSC distinguishes antibiotic timing between shock and sepsis without shock?
options: The association between delay and mortality is strongest in shock, while over-treatment of non-infected patients carries harm
Antibiotics are ineffective in shock
Randomised trials proved harm of early antibiotics in sepsis without shock
Patients without shock never have bacteraemia
Blood cultures are only positive in shock
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Observational data show the strongest association between antibiotic delay and mortality in **septic shock**, whereas in sepsis without shock the association is weaker and over-treating non-infected patients causes harm (resistance, C. difficile, toxicity, missed alternative diagnoses). Hence 1 h in shock and a time-limited assessment (up to 3 h) in possible sepsis without shock.

**Why not the others:**

- B – Antibiotics are lifesaving in shock; that is why they are given fastest.
- C – No RCT has shown harm from early antibiotics; the evidence is mainly observational.
- D – Bacteraemia also occurs in patients without shock.
- E – Blood cultures are positive in a minority overall, with or without shock.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812. Seymour CW, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2017;376:2235–2244.

questions.stem: Vasopressor administration in early sepsis (SSC 2026):
options: Strong evidence defines the safe maximal duration of peripheral vasopressors.
Initial crystalloid bolus is suggested before vasopressors in sepsis-induced hypotension.
Vasopressors may be started peripherally rather than delaying until central access is secured.
The recommendation on peripheral vasopressors is conditional.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Data on the safe duration, dose and route of peripheral vasopressors are insufficient.
- B (True) – In sepsis-induced hypotension an initial crystalloid bolus is suggested, followed by a vasopressor if hypotension persists (conditional, very low).
- C (True) – Vasopressors may be started peripherally rather than delaying until central access is secured (large proximal cannula, extravasation checks).
- D (True) – The peripheral-vasopressor recommendation is conditional, very low certainty.

**EDIC trap:** "a central line is required before noradrenaline" – false.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with fever, confusion and BP 78/45 mmHg is picked up by a rural ambulance service that uses a structured sepsis screening protocol; the expected time to in-hospital evaluation is 90 min. According to SSC 2026, the most appropriate antimicrobial strategy is:
options: Withhold antimicrobials until blood cultures can be taken in hospital
Give antimicrobials in the ambulance (conditional recommendation, very low certainty)
Give antimicrobials in the ambulance only if qSOFA is 3
Give oral antibiotics and defer IV therapy until arrival
Give antimicrobials in the ambulance for all patients with suspected infection, irrespective of shock or transport time
questions.expl:
**Why B:** New in SSC 2026: in definite or probable sepsis **with hypotension** (septic shock) and an anticipated time to in-hospital evaluation of **> 60 min**, antimicrobials are suggested in the ambulance or flight (conditional, very low certainty), but only once a structured prehospital screening process is in place. This patient meets all three conditions.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Withholding for 90 min contradicts the time-critical approach to septic shock.
- C – qSOFA is not used as a trigger for antimicrobials.
- D – Oral antibiotics are inappropriate in shock.
- E – The suggestion is limited to septic shock with transport > 60 min, not all suspected infections.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Regarding blood cultures and source control in SSC 2026:
options: Blood cultures should be collected as soon as possible, ideally before antimicrobials – a strong recommendation.
The blood culture recommendation is based on high-certainty evidence.
Early source control is suggested, ideally within 6 hours of diagnosis of sepsis requiring source control.
The source control timing recommendation is strong with moderate certainty.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Blood cultures as soon as possible, ideally before antimicrobials if this causes no substantial delay – strong recommendation.
- B (False) – Strong recommendation, but only **low** certainty of evidence.
- C (True) – Early source control is suggested, ideally within 6 h of diagnosis of sepsis requiring it (new explicit time window in 2026).
- D (False) – The source-control timing recommendation is **conditional, very low** certainty.

**EDIC trap:** a strong recommendation can rest on low certainty – read strength and certainty separately.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

open.q: Outline your approach to the timing of antimicrobials according to SSC 2026 in (a) a patient with septic shock, (b) probable sepsis without shock, (c) possible sepsis without shock, and (d) possible sepsis with a low likelihood of infection. Explain the rationale for these differences.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Septic shock (possible or definite): antibiotics immediately, ideally within 1 h of recognition – strong recommendation, very low certainty.
- Probable/definite sepsis without shock: also immediately, ideally within 1 h – strong, very low certainty.
- Possible sepsis without shock: time-limited rapid assessment; if concern persists, antibiotics within 3 h of first suspicion – conditional.
- Low likelihood of infection without shock: defer antibiotics with close monitoring (new in 2026) – conditional.
- Rationale: in observational data each hour of delay in shock is associated with higher mortality; the association is weaker without shock.
- Overuse of antibiotics has real costs: resistance, C. difficile, toxicity, missing an alternative diagnosis – hence emphasis on stewardship.
- Take blood cultures before antibiotics if this does not substantially delay them; do not use PCT to decide on starting antibiotics.

open.q: Explain how a recommendation can be "strong" while resting on "very low certainty" evidence in the GRADE system, using an example from SSC 2026.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- GRADE separates strength of recommendation from certainty of evidence (high / moderate / low / very low).
- "We recommend" = strong (most informed clinicians would act this way); "we suggest" = conditional, with reasonable variability.
- Best practice statements are ungraded but self-evident.
- A strong recommendation can be issued when the benefit/risk balance is clear despite low-quality evidence.
- Example: antibiotics within 1 h in septic shock – strong / very low certainty, based on observational delay–mortality data.
- In SSC 2026 ~63 % of the 129 statements are conditional.

title: W01 · D3 – Fluids in sepsis: how much, which and when to stop

questions.stem: In the CLASSIC trial, patients were randomised:
options: In the ICU after receiving at least 1 L of IV fluid, with shock onset < 12 h
After 72 hours of ICU stay
In the emergency department before any fluid
Only if they required renal replacement therapy
In the operating room during major surgery
questions.expl:
**Why A:** CLASSIC randomised 1554 adults in 31 European ICUs with septic shock of < 12 h who had **already received ≥ 1 L** of IV fluid, testing restriction after initial resuscitation. The restrictive arm received a median 1798 vs 3811 mL in the ICU, with no difference in 90-day mortality (42.3 % vs 42.1 %) and no signal of harm.

**Why not the others:**

- B – Randomisation was early (shock < 12 h), not after 72 h of ICU stay.
- C – CLASSIC was an ICU trial; CLOVERS randomised in the ED, and only after 1–3 L of crystalloid.
- D – Renal replacement therapy was not an inclusion criterion.
- E – Perioperative restriction was tested in RELIEF (major abdominal surgery), not CLASSIC.

**EDIC trap:** CLASSIC = ICU, Europe, after resuscitation; CLOVERS = ED, USA, first 24 h.

**Ref:** Meyhoff TS, et al. CLASSIC. *N Engl J Med* 2022;386:2459–2470.

questions.stem: Regarding the CLOVERS trial:
options: The protocol period was 72 hours.
Patients had already received 1–3 L of crystalloid before randomisation.
It enrolled patients with sepsis-induced hypotension, mostly in the emergency department.
The restrictive arm showed significantly lower mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – The protocol period was **24 hours**.
- B (True) – Patients had already received 1–3 L of crystalloid before randomisation.
- C (True) – 1563 patients with sepsis-induced hypotension in 60 US centres, mostly enrolled in the emergency department.
- D (False) – Death before discharge home by day 90 was 14.0 % vs 14.9 % (NS), despite ~2.1 L less fluid and earlier vasopressors in the restrictive arm.

**EDIC trap:** both CLASSIC and CLOVERS were "negative" – less fluid gave the same mortality.

**Ref:** Shapiro NI, et al. CLOVERS. *N Engl J Med* 2023;388:499–510.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with septic shock and a concomitant severe traumatic brain injury requires fluid resuscitation. The most appropriate fluid is:
options: 6 % hydroxyethyl starch
4 % albumin
Ringer's lactate
0.9 % sodium chloride
Plasma-Lyte 148
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In TBI, 0.9 % saline is preferred: balanced solutions are mildly hypotonic and may worsen cerebral oedema, which is why SSC 2026 excepts TBI from its "balanced over saline" suggestion. Albumin increased mortality in SAFE-TBI, and starches are not used at all.

**Why not the others:**

- A – 6 % HES increases mortality and RRT (6S) and should not be used.
- B – 4 % albumin was associated with higher mortality in the TBI subgroup of SAFE (probably via raised ICP).
- C – Ringer's lactate is hypotonic relative to plasma.
- E – Plasma-Lyte 148 is a balanced solution; meta-analyses show a signal of harm for balanced fluids in TBI.

**EDIC trap:** "balanced crystalloids for everyone" – the exception is TBI.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; SAFE Study Investigators. *N Engl J Med* 2007;357:874–884.

questions.stem: Regarding 0.9 % saline:
options: In SMART, balanced crystalloids reduced the composite MAKE30 compared with saline.
Its chloride concentration is approximately 154 mmol/L.
Large volumes reduce the strong ion difference.
It causes hyperchloraemic metabolic alkalosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SMART (15,802 ICU adults, cluster-crossover): MAKE30 14.3 % vs 15.4 % in favour of balanced crystalloids.
- B (True) – 0.9 % NaCl contains 154 mmol/L each of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (plasma Cl⁻ ~100 mmol/L).
- C (True) – Saline has an SID of 0, so large volumes lower plasma SID (Stewart approach).
- D (False) – A falling SID causes **hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis**, not alkalosis; chloride also causes renal vasoconstriction via tubuloglomerular feedback.

**Ref:** Semler MW, et al. SMART. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:829–839.

questions.stem: Which trial showed increased mortality and renal replacement therapy with hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.42 in severe sepsis?
options: 6S
SAFE
PLUS
ALBIOS
SMART
questions.expl:
**Why A:** 6S randomised 804 patients with severe sepsis to HES 130/0.42 or Ringer's acetate: 90-day mortality was 51 % vs 43 %, and more patients needed RRT (22 % vs 16 %). Together with CHEST (more RRT) this led to EMA restrictions and an SSC recommendation against starches.

**Why not the others:**

- B – SAFE compared 4 % albumin with saline; no difference in mortality.
- C – PLUS compared Plasma-Lyte 148 with saline; no difference in 90-day mortality.
- D – ALBIOS compared 20 % albumin plus crystalloid with crystalloid alone; no difference.
- E – SMART compared balanced crystalloids with saline; MAKE30 favoured balanced.

**Ref:** Perner A, et al. 6S. *N Engl J Med* 2012;367:124–134.

questions.stem: According to SSC 2026, regarding fluid responsiveness assessment:
options: Central venous pressure is the preferred guide to fluid therapy.
Passive leg raising is an example of a static measure.
Physical examination alone is suggested as sufficient to guide further fluids.
The recommendation is strong with high certainty.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – CVP is a static measure; SSC suggests against using static measures alone to guide fluids.
- B (False) – Passive leg raising is a **dynamic** test: a reversible autotransfusion, with a response judged by the rise in SV or CO.
- C (False) – Dynamic measures (PLR, PPV, SVV, change in SV) are suggested over physical examination or static measures alone.
- D (False) – The recommendation is **conditional, low certainty**.

**EDIC trap:** an all-false K′ item is uncommon but legitimate.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Monnet X, et al. *Crit Care* 2015;19:18.

questions.stem: In the ALBIOS trial, albumin supplementation targeting serum albumin ≥ 30 g/L in severe sepsis:
options: Increased the need for renal replacement therapy
Did not reduce 90-day mortality compared with crystalloids alone
Was stopped early for harm
Increased mortality in patients with TBI
Reduced 90-day mortality in all patients
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ALBIOS randomised 1818 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock to 20 % albumin targeting serum albumin ≥ 30 g/L plus crystalloid, or crystalloid alone. 90-day mortality was 41.1 % vs 43.6 % (NS). A post-hoc benefit in septic shock was only hypothesis-generating.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Albumin did not increase the need for RRT.
- C – The trial was not stopped early for harm.
- D – The TBI harm signal came from SAFE-TBI; ALBIOS did not address TBI.
- E – There was no overall reduction in mortality.

**Ref:** Caironi P, et al. ALBIOS. *N Engl J Med* 2014;370:1412–1421.

questions.stem: De-resuscitation in septic shock (SSC 2026):
options: It is supported by high-certainty evidence.
Diuretics are the first step.
Active fluid removal is suggested during the first hours of resuscitation.
Ultrafiltration may be used if diuretics are insufficient.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – The de-resuscitation recommendation rests on **very low** certainty evidence.
- B (True) – Diuretics are the first step of active fluid removal.
- C (False) – Active fluid removal is suggested only **after** the acute resuscitation phase (the "E" of ROSE), not during the first hours.
- D (True) – Ultrafiltration may be used if diuretics are insufficient.

**EDIC trap:** know in which ROSE phase each intervention belongs – rescue, optimisation, stabilisation, evacuation.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Malbrain MLNG, et al. *Ann Intensive Care* 2018;8:66.

questions.stem: The initial crystalloid volume suggested by SSC 2026 for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock is:
options: At least 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours, individualised
2 L for all patients irrespective of weight
30 mL/kg within 6 hours, fixed
Fluids only after a vasopressor is started
10 mL/kg over 1 h, then reassess
questions.expl:
**Why A:** SSC 2026 suggests at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid within the first 3 h for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, with the volume **individualised** by frequent reassessment (conditional, low certainty). In obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m²) adjusted or ideal body weight is used.

**Why not the others:**

- B – A fixed 2 L ignores body weight and is not the SSC suggestion.
- C – The window is 3 h, not 6 h, and the volume is individualised, not fixed.
- D – Initial fluid precedes or accompanies vasopressors; it is not given only after them.
- E – 10 mL/kg is well below the suggested initial volume.

**EDIC trap:** "30 mL/kg" is a starting point, not a mandatory fixed dose.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Which statements regarding the PLUS and BaSICS trials are correct?
options: Both compared a balanced solution with 0.9 % saline.
BaSICS was conducted in Brazil.
PLUS was conducted in North America.
Both showed significantly lower 90-day mortality with balanced solutions.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Both compared Plasma-Lyte 148 with 0.9 % saline (BaSICS also tested infusion rate in a factorial design).
- B (True) – BaSICS enrolled ~11,000 ICU patients in Brazil.
- C (False) – PLUS (5037 patients) was conducted in **Australia and New Zealand**.
- D (False) – Neither showed a 90-day mortality difference (PLUS 21.8 % vs 22.0 %; BaSICS ~26 % vs ~27 %).

**EDIC trap:** only SMART was "positive", and only for the composite MAKE30.

**Ref:** Zampieri FG, et al. BaSICS. *JAMA* 2021;326:818–829; Finfer S, et al. PLUS. *N Engl J Med* 2022;386:815–826.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with septic shock from pyelonephritis has received 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid but still has signs of hypoperfusion. According to SSC 2026, regarding further fluid strategy:
options: A restrictive strategy is recommended (strong, high certainty) based on CLASSIC
A liberal strategy is recommended until lactate normalises
Either a liberal or a restrictive strategy is suggested, depending on patient and health-system factors
No further fluid may be given once 30 mL/kg has been reached
There is insufficient evidence to make any recommendation
questions.expl:
**Why C:** New in SSC 2026: after the initial 30 mL/kg with persistent hypoperfusion, **either a liberal or a restrictive** fluid strategy is suggested, chosen according to patient and health-system factors (conditional, low certainty). CLASSIC and CLOVERS showed similar mortality with less fluid; SSC 2021 had made no recommendation.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Restriction is not strongly recommended; CLASSIC showed safety but no mortality benefit.
- B – Fluids should not be continued merely to normalise lactate.
- D – Further fluid guided by dynamic measures is allowed after 30 mL/kg.
- E – Insufficient evidence was the 2021 position; 2026 makes a conditional recommendation.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Meyhoff TS, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2022; Shapiro NI, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding the SSC 2026 statement on fluids after initial resuscitation:
options: It is a strong recommendation.
It recommends a restrictive strategy in all patients after 30 mL/kg.
It is supported by high-certainty evidence.
The choice between liberal and restrictive fluids may take health-system factors into account.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – It is a **conditional** recommendation.
- B (False) – It suggests **either** a liberal **or** a restrictive strategy, not restriction for everyone.
- C (False) – The certainty of evidence is **low**.
- D (True) – The choice may take patient and health-system factors into account.

**EDIC trap:** two neutral RCTs (CLASSIC, CLOVERS) support an "either approach" recommendation, not a preference.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

open.q: Explain why CLASSIC and CLOVERS were both "negative" for mortality yet tested different questions. What do they together imply for fluid management in septic shock?
open.model:
Key points expected:
- CLASSIC (NEJM 2022): ICU, Europe, septic shock < 12 h after ≥ 1 L of fluid – tested restriction after initial resuscitation.
- CLASSIC separation 1798 vs 3811 mL; 90-day mortality ~42 % in both arms, no signal of harm.
- CLOVERS (NEJM 2023): 60 US centres, mainly ED, 1563 patients with sepsis-induced hypotension after 1–3 L, 24 h protocol.
- CLOVERS: restrictive = early vasopressors vs liberal = further boluses; ~2.1 L less fluid; mortality 14.0 vs 14.9 % (NS).
- They randomised at different phases (rescue/early ED vs ICU optimisation/stabilisation – ROSE concept).
- Together: less fluid gives the same mortality; no need to push large volumes before vasopressors, and restriction is safe.
- Practice: ≥ 30 mL/kg within 3 h individualised, then dynamic measures, then active de-resuscitation after the acute phase.

open.q: Outline your choice of resuscitation fluid in septic shock, including special situations (TBI, cirrhosis, large crystalloid volumes), and justify it with trial evidence.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Crystalloids first choice (strong, moderate certainty); balanced over 0.9 % NaCl (conditional, moderate certainty).
- Saline (154 mmol/L Cl⁻) → hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis (fall in SID) and renal vasoconstriction; SMART MAKE30 14.3 vs 15.4 % favouring balanced.
- BaSICS and PLUS showed no mortality difference – hence only a conditional recommendation.
- TBI: use 0.9 % NaCl (hypotonicity of balanced solutions); avoid albumin (higher mortality in SAFE-TBI).
- Albumin not routinely (SAFE and ALBIOS no mortality benefit); consider after large crystalloid volumes or in cirrhosis.
- No HES (6S: ↑ mortality and ↑ RRT; CHEST: ↑ RRT; EMA restriction); avoid gelatins.

title: W01 · D4 – Vasopressors and target MAP in septic shock

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with septic shock from cholangitis is on noradrenaline. According to SSC 2026, the suggested initial MAP target is:
options: 80–85 mmHg
70–75 mmHg
60–65 mmHg
55–60 mmHg
MAP target guided only by lactate
questions.expl:
**Why C:** For patients aged ≥ 65 years SSC 2026 newly suggests an initial MAP target of **60–65 mmHg** rather than higher (conditional, low certainty). It is based on the 65 trial (~2600 patients ≥ 65 y): permissive hypotension reduced vasopressor exposure, 90-day mortality was 41.0 % vs 43.8 % (NS) and there was no signal of harm.

**Why not the others:**

- A – 80–85 mmHg (SEPSISPAM) brought no survival benefit and more atrial fibrillation.
- B – A higher target only adds catecholamine exposure without proven benefit.
- D – MAP below ~60 mmHg is associated with organ injury and has not been tested as a target.
- E – Lactate helps assess perfusion but does not replace a MAP target.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Lamontagne F, et al. 65 trial. *JAMA* 2020;323:938–949.

questions.stem: Regarding the SEPSISPAM trial:
options: It compared MAP targets of 80–85 versus 65–70 mmHg.
Mortality was significantly lower with the higher target.
In chronically hypertensive patients, the higher target was associated with less renal replacement therapy.
Atrial fibrillation was more frequent with the higher target.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 776 patients with septic shock were randomised to MAP 80–85 vs 65–70 mmHg.
- B (False) – There was **no difference** in 28-day (or 90-day) mortality.
- C (True) – In chronic hypertension the higher target reduced creatinine doubling and RRT, without a mortality effect – hypothesis-generating only.
- D (True) – Atrial fibrillation was more frequent with the higher target (~6.7 % vs 2.8 %), reflecting greater catecholamine exposure.

**EDIC trap:** the hypertensive subgroup is not a reason to target a routinely higher MAP.

**Ref:** Asfar P, et al. SEPSISPAM. *N Engl J Med* 2014;370:1583–1593.

questions.stem: In SOAP II, compared with noradrenaline, dopamine was associated with:
options: Better renal outcomes
Lower lactate levels
More arrhythmic events and higher mortality in cardiogenic shock
Less tachycardia
Lower mortality in septic shock
questions.expl:
**Why C:** SOAP II randomised 1679 patients with shock of any type to dopamine or noradrenaline. There was no overall difference in 28-day mortality, but arrhythmic events were roughly twice as frequent with dopamine (24 % vs 12 %) and mortality was higher in the cardiogenic shock subgroup. SSC therefore recommends noradrenaline over dopamine (strong, high certainty).

**Why not the others:**

- A – Dopamine has no renal benefit; "renal-dose dopamine" is a myth.
- B – Lactate was not lower with dopamine.
- D – Dopamine causes more, not less, tachycardia (β1 effect).
- E – There was no mortality benefit in the septic shock subgroup.

**Ref:** De Backer D, et al. SOAP II. *N Engl J Med* 2010;362:779–789.

questions.stem: Vasopressin in septic shock:
options: It is usually titrated up to 0.5 U/min.
SSC 2026 suggests adding it in patients on escalating noradrenaline doses.
Its endogenous levels are typically markedly elevated throughout septic shock.
Acts via V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Vasopressin is given at a fixed low dose, usually up to ~0.03 U/min (max ~0.04); it is not titrated like noradrenaline, and higher doses cause digital, mesenteric and myocardial ischaemia.
- B (True) – SSC 2026 suggests adding vasopressin when noradrenaline doses escalate (conditional, moderate; in practice at ~0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min).
- C (False) – After an early surge, levels become inappropriately low – septic shock is a state of **relative vasopressin deficiency**.
- D (True) – Vasoconstriction is mediated by V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle, independently of adrenergic receptors and relatively preserved in acidosis.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Landry DW, et al. *Circulation* 1997;95:1122–1125.

questions.stem: The VASST trial compared vasopressin with noradrenaline in septic shock. The main finding was:
options: Trial stopped early for digital ischaemia
Vasopressin was superior in severe shock only
Higher mortality with vasopressin
Significantly lower 28-day mortality with vasopressin overall
No significant difference in 28-day mortality overall
questions.expl:
**Why E:** VASST randomised 778 patients already on vasopressors to low-dose vasopressin (0.01–0.03 U/min) or noradrenaline. 28-day mortality was 35.4 % vs 39.3 %, not significant. A predefined subgroup with **less severe** shock had lower mortality with vasopressin – hypothesis-generating only.

**Why not the others:**

- A – The trial was not stopped early; serious adverse events, including digital ischaemia, were similar.
- B – The benefit signal was in less severe, not severe, shock.
- C – Mortality was not higher with vasopressin.
- D – The overall mortality difference was not significant.

**EDIC trap:** "severe" vs "less severe" shock subgroup – a classic swap.

**Ref:** Russell JA, et al. VASST. *N Engl J Med* 2008;358:877–887.

questions.stem: In SSC 2026, regarding first-line vasopressor choice:
options: Noradrenaline is suggested over vasopressin as first line.
Noradrenaline is suggested over angiotensin II as first-line agent.
Noradrenaline is recommended over selepressin.
Noradrenaline is recommended over dopamine with high certainty of evidence.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Noradrenaline over vasopressin as first line: conditional, low certainty.
- B (True) – Noradrenaline over angiotensin II: conditional, very low; ATHOS-3 raised MAP but did not demonstrate a mortality benefit, so angiotensin II is a 2nd/3rd-line agent.
- C (True) – Noradrenaline over selepressin: strong, low certainty (SEPSIS-ACT showed no benefit).
- D (True) – Noradrenaline over dopamine: strong, **high** certainty (SOAP II and meta-analyses).

**EDIC trap:** only the dopamine comparison carries high certainty.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Khanna A, et al. ATHOS-3. *N Engl J Med* 2017;377:419–430; Laterre PF, et al. SEPSIS-ACT. *JAMA* 2019;322:1476–1485.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock has an adequate MAP on noradrenaline and vasopressin, but persistent hypoperfusion; echocardiography shows severe LV systolic dysfunction. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Switch noradrenaline to dopamine
Increase MAP target to 85 mmHg
Add levosimendan
Add dobutamine
Give 2 L of crystalloid
questions.expl:
**Why D:** With cardiac dysfunction and persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate MAP and fluid status, SSC 2026 suggests inotropes over none – dobutamine **added** to noradrenaline, or adrenaline alone (conditional, very low certainty). Inotropes are given on top of, not instead of, vasopressors.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Dopamine causes more arrhythmias and higher mortality in cardiogenic shock (SOAP II).
- B – Raising MAP does not correct low cardiac output; SEPSISPAM showed no benefit and more AF.
- C – Levosimendan is suggested against (LeoPARDS: no organ benefit, more tachyarrhythmias).
- E – A blind 2-L bolus without evidence of fluid responsiveness risks pulmonary oedema in severe LV dysfunction.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Gordon AC, et al. LeoPARDS. *N Engl J Med* 2016;375:1638–1648.

questions.stem: In the 65 trial:
options: Patients aged ≥ 65 years with vasodilatory hypotension were included.
90-day mortality was significantly lower in the primary analysis.
Patients in the permissive arm had higher vasopressor exposure.
The intervention arm targeted MAP 75–80 mmHg.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ~2600 patients aged ≥ 65 y with vasodilatory hypotension in 65 UK ICUs.
- B (False) – 90-day mortality 41.0 % vs 43.8 % – **not significant** in the primary analysis (adjusted analysis suggested possible benefit).
- C (False) – The permissive arm had **less** vasopressor exposure and a lower achieved MAP.
- D (False) – Permissive hypotension targeted **MAP 60–65 mmHg**; usual-care clinicians targeted higher values.

**EDIC trap:** a neutral trial with no harm can still change a guideline (SSC 2026: 60–65 mmHg if ≥ 65 y).

**Ref:** Lamontagne F, et al. 65 trial. *JAMA* 2020;323:938–949.

questions.stem: Adrenaline used as a vasopressor in septic shock commonly causes:
options: Bradycardia
Hypoglycaemia
Hyponatraemia
A fall in lactate due to improved perfusion only
A rise in lactate partly due to β2-mediated aerobic glycolysis
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Adrenaline stimulates β2 receptors in skeletal muscle, accelerating aerobic glycolysis and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, so lactate rises independently of hypoperfusion. This complicates lactate-guided resuscitation; adrenaline also causes tachycardia and hyperglycaemia.

**Why not the others:**

- A – β1 stimulation causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.
- B – Adrenaline causes hyperglycaemia (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, reduced insulin release).
- C – Hyponatraemia is an adverse effect of vasopressin, not adrenaline.
- D – The lactate rise is partly metabolic, not only a reflection of perfusion.

**EDIC trap:** a rising lactate on adrenaline does not automatically mean worsening shock.

**Ref:** Myburgh JA, et al. CAT. *Intensive Care Med* 2008;34:2226–2234; Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Concerning the LeoPARDS trial (levosimendan in sepsis):
options: It supports routine use of levosimendan in septic shock.
Supraventricular tachyarrhythmias were less frequent with levosimendan.
Weaning from mechanical ventilation was less likely with levosimendan.
Levosimendan reduced organ dysfunction scores.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – SSC 2026 suggests **against** levosimendan (conditional, low certainty).
- B (False) – Supraventricular tachyarrhythmias were **more** frequent with levosimendan.
- C (True) – Patients receiving levosimendan were less likely to be successfully weaned from mechanical ventilation.
- D (False) – Mean daily SOFA did not differ from placebo.

**EDIC trap:** an inodilator is not a "better dobutamine" in sepsis.

**Ref:** Gordon AC, et al. LeoPARDS. *N Engl J Med* 2016;375:1638–1648.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with septic shock remains below the MAP target despite noradrenaline 0.6 µg/kg/min and vasopressin 0.03 U/min. Echocardiography shows a hyperdynamic LV. According to SSC 2026, the suggested next agent is:
options: Terlipressin
Adrenaline
Esmolol
Levosimendan
Methylene blue, which is recommended as standard rescue therapy
questions.expl:
**Why B:** When MAP remains inadequate despite noradrenaline and vasopressin, SSC 2026 suggests **adding adrenaline** (conditional, very low certainty); where vasopressin is unavailable, adrenaline can be added to noradrenaline alone. A hyperdynamic LV points to vasoplegia, not a need for an inodilator.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Terlipressin is suggested against (conditional, low certainty).
- C – Beta-blockers such as esmolol are suggested against as a treatment for septic shock.
- D – Levosimendan is suggested against (LeoPARDS), and the LV here is hyperdynamic.
- E – For methylene blue the evidence is insufficient for any recommendation; it is not standard rescue therapy.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: According to SSC 2026, in adults with septic shock:
options: Beta-blockers are suggested against as a treatment for septic shock; the evidence comes from short-acting IV agents such as esmolol and landiolol.
Terlipressin is suggested against (conditional, low certainty).
In concomitant cardiac dysfunction, either noradrenaline or adrenaline may be used as the first vasopressor.
When inotropes are used for persistent hypoperfusion with cardiac dysfunction, they are given in addition to, not instead of, vasopressors.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – New 2026: beta-blockers are suggested against as a treatment for septic shock (conditional, very low); the evidence comes from short-acting IV agents (esmolol, landiolol – e.g. STRESS-L).
- B (True) – Terlipressin is suggested against (conditional, low certainty).
- C (True) – In cardiac dysfunction either noradrenaline or adrenaline may be the first vasopressor (conditional, very low; NA with tachyarrhythmia, adrenaline with bradyarrhythmia).
- D (True) – Inotropes for persistent hypoperfusion with cardiac dysfunction are an add-on to vasopressors (conditional, very low).

**EDIC trap:** rate control with esmolol/landiolol is not a treatment for septic shock.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Whitehouse T, et al. STRESS-L. *JAMA* 2023;330:1641–1652.

open.q: A 72-year-old man with septic shock from pneumonia remains hypotensive after initial fluids. Outline your vasopressor strategy, including the MAP target, choice of agents, escalation and the role of inotropes.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Start noradrenaline (first choice; recommended over dopamine – strong/high certainty); may start peripherally without delaying for a central line; arterial catheter with escalating/high-dose vasopressors (SSC 2026 accepts invasive or non-invasive BP monitoring).
- Initial MAP target 60–65 mmHg because he is ≥ 65 y (SSC 2026 conditional, based on the 65 trial); otherwise 65 mmHg (strong).
- Avoid dopamine (SOAP II: ~2× more arrhythmias, higher mortality in cardiogenic shock).
- With escalating NA (practically ~0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min) add vasopressin (V1, catecholamine-sparing) up to ~0.03 U/min, not titrated like NA.
- Adrenaline as alternative/add-on, aware of ↑ lactate, tachycardia, hyperglycaemia; angiotensin II only as 2nd/3rd line.
- If cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate MAP and volume → dobutamine or adrenaline; no levosimendan (LeoPARDS).

open.q: Explain why SEPSISPAM and the 65 trial do not support a higher MAP target in septic shock, and what the chronic hypertension subgroup finding means.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- SEPSISPAM: 776 patients, MAP 80–85 vs 65–70 – no difference in 28-d mortality.
- Higher target caused more atrial fibrillation (more catecholamine exposure).
- In chronic hypertension the higher MAP reduced creatinine doubling and RRT but not mortality – hypothesis-generating only.
- 65 trial: ~2600 patients ≥ 65 y; permissive MAP 60–65 → less vasopressor exposure, MAP ~6 mmHg lower.
- 90-d mortality 41.0 vs 43.8 % (NS in primary analysis), adjusted analysis suggested possible benefit, no signal of harm including renal.
- Conclusion: MAP 65 (strong) and 60–65 in older patients (conditional); a higher target means more catecholamines without benefit.

title: W01 · D5 – Corticosteroids in septic shock

questions.stem: In the ADRENAL trial, hydrocortisone 200 mg/day by continuous infusion in ventilated patients with septic shock:
options: Was given together with fludrocortisone
Did not significantly reduce 90-day mortality but hastened resolution of shock
Significantly reduced 90-day mortality
Was given only to ACTH non-responders
Increased the rate of recurrent shock and mortality
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ADRENAL randomised 3800 ventilated patients with septic shock on vasopressors to hydrocortisone 200 mg/day by continuous infusion for 7 days or placebo. 90-day mortality was 27.9 % vs 28.8 % (NS), but shock resolved faster, initial ventilation was shorter and fewer transfusions were needed.

**Why not the others:**

- A – No fludrocortisone was given; that was APROCCHSS.
- C – The mortality reduction was not significant.
- D – Patients were not selected by ACTH testing (non-responders were the focus of Annane 2002).
- E – Mortality was not increased, and serious adverse events were rare.

**Ref:** Venkatesh B, et al. ADRENAL. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:797–808.

questions.stem: Regarding APROCCHSS:
options: Hyperglycaemia was less frequent in the treatment group.
Patients were selected based on a short ACTH stimulation test.
Hydrocortisone was combined with fludrocortisone.
90-day all-cause mortality was significantly lower in the treatment group.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Hyperglycaemia was **more** frequent with hydrocortisone, as in other steroid trials.
- B (False) – Patients were not selected by an ACTH test; all adults with septic shock meeting the criteria were eligible.
- C (True) – Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 h plus fludrocortisone 50 µg enterally once daily for 7 days.
- D (True) – 90-day mortality 43.0 % vs 49.1 %, significantly lower.

**EDIC trap:** APROCCHSS = "the one with fludrocortisone" and the only large trial with a mortality benefit.

**Ref:** Annane D, et al. APROCCHSS. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:809–818.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with septic shock has been on noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min for 5 hours despite adequate fluids. The most appropriate corticosteroid regimen is:
options: Methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days
Corticosteroids are not indicated
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (e.g. 50 mg every 6 h)
Dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 10 days
Await short Synacthen test before deciding
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Septic shock on noradrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥ 4 h after adequate fluids meets the practical starting criterion (SSC 2021); SSC 2026 suggests IV corticosteroids in septic shock (conditional, low certainty). The regimen is hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg every 6 h or continuous), fludrocortisone optional, for about 5–7 days.

**Why not the others:**

- A – High-dose methylprednisolone pulses showed no benefit in septic shock in older trials.
- B – He meets the criteria, so corticosteroids are indicated.
- D – Dexamethasone 6 mg for 10 days is the COVID-19 (RECOVERY) regimen.
- E – The ACTH test does not identify who benefits (CORTICUS) and should not delay treatment.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Evans L, et al. SSC 2021. *Intensive Care Med* 2021;47:1181–1247.

questions.stem: Regarding the CORTICUS trial:
options: Shock reversal was faster with hydrocortisone.
A signal of more superinfections was observed with hydrocortisone.
The ACTH stimulation test identified patients who benefited.
Hydrocortisone did not reduce 28-day mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Shock reversal was faster with hydrocortisone.
- B (True) – There was a signal of more superinfections, including new sepsis and septic shock.
- C (False) – The ACTH test did **not** identify who benefited; there was no mortality benefit in non-responders either.
- D (True) – 28-day mortality was not reduced (~34 % vs ~32 %, NS) in ~500 patients.

**EDIC trap:** CORTICUS is the reason we no longer use the Synacthen test to select patients.

**Ref:** Sprung CL, et al. CORTICUS. *N Engl J Med* 2008;358:111–124.

questions.stem: Which mechanism does NOT contribute to the benefit of corticosteroids in septic shock?
options: Direct bactericidal effect
Attenuation of the inflammatory response
Increased vascular responsiveness to catecholamines
Upregulation of adrenergic receptors
Reduced inducible nitric oxide synthase activity
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Corticosteroids have no antimicrobial effect; their benefit in septic shock comes from haemodynamic and immunomodulatory actions that counter CIRCI. They are therefore given with, never instead of, antibiotics and source control.

**Why not the others:**

- B – Attenuating the inflammatory response (e.g. NF-κB inhibition) is a genuine mechanism.
- C – Increased vascular responsiveness to catecholamines underlies faster shock reversal.
- D – Upregulation of adrenergic (α) receptors contributes to that responsiveness.
- E – Reduced iNOS activity means less NO-mediated vasodilatation.

**EDIC trap:** in a negatively phrased item, the four true mechanisms are the distractors.

**Ref:** Annane D, et al. CIRCI guidelines (SCCM/ESICM). *Intensive Care Med* 2017;43:1751–1763.

questions.stem: Critical illness–related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI):
options: Can involve tissue resistance to glucocorticoids.
Can involve reduced cortisol clearance.
Is reliably diagnosed by a random cortisol below a fixed threshold in all septic patients.
Is one rationale for low-dose hydrocortisone in septic shock.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Tissue resistance to glucocorticoids (fewer or less functional receptors) is one component of CIRCI.
- B (True) – Reduced cortisol clearance (impaired breakdown) occurs alongside HPA-axis dysfunction.
- C (False) – No random cortisol threshold reliably diagnoses CIRCI in sepsis; total cortisol is distorted by low binding proteins, and treatment does not depend on a level.
- D (True) – CIRCI is one rationale for low-dose hydrocortisone in septic shock.

**EDIC trap:** "measure cortisol before steroids" – false; the decision is clinical.

**Ref:** Annane D, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2017;43:1751–1763; Boonen E, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2013;368:1477–1488.

questions.stem: In CAPE COD (severe community-acquired pneumonia), hydrocortisone:
options: Increased 28-day mortality
Was compared with dexamethasone
Showed benefit only in patients with septic shock
Reduced 28-day mortality; patients with septic shock were excluded
Reduced mortality only in influenza pneumonia
questions.expl:
**Why D:** CAPE COD randomised 800 ICU patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia to hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (4 or 8 days, then tapered) or placebo. 28-day mortality was 6.2 % vs 11.9 %. Septic shock and influenza were exclusion criteria, so the result does not transfer directly to septic shock.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Mortality was reduced, not increased.
- B – The comparator was placebo, not dexamethasone.
- C – Patients with septic shock were excluded.
- E – Influenza was excluded, and steroids tend to harm in influenza pneumonia (observational data).

**Ref:** Dequin PF, et al. CAPE COD. *N Engl J Med* 2023;388:1931–1941.

questions.stem: According to SSC guidance:
options: Corticosteroids are suggested in sepsis without shock.
The 2026 recommendation on corticosteroids is strong with high certainty.
Corticosteroids are suggested in septic shock (SSC 2026).
SSC 2021 suggested starting when noradrenaline or adrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for at least 4 h.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Corticosteroids are **not** suggested in sepsis without shock; HYPRESS showed no prevention of shock.
- B (False) – The 2026 recommendation is **conditional, low certainty**.
- C (True) – SSC 2026 suggests IV corticosteroids in septic shock.
- D (True) – SSC 2021 gave the practical start criterion: noradrenaline or adrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for at least 4 h after initiation.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Evans L, et al. SSC 2021. *Intensive Care Med* 2021;47:1181–1247; Keh D, et al. HYPRESS. *JAMA* 2016;316:1775–1785.

questions.stem: Which difference between ADRENAL and APROCCHSS is most often cited to explain their discordant mortality results?
options: ADRENAL used dexamethasone
ADRENAL excluded ventilated patients
APROCCHSS gave steroids for 28 days
ADRENAL was conducted only in the USA
APROCCHSS added fludrocortisone and enrolled sicker patients
questions.expl:
**Why E:** APROCCHSS added **fludrocortisone 50 µg** and enrolled sicker patients (control mortality ~49 % vs ~29 % in ADRENAL). Bolus vs continuous hydrocortisone and different inclusion criteria (ventilation required in ADRENAL) are also cited. These differences are used to explain why only APROCCHSS reduced mortality.

**Why not the others:**

- A – ADRENAL used hydrocortisone 200 mg/day, not dexamethasone.
- B – ADRENAL required mechanical ventilation.
- C – Both trials gave steroids for 7 days.
- D – ADRENAL was conducted mainly in Australia, New Zealand and the UK (plus Saudi Arabia and Denmark), not the USA.

**Ref:** Venkatesh B, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:797–808; Annane D, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:809–818.

questions.stem: Adverse effects observed more frequently with hydrocortisone in septic shock trials include:
options: A consistent, large increase in mortality from secondary infections across ADRENAL and APROCCHSS
Hyperglycaemia
Hypernatraemia (particularly with mineralocorticoid effect)
Hypoglycaemia
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Neither ADRENAL nor APROCCHSS found a significant increase in serious infections; the superinfection signal came from CORTICUS.
- B (True) – Hyperglycaemia is the most common adverse effect.
- C (True) – Hypernatraemia occurs, particularly with mineralocorticoid effect (fludrocortisone; hydrocortisone itself at 200 mg/day).
- D (False) – Glucocorticoids cause hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia.

**Ref:** Venkatesh B, et al. ADRENAL. *N Engl J Med* 2018; Annane D, et al. APROCCHSS. *N Engl J Med* 2018; Sprung CL, et al. CORTICUS. *N Engl J Med* 2008.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock has pH 7.15, lactate 8 mmol/L and KDIGO/AKIN stage 3 acute kidney injury. According to SSC 2026, sodium bicarbonate:
options: Is recommended for all septic shock patients with lactate > 4 mmol/L
Is suggested against in all circumstances
Is recommended (strong) to reduce vasopressor requirements
Is suggested in this patient because of pH ≤ 7.2 with AKI stage 2–3 (conditional, very low certainty)
Should be replaced by THAM as first choice
questions.expl:
**Why D:** SSC 2026 suggests sodium bicarbonate in septic shock with severe metabolic acidaemia (**pH ≤ 7.2**) and **AKI stage 2–3** (conditional, very low certainty). This is based on the predefined AKIN 2–3 stratum of BICAR-ICU, where bicarbonate lowered 28-day mortality and RRT use. To improve haemodynamics in lactic acidaemia, bicarbonate is suggested against (conditional, low).

**Why not the others:**

- A – A lactate threshold is not an indication, and there is no strong recommendation.
- B – The pH ≤ 7.2 plus AKI 2–3 group is an explicit exception.
- C – Bicarbonate is suggested against for reducing vasopressor requirements.
- E – SSC makes no recommendation for THAM.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Jaber S, et al. BICAR-ICU. *Lancet* 2018;392:31–40.

questions.stem: Regarding adjunctive therapies in SSC 2026:
options: IV vitamin C is suggested for septic shock.
Blood purification techniques, including haemoperfusion, are suggested.
Antipyretic therapy is suggested to improve clinical outcomes in sepsis.
IV immunoglobulins are suggested against.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – IV vitamin C is suggested **against** (conditional, low); LOVIT showed a higher risk of death or persistent organ dysfunction.
- B (False) – Blood purification, including haemoperfusion such as polymyxin B, is suggested against (conditional, very low; EUPHRATES negative).
- C (False) – Antipyretics to improve outcomes are suggested against (conditional, very low; new 2026); treating fever for comfort is still allowed.
- D (True) – IV immunoglobulins are suggested against (conditional, low).

**EDIC trap:** nearly every adjunct in SSC 2026 is "against" – the exceptions are corticosteroids and bicarbonate in pH ≤ 7.2 with AKI.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Lamontagne F, et al. LOVIT. *N Engl J Med* 2022;386:2387–2398; Dellinger RP, et al. EUPHRATES. *JAMA* 2018;320:1455–1463.

open.q: Explain why ADRENAL and APROCCHSS reached different conclusions on mortality, and how this shapes current recommendations for corticosteroids in septic shock.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ADRENAL (3800, ventilated patients on vasopressors): HC 200 mg/d continuous for 7 d, no fludrocortisone – 90-d mortality 27.9 vs 28.8 % (NS).
- APROCCHSS (1241): HC 50 mg q6h + fludrocortisone 50 µg for 7 d – 90-d mortality 43.0 vs 49.1 % (significantly lower).
- Differences cited: fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid effect), bolus vs continuous infusion, sicker patients in APROCCHSS (higher control mortality), different inclusion criteria (MV in ADRENAL; stricter shock criteria and longer time to enrolment in APROCCHSS).
- Common findings: faster shock resolution, more hyperglycaemia, no significant increase in serious infections.
- SSC 2026: IV corticosteroids suggested in septic shock (conditional, low certainty); not in sepsis without shock.
- Practical regimen: hydrocortisone 200 mg/d when NA/adrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥ 4 h, fludrocortisone optional, ~5–7 days, no ACTH test.

open.q: A colleague wants to perform a short Synacthen test before starting hydrocortisone in a patient with septic shock, citing CAPE COD as further evidence for steroids. Explain why you disagree on both points.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- CIRCI involves HPA axis dysfunction, reduced cortisol clearance and tissue glucocorticoid resistance – a cortisol level does not reliably reflect it.
- CORTICUS showed the ACTH test does not identify who benefits; SSC advises against ACTH testing to select patients.
- Decision is clinical: septic shock with NA/adrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥ 4 h → hydrocortisone 200 mg/d.
- CAPE COD (NEJM 2023): hydrocortisone in severe CAP reduced 28-d mortality 6.2 vs 11.9 %.
- But septic shock (and influenza) were exclusion criteria – the result does not transfer directly to septic shock.
- It shows benefit in correctly selected patients; influenza pneumonia is a setting where steroids tend to harm (observational data).

title: W01 · Saturday – weekly review: Sepsis I

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with fever, RR 24/min, GCS 14 and BP 105/60 mmHg. Lactate 1.8 mmol/L, creatinine rose from 80 to 190 µmol/L, platelets normal. Which statement is correct?
options: He has severe sepsis
He meets qSOFA ≥ 2, which by itself defines sepsis
He has septic shock
He likely has sepsis because of an acute rise in SOFA ≥ 2 attributable to infection
He cannot have sepsis because SBP > 100 mmHg
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Creatinine 190 µmol/L scores 2 renal SOFA points (171–299 µmol/L) and GCS 14 scores 1 CNS point, so Δ SOFA = 3 attributable to infection – sepsis by Sepsis-3. MAP ~75 mmHg without vasopressors scores 0 cardiovascular points.

**Why not the others:**

- A – "Severe sepsis" was abandoned in 2016.
- B – qSOFA is 2 here (RR, GCS), but qSOFA does not define sepsis.
- C – No vasopressor and lactate 1.8 mmol/L – septic shock criteria are not met.
- E – SBP matters only for qSOFA; sepsis is defined by Δ SOFA.

**EDIC trap:** calculate SOFA from the numbers in the stem; ignore the qSOFA bait.

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. Sepsis-3. *JAMA* 2016;315:801–810; Vincent JL, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 1996;22:707–710.

questions.stem: Regarding antibiotics in sepsis (SSC 2026):
options: In possible sepsis with low likelihood of infection and no shock, antibiotics may be deferred with close monitoring.
In septic shock antibiotics should be given immediately, ideally within 1 hour.
In possible sepsis without shock, a time-limited rapid investigation is suggested.
Anaerobic coverage is suggested for all patients with sepsis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – New in 2026: with a low likelihood of infection and no shock, antibiotics may be deferred with close monitoring (conditional, very low).
- B (True) – Septic shock: antibiotics immediately, ideally within 1 h (strong, very low).
- C (True) – Possible sepsis without shock: time-limited rapid assessment; antibiotics within 3 h if concern persists (conditional).
- D (False) – Anaerobic coverage only with risk factors for anaerobic infection (e.g. intra-abdominal source) – new 2026, conditional.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Which trial randomised ED patients with sepsis-induced hypotension, after 1–3 L of crystalloid, to restrictive vs liberal fluids for 24 hours?
options: ProCESS
CLOVERS
SMART
CLASSIC
ALBIOS
questions.expl:
**Why B:** CLOVERS randomised 1563 patients with sepsis-induced hypotension in 60 US centres, mostly in the ED, after 1–3 L of crystalloid, to a restrictive (early vasopressor) or liberal strategy for 24 h. Mortality was 14.0 % vs 14.9 % (NS).

**Why not the others:**

- A – ProCESS tested protocolised EGDT vs standard care in the ED, not restrictive vs liberal fluids.
- C – SMART compared balanced crystalloids with saline.
- D – CLASSIC tested restriction in European ICUs after ≥ 1 L.
- E – ALBIOS tested albumin replacement in severe sepsis.

**Ref:** Shapiro NI, et al. CLOVERS. *N Engl J Med* 2023;388:499–510.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with septic shock is on noradrenaline 0.35 µg/kg/min (rising) after appropriate fluids. Reasonable next steps include:
options: Increasing the MAP target to 80–85 mmHg because of age
Starting dexamethasone 6 mg/day for 10 days
Adding levosimendan
Replacing noradrenaline with dopamine
questions.expl:
- A (False) – At ≥ 65 y SSC 2026 suggests MAP 60–65 mmHg (65 trial); 80–85 mmHg gave no benefit and more AF (SEPSISPAM).
- B (False) – Dexamethasone 6 mg for 10 days is the COVID-19 regimen; with NA ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥ 4 h the choice is hydrocortisone 200 mg/day.
- C (False) – Levosimendan is suggested against (LeoPARDS), and no cardiac dysfunction is described.
- D (False) – Noradrenaline is recommended over dopamine (strong, high; SOAP II).

**What would be reasonable:** add vasopressin (up to ~0.03 U/min) for the escalating NA dose and start hydrocortisone.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: The fluid with the strongest evidence of harm in septic patients is:
options: 20 % albumin
Ringer's lactate
Plasma-Lyte 148
0.9 % saline
Hydroxyethyl starch
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Hydroxyethyl starch has the strongest evidence of harm: in 6S, HES 130/0.42 increased 90-day mortality (51 % vs 43 %) and RRT, and CHEST also showed more RRT. HES licences were suspended in the EU (EMA, 2022) and SSC recommends against starches.

**Why not the others:**

- A – 20 % albumin was neutral in ALBIOS.
- B – Ringer's lactate is a balanced crystalloid, suggested over saline.
- C – Plasma-Lyte 148 was neutral in PLUS and BaSICS.
- D – Saline has at most a small signal of harm (SMART MAKE30), far weaker than HES.

**Ref:** Perner A, et al. 6S. *N Engl J Med* 2012;367:124–134; Myburgh JA, et al. CHEST. *N Engl J Med* 2012;367:1901–1911.

questions.stem: Which of the following are correctly matched?
options: VASST – vasopressin vs noradrenaline
SOAP II – dopamine vs noradrenaline
ADRENAL – hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone
SEPSISPAM – MAP 80–85 vs 65–70 mmHg
questions.expl:
- A (True) – VASST: vasopressin vs noradrenaline (778 patients; 28-day mortality NS).
- B (True) – SOAP II: dopamine vs noradrenaline (1679 patients; more arrhythmias with dopamine).
- C (False) – ADRENAL used hydrocortisone **alone** by continuous infusion; fludrocortisone was added in **APROCCHSS** (and Annane 2002).
- D (True) – SEPSISPAM: MAP 80–85 vs 65–70 mmHg (776 patients; mortality NS, more AF).

**Ref:** Russell JA, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2008; De Backer D, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2010; Venkatesh B, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2018; Asfar P, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2014.

questions.stem: Which screening approach for sepsis in hospitalised acutely ill patients is recommended by SSC 2026?
options: Procalcitonin alone
NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS rather than qSOFA as a single tool
SOFA-2 calculated every hour
Lactate > 4 mmol/L alone
qSOFA alone
questions.expl:
**Why B:** SSC 2026 recommends NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS over qSOFA as a single screening tool in acutely ill hospitalised patients (strong, moderate certainty), because qSOFA has low sensitivity.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Procalcitonin is neither a screening tool nor used to start antibiotics.
- C – SOFA-2 describes organ dysfunction; it is not a ward screening tool, let alone hourly.
- D – Lactate alone is insensitive, and the 4 mmol/L threshold is obsolete.
- E – qSOFA alone is recommended against.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Regarding albumin in sepsis:
options: Albumin is preferred in traumatic brain injury.
SSC 2026 suggests crystalloids alone over adding albumin routinely.
Albumin may be appropriate after large volumes of crystalloid.
The SAFE trial showed significantly lower overall mortality with 4 % albumin than with saline.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Albumin should be avoided in TBI (higher mortality in SAFE-TBI).
- B (True) – SSC 2026 suggests crystalloids alone rather than routine added albumin (conditional, moderate).
- C (True) – Albumin may be appropriate after large volumes of crystalloid, or in cirrhosis.
