questions.expl:
**Why E:** The trial enrolled 339 critically ill adults (13 ICUs, Australia/New Zealand) with refeeding hypophosphataemia. Restriction meant 20 kcal/h for ≥ 2 days, then a gradual return to target over 2–3 days. The primary outcome (days alive after ICU discharge) improved by 4.9 days, which was not significant (p = 0.19). Survival at day 60 was higher (~91 % vs ~79 %, p = 0.002).

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality was lower, not higher, with restriction.
- B – energy was reduced to 20 kcal/h, not stopped, and only for ≥ 48 h.
- C – it was a general ICU population, not patients with anorexia nervosa.
- D – the primary outcome did not reach significance.

**EDIC trap:** the survival benefit is a secondary outcome, but it underpins ESPEN's advice to restrict energy for 48 h in refeeding hypophosphataemia.

**Ref:** Doig GS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2015;3:943–952; Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79.

questions.stem: Consequences of severe hypophosphataemia include:
options: Hypercalcaemia
Respiratory muscle weakness and difficult weaning
Haemolysis and rhabdomyolysis
Right shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve due to increased 2,3-DPG
questions.expl:
- A (False) – hypophosphataemia does not raise calcium. Rapid IV phosphate can instead **lower** iCa²⁺ through Ca–P precipitation.
- B (True) – ATP depletion weakens the diaphragm and other respiratory muscles, which causes weaning failure (and also reduces myocardial contractility).
- C (True) – ATP depletion makes red cells rigid (haemolysis) and injures muscle (rhabdomyolysis), especially when Pi is < 0.32 mmol/L.
- D (False) – low phosphate **reduces** 2,3-DPG, which shifts the curve to the **left** and impairs O₂ release to tissues.

**Ref:** Geerse DA et al., Crit Care 2010;14:R147; Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic lung cancer is confused and dehydrated; total calcium 3.9 mmol/L, creatinine mildly raised. The most appropriate initial management is:
options: Hydrocortisone as first-line therapy
Furosemide alone
Oral calcium restriction only
Calcium gluconate
IV isotonic fluid plus an IV bisphosphonate
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Total Ca 3.9 mmol/L (≥ 3.5 = severe) with confusion in a patient with lung cancer is most likely PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia of malignancy. Hypercalcaemia causes nephrogenic DI, and the resulting volume depletion lowers GFR and calcium excretion, so the first step is IV isotonic fluid. An IV bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid 4 mg) is given at the same time and acts in 2–4 days; calcitonin can bridge the first 48 h.

**Why not the others:**
- A – glucocorticoids work in calcitriol-mediated disease (lymphoma, granulomas, vitamin D intoxication), not in PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia from solid tumours.
- B – furosemide alone worsens the dehydration; use it only after volume repletion if the patient is fluid overloaded.
- C – restricting oral calcium does little when bone resorption drives the hypercalcaemia.
- D – calcium gluconate would make the hypercalcaemia worse.

**EDIC trap:** if renal failure limits bisphosphonate use, denosumab is the alternative (watch for hypocalcaemia).

**Ref:** Walker MD, Shane E, JAMA 2022;328:1624–1636; El-Hajj Fuleihan G et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108:507–528.

questions.stem: Regarding refeeding syndrome:
options: Thiamine should be withheld until feeding has reached the energy target.
Insulin release drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium out of cells.
ESPEN 2019 recommends continuing full energy targets despite refeeding hypophosphataemia.
In the Doig trial, refeeding hypophosphataemia was defined as phosphate < 0.65 mmol/L with a fall > 0.16 mmol/L within 72 hours of starting feeding.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – give thiamine (with other B vitamins) **before** the first feed and during the first 10 days. A carbohydrate load uses up thiamine and can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy and lactic acidosis.
- B (False) – insulin drives phosphate, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ **into** cells, which is why their serum levels fall.
- C (False) – ESPEN 2019 recommends restricting energy for 48 h, then increasing it gradually, and measuring phosphate 2–3 times daily.
- D (True) – this is the Doig trial's definition of refeeding hypophosphataemia.

**Ref:** NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults (2006, updated 2017); Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79; Doig GS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2015;3:943–952.

questions.stem: Which patient meets a single criterion for high risk of refeeding problems according to NICE?
options: BMI 17.5 kg/m² alone
Little or no intake for 6 days alone
BMI 15 kg/m²
Weight loss of 8 % over 4 months alone
History of alcohol misuse alone
questions.expl:
**Why C:** NICE CG32 lists four criteria that are each enough on their own: BMI < 16, unintentional weight loss > 15 % in 3–6 months, little or no intake for > 10 days, and low K⁺/PO₄/Mg²⁺ before feeding. A BMI of 15 qualifies alone. Start at ≤ 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg/day in extreme cases, e.g. BMI < 14) and give thiamine first.

**Why not the others:**
- A – BMI < 18.5 is a minor criterion and needs a second one.
- B – little intake for > 5 days is minor; the single criterion requires > 10 days.
- D – 8 % weight loss does not even meet the minor threshold (> 10 %).
- E – a history of alcohol misuse is a minor criterion and needs a second one.

**Ref:** NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults (2006, updated 2017).

questions.stem: Regarding treatment of hypercalcaemia:
options: Glucocorticoids are useful when hypercalcaemia is mediated by vitamin D (e.g. granulomatous disease).
PTHrP is the most common mediator of hypercalcaemia of malignancy.
Denosumab may be used when kidney failure limits bisphosphonate use.
Calcitonin has a durable effect without tachyphylaxis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – granulomas and some lymphomas produce calcitriol through 1α-hydroxylase. Glucocorticoids suppress this, and they also help in vitamin D intoxication.
- B (True) – PTHrP (humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy) causes most cases; osteolytic metastases and ectopic calcitriol cause the rest.
- C (True) – denosumab (a RANKL antibody) is not renally cleared, so it is useful in kidney failure or bisphosphonate-refractory disease. It can cause severe hypocalcaemia.
- D (False) – calcitonin lowers Ca within hours, but tachyphylaxis develops within ~48 h (receptor down-regulation), so it serves only as a bridge.

**Ref:** Walker MD, Shane E, JAMA 2022;328:1624–1636; El-Hajj Fuleihan G et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108:507–528.

questions.stem: A laboratory reports phosphate as 1.5 mg/dL. In mmol/L this is approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Phosphorus has a molar mass of ≈ 31 g/mol, so 1 mg/dL = 10 mg/L / 31 ≈ 0.323 mmol/L. Therefore 1.5 mg/dL × 0.323 = **0.48 mmol/L**. This is moderate hypophosphataemia (0.32–0.65 mmol/L), below the normal range of ~0.8–1.45 mmol/L.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 1.50 simply relabels mg/dL as mmol/L.
- B – 0.15 divides by 10 instead of applying the molar conversion.
- C – 0.32 mmol/L corresponds to 1.0 mg/dL, the threshold for severe hypophosphataemia.
- D – 0.75 halves the value instead of multiplying by 0.323 (≈ 1/3.1).

**Ref:** Geerse DA et al., Treatment of hypophosphatemia in the ICU, Crit Care 2010;14:R147.

questions.stem: Causes of hypocalcaemia in the ICU include:
options: Hyperphosphataemia
Acute pancreatitis
Hypomagnesaemia
Massive transfusion
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Ca–P precipitates in tissues and calcitriol production falls (AKI, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis).
- B (True) – free fatty acids in peripancreatic fat necrosis bind calcium (saponification), and hypocalcaemia is a marker of severity.
- C (True) – hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and action, so correct Mg²⁺ first or at the same time.
- D (True) – citrate in blood products chelates ionised calcium, especially with liver dysfunction, hypothermia or shock. The European bleeding guideline recommends monitoring iCa²⁺ and keeping it in the normal range.

**Ref:** Rossaint R et al., European guideline on management of major bleeding, Crit Care 2023;27:80; Aberegg SK, Chest 2016;149:846–855.

questions.stem: A 46 kg woman (BMI 16.5) with alcohol use disorder and 8 days of minimal intake is ventilated for aspiration pneumonia. Enteral feeding was started at 25 kcal/kg/day. On day 3, phosphate has fallen from 1.10 to 0.40 mmol/L, K⁺ is 3.0 and Mg²⁺ 0.55 mmol/L; she fails a spontaneous breathing trial with rapid shallow breathing. The most appropriate management is:
options: Replace the feed with glucose 10 % infusion to avoid protein overload
Stop all nutrition for 7 days
No change – a fall in phosphate is expected and harmless during refeeding
Reduce energy intake (e.g. 20 kcal/h for ≥ 48 h), give IV phosphate, K⁺, Mg²⁺ and thiamine, then increase feeding gradually
Continue full feeding and give oral phosphate only
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Phosphate fell from 1.10 to 0.40 mmol/L, a fall of 0.70 / 1.10 ≈ 64 % within 5 days of feeding. With organ dysfunction (respiratory muscle weakness → failed SBT), this is **severe** refeeding syndrome by ASPEN 2020 (falls of 10–20 % mild, 20–30 % moderate, > 30 % or organ dysfunction severe). She met NICE high-risk criteria (≥ 2 minor), so feeding should have started at ≤ 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamine. Now restrict energy for 48 h (Doig: 20 kcal/h), replace phosphate, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ IV, give thiamine, then increase feeding gradually.

**Why not the others:**
- A – glucose alone maximises insulin release and the phosphate shift.
- B – stopping nutrition for 7 days prolongs starvation; the evidence supports restriction, not cessation.
- C – Pi 0.40 mmol/L with weaning failure is harmful and needs treatment.
- E – full feeding sustains the shift, and oral phosphate is inadequate for a severe deficit.

See also the PCP/refeeding case in [W03/D4](#W03-D4) and the [EDIC II-style cases workshop](#extra-clinical-cases-workshop).

**Ref:** da Silva JSV et al., ASPEN consensus, Nutr Clin Pract 2020;35:178–195; Doig GS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2015;3:943–952; Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79; NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults (2006, updated 2017).

open.q: A 50-kg woman with BMI 15 has eaten almost nothing for 2 weeks and is admitted to the ICU. Outline how you would start nutrition, and how you would respond if her phosphate falls from 1.0 to 0.50 mmol/L on day 2.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- High risk of refeeding syndrome by NICE CG32 (BMI < 16 and little/no intake > 10 days; one criterion is enough).
- Thiamine and B vitamins before the first feed and during the first 10 days.
- Start cautiously: max. 10 kcal/kg/day (= 500 kcal/day), increase gradually; prophylactic K⁺, PO₄, Mg²⁺ according to levels.
- Monitor phosphate at least daily in the first week (2–3 times daily once refeeding hypophosphataemia develops – ESPEN 2019).
- Day 2: Pi 0.50 (< 0.65) with a fall of 0.50 (> 0.16) within 72 h = refeeding hypophosphataemia (Doig definition).
- Restrict to 20 kcal/h for ≥ 48 h, then return gradually to target over 2–3 days, plus IV phosphate; monitor Ca²⁺ and K⁺ during replacement.
- Evidence: Doig 2015 – primary outcome NS (+4.9 days, p = 0.19) but higher 60-day survival (~91 % vs ~79 %, p = 0.002).

open.q: A septic patient on citrate CRRT has total Ca 2.40 mmol/L, iCa²⁺ 0.85 mmol/L and a worsening high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Interpret these results and explain why the albumin-corrected calcium is unhelpful here.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Total/ionised Ca ratio = 2.40 / 0.85 ≈ 2.8 (> ~2.5) → citrate accumulation.
- Citrate accumulation is typical with citrate CRRT in liver failure/shock: ↓ iCa²⁺, ↑ total/iCa ratio, high-AG metabolic acidosis.
- Only iCa²⁺ (~45–50 % of plasma Ca) is biologically active; complexed Ca (citrate) increases total Ca without raising iCa²⁺.
- Corrected Ca (+ 0.02 × (40 − albumin)) is inaccurate in the ICU (altered pH, complexes, hypoalbuminaemia) → measure iCa²⁺.
- Consequences of low iCa²⁺: tetany, seizures, prolonged QT, hypotension, ↓ contractility, impaired coagulation.
- Management: treat symptomatic/severe hypocalcaemia with IV Ca gluconate, correct Mg²⁺, and reassess the citrate anticoagulation.

title: W06 · Saturday – weekly review: Electrolytes

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with chronic thiazide-induced hyponatraemia (Na⁺ 112 mmol/L) received 3 % saline boluses for confusion. After stopping the thiazide, urine output is 400 mL/h and Na⁺ is 124 mmol/L at 12 hours. The best next step is:
options: Start tolvaptan
Continue observation; the correction is within limits
Give 0.9 % saline to replace urine output
Stop sodium-containing fluids, give electrolyte-free water (about 10 mL/kg over 1 h) and consider desmopressin 2 µg IV
Give furosemide
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Na⁺ rose from 112 to 124 = +12 mmol/L in 12 h, which already exceeds the 10 mmol/L/24 h limit. Stopping the thiazide caused an aquaresis of dilute urine at 400 mL/h and Na⁺ will keep climbing. The guideline advises stopping active treatment and giving 10 mL/kg of electrolyte-free water (e.g. 5 % glucose) over 1 h under close monitoring, ± desmopressin 2 µg IV (no more often than every 8 h).

**Why not the others:**
- A – tolvaptan would increase the aquaresis and worsen the overcorrection.
- B – the limit is already exceeded at 12 h, and the ongoing aquaresis will push Na⁺ higher.
- C – 0.9 % saline (154 mmol/L) is far more concentrated than the dilute urine, so replacing urine with it would raise Na⁺ further.
- E – furosemide produces urine that is hypotonic to plasma, which raises Na⁺ further.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331; Sterns RH, N Engl J Med 2015;372:55–65.

questions.stem: According to the European hyponatraemia guideline:
options: Hyponatraemia of unknown duration should be treated as acute.
In severe symptoms, the target is a rise of about 5 mmol/L in the first hour.
Profound hyponatraemia is defined as Na⁺ < 130 mmol/L.
Vomiting and somnolence are severe symptoms.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – hyponatraemia of unknown duration is treated as **chronic**, because the brain may already have adapted and rapid correction risks ODS.
- B (True) – with severe symptoms, the aim is a rise of ~5 mmol/L in the first hour (150 mL 3 % NaCl over 20 min, up to 3 times). This usually improves symptoms.
- C (False) – profound is < 125 mmol/L; moderate is 125–129 and mild 130–135.
- D (True) – severe symptoms are vomiting, cardiorespiratory distress, abnormal deep somnolence, seizures and coma (GCS ≤ 8). Nausea without vomiting, confusion and headache are moderately severe.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331.

questions.stem: A 70-kg man (TBW 42 L) with Na⁺ 120 mmol/L receives 1 L of 0.9 % saline (Na⁺ 154 mmol/L). The Adrogué–Madias formula predicts a rise in Na⁺ of approximately:
options: 12 mmol/L
3.4 mmol/L
5 mmol/L
0.8 mmol/L
8 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ΔNa⁺ = (154 + 0 − 120) / (42 + 1) = 34 / 43 ≈ **0.8 mmol/L**. Isotonic saline hardly raises Na⁺ at all. In SIAD, if urine osmolality exceeds that of saline (~308 mOsm/kg), the infused Na⁺ is excreted in a smaller volume and the water is retained, so serum Na⁺ can even fall ("desalination").

**Why not the others:**
- A – 12 mmol/L is more than even 1 L of 3 % saline would achieve here: (513 − 120) / 43 ≈ 9.1.
- B – 3.4 is a decimal slip (34 / 10).
- C – 5 mmol/L is the first-hour target for 3 % boluses in severe symptoms, not the effect of 0.9 % saline.
- E – 8 mmol/L is the daily correction ceiling for high-risk patients, not the effect per litre.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1581–1589; Spasovski G et al., Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331.

questions.stem: Regarding emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia:
options: Hypoglycaemia is a common complication of insulin–glucose therapy.
Dialysis has no role in refractory severe hyperkalaemia.
Calcium is given to lower the serum potassium when ECG changes are present.
Salbutamol alone is sufficient treatment for severe hyperkalaemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – hypoglycaemia is the most common complication, especially with low baseline glucose or renal failure. ERC 2025 adds a 10 % glucose infusion if pre-treatment glucose is < 7 mmol/L.
- B (False) – dialysis is the definitive treatment to remove K⁺ in refractory severe hyperkalaemia, particularly with renal failure.
- C (False) – calcium stabilises the myocardial membrane but does not change the serum K⁺.
- D (False) – salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised is an adjunct to insulin–glucose. It is insufficient alone, and some patients do not respond.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: According to ERC 2025, a serum K⁺ of 6.2 mmol/L is classified as:
options: Life-threatening only if ECG changes are absent
Normal
Moderate hyperkalaemia
Severe hyperkalaemia
Mild hyperkalaemia
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ERC 2025 classifies hyperkalaemia as **moderate at 6.0–6.4 mmol/L** and severe at ≥ 6.5 mmol/L, so 6.2 mmol/L is moderate. Treatment urgency also depends on ECG changes, the rate of rise and the clinical context. Moderate hyperkalaemia is treated with insulin–glucose ± salbutamol and K⁺ removal.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ECG changes make hyperkalaemia more dangerous; their absence does not make it life-threatening.
- B – the normal range is ~3.5–5.0 mmol/L.
- D – severe hyperkalaemia starts at 6.5 mmol/L.
- E – ERC 2025 does not use a separate mild category for this value (the older 5.5–5.9 band); 6.2 falls in the moderate band.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: Regarding hypokalaemia:
options: Hypomagnesaemia causes renal potassium wasting.
A small fall in serum potassium reflects only a small total body deficit.
IV potassium should preferably be diluted in 5 % glucose.
Metabolic alkalosis shifts potassium into cells.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Mg²⁺ deficiency releases the inhibition of ROMK channels, so renal K⁺ wasting continues until magnesium is replaced.
- B (False) – ~98 % of K⁺ is intracellular, so even a 1 mmol/L fall in serum K⁺ reflects a deficit of the order of 200–400 mmol.
- C (False) – glucose stimulates insulin, which shifts K⁺ into cells and can deepen the hypokalaemia; dilute KCl in 0.9 % saline.
- D (True) – in alkalosis H⁺ leaves cells in exchange for K⁺, and bicarbonaturia increases renal K⁺ loss.

**Ref:** Gennari FJ, N Engl J Med 1998;339:451–458.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old woman, 50 kg (TBW 0.45 × weight), has Na⁺ 168 mmol/L. The free water deficit is approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why B:** TBW = 0.45 × 50 = 22.5 L. Deficit = 22.5 × (168/140 − 1) = 22.5 × 0.2 = **4.5 L**, to which ongoing losses must be added. At ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/24 h, correcting chronic hypernatraemia from 168 to ~145 mmol/L takes about 2–3 days.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 7.0 L would need a TBW of 35 L (0.7 × weight), far too high for an elderly woman.
- C – 2.5 L would match a Na⁺ of only ~155 mmol/L.
- D – 5.5 L assumes a TBW of 0.55 × weight.
- E – 3.5 L would need a TBW of ~17.5 L (0.35 × weight), which underestimates the deficit.

**EDIC trap:** use the TBW fraction for age and sex: 0.6 young men, 0.5 young women and elderly men, 0.45 elderly women.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, Hypernatremia, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

questions.stem: Regarding calcium disorders:
options: Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy account for about 90 % of hypercalcaemia.
Hyperphosphataemia from rhabdomyolysis can cause hypocalcaemia.
Severe hypercalcaemia is defined as total calcium ≥ 3.5 mmol/L.
Hypercalcaemia typically prolongs the QT interval.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – primary hyperparathyroidism (mostly outpatients) and malignancy (mostly inpatients) together cause ~90 % of hypercalcaemia.
- B (True) – Ca–P precipitates in damaged muscle in rhabdomyolysis; rebound hypercalcaemia can occur in the recovery phase.
- C (True) – severe hypercalcaemia is total Ca ≥ 3.5 mmol/L (≥ 14 mg/dL), or iCa²⁺ ≥ 2.5 mmol/L.
- D (False) – hypercalcaemia **shortens** the QT interval (short ST segment); a prolonged QT points to hypocalcaemia.

**Ref:** Walker MD, Shane E, JAMA 2022;328:1624–1636.

questions.stem: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder starts parenteral nutrition. On day 3 he fails a spontaneous breathing trial; phosphate is 0.25 mmol/L. The most likely explanation is:
options: Refeeding hypophosphataemia causing respiratory muscle weakness
Critical illness polyneuropathy
Hypermagnesaemia
Hypercalcaemia
Metabolic alkalosis from parenteral nutrition
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Malnutrition and alcohol misuse put him at high risk of refeeding. The glucose in parenteral nutrition triggers insulin release, which shifts phosphate into cells; a Pi of 0.25 mmol/L (< 0.32) is severe. ATP and 2,3-DPG depletion weakens the diaphragm, which explains the failed SBT. Treat with IV phosphate, restrict energy for 48 h (ESPEN), give thiamine and replace K⁺ and Mg²⁺.

**Why not the others:**
- B – critical illness polyneuropathy follows prolonged sepsis or multiorgan failure and does not explain a Pi of 0.25 mmol/L on day 3.
- C – refeeding causes **hypo**magnesaemia; hypermagnesaemia needs renal failure or iatrogenic loading.
- D – hypercalcaemia is not a feature of refeeding, and IV phosphate can even lower calcium.
- E – metabolic alkalosis from PN is uncommon and does not explain severe hypophosphataemia.

**Ref:** Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79; da Silva JSV et al., Nutr Clin Pract 2020;35:178–195.

questions.stem: Regarding the Doig refeeding trial (Lancet Respir Med 2015):
options: The primary outcome was significantly improved.
It enrolled critically ill adults in Australia and New Zealand.
The intervention was 20 kcal/h for at least 2 days, then a gradual return to goal.
Fewer patients were alive at day 60 in the restricted group.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the primary outcome (days alive after ICU discharge) improved by 4.9 days, which was not significant (p = 0.19).
- B (True) – the trial randomised 339 critically ill adults in 13 ICUs in Australia and New Zealand.
- C (True) – the intervention was 20 kcal/h for ≥ 2 days, followed by a gradual return to goal over 2–3 days.
- D (False) – **more** patients were alive at day 60 in the restricted group (~91 % vs ~79 %, p = 0.002), a secondary outcome.

**Ref:** Doig GS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2015;3:943–952.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man, 80 kg (TBW 40 L), has Na⁺ 160 mmol/L. The expected effect of 1 L of 5 % glucose on serum Na⁺ (Adrogué–Madias) is:
options: −2.0 mmol/L
−6.0 mmol/L
−10 mmol/L
−3.9 mmol/L
−1.0 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ΔNa⁺ = (0 − 160) / (40 + 1) = −160 / 41 ≈ **−3.9 mmol/L** per litre of 5 % glucose. To lower Na⁺ by 10 mmol/L in 24 h, about 10 / 3.9 ≈ 2.6 L is needed, plus replacement of ongoing (insensible, urinary) losses.

**Why not the others:**
- A – −2.0 mmol/L is the predicted effect of 1 L of 0.45 % saline: (77 − 160) / 41 ≈ −2.0.
- B – −6.0 mmol/L would need a TBW of only ~26 L.
- C – −10 mmol/L is the daily target, not the effect of one litre.
- E – −1.0 mmol/L underestimates the effect about fourfold; such small changes come from near-isotonic fluids, e.g. Hartmann's (130 − 160) / 41 ≈ −0.7.

**EDIC trap:** the formula ignores urine output, so check Na⁺ frequently, especially with DI or osmotic diuresis.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

questions.stem: Essential features for diagnosing SIAD include:
options: Effective serum osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg
Clinical hypervolaemia with oedema
Exclusion of hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency
questions.expl:
- A (True) – an effective serum osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg confirms hypotonicity (exclude glucose, mannitol and pseudohyponatraemia).
- B (True) – urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg shows inappropriately concentrated urine, i.e. ADH is active.
- C (False) – SIAD requires clinical **euvolaemia**. Oedema points to hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).
- D (True) – hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (including secondary) must be excluded, as must recent diuretic use and renal failure. Urine Na⁺ is > 30 mmol/L on a normal intake.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331.

questions.stem: A patient with essential thrombocythaemia (platelets 1100 × 10⁹/L) has serum K⁺ 6.4 mmol/L, a normal ECG and normal renal function. The best next step is:
options: Arrange urgent dialysis
Start insulin–glucose
Measure potassium in a heparinised whole-blood sample (blood gas analyser)
Give sodium bicarbonate
Give calcium chloride immediately
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Platelets release K⁺ while blood clots in a serum tube, so extreme thrombocytosis produces **pseudohyperkalaemia**. A normal ECG and normal renal function support this. Measure K⁺ in heparinised whole blood (blood gas analyser) or plasma; a serum–plasma difference of > ~0.4 mmol/L confirms it.

**Why not the others:**
- A – dialysis is for confirmed, refractory hyperkalaemia, not an unverified result.
- B – insulin–glucose for an artefactual value risks hypoglycaemia and true hypokalaemia.
- D – bicarbonate is not first-line even for true hyperkalaemia outside acidosis or arrest.
- E – calcium is indicated for severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes; the ECG here is normal and 6.4 mmol/L is moderate.

**EDIC trap:** extreme leucocytosis (e.g. CLL), haemolysis and fist clenching cause the same artefact.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753; Clase CM et al. (KDIGO), Kidney Int 2020;97:42–61.

questions.stem: According to NICE CG32, which of the following alone (as a single criterion) places a patient at high risk of refeeding problems?
options: History of alcohol misuse
BMI < 18.5 kg/m²
Little or no nutritional intake for > 5 days
Unintentional weight loss > 15 % within 3–6 months
questions.expl:
- A (False) – a history of alcohol misuse (or drugs such as insulin, chemotherapy, antacids, diuretics) is a minor criterion and needs at least one other.
- B (False) – BMI < 18.5 is minor; the single criterion is BMI < 16.
- C (False) – little intake for > 5 days is minor; the single criterion is > 10 days.
- D (True) – unintentional weight loss > 15 % within 3–6 months is a single high-risk criterion, as are BMI < 16, little intake for > 10 days and low K⁺/PO₄/Mg²⁺ before feeding.

**Ref:** NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults (2006, updated 2017).

questions.stem: Total calcium 2.00 mmol/L, albumin 25 g/L, ionised calcium 0.92 mmol/L in a septic patient. Which statement is correct?
options: Calcium must be given routinely to all septic patients with this result
Ionised calcium is not affected by pH
Corrected calcium is 2.30 mmol/L, so calcium status is normal
Corrected calcium is 1.70 mmol/L
Corrected calcium is 2.30 mmol/L, but the ionised value shows true hypocalcaemia
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Corrected Ca = 2.00 + 0.02 × (40 − 25) = 2.00 + 0.30 = 2.30 mmol/L, which looks normal. The measured iCa²⁺ of 0.92 mmol/L (normal ~1.1–1.3) shows true hypocalcaemia. The albumin formula performs poorly in critically ill patients, so the ionised value decides.

**Why not the others:**
- A – routine supplementation of asymptomatic mild hypocalcaemia in sepsis has no proven benefit; treat symptomatic or severe cases or specific settings (massive transfusion, hyperkalaemia).
- B – pH changes iCa²⁺: alkalosis lowers it and acidosis raises it.
- C – the arithmetic is right but the interpretation is wrong, because iCa²⁺ is low.
- D – 1.70 subtracts the correction instead of adding it.

**Ref:** Aberegg SK, Ionized calcium in the ICU, Chest 2016;149:846–855.

title: W07 · D1 – Cardiogenic shock: definition, SCAI SHOCK, diagnosis, recommendations

questions.stem: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, which statement about the definition of cardiogenic shock is correct?
options: A cardiac index < 1.8 L/min/m² must be documented
Pulmonary congestion on chest X-ray is required
It is critical end-organ hypoperfusion due to primary cardiac dysfunction, without a fixed blood pressure cut-off
Lactate must exceed 4 mmol/L
Systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg for ≥ 30 minutes is mandatory
questions.expl: ESC 2026 defines CS as critical hypoperfusion due to primary cardiac dysfunction; lactate > 2 mmol/L supports the diagnosis, no fixed BP cut-off is set.

questions.stem: Regarding the SCAI SHOCK classification (2022 update):
options: Stage C can be assigned without hypotension if hypoperfusion requires intervention.
A lactate ≥ 8 mmol/L is typical of stage E.
Stage B describes haemodynamic instability (relative hypotension or tachycardia) without hypoperfusion.
The cardiac arrest modifier applies to patients who are comatose after cardiac arrest.
questions.expl: A: what matters is hypoperfusion requiring intervention; hypotension is not required.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with anterior STEMI has BP 96/60 mmHg, cool extremities and lactate 3.4 mmol/L, requiring dobutamine to maintain urine output. One hour later he is stable on the same dose. His SCAI stage is:
options: A
B
D
C
E
questions.expl: Hypoperfusion (lactate ≥ 2) requiring one intervention beyond fluids, without deterioration = Classic.

questions.stem: Regarding haemodynamic assessment in cardiogenic shock:
options: Cardiac power output is calculated as MAP × CO / 451.
The ESICM 2025 guidelines consider echocardiography the first-line tool to determine the type of shock.
Mixed venous oxygen saturation is typically high in cardiogenic shock.
A high pulmonary artery pulsatility index (PAPi) suggests right ventricular failure.
questions.expl: C: it is low – increased extraction with low CO. D: a low PAPi suggests RV failure.

questions.stem: In the SHOCK trial (NEJM 1999), emergency revascularisation compared with initial medical stabilisation in AMI-related cardiogenic shock:
options: Was stopped early for harm
Increased mortality at 6 months
Showed benefit only with fibrinolysis
Did not significantly reduce 30-day mortality but reduced 6-month mortality
Significantly reduced 30-day mortality

questions.stem: Regarding vasoactive drugs in cardiogenic shock:
options: In SOAP II, dopamine was associated with more arrhythmic events than norepinephrine.
In the cardiogenic shock subgroup of SOAP II, dopamine was associated with higher 28-day mortality.
The 2026 ESC guidelines give a class I recommendation for norepinephrine in cardiogenic shock.
An individual-patient meta-analysis associated epinephrine with higher short-term mortality in cardiogenic shock.
questions.expl: C: IIb, C. D: Léopold, ICM 2018 – observational data.

questions.stem: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, which recommendation regarding temporary mechanical circulatory support carries class I?
options: Routine IABP in all cardiogenic shock
Microaxial flow pump in all AMI-related cardiogenic shock
A multidisciplinary Shock Team to guide device selection
VA-ECMO in all patients with lactate > 4 mmol/L
Temporary MCS in unselected AMI-CS
questions.expl: Shock team I, C. Microaxial pump only in selected STEMI-CS (IIa); routine IABP and unselected MCS = III.

questions.stem: Haemodynamic profiles of cardiogenic shock:
options: The "cold and wet" profile is the most common.
Results of AMI-CS device trials can be directly extrapolated to non-ischaemic HF-related shock.
Isolated right ventricular failure typically shows low right atrial pressure with a high PCWP.
A "warm and wet" profile suggests low systemic vascular resistance, e.g. a systemic inflammatory response after MI.
questions.expl: C: isolated RV failure shows high RAP with a normal or low PCWP. B: all key MCS RCTs were in AMI-CS; their results should not be automatically extrapolated to HF-CS.

questions.stem: A patient with NSTEMI develops cardiogenic shock. According to the 2023 ESC ACS guidelines, the appropriate invasive strategy is:
options: Fibrinolysis first, then angiography within 24 hours
Invasive strategy within 72 hours
Early invasive strategy within 24 hours
Immediate invasive strategy
Selective invasive strategy after non-invasive testing
questions.expl: CS is a very-high-risk criterion in NSTE-ACS → immediate invasive strategy.

questions.stem: Regarding the 2022 SCAI SHOCK update:
options: Mortality increases progressively across stages A to E in validation studies.
It was endorsed by the ESC Association for Acute CardioVascular Care.
Age and frailty are considered modifiable risk factors.
It introduced a three-axis model including shock severity, phenotype/aetiology and risk modifiers.
questions.expl: C: they are non-modifiable risk factors.

open.q: A 58-year-old man with anterior STEMI arrives with BP 92/58 mmHg, cool mottled extremities, oliguria and lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Outline your initial diagnostic work-up and management during the first hours.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Recognise CS (hypoperfusion from a primary cardiac cause; lactate > 2 supports it, no fixed BP cut-off) and stage it – hypoperfusion needing intervention = at least SCAI C; reassess for deterioration (D).
- ECG, troponin, lactate, ABG, creatinine, liver tests, NT-proBNP; echocardiography as first-line tool – LVEF, regional wall motion, mechanical complications (VSD, acute MR, tamponade), RV function.
- Immediate coronary angiography and PCI of the infarct-related artery (SHOCK trial: ↓ 6-month mortality); emergency CABG if PCI not feasible; culprit-only PCI in multivessel disease.
- Arterial line; consider PAC/TPTD if CO monitoring needed (CPO, PAPi, SvO₂).
- Norepinephrine as preferred vasopressor, initial MAP target ≥ 65 mmHg individualised to perfusion; avoid dopamine and routine epinephrine.
- Inotrope (e.g. dobutamine) if hypoperfusion persists despite standard treatment incl. fluid challenge – lowest dose, shortest time.
- Activate the shock team (I, C); consider microaxial pump only in selected STEMI-CS without risk of hypoxic brain injury (IIa); no routine IABP or unselected MCS (III).
- Monitor perfusion targets: lactate clearance, CRT, urine output, mental status.

open.q: Explain why mixed venous saturation helps distinguish cardiogenic from septic shock, and how PAC-derived indices help identify right ventricular failure.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- In CS, low CO leads to increased O₂ extraction → SvO₂/ScvO₂ typically low.
- In septic shock ScvO₂ is often normal or high.
- Low SvO₂ + high PCWP + low CI = classic CS profile.
- PAPi = (sPAP − dPAP) / RAP; a low value signals RV failure.
- High RAP/PCWP ratio = predominant RV failure; isolated RV failure shows ↑ CVP/RAP with normal or low PCWP.
- CPO = MAP × CO / 451 integrates pressure and flow and is a strong predictor of mortality.

title: W07 · D2 – Mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock

questions.stem: In IABP-SHOCK II, intra-aortic balloon pump support in AMI-related cardiogenic shock:
options: Reduced 30-day mortality by 25 %
Did not reduce 30-day mortality
Was only tested in patients not undergoing revascularisation
Increased the stroke rate significantly
Increased major bleeding significantly
questions.expl: 39.7 vs 41.3% (NS); neither bleeding nor stroke differed significantly; patients were planned for early revascularisation.

questions.stem: Regarding the ECLS-SHOCK trial:
options: Peripheral ischaemic vascular complications were more frequent with ECLS.
30-day mortality was significantly lower with early ECLS.
It enrolled patients with AMI-related cardiogenic shock with lactate > 3 mmol/L planned for revascularisation.
Moderate or severe bleeding was less frequent with ECLS.
questions.expl: B: 47.8 vs 49.0%. D: more frequent with ECLS, 23.4 vs 9.6%. A: 11.0 vs 3.8%.

questions.stem: Which patient best matches the population in which DanGer Shock showed a mortality benefit?
options: 62-year-old comatose after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with STEMI and shock
66-year-old with isolated right ventricular infarction
45-year-old with fulminant myocarditis and biventricular failure
70-year-old with NSTEMI, LVEF 55 %, lactate 1.5 mmol/L
58-year-old with anterior STEMI, LVEF 25 %, lactate 4 mmol/L, awake, on norepinephrine
questions.expl: STEMI-CS, EF < 45%, lactate ≥ 2.5, not comatose after OHCA; myocarditis or isolated RV infarction do not match the trial population (STEMI with LV failure).

questions.stem: Regarding DanGer Shock (NEJM 2024):
options: The composite of adverse events was more frequent with the pump.
Limb ischaemia requiring intervention was more frequent with the pump.
Renal replacement therapy was less frequent in the pump group.
All-cause death at 180 days was 45.8 % with the microaxial flow pump vs 58.5 % with standard care.
questions.expl: A: 24.0 vs 6.2%. C: 41.9 vs 26.7% – more frequent.

questions.stem: A patient on femoral VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock with severe ARDS shows recovering LV function. Right radial PaO₂ is 6 kPa, femoral arterial PaO₂ 35 kPa. The most appropriate intervention is:
options: Improve native lung gas exchange and consider conversion to V-AV ECMO
Increase FiO₂ on the oxygenator
Increase sweep gas flow
Reduce ECMO flow to the minimum
Insert a distal perfusion cannula
questions.expl: Harlequin syndrome – the heart ejects hypoxic blood from the failing lungs into the aortic root; oxygenator FiO₂ does not change that. Reducing flow would move the mixing zone even more distally.

questions.stem: Signs suggesting left ventricular distension on peripheral VA-ECMO include:
options: Aortic valve remaining closed on echocardiography
Loss of arterial pulse pressure
Spontaneous echo contrast ("smoke") in the left ventricle
Rapid resolution of pulmonary oedema
questions.expl: D: pulmonary oedema progresses.

questions.stem: The haemodynamic effect of a transvalvular microaxial flow pump (Impella) on the left ventricle is:
options: Increase in LV afterload
Right ventricular unloading
Direct LV unloading with reduced end-diastolic pressure
Full biventricular and respiratory support
Diastolic augmentation only
questions.expl: Impella aspirates blood from the LV into the ascending aorta → direct LV unloading; it provides neither oxygenation nor RV support (that is VA-ECMO or Impella RP).

questions.stem: Regarding left ventricular unloading during VA-ECMO:
options: Inotropes are contraindicated because they prevent aortic valve opening.
In EARLY-UNLOAD, early routine transseptal left atrial venting reduced 30-day mortality.
In ECLS-SHOCK, active LV unloading was used in the majority of ECLS patients.
An IABP or microaxial flow pump cannot be used to unload the LV.
questions.expl: A: inotropes may help open the aortic valve. B: 46.6 vs 44.8%, NS. C: only ~6%. D: both an IABP and a microaxial flow pump can be used to unload the LV.

questions.stem: Which statement about the IPD meta-analysis of VA-ECMO trials in infarct-related cardiogenic shock (Lancet 2023) is correct?
options: It included only observational studies
It showed benefit only in patients older than 75 years
VA-ECMO reduced 30-day mortality by about one third
VA-ECMO did not reduce 30-day mortality and increased major bleeding and vascular complications
It found fewer vascular complications with VA-ECMO
questions.expl: 4 RCTs, 567 patients; mortality OR 0.93 (NS); bleeding OR 2.44, vascular complications OR 3.53.

questions.stem: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines:
options: IABP is not recommended in unselected cardiogenic shock.
Temporary MCS is not recommended in unselected AMI-related cardiogenic shock.
Temporary MCS should be considered as a bridge in mechanical complications of MI.
Routine use of microaxial flow pumps in all cardiogenic shock is recommended.
questions.expl: A: III, B1. B: III, B1. C: IIa, C.

open.q: Explain why ECLS-SHOCK was negative while DanGer Shock showed a mortality benefit, and what this means for device selection in AMI-related cardiogenic shock.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Different devices and physiology: VA-ECMO gives full circulatory support but increases LV afterload; Impella directly unloads the LV.
- ECLS-SHOCK: unselected AMI-CS (STEMI and NSTEMI), lactate > 3, large proportion after CPR; 30-d mortality 47.8 vs 49.0% (NS).
- ECLS-SHOCK: more BARC 3–5 bleeding (23.4 vs 9.6%) and vascular complications (11.0 vs 3.8%); active LV unloading in only ~6%.
- DanGer Shock: carefully selected STEMI-CS, LVEF < 45%, lactate ≥ 2.5, comatose OHCA patients excluded; 180-d mortality 45.8 vs 58.5% (HR 0.74).
- DanGer Shock benefit came at the cost of more adverse events (24.0 vs 6.2%), limb ischaemia and RRT.
- Implication (ESC 2026): microaxial pump IIa only in selected STEMI-CS without risk of hypoxic brain injury; unselected MCS and routine IABP III; shock team I.
- Rescue/individualised VA-ECMO still has a role (refractory CS, ECPR, myocarditis, bridge to transplant/VAD).

open.q: A patient on femoral VA-ECMO shows loss of arterial pulse pressure and worsening pulmonary oedema. Explain the mechanism and outline your management.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Retrograde femoral return increases LV afterload; a weak LV cannot open the aortic valve.
- Result: ↑ LVEDP and LA pressure → pulmonary oedema, LV/aortic root stasis and thrombus, subendocardial ischaemia.
- Confirm with echo: aortic valve not opening, "smoke" in the LV; rising PCWP.
- Reduce ECMO flow to the minimum that maintains perfusion.
- Inotrope to open the aortic valve; vasodilation to reduce afterload.
- Unload with IABP or Impella (ECPELLA), or surgical/percutaneous vent (transseptal LA cannula, septostomy).
- Note: EARLY-UNLOAD showed no benefit of early routine unloading (46.6 vs 44.8%).

title: W07 · D3 – ACS in the ICU: STEMI/NSTEMI, CULPRIT-SHOCK, mechanical complications of MI

questions.stem: In CULPRIT-SHOCK, culprit-lesion-only PCI compared with immediate multivessel PCI in AMI-related cardiogenic shock:
options: Enrolled only patients with single-vessel disease
Reduced the 30-day composite of death or severe renal failure requiring RRT
Showed no difference at 30 days
Increased the 30-day composite of death or renal replacement therapy
Was associated with more renal replacement therapy
questions.expl: 45.9 vs 55.4% (RR 0.83); the RRT component was numerically lower (NS).

questions.stem: Regarding revascularisation strategies in STEMI with multivessel disease:
options: In haemodynamically stable STEMI, COMPLETE showed that complete revascularisation did not reduce cardiovascular death or MI.
In CULPRIT-SHOCK, the mortality difference was no longer present at 1 year.
In cardiogenic shock, PCI during the index procedure should be restricted to the infarct-related artery.
CULPRIT-SHOCK and COMPLETE studied the same population.
questions.expl: A: complete revascularisation reduced CV death or MI. D: shock vs stable STEMI. B: 1 year 50.0 vs 56.9%.

questions.stem: Three days after a late-presenting inferior STEMI, a patient develops sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension. No new murmur is heard. PCWP tracing shows large v waves. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Dressler syndrome
Ventricular septal rupture
Right ventricular infarction
Papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation
Free wall rupture
questions.expl: Posteromedial papillary muscle (single supply from the PDA) in inferior MI; the murmur may be soft/absent; large v waves = acute MR.

questions.stem: Regarding ventricular septal rupture after MI:
options: A new harsh holosystolic murmur is a common finding.
It causes a right-to-left shunt.
A step-down in oxygen saturation between the right atrium and pulmonary artery is typical.
IABP or temporary MCS can be used as a bridge to closure.
questions.expl: B: the shunt is left-to-right. C: the left-to-right shunt causes a step-up in saturation.

questions.stem: A patient with NSTEMI develops recurrent ventricular tachycardia and acute heart failure. According to ESC 2023, coronary angiography should be performed:
options: Only after non-invasive ischaemia testing
After 6 weeks of medical therapy
Immediately
Within 24 hours
Within 72 hours
questions.expl: Life-threatening arrhythmias and acute HF = very high risk → immediate invasive strategy.

questions.stem: Regarding right ventricular infarction:
options: ST elevation in V4R supports the diagnosis.
Maintenance of AV synchrony is important.
It is typically associated with inferior STEMI due to proximal RCA occlusion.
Nitrates are the first-line treatment of the associated hypotension.
questions.expl: D: nitrates reduce preload – avoid them.

questions.stem: Regarding mechanical complications of MI, the ESC 2023 ACS guidelines state that:
options: IABP is contraindicated in mechanical complications
Surgery is regarded as the treatment of choice, with strategy decided by the Heart Team
Fibrinolysis is the preferred reperfusion strategy
Medical therapy alone is the treatment of choice
Revascularisation should never be performed at the time of surgery
questions.expl: Surgery is the treatment of choice; consider IABP while awaiting surgery; CABG at the same time as repair if revascularisation is needed.

questions.stem: In STEMI management (ESC 2023):
options: Routine oxygen is recommended irrespective of SpO₂.
If the anticipated time from diagnosis to PCI exceeds 120 minutes, fibrinolysis should be considered.
Before fibrinolysis in cardiogenic shock, a mechanical complication should be excluded.
Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy within 12 hours of symptom onset.
questions.expl: A: only if SpO₂ < 90%.

questions.stem: A patient presents 6 days after an untreated anterior MI with sudden pulseless electrical activity. Bedside echo shows a large pericardial effusion with tamponade. The most likely cause is:
options: Right ventricular infarction
Papillary muscle rupture
Dressler syndrome
Left ventricular thrombus
Free wall rupture
questions.expl: Free wall rupture → haemopericardium, tamponade, PEA; treatment is pericardiocentesis as a bridge and emergency surgery.

questions.stem: Regarding acute coronary syndromes in the ICU:
options: Oral P2Y12 inhibitor absorption may be delayed in shocked, ventilated patients receiving opioids.
Type 2 MI is caused by supply–demand imbalance, e.g. shock or tachyarrhythmia.
An LV thrombus is a contraindication to Impella insertion.
Type 2 MI always requires an immediate invasive strategy.
questions.expl: D: treat the underlying cause.

open.q: Explain why CULPRIT-SHOCK and COMPLETE reached different conclusions about multivessel PCI, and how you would apply them in practice.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Different populations: CULPRIT-SHOCK = AMI-CS with multivessel CAD (n = 706); COMPLETE = haemodynamically stable STEMI after successful culprit PCI (n = 4041).
- CULPRIT-SHOCK: culprit-only reduced death or RRT at 30 d (45.9 vs 55.4%, RR 0.83); 1-year mortality 50.0 vs 56.9%.
- COMPLETE: complete revascularisation reduced CV death or MI (7.8 vs 10.5%, HR 0.74).
- In shock, extra lesions add contrast load, procedure time and ischaemia during further interventions.
- The trials do not conflict – presence of shock decides.
- Practice: in CS treat only the IRA during the index procedure, stage other lesions; in stable STEMI aim for complete (staged) revascularisation.
- If anatomy unsuitable for PCI in CS → emergency CABG.

open.q: Four days after a late-presenting MI, a patient becomes acutely hypotensive. Outline how you would differentiate the possible mechanical complications at the bedside and their management.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Urgent echocardiography for any sudden deterioration or new murmur.
- VSR: new holosystolic murmur with thrill, biventricular failure, left-to-right shunt, O₂ saturation step-up RA→PA, Qp/Qs > 1.
- Papillary muscle rupture (posteromedial, inferior MI, single PDA supply): sudden pulmonary oedema, murmur may be absent, flail leaflet, large v waves on PCWP.
- Free wall rupture: tamponade, PEA, sudden death → pericardiocentesis as bridge and emergency surgery.
- Also consider RV infarction (hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs, V4R) – preserve preload, avoid nitrates.
- Surgery is the treatment of choice, decided by the Heart Team; CABG at the same time if needed.
- Bridge with afterload reduction, IABP or temporary MCS (ESC 2026 IIa, C).

title: W07 · D4 – Acute (decompensated) heart failure, inotropes, NIV

questions.stem: In the DOREMI trial (NEJM 2021), milrinone compared with dobutamine in cardiogenic shock:
options: Significantly reduced in-hospital mortality
Did not significantly differ in the primary composite outcome
Caused significantly more arrhythmias
Was compared in an open-label design
Was tested only in SCAI stage E
questions.expl: 49 vs 54% (RR 0.90; NS); double-blind trial, SCAI B–E.

questions.stem: Regarding the 3CPO trial:
options: NIPPV was superior to CPAP for death or intubation.
Non-invasive ventilation did not improve acidosis or hypercapnia faster than oxygen.
Non-invasive ventilation reduced 7-day mortality.
It compared CPAP with high-flow nasal oxygen in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
questions.expl: C: 9.5 vs 9.8%. A: 11.1 vs 11.7%, NS. B: NIV improved acidosis and hypercapnia faster. D: it compared standard oxygen, CPAP and NIPPV.

questions.stem: Which statement about the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines is correct?
options: Inotropes carry a class I recommendation in cardiogenic shock
HFmrEF is defined as LVEF 41–49 %
Heart failure with LVEF < 50 % is classified as HFrEF
Routine opioids are recommended in acute pulmonary oedema
The term "acute heart failure" was retained
questions.expl: HFmrEF was abolished; "decompensated HF"; opioids III; inotropes IIb.

questions.stem: Regarding levosimendan:
options: In SURVIVE, it significantly reduced 180-day mortality compared with dobutamine.
It sensitises troponin C to calcium.
It blocks ATP-sensitive potassium channels, causing vasoconstriction.
ESC 2026 notes it may be preferred over dobutamine in patients on beta-blockers.
questions.expl: A: 26 vs 28%, NS. C: it opens K-ATP channels, causing vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP 190/105 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO₂ 86 % on oxygen. Besides NIV, the most appropriate initial drug therapy is:
options: Intravenous nitrate (vasodilator)
Intravenous morphine as routine
Dobutamine infusion
Milrinone
Norepinephrine
questions.expl: APO with hypertension = fluid redistribution, ↑ afterload → vasodilators (SBP > 110); no routine opioids.

questions.stem: Regarding decongestion in decompensated heart failure (ESC 2026):
options: IV loop diuretics are recommended for patients admitted with fluid overload.
Adding acetazolamide or hydrochlorothiazide may be considered in patients already on loop diuretics.
In ADVOR, acetazolamide did not increase successful decongestion.
SGLT2 inhibitors should be avoided during hospitalisation.
questions.expl: A: I, A. B: IIa, B1. C: it did, 42.2 vs 30.5%. D: start during hospitalisation, class I.

questions.stem: The STRONG-HF trial showed that rapid up-titration of heart failure therapy before and shortly after discharge:
options: Increased mortality
Had no effect on outcomes
Was associated with fewer adverse events overall
Was tested only in outpatients with stable HF
Reduced death or heart failure readmission at 180 days
questions.expl: 15.2 vs 23.3%; adverse events were more frequent, serious ones were similar.

questions.stem: Regarding inotropes and vasopressors in cardiogenic shock:
options: Milrinone acts independently of beta-adrenergic receptors.
Dobutamine's effect may be attenuated by beta-blockade.
Inotropes have been shown to improve long-term survival.
Milrinone accumulates in renal failure.
questions.expl: A: PDE-3 inhibition.

questions.stem: According to ESC 2026, non-invasive positive pressure ventilation in decompensated HF is suggested in patients with:
options: Only when PaCO₂ exceeds 8 kPa
Cardiogenic shock with SBP < 70 mmHg as first-line therapy
Only after failure of high-flow nasal oxygen
Respiratory distress (RR > 25/min, SpO₂ < 90 %), started early
Any dyspnoea, regardless of oxygenation
questions.expl: IIa, B2 – early, to reduce the risk of intubation.

questions.stem: Regarding the SURVIVE and SOAP II trials:
options: SOAP II showed significantly lower overall 28-day mortality with dopamine.
SURVIVE compared levosimendan with dobutamine.
SOAP II found more arrhythmic events with dopamine than norepinephrine.
Levosimendan produced a greater reduction in BNP.
questions.expl: A: 52.5 vs 48.5% for dopamine, NS.

open.q: A 72-year-old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP 190/105 mmHg, RR 32/min and SpO₂ 86%. Outline your management according to ESC 2026 and the supporting evidence.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Recognise APO: mainly fluid redistribution with ↑ afterload, not total volume overload.
- O₂ for SpO₂ < 90% (I, C); early NIV (CPAP or NIPPV) for RR > 25/min and SpO₂ < 90% (IIa, B2).
- 3CPO: NIV did not reduce mortality but improved dyspnoea, acidosis and hypercapnia faster; CPAP = NIPPV.
- IV vasodilators (nitrates) since SBP > 110 mmHg (IIb, C) – fewer intubations; caution with severe AS/RV infarction.
- IV loop diuretic if fluid overloaded (I, A) – but fewer diuretics needed than in left-sided DHF.
- No routine opioids (III, C).
- Intubate if respiratory failure persists/progresses despite O₂ or NIV (I, C).

open.q: Compare dobutamine, milrinone and levosimendan and explain how you would choose between them in a hypoperfused patient on chronic beta-blocker therapy.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Dobutamine: β1 agonist; arrhythmias, ischaemia; effect attenuated by β-blockade.
- Milrinone: PDE-3 inhibitor acting independently of β-receptors; inodilator, ↓ PVR; hypotension; accumulates in renal failure.
- Levosimendan: Ca²⁺ sensitisation of troponin C + K-ATP opening; long-acting metabolite; hypotension, hypokalaemia, AF.
- DOREMI: milrinone = dobutamine (composite 49 vs 54%, NS); SURVIVE: levosimendan = dobutamine (180-d mortality 26 vs 28%).
- ESC 2026: levosimendan or PDE-3 inhibitor may be preferred over dobutamine in patients on β-blockers.
- Inodilators often need norepinephrine to counter hypotension.
- Inotropes do not improve survival – use for SBP < 90 with hypoperfusion (IIb, C), lowest dose, shortest time.

title: W07 · D5 – Right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension in the ICU

questions.stem: According to the 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines, pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension is defined as:
options: mPAP ≥ 25 mmHg, PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg, PVR ≥ 3 WU
sPAP > 40 mmHg on echocardiography
mPAP > 30 mmHg irrespective of PAWP
mPAP > 20 mmHg, PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg, PVR > 2 WU
mPAP > 20 mmHg, PAWP > 15 mmHg, PVR ≤ 2 WU
questions.expl: E is isolated post-capillary PH; A is the old definition.

questions.stem: Regarding ventricular interdependence:
options: Volume loading of a failing, dilated RV reliably increases cardiac output.
It can reduce left ventricular filling and stroke volume despite normal LV contractility.
Systemic hypotension may worsen RV function by reducing RV coronary perfusion.
A pressure-overloaded right ventricle shifts the septum towards the left ventricle.
questions.expl: A: volume loading of a failing RV may reduce CO.

questions.stem: Which factor was NOT part of the risk score for acute cor pulmonale in ARDS (Mekontso Dessap, ICM 2016)?
options: PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg
Age > 65 years
Pneumonia as the cause of ARDS
PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg
Driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O
questions.expl: The score comprised pneumonia, driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O, PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg and PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg.

questions.stem: Regarding inhaled nitric oxide:
options: It acts predominantly in ventilated lung units, improving V/Q matching.
It causes marked systemic hypotension.
It can be stopped abruptly without risk of rebound pulmonary hypertension.
It improves survival in ARDS.
questions.expl: C: abrupt withdrawal may cause rebound pulmonary hypertension – wean gradually. B: it is inactivated by haemoglobin. D: oxygenation improves only transiently.

questions.stem: A patient with known pulmonary arterial hypertension is admitted with pneumonia, BP 82/50 mmHg, CVP 18 mmHg, lactate 3.5 mmol/L and a dilated RV with D-sign. The most appropriate initial haemodynamic intervention is:
options: Urgent intubation to reduce work of breathing
1 L crystalloid bolus
Norepinephrine to restore systemic pressure, with consideration of an inotrope
Intravenous nitroglycerin
Beta-blocker to control heart rate
questions.expl: Maintain MAP (> 60 mmHg) for RV perfusion; fluids are more likely to harm, and intubation should be avoided if possible.

questions.stem: According to the ESC/ERS 2022 guidelines on ICU management of PAH with right heart failure:
options: Intubation should be avoided whenever possible.
Most patients require a positive fluid balance.
VA-ECMO is never used in PAH.
Norepinephrine or vasopressin may be required for persistent hypotension.
questions.expl: B: most patients require a negative fluid balance. C: it is used as a bridge to transplantation, or to recovery.

questions.stem: In a mechanically ventilated patient, pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest at:
options: Lung volumes associated with atelectasis
Maximal PEEP
Functional residual capacity
Total lung capacity
Residual volume
questions.expl: The PVR–lung volume relationship is "U"-shaped – both atelectasis and hyperinflation increase PVR.

questions.stem: "RV-protective" ventilation in ARDS includes:
options: Maximising PEEP to the highest tolerated level
Avoiding hypercapnia
Prone positioning
Limiting driving pressure
questions.expl: A: overdistension ↑ PVR.

questions.stem: Which echocardiographic finding is most typical of RV pressure overload?
options: Paradoxical septal motion with a D-shaped LV in short axis
Small RV with hyperdynamic LV
Isolated LV apical akinesia
Collapsible inferior vena cava
Mitral valve systolic anterior motion
questions.expl: The pressure-loaded RV shifts the septum to the left (D-sign); the IVC is typically dilated without respiratory variation.

questions.stem: Regarding acute right ventricular failure in the ICU:
options: Venous congestion does not affect liver or kidney function.
The right ventricle tolerates acute increases in afterload better than volume load.
Pulmonary embolism and RV infarction should be excluded in right-sided decompensated HF.
Hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis increase pulmonary vascular resistance.
questions.expl: A: congestive hepatopathy and nephropathy may result. B: the opposite is true. C: ESC 2026.

open.q: A patient with known PAH is admitted with pneumonia, BP 82/50 mmHg, CVP 18 mmHg, lactate 3.5 mmol/L and a dilated RV with D-sign. Outline your management and explain the physiological rationale.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Vicious circle: ↑ RV afterload → dilatation, TR → ↓ LV filling → hypotension → ↓ RV coronary perfusion → ischaemia.
- Treat the trigger (pneumonia – antibiotics; check arrhythmia, anaemia, interrupted PAH therapy).
- Restore systemic pressure – MAP > 60 mmHg with norepinephrine or vasopressin (vasopressin raises SVR without marked rise in PVR).
- Avoid fluid boluses – dilated RV compresses the LV; most need negative balance (diuretics, RRT/ultrafiltration).
- Inotrope for low output (dobutamine, milrinone; levosimendan alternative), with vasopressor if inodilator causes hypotension.
- Reduce RV afterload: correct hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidosis; inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (iNO, inhaled prostacyclins).
- Maintain sinus rhythm/AV synchrony; avoid intubation if possible (if needed: vasopressor running before induction, gentle induction).
- Consider VA-ECMO as a bridge to transplantation or recovery.

open.q: A ventilated ARDS patient has driving pressure 20 cmH₂O, PaCO₂ 55 mmHg and a D-sign on echo. Explain why the RV is failing and describe RV-protective ventilation.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Acute cor pulmonale occurs in ~22% of moderate/severe ARDS; this patient has risk factors (DP ≥ 18, PaCO₂ ≥ 48).
- Positive pressure ↑ RV afterload and ↓ preload; hypercapnia and acidosis ↑ PVR.
- PVR–lung volume relationship is U-shaped – lowest at FRC; atelectasis and hyperinflation both raise PVR.
- Limit plateau and driving pressure (target < 18 cmH₂O).
- Keep PaCO₂ < 48 mmHg; correct hypoxaemia.
- Titrate PEEP – enough to recruit, avoid overdistension; do not simply increase PEEP or give fluids.
- Prone positioning unloads the RV; consider VV-ECMO for refractory ACP; vasopressor to maintain RV perfusion.

title: W07 · Saturday – weekly review: Cardio I

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with anterior STEMI has BP 88/56 mmHg and HR 112/min, warm extremities, normal mentation, urine output 1 mL/kg/h and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. His SCAI SHOCK stage is:
options: C
A
E
B
D
questions.expl: Hypotension and tachycardia **without hypoperfusion** (normal lactate, urine output, mentation) = Beginning.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is in AMI-related cardiogenic shock with three-vessel disease. Regarding revascularisation:
options: Emergency CABG has no role, even if coronary anatomy is unsuitable for PCI.
All significant lesions should be treated during the index procedure.
CULPRIT-SHOCK showed a lower 30-day rate of death or RRT with culprit-only PCI.
Immediate coronary angiography with PCI of the infarct-related artery is recommended.
questions.expl: A: emergency CABG is an option if anatomy is unsuitable for PCI. B: CULPRIT-SHOCK. C: 45.9 vs 55.4%.

questions.stem: Five days after an inferior STEMI treated late, a patient becomes hypotensive with a new harsh holosystolic murmur. PAC shows SpO₂ 62 % in the right atrium and 84 % in the pulmonary artery. The diagnosis is:
options: Acute mitral regurgitation
Ventricular septal rupture
Free wall rupture
Pulmonary embolism
Right ventricular infarction
questions.expl: O₂ saturation step-up between RA and PA = left-to-right shunt at ventricular level.

questions.stem: Regarding mechanical circulatory support trials in infarct-related cardiogenic shock:
options: Both ECLS-SHOCK and DanGer Shock showed more bleeding complications with the device.
ECLS-SHOCK showed no reduction in 30-day mortality with early routine VA-ECMO.
DanGer Shock showed lower 180-day mortality with a microaxial flow pump in STEMI-related shock.
IABP-SHOCK II showed no reduction in 30-day mortality with IABP.
questions.expl: A: both ECLS-SHOCK and DanGer Shock showed more bleeding.

questions.stem: A patient on peripheral femoral VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock develops progressive pulmonary oedema. The arterial line shows a flat trace without pulsatility, and echo shows a closed aortic valve with spontaneous contrast in the LV. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Increase ECMO flow to maximum
Convert to VV-ECMO immediately
Give a fluid bolus
Increase PEEP to 20 cmH₂O and continue unchanged
Start an inotrope and consider LV unloading (IABP or microaxial pump)
questions.expl: LV distension due to ↑ afterload from retrograde flow; ↑ flow would increase afterload even further.

questions.stem: A patient on femoral VA-ECMO with severe lung injury has a recovering left ventricle. Regarding differential (Harlequin) hypoxaemia:
options: Increasing FiO₂ on the oxygenator corrects cerebral hypoxaemia.
Conversion to V-AV ECMO is a possible solution.
Oxygenation should be monitored from a femoral arterial line.
The upper body, including the brain and coronaries, may be perfused by poorly oxygenated blood.
questions.expl: C: monitor from the right radial artery, which reflects blood reaching the brain; femoral blood is mainly ECMO-oxygenated. A: the oxygenator only oxygenates ECMO blood, not blood ejected from the failing lungs.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on long-term bisoprolol is admitted with low-output heart failure (SBP 92 mmHg, cold extremities, lactate 3 mmol/L) and remains hypoperfused after cautious fluids. According to ESC 2026, which inotrope may be preferred over dobutamine?
options: Isoprenaline
Dopamine
Vasopressin
Phenylephrine
Levosimendan or a PDE-3 inhibitor
questions.expl: With β-blockade the effect of dobutamine is attenuated; levosimendan/milrinone act outside the β-receptor.

questions.stem: Regarding trials of inotropes:
options: In SURVIVE, 180-day mortality did not differ significantly.
DOREMI compared milrinone with dobutamine in cardiogenic shock.
SURVIVE compared levosimendan with dobutamine in acute decompensated heart failure.
DOREMI found a significant mortality benefit with milrinone.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP 200/110 mmHg, RR 34/min, SpO₂ 84 %, pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 7.5 kPa, alert and cooperative. The best initial respiratory support is:
options: Heliox
Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or NIPPV)
Intravenous morphine and oxygen
Immediate intubation
Low-flow oxygen 2 L/min only
questions.expl: NIV corrects acidosis and hypercapnia faster (3CPO); CPAP and NIPPV are equivalent; intubate if NIV fails.

questions.stem: Regarding the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines:
options: The term "decompensated heart failure" replaces "acute heart failure".
HFmrEF remains a separate category.
Vasopressors, preferably norepinephrine, may be considered in cardiogenic shock.
Intensive rapid up-titration of foundational therapy before and after discharge is recommended.
questions.expl: C: IIb, C. D: I, B2 – STRONG-HF.

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS from pneumonia has driving pressure 19 cmH₂O, PaO₂/FiO₂ 110 mmHg and PaCO₂ 52 mmHg (7 kPa). Echo shows a dilated RV with paradoxical septal motion. Which measure is most likely to help the right ventricle?
options: Fluid bolus of 1 L
Increase PEEP to maximal tolerated values
Start a beta-blocker
Prone positioning with reduction of driving pressure and PaCO₂
Permissive hypercapnia with PaCO₂ target 8 kPa
questions.expl: All 4 ACP risk factors are present; prone positioning and RV-protective ventilation reduce RV afterload.

questions.stem: Regarding pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure:
options: In PAH with right heart failure, intubation should be avoided whenever possible.
Group 2 PH is associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia.
Pulmonary hypertension is defined by mPAP > 20 mmHg (ESC/ERS 2022).
Isolated post-capillary PH has PAWP > 15 mmHg and PVR > 2 WU.
questions.expl: B: group 2 = left heart disease; lung disease = group 3. D: isolated post-capillary PH has PVR ≤ 2 WU; PVR > 2 WU = combined post- and pre-capillary PH.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with inferior STEMI is hypotensive (82/50 mmHg) with distended neck veins and clear lungs. ST elevation is present in V4R. Which initial treatment should be avoided?
options: Temporary pacing for complete AV block
Cautious fluid challenge
Primary PCI of the right coronary artery
Dobutamine if hypoperfusion persists
Intravenous nitrates
questions.expl: RV infarction is preload-dependent – nitrates (and diuretics) may cause severe hypotension.

questions.stem: Regarding diagnostics in cardiogenic shock:
options: ESICM 2025 considers echocardiography the first-line tool to determine the type of shock.
Mixed venous saturation is typically low.
Large v waves on PCWP tracing suggest acute mitral regurgitation.
A lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L is required for SCAI stage B.
questions.expl: D: stage B has normal lactate; ≥ 2 is stage C.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with anterior STEMI and cardiogenic shock (LVEF 25 %, lactate 5 mmol/L) is awake and was not resuscitated. He remains hypoperfused despite norepinephrine after primary PCI. According to ESC 2026, which option has class IIa support?
options: Dopamine as first-line vasopressor
No mechanical support should be considered
Routine VA-ECMO for all AMI-CS
Microaxial flow pump
Routine IABP
questions.expl: Selected STEMI-CS with LV dysfunction and no risk of hypoxic brain injury (DanGer Shock) – IIa, B1; routine IABP III; unselected MCS III.

title: W08 · D1 – Arrhythmias in the ICU: AF, VT/electrical storm, bradyarrhythmias

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with septic shock on noradrenaline develops new atrial fibrillation at 165/min. BP falls to 70/40 mmHg with rising lactate despite adequate filling. According to ERC 2025, the most appropriate immediate step is:
options: IV digoxin loading
Synchronised cardioversion with an initial shock at maximum defibrillator output
Synchronised cardioversion starting at 50 J with stepwise escalation
Wait 48 hours for spontaneous conversion
IV diltiazem bolus
questions.expl:
**Why B:** AF with shock, ischaemia or acute heart failure is an indication for emergency synchronised electrical cardioversion (ESC 2024, class I C). ERC 2025 changed the energy advice for AF: the first synchronised shock should be delivered at **maximum defibrillator output** instead of escalating, because the first-shock success is higher and repeated shocks are avoided. If it fails, give amiodarone 300 mg IV and shock again.

**Why not the others:**
- A – digoxin acts slowly (hours) and does not treat shock caused by the arrhythmia.
- C – a low start with stepwise escalation is the old approach; ERC 2025 recommends maximum energy for AF (70–120 J is for flutter/SVT).
- D – "wait-and-see" within 48 h is only for haemodynamically stable patients.
- E – diltiazem is negatively inotropic and a vasodilator, so it would worsen the hypotension.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult ALS, Resuscitation 2025;215:110769; Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

questions.stem: Regarding rate control of atrial fibrillation according to the 2024 ESC guidelines:
options: Lenient rate control with a resting heart rate < 110/min should be considered as the initial target.
Diltiazem and verapamil should be avoided when LVEF is ≤ 40 %.
Digoxin can be used irrespective of left ventricular ejection fraction.
In haemodynamic instability, IV amiodarone, digoxin, esmolol or landiolol may be considered.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESC 2024 recommends lenient rate control (resting HR < 110/min) as the initial target (IIa B), based on RACE II.
- B (True) – non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negatively inotropic and can cause decompensation in HFrEF, so they are used only if LVEF > 40%.
- C (True) – digoxin (like beta-blockers) can be used at any LVEF; it is slower and less effective at high sympathetic tone, but it does not lower blood pressure.
- D (True) – in haemodynamic instability or severely reduced LVEF, IV amiodarone, digoxin, esmolol or landiolol may be considered (IIb B).

**EDIC trap:** All four are true – a K′ item can have four true statements.

**Ref:** Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414; Van Gelder IC et al. (RACE II), N Engl J Med 2010;362:1363–1373.

questions.stem: In the STRESS-L trial of landiolol in septic shock with heart rate ≥ 95/min:
options: There was no improvement in organ failure and the trial was stopped early with a possible signal of harm
Landiolol significantly reduced 28-day mortality
Landiolol significantly reduced the mean SOFA score
Landiolol was compared with esmolol
Only patients with atrial fibrillation were enrolled
questions.expl:
**Why A:** STRESS-L (126 adults with septic shock, noradrenaline > 0.1 µg/kg/min for > 24 h, HR ≥ 95/min) randomised landiolol titrated to HR 80–94/min vs standard care. Mean SOFA over 14 days did not differ (8.8 vs 8.1). The trial was stopped early because benefit was unlikely; 28-day mortality was 37.1% vs 25.4% and 90-day mortality 43.5% vs 28.6% (not significant), a possible signal of harm.

**Why not the others:**
- B – 28-day mortality was numerically **higher** with landiolol, not lower.
- C – there was no difference in mean SOFA score, the primary outcome.
- D – the comparator was standard care, not esmolol.
- E – most patients had sinus tachycardia; the entry criterion was heart rate, not AF.

**EDIC trap:** Do not confuse STRESS-L with Morelli's single-centre esmolol trial (JAMA 2013), which suggested benefit.

**Ref:** Whitehouse T et al. (STRESS-L), JAMA 2023;330:1641–1652.

questions.stem: Concerning anticoagulation and cardioversion in atrial fibrillation (ESC 2024):
options: The CHA₂DS₂-VA score adds one point for female sex.
A score of ≥ 2 is an indicator to start oral anticoagulation.
Early cardioversion without anticoagulation or TOE is acceptable if AF has lasted up to 72 hours.
Atrial fibrillation triggered by a reversible precipitant never requires long-term anticoagulation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – CHA₂DS₂-**VA** (ESC 2024) dropped female sex; it is no longer counted as a risk factor.
- B (True) – a score ≥ 2 means oral anticoagulation is recommended (I C); a score of 1 means it should be considered (IIa C).
- C (False) – the threshold in ESC 2024 is **24 h**: early cardioversion without anticoagulation or TOE is not recommended if AF has lasted > 24 h (III C).
- D (False) – AF triggered by a reversible precipitant (e.g. sepsis, surgery) often recurs; long-term OAC should be **considered** in patients at increased thromboembolic risk (IIa C).

**EDIC trap:** Older sources use 48 h and CHA₂DS₂-VASc – ESC 2024 uses 24 h and CHA₂DS₂-VA.

**Ref:** Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25 %) has haemodynamically stable recent-onset AF. Pharmacological cardioversion is requested. The most appropriate agent is:
options: Vernakalant
Verapamil
Flecainide
Propafenone
Amiodarone
questions.expl:
**Why E:** In structural heart disease – HFrEF, coronary artery disease or severe LVH – IV amiodarone is the recommended agent for pharmacological cardioversion (ESC 2024, I A). Its effect is delayed (often 8–12 h or more), but it is safe in a low-EF heart and also slows the ventricular rate in the meantime. Watch for hypotension, bradycardia and QT prolongation with IV use.

**Why not the others:**
- A – vernakalant is contraindicated in HFrEF, recent ACS and severe aortic stenosis.
- B – verapamil is a rate-control drug, not a cardioversion drug, and is contraindicated with LVEF ≤ 40%.
- C – flecainide (class IC) is contraindicated in CAD and HFrEF because it is proarrhythmic in a scarred ventricle (CAST).
- D – propafenone (class IC) has the same contraindications as flecainide.

**Ref:** Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

questions.stem: Regarding electrical storm (ESC 2022):
options: It is defined as ≥ 3 episodes of sustained ventricular arrhythmia within 7 days, each requiring intervention.
Catheter ablation is contraindicated during electrical storm.
Sedation is part of the initial management.
A non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol combined with amiodarone is commonly used.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – electrical storm is ≥ 3 episodes of sustained ventricular arrhythmia within **24 hours**, separated by ≥ 5 min, each needing intervention (e.g. ICD shock or ATP).
- B (False) – catheter ablation is a key treatment of storm and is preferred in incessant monomorphic VT.
- C (True) – sedation breaks the cycle of shocks, fear and sympathetic drive; deep sedation or intubation is used if the storm is refractory.
- D (True) – non-selective beta-blockade (propranolol) plus amiodarone is the most common drug combination; landiolol is an option for amiodarone-resistant VT.

**EDIC trap:** "7 days" is a wrong definition; the window is 24 h.

**Ref:** Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997–4126.

questions.stem: A patient on haloperidol and ciprofloxacin with QTc 590 ms develops recurrent runs of torsade de pointes. Serum magnesium is normal. The first-line drug is:
options: Adenosine
Intravenous magnesium sulfate
Procainamide
Sotalol
Amiodarone
questions.expl:
**Why B:** This is drug-induced long-QT torsade de pointes (haloperidol + ciprofloxacin, QTc 590 ms). IV magnesium sulfate (e.g. 2 g) stops and prevents recurrences even when serum magnesium is normal, probably by blocking early afterdepolarisations. Also correct K⁺ to high-normal and stop the QT-prolonging drugs; for recurrences raise the heart rate with isoprenaline or overdrive pacing.

**Why not the others:**
- A – adenosine is for re-entrant SVT and has no role in TdP.
- C – procainamide (class IA) prolongs the QT interval and can worsen TdP.
- D – sotalol has class III action and is itself a common cause of TdP.
- E – amiodarone prolongs QT further and is avoided in long-QT TdP.

**EDIC trap:** Unstable or pulseless TdP needs an unsynchronised shock (defibrillation).

**Ref:** Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997–4126.

questions.stem: Bradycardia with adverse features (ERC 2025):
options: Transcutaneous pacing can be used as a bridge to transvenous pacing.
The initial atropine dose is 500 µg IV, repeated up to a total of 3 mg.
Isoprenaline or adrenaline are second-line options when atropine fails.
Atropine is the drug of choice after heart transplantation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – transcutaneous pacing is a bridge when drugs fail and transvenous pacing is not yet available.
- B (True) – ERC 2025: atropine 500 µg IV, repeated every 3–5 min up to a total of 3 mg.
- C (True) – if atropine is ineffective, isoprenaline (start 5 µg/min) or adrenaline 2–10 µg/min are second-line drugs; aminophylline and glucagon are used in specific situations.
- D (False) – after heart transplantation the heart is denervated, so atropine does not work and can cause paradoxical high-degree AV block; aminophylline is the alternative.

**EDIC trap:** Atropine is also unlikely to work in high-degree AV block with broad QRS (block below the His bundle) – go to pacing.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult ALS, Resuscitation 2025;215:110769; Glikson M et al., 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427–3520.

questions.stem: In a large cohort of patients hospitalised with severe sepsis (Walkey, JAMA 2011), new-onset atrial fibrillation was associated with:
options: No difference in stroke
Higher in-hospital stroke and mortality
A protective effect of anticoagulation on mortality
Lower in-hospital mortality
Reduced length of stay
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In over 49,000 patients with severe sepsis, new-onset AF occurred in 5.9%. It was associated with more in-hospital ischaemic stroke (2.6% vs 0.6%) and higher in-hospital mortality (56% vs 39%). This is an observational association – NOAF is a marker of illness severity, not proven to cause the outcomes.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stroke was about four times more frequent with NOAF.
- C – the study did not show a protective effect of anticoagulation; ICU data do not support routine therapeutic anticoagulation in acute sepsis.
- D – mortality was higher, not lower.
- E – NOAF is associated with a longer, not shorter, stay.

**Ref:** Walkey AJ et al., JAMA 2011;306:2248–2254; Wetterslev M et al., Intensive Care Med 2019;45:928–938.

questions.stem: Regarding sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (ESC 2022):
options: In PROCAMIO, amiodarone terminated more tachycardias than procainamide.
Haemodynamic instability is an indication for IV amiodarone before any attempt at cardioversion.
A haemodynamically tolerated VT may be left untreated if blood pressure is normal.
