questions.expl: COMPLETE (stable STEMI): CV death or MI 7.8 vs 10.5 % (HR 0.74). CULPRIT-SHOCK applies to **shock** (culprit lesion only during the index procedure). The presence of shock decides. ([W07/D3](#W07-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding mechanical complications of myocardial infarction:
options: The posteromedial papillary muscle is vulnerable because it has a single blood supply (from the PDA).
Ventricular septal rupture after inferior MI (basal septum) carries a worse prognosis than after anterior MI.
IABP is contraindicated as a bridge to surgery in ventricular septal rupture.
Free wall rupture typically presents with gradually progressive heart failure over several days.
questions.expl: C: IABP/MCS as a bridge – should be considered. D: free wall rupture typically presents with sudden tamponade and PEA. ([W07/D3](#W07-D3))

questions.stem: A patient with cardiogenic shock and anuric acute kidney injury needs inotropic support. Which drug is most likely to accumulate because of the renal failure?
options: Noradrenaline
Adrenaline
Milrinone
Dobutamine
Dopamine
questions.expl: Milrinone (PDE-3 inhibitor) accumulates in renal failure and causes hypotension. In DOREMI milrinone and dobutamine did not differ (49 vs 54 %, NS). ([W07/D4](#W07-D4))

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman develops sudden pulmonary oedema with BP 205/110 mmHg; her weight is unchanged from baseline. Which description best fits this presentation and its treatment?
options: Fluid redistribution with increased afterload – IV vasodilators are central, aiming for SBP < 140 mmHg promptly
Routine IV morphine to reduce anxiety and preload
Cardiogenic shock – start inotropes
Total body volume overload – high-dose diuretics are the main therapy
Isolated right ventricular failure – give a fluid bolus
questions.expl: ESC 2026: acute pulmonary oedema = mainly **fluid redistribution** (↑ afterload) → fewer diuretics, more vasodilators (IV vasodilators with SBP > 110 – IIb); ESC/ESH 2018: pulmonary oedema – SBP < 140 immediately (nitroglycerin/nitroprusside + loop diuretic). No routine opioids (III). ([W07/D4](#W07-D4), [W08/D4](#W08-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding decongestion in decompensated heart failure (ESC 2026 and related trials):
options: IV loop diuretics in patients with fluid overload carry only a class IIb recommendation.
In ADVOR, IV acetazolamide 500 mg added to loop diuretics increased successful decongestion within 3 days.
Ultrafiltration is recommended as first-line decongestive therapy (class I).
Routine opioids are recommended in acute pulmonary oedema.
questions.expl: A: I, A. B: 42.2 vs 30.5 %. C: ultrafiltration may be considered only for refractory congestion (IIb, C). D: III, C. ([W07/D4](#W07-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding the definition and organisation of care in cardiogenic shock:
options: According to ESC 2026, a lactate > 2 mmol/L supports the diagnosis.
According to ESC 2026, a systolic BP < 90 mmHg is mandatory for the diagnosis.
A multidisciplinary Shock Team for MCS candidates has a class I recommendation in ESC 2026.
The key MCS trials (IABP-SHOCK II, ECLS-SHOCK, DanGer Shock) enrolled AMI-related shock, so their results should not be automatically applied to HF-related shock.
questions.expl: B: no fixed BP threshold is defined – "normotensive CS". C: I, C. ([W07/D1](#W07-D1))

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing HFrEF undergoes right heart catheterisation: mPAP 32 mmHg, PAWP 22 mmHg, PVR 4 WU. According to ESC/ERS 2022, this is:
options: No pulmonary hypertension
Pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension
Group 3 pulmonary hypertension
Isolated post-capillary pulmonary hypertension
Combined post- and pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension
questions.expl: mPAP > 20, PAWP > 15 **and** PVR > 2 WU = CpcPH. IpcPH would have PVR ≤ 2 WU; pre-capillary PAWP ≤ 15. Left heart disease = group 2. ([W07/D5](#W07-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding management of acute right ventricular failure:
options: Vasopressin increases systemic vascular resistance without a marked increase in PVR.
ESC/ERS 2022 advises maintaining MAP > 60 mmHg to preserve RV perfusion.
Inhaled nitric oxide may worsen pulmonary oedema in severe LV dysfunction.
Inhaled nitric oxide does not cause systemic hypotension because it is rapidly inactivated by haemoglobin.
questions.expl: iNO also carries a risk of rebound PH on abrupt withdrawal and methaemoglobinaemia; it does not improve survival in ARDS. ([W07/D5](#W07-D5))

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS due to pneumonia has driving pressure 16 cmH₂O, PaO₂/FiO₂ 130 mmHg and PaCO₂ 50 mmHg. How many risk factors for acute cor pulmonale (Mekontso Dessap score) are present?
questions.expl: Pneumonia ✓, P/F < 150 ✓, PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg ✓; driving pressure 16 < 18 ✗ → **3**. ACP was present in ~22 % of ARDS patients; RV-protective ventilation = ↓ ΔP, correction of hypercapnia, prone positioning. ([W07/D5](#W07-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding ventilatory support in decompensated heart failure:
options: Positive intrathoracic pressure increases LV transmural pressure (afterload).
In 3CPO, CPAP was superior to NIPPV for death or intubation.
ESC 2026 recommends oxygen for all patients with decompensated HF, regardless of SpO₂.
In RV failure or hypovolaemia, PEEP reliably increases cardiac output.
questions.expl: A: positive intrathoracic pressure **reduces** LV transmural pressure (afterload). B: 11.7 vs 11.1 %, NS – equivalent. C: O₂ if SpO₂ < 90 % or PaO₂ < 60 mmHg. D: in RV failure or hypovolaemia, PEEP may **reduce** cardiac output. ([W07/D4](#W07-D4))

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on day 2 after colectomy has septic shock from an anastomotic leak. He is haemodynamically stable on low-dose noradrenaline (MAP 72 mmHg) when atrial fibrillation at 128/min starts; it has lasted 6 hours. K⁺ 3.2 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ 0.5 mmol/L, LVEF 55 %. The most appropriate approach is:
options: Immediate synchronised cardioversion at maximum energy
Landiolol titrated to a heart rate of 80–94/min
Treat the triggers (source control, correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺), rate control if needed, and allow time for spontaneous conversion
Immediate full-dose unfractionated heparin
Elective cardioversion without anticoagulation or TOE on day 3 of AF
questions.expl: In a stable patient treat triggers first; sinus rhythm returns spontaneously after treating the cause in up to 83 % within 48 h ("wait-and-see" IIa B). STRESS-L: landiolol for tachycardia in septic shock without benefit and with a signal of harm; anticoagulation in acute sepsis unclear; cardioversion without OAC/TOE in AF > 24 h – III. ([W08/D1](#W08-D1))

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes mellitus develops atrial fibrillation (ESC 2024):
options: Her CHA₂DS₂-VA score is 4.
Female sex adds one point to her score.
Oral anticoagulation is recommended.
If AF has lasted more than 24 hours, early cardioversion without anticoagulation or TOE is acceptable.
questions.expl: A: age 65–74 = 1, HT = 1, DM = 1 → 3. B: sex has been removed. C: ≥ 2 → I C. D: not recommended (III C) unless she is unstable. ([W08/D1](#W08-D1))

questions.stem: A 54-year-old after an intentional verapamil overdose has a heart rate of 32/min and BP 70/40 mmHg despite atropine 3 mg. Besides pacing and adrenaline/isoprenaline, which drug is specifically suggested by ERC 2025 for this cause?
options: Aminophylline
Amiodarone
Further atropine up to 6 mg
Adenosine
Glucagon
questions.expl: Glucagon for bradycardia due to beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers. Aminophylline is for the transplanted heart and spinal cord injury; atropine max. 3 mg. ([W08/D1](#W08-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding bradycardia with adverse features (ERC 2025):
options: Transcutaneous pacing can be used as a bridge when transvenous pacing is not immediately available.
Isoprenaline is contraindicated in bradycardia.
Raised intracranial pressure (Cushing reflex) is a recognised cause of bradycardia.
Atropine is unlikely to help in high-grade AV block with a broad QRS complex.
questions.expl: D: block below the His level. B: isoprenaline 5 µg/min is second line. ([W08/D1](#W08-D1))

questions.stem: A normotensive patient with PE has sPESI 0, an RV/LV ratio of 1.2 on CT and a normal troponin. According to ESC 2019, the risk category is:
options: Low
Cannot be classified without the full PESI
High
Intermediate-high
Intermediate-low
questions.expl: A patient with low PESI/sPESI but with RV dysfunction **or** positive biomarkers is intermediate-low risk. Intermediate-high = RV dysfunction **and** troponin. ([W08/D2](#W08-D2))

questions.stem: Haemodynamic and airway management in severe PE:
options: The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline considers systemic thrombolysis reasonable in category C1.
ESC 2019 advises generous fluid loading (> 2 L) to support the RV.
The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline classifies deep sedation and mechanical ventilation, when not essential, as harmful in categories C–E.
Noradrenaline (0.2–1.0 µg/kg/min) improves systemic pressure and RV perfusion.
questions.expl: B: limit fluid loading to ≤ 500 mL. C: Class 3: Harm. A: in A to C2 systemic thrombolysis is harmful. ([W08/D2](#W08-D2))

questions.stem: Considering PEITHO (systemic tenecteplase) and the catheter-directed thrombolysis trials HI-PEITHO and PRAGUE-26 in intermediate-high risk PE, the common finding was:
options: No effect on any clinical outcome
A significant reduction in all-cause mortality
A reduction in early haemodynamic/cardiorespiratory decompensation without a proven mortality benefit
No intracranial bleeding in any of the trials
Benefit only in low-risk patients
questions.expl: PEITHO: death/decompensation 2.6 vs 5.6 %, mortality NS, ↑ bleeding and stroke (2.4 vs 0.2 %); HI-PEITHO and PRAGUE-26 driven by decompensation, mortality no different; in PRAGUE-26 2 intracranial haemorrhages in the CDT arm. ([W08/D2](#W08-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding classification and imaging of acute aortic syndromes (ESC 2024):
options: A dissection diagnosed 20 hours after symptom onset is classified as subacute.
DeBakey type II involves only the ascending aorta.
A negative transthoracic echo does not exclude dissection.
Stanford type A corresponds to DeBakey types I and II.
questions.expl: A: < 24 h = hyperacute; subacute 15–90 days. C: TTE has low sensitivity, e.g. < 40 % for IMH. ([W08/D3](#W08-D3))

questions.stem: A patient with acute type A dissection extending into the left subclavian artery has BP 92/60 mmHg in the left arm and 158/90 mmHg in the right arm. The arterial line should preferably be placed in the:
options: Left radial artery
Right radial artery
Left brachial artery
Either radial artery – the readings are equivalent
Dorsalis pedis artery only
questions.expl: With left subclavian involvement the left arm may show falsely low BP. Target SBP < 120 and HR ≤ 60/min – BB first, then a vasodilator; type A → immediate surgery. ([W08/D3](#W08-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding cardiac tamponade (ESC 2025):
options: An end-diastolic effusion of 15 mm is classified as moderate.
A triage score > 6 points (from at least two categories) indicates immediate pericardiocentesis.
Right atrial collapse is a later but more specific sign than right ventricular diastolic collapse.
Electrical alternans is explained by the "swinging heart".
questions.expl: A: 10–20 mm. C: RA collapse is the earliest and sensitive sign; RV diastolic collapse is more specific. ([W08/D3](#W08-D3))

questions.stem: A 68-year-old presents with BP 214/122 mmHg and acute pulmonary oedema. Which management is correct?
options: Reduce MAP by 20–25 % over several hours with labetalol
Reduce SBP to < 140 mmHg immediately with IV nitroglycerin or nitroprusside plus a loop diuretic
SBP < 120 mmHg and HR < 60/min with esmolol
No IV therapy, because BP is below 180/110 mmHg
SBP < 160 mmHg and DBP < 105 mmHg with magnesium sulphate
questions.expl: Acute organ damage, not the absolute BP value, defines an emergency. Pulmonary oedema is one of the exceptions to the "slowly" rule (ESC/ESH 2018). A = malignant HT, C = dissection, E = pre-eclampsia. ([W08/D4](#W08-D4))

questions.stem: Blood pressure management in acute stroke (trials and ESC 2024):
options: In INTERACT2, the ordinal analysis of mRS favoured standard BP lowering.
In ATACH-2, renal adverse events within 7 days were less frequent with intensive lowering.
Before mechanical thrombectomy, BP should be < 185/110 mmHg, the same target as for thrombolysis.
In ischaemic stroke without reperfusion and BP ≥ 220/110 mmHg, a reduction of about 50 % during the first 24 h is reasonable.
questions.expl: A: the ordinal analysis favoured **intensive** lowering (p = 0.04); primary outcome NS. B: **more** frequent with intensive lowering (9.0 % vs 4.0 %). C: thrombectomy < 180/105; thrombolysis < 185/110. D: about 15 % (IIa C). ([W08/D4](#W08-D4))

questions.stem: A 41-year-old with a known adrenal mass has paroxysmal headache, sweating and BP 240/130 mmHg with hypertensive encephalopathy. The preferred first drug is:
options: Propranolol alone
Esmolol alone
Furosemide
Sublingual nifedipine
Phentolamine
questions.expl: Phaeochromocytoma crisis: α-blockade (phentolamine, doxazosin, terazosin, labetalol). A β-blocker alone without α-blockade → unopposed α-vasoconstriction. ([W08/D4](#W08-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding valvular disease and haemodynamic support in critically ill patients:
options: Severe aortic stenosis is a contraindication to Impella.
An IABP is a useful bridge in acute severe aortic regurgitation.
In low-flow, low-gradient AS with reduced EF, a rise in stroke volume ≥ 20 % during dobutamine echo indicates contractile (flow) reserve.
TAVI in cardiogenic shock has a 30-day mortality of about 13–19 %.
questions.expl: B: IABP is contraindicated in AR – diastolic augmentation ↑ regurgitation. ([W08/D5](#W08-D5), [W07/D2](#W07-D2))

questions.stem: A patient with native mitral valve IE (*S. aureus*) has a 12-mm vegetation and a splenic embolus despite appropriate antibiotics; there is no heart failure.
options: Urgent surgery (within 3–5 days) is indicated.
In EASE, early surgery significantly reduced 6-month all-cause mortality.
Gentamicin should be added for staphylococcal native valve IE.
A significant intracranial haemorrhage is never a reason to delay surgery.
questions.expl: A: vegetation ≥ 10 mm after ≥ 1 embolism despite antibiotics. C: no aminoglycosides in staphylococcal NVE. B: 3 vs 5 %, NS; benefit via ↓ embolism. D: after significant intracranial haemorrhage, delaying surgery for ≥ 4 weeks should be considered. ([W08/D5](#W08-D5))

questions.stem: During an in-hospital VF arrest, amiodarone 300 mg was given after the third shock. VF persists and the fifth shock has just been delivered. According to ERC 2025, which antiarrhythmic dose is now due?
options: Lidocaine 100 mg
No further antiarrhythmic
Amiodarone 150 mg
Amiodarone 300 mg
Magnesium sulphate 2 g
questions.expl: Amiodarone 300 mg after the 3rd shock, 150 mg after the 5th shock (alternative lidocaine 100 mg + 50 mg). Adrenaline 1 mg continues every 3–5 min. ([W09/D1](#W09-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding airway management and ventilation during CPR (ERC 2025):
options: Chest compressions may be paused for up to 10 seconds for tracheal intubation.
Each breath should last about 1 second with visible chest rise.
Video laryngoscopy is preferred if immediately available.
Inspired oxygen should be titrated to SpO₂ 88–92 % during CPR.
questions.expl: A: interruption < 5 s. D: use the highest feasible inspired oxygen during CPR. ([W09/D1](#W09-D1))

questions.stem: A haemodialysis patient has a cardiac arrest; point-of-care K⁺ is 8.5 mmol/L. In addition to standard ALS, the most appropriate drug management is:
options: 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ and 50 mmol NaHCO₃ (separate lines or with flushing), insulin–glucose, and consider dialysis or ECPR
Calcium gluconate and sodium bicarbonate mixed in one syringe
Insulin–glucose only, withholding calcium during CPR
Stop resuscitation – hyperkalaemic arrest is not survivable
Oral sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g
questions.expl: ERC 2025 – hyperkalaemic arrest: 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ + 50 mmol NaHCO₃ via separate lines/with flushing (otherwise CaCO₃ precipitates), insulin/glucose, dialysis, ECPR if these fail. ([W09/D5](#W09-D5), [W06/D2](#W06-D2))

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient has cardiac arrest from local anaesthetic systemic toxicity. The maximum cumulative dose of 20 % lipid emulsion according to ERC 2025 is approximately:
options: 105 mL
420 mL
840 mL
questions.expl: Max. 12 mL/kg × 70 kg = **840 mL**. Bolus 1.5 mL/kg = 105 mL, infusion 15 mL/kg/h = 1050 mL/h; consider prolonged CPR (> 1 h) and ECPR. ([W09/D5](#W09-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding post-ROSC care (ERC-ESICM 2025 and BOX):
options: In BOX, a liberal PaO₂ target of 13–14 kPa improved outcomes compared with 9–10 kPa.
Normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa) is targeted.
Both hypokalaemia and hyperkalaemia should be avoided.
A SBP > 100 mmHg is mentioned in addition to MAP > 60–65 mmHg.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old is resuscitated from OHCA with an initial VF rhythm. The post-ROSC ECG shows no ST elevation, but he has recurrent VT requiring shocks and needs escalating noradrenaline. According to ERC-ESICM 2025, the most appropriate approach is:
options: Systemic thrombolysis
Early coronary angiography, because electrical and haemodynamic instability strongly suggest acute coronary occlusion
Defer angiography until neuroprognostication at 72 h
Coronary CT angiography only
Defer angiography in all patients without ST elevation
questions.expl: Without ST elevation catheterisation is deferred (COACT, TOMAHAWK) **unless** the clinical picture strongly suggests acute coronary occlusion (haemodynamic or electrical instability, ongoing ischaemia). Parallel: NSTE-ACS with life-threatening arrhythmias = very high risk → immediate. ([W09/D2](#W09-D2), [W07/D3](#W07-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding temperature control trials after cardiac arrest:
options: HYPERION enrolled both in-hospital and out-of-hospital arrests with a non-shockable rhythm.
In TTM2, rewarming was performed at up to 1 °C/h.
In HYPERION, mortality was significantly lower at 33 °C.
TTM2 included in-hospital cardiac arrests.
questions.expl: B: rewarming was limited to 0.3 °C/h. D: OHCA only – generalisation to IHCA is less well supported. C: only CPC 1–2 10.2 vs 5.7 %; no difference in mortality. ([W09/D3](#W09-D3))

questions.stem: A patient treated with controlled hypothermia at 33 °C is being rewarmed. Which electrolyte disturbance is most expected during rewarming?
options: Hypercalcaemia
Hyperkalaemia
Hypernatraemia
Hypermagnesaemia
Hypokalaemia
questions.expl: K⁺ shifts: hypokalaemia during cooling, hyperkalaemia during rewarming → rewarm slowly, monitor K⁺. ([W09/D3](#W09-D3))

questions.stem: A 46-year-old remains unconscious (GCS motor 2) 96 h after OHCA; sedation was stopped 60 h ago, he is normothermic and has not received NMB. NSE is 72 µg/L at 48 h and 95 µg/L at 72 h; EEG at 36 h shows burst-suppression.
options: Haemolysis would falsely elevate NSE.
Two predictors are present, so a poor outcome is likely according to ERC-ESICM 2025.
Sedatives such as propofol can induce EEG suppression and must be considered when interpreting the EEG.
The decision to withdraw life-sustaining therapy should be based solely on these results.
questions.expl: B: NSE > 60 at 48/72 h + highly malignant EEG > 24 h. D: separate WLST from prognosis – age, comorbidities, preferences. ([W09/D4](#W09-D4))

questions.stem: Which finding is a valid ERC-ESICM 2025 predictor of poor outcome at the time point stated?
options: Bilaterally absent N20 SSEP waves at 30 h
Motor response M3 at 72 h as the sole predictor
Bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at 48 h
NSE > 60 µg/L at 24 h
Status myoclonus first appearing on day 5
questions.expl: N20 is assessed at ≥ 24 h. Reflexes at ≥ 72 h; NSE at 48 h and/or 72 h; status myoclonus ≤ 72 h; M ≤ 3 is used to select patients, not as a predictor. ([W09/D4](#W09-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding ECPR trials in refractory OHCA:
options: ARREST was stopped early for futility.
In INCEPTION, the median time from arrest to ECMO flow was about 74 minutes.
INCEPTION was a single-centre trial.
Prague OHCA enrolled witnessed arrests in patients aged 18–65 years without ROSC after 5 minutes of ALS.
questions.expl: A: stopped early after crossing a Bayesian **superiority** boundary (43 vs 7 %, n = 30). C: 10 centres in the Netherlands. ([W09/D5](#W09-D5))

questions.stem: A patient with accidental hypothermia (core temperature 32 °C) is in PEA. According to ERC 2025, adrenaline should be given:
options: Only after ROSC
Every 3–5 minutes
Every 6–10 minutes
At double dose every 3–5 minutes
Not at all until the temperature exceeds 35 °C
questions.expl: 30–35 °C → intervals of 6–10 min; < 30 °C do not give adrenaline (accumulation) unless ECPR is started immediately. ([W09/D5](#W09-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding drug trials during cardiac arrest:
options: In ALPS, lidocaine was significantly superior to amiodarone.
In PARAMEDIC2, survival to hospital admission was 23.8 % with adrenaline vs 8.0 % with placebo.
In ALPS, both drugs were associated with higher survival than placebo in bystander-witnessed arrests.
In PARAMEDIC2, the number needed to treat with adrenaline for one additional 30-day survivor was about 112.

questions.stem: Regarding defibrillation (ERC 2025):
options: For pulsed biphasic devices, the first shock is 360 J.
Stacked shocks are recommended for all out-of-hospital VF arrests.
The RCUK 2025 guidelines recommend routine double sequential external defibrillation.
If the defibrillator type is unknown, the lowest available energy should be used.
questions.expl: A: 130–150 J for pulsed biphasic devices. B: up to 3 shocks only in a witnessed, monitored arrest with a defibrillator immediately available. C: no routine DSED; a change of vector (AP) is considered. D: use the highest energy if the device type is unknown. ([W09/D1](#W09-D1))

questions.stem: During CPR for PEA in a 50-year-old after hip surgery, point-of-care ultrasound shows a dilated right ventricle. Which statement is correct?
options: Thrombolysis is contraindicated during CPR
Absence of myocardial contractility on ultrasound is alone a reason to stop CPR
A low ETCO₂ alone is sufficient to terminate resuscitation
RV dilatation confirms PE
RV dilatation alone does not confirm PE; if PE is suspected, thrombolysis may be considered and CPR continued long enough for it to act
questions.expl: The right ventricle dilates in every cardiac arrest – isolated RV dilatation is not a diagnosis of PE. In arrest from PE an accelerated alteplase regimen of 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min is used (max. 50 mg, off-label); also consider ECPR. ([W09/D1](#W09-D1), [W08/D2](#W08-D2))

questions.stem: An intubated patient with pneumonia has bilateral B-lines and consolidations on lung ultrasound and a normal echocardiogram. On PEEP 8 cmH₂O and FiO₂ 0.5, SpO₂ is 94 %; no arterial blood gas is available. According to the global definition (2024), this is:
options: Moderate ARDS
Not ARDS – an arterial blood gas is mandatory
Mild ARDS
Not assessable – S/F is invalid when SpO₂ < 97 %
Severe ARDS
questions.expl: S/F = 94 / 0.5 = **188** → 148 < S/F ≤ 235 = moderate. S/F is valid with SpO₂ ≤ 97 %; lung ultrasound is acceptable imaging. ([W10/D1](#W10-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding the evolution of ARDS definitions:
options: AECC 1994 used PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 300 for ALI and ≤ 200 for ARDS.
The Berlin definition requires invasive mechanical ventilation.
The Berlin definition allows patients on high-flow nasal oxygen.
The Berlin definition markedly improved predictive validity, with an AUROC above 0.8.
questions.expl: B: NIV or CPAP with PEEP ≥ 5 cmH₂O is acceptable. C: HFNO has no defined PEEP – the main reason for the revision. D: AUROC 0.577 vs 0.536 – still weak. ([W10/D1](#W10-D1))

questions.stem: A 175-cm man weighing 130 kg is intubated for ARDS. A tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight is approximately:
options: 350 mL
780 mL
600 mL
423 mL
525 mL

questions.stem: A ventilated ARDS patient has VT 480 mL, PEEP 12 cmH₂O, peak pressure 40 cmH₂O and plateau pressure 30 cmH₂O.
options: The static compliance of the respiratory system is about 16 mL/cmH₂O.
The 10 cmH₂O difference between peak and plateau pressure reflects the resistive component.
Because plateau pressure does not exceed 30 cmH₂O, ventilation is safe and driving pressure is irrelevant.
The driving pressure is 18 cmH₂O.
questions.expl: D: 30 − 12. A: Crs = VT / ΔP = 480 / 18 ≈ 26.7 mL/cmH₂O. C: in Amato's analysis ΔP was the strongest predictor of survival even with a "protective" Pplat. ([W10/D2](#W10-D2))

questions.stem: A patient with morbid obesity and intra-abdominal hypertension has ARDS; plateau pressure is 32 cmH₂O on VT 6 mL/kg PBW. The best way to assess the true stress on the lung is to:
options: Perform a recruitment manoeuvre at 45 cmH₂O for 2 minutes
Increase PEEP to 25 cmH₂O without further monitoring
Ignore plateau pressure in obese patients
Measure oesophageal pressure to estimate transpulmonary pressure
Switch to pressure support to lower plateau pressure
questions.expl: The lungs "feel" transpulmonary pressure (P_aw − P_es); with a stiff chest wall Pplat overestimates lung stress. Prolonged high-pressure RMs – ESICM strongly against. ([W10/D2](#W10-D2), [W10/D3](#W10-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding trials of PEEP strategies:
options: In ALVEOLI, recruitment manoeuvres were used throughout the trial in the higher PEEP group.
EXPRESS increased ventilator-free days (7 vs 3) and organ-failure-free days without a significant mortality difference.
In EPVent-2, oesophageal pressure–guided PEEP was compared with a low PEEP/FiO₂ table.
In LOVS, recruitment manoeuvres were performed at 40 cmH₂O for 40 seconds.
questions.expl: A: only in the first 80 patients, then abandoned. C: control = empirical high PEEP/FiO₂. ([W10/D3](#W10-D3))

questions.stem: In a patient with ARDS, PEEP is increased from 10 to 15 cmH₂O at constant VT 450 mL. Plateau pressure rises from 25 to 27 cmH₂O. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Driving pressure fell, but compliance decreased
Compliance is unchanged
Airway resistance has increased
Recruitment predominates; driving pressure fell from 15 to 12 cmH₂O and compliance rose from 30 to 37.5 mL/cmH₂O
Overdistension predominates; driving pressure rose from 15 to 17 cmH₂O
questions.expl: ΔP: 25 − 10 = 15 → 27 − 15 = 12; Crs: 450/15 = 30 → 450/12 = 37.5 mL/cmH₂O. If ΔP had risen (and Pplat > 30, ↓ BP), overdistension would predominate. ([W10/D2](#W10-D2), [W10/D3](#W10-D3))

questions.stem: Practical aspects of prone positioning:
options: Enteral nutrition can be continued during prone sessions.
Raised intracranial pressure is a relative contraindication.
In PROSEVA, proning was stopped when PaO₂/FiO₂ was ≥ 150 mmHg with PEEP ≤ 10 and FiO₂ ≤ 0.6 at least 4 h after a session in the supine position.
ECMO was an exclusion criterion in PROSEVA.
questions.expl: A: feeding in the prone position is possible; intolerance may be a complication. ([W10/D4](#W10-D4))

questions.stem: In PROSEVA, 28-day mortality was 16.0 % with prone positioning vs 32.8 % supine. The number needed to treat to prevent one death is approximately:
Regarding neuromuscular blockade in ARDS:
options: In ACURASYS, crude 90-day mortality was significantly lower with cisatracurium.
ATS 2024 strongly recommends against neuromuscular blockade in early severe ARDS.
In ACURASYS, cisatracurium was given as a 15 mg bolus followed by 37.5 mg/h for 48 hours.
ROSE was stopped early for efficacy.
questions.expl: A: crude 31.6 vs 40.7 %, p = 0.08; only the adjusted HR 0.68 was significant. D: ROSE was stopped for **futility** (42.5 vs 42.8 %). B: ATS conditionally suggests NMBA in early severe ARDS; it is ESICM that is strongly against routine infusion. ([W10/D4](#W10-D4))

questions.stem: In RECOVERY, dexamethasone 6 mg/day in hospitalised COVID-19 patients who were not receiving oxygen:
options: Showed no benefit (17.8 % vs 14.0 %, not significant)
Reduced mortality from 41.4 % to 29.3 %
Produced the largest mortality benefit of all subgroups
Was given at 20 mg/day
Was not included in the trial
questions.expl: The largest benefit was in invasively ventilated patients (29.3 vs 41.4 %); overall 22.9 vs 25.7 %. 20 mg/d was the DEXA-ARDS regimen. ([W10/D4](#W10-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding non-invasive respiratory support in the ESICM 2023 guidelines:
options: A helmet interface is recommended over a face mask.
In COVID-19, CPAP/NIV is suggested over HFNO to reduce intubation.
In non-COVID AHRF, no recommendation is made for HFNO versus CPAP/NIV.
HFNO is strongly recommended over conventional oxygen to reduce mortality.
questions.expl: A: no recommendation, very low certainty. D: strong recommendation only for ↓ intubation; no recommendation for mortality. ([W10/D5](#W10-D5))

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS has been proned and is ventilated with VT 6 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 12 cmH₂O, RR 35/min and plateau pressure 31 cmH₂O. For the past 7 hours, pH has been 7.22 with PaCO₂ 65 mmHg; PaO₂/FiO₂ is 110 mmHg. Which statement is correct?
options: He meets the hypercapnic EOLIA criterion, and ESICM 2023 recommends VV-ECMO in an ECMO centre meeting organisational standards
He does not meet any EOLIA criterion because PaO₂/FiO₂ is above 80 mmHg
ECCO₂R is the recommended next step
EOLIA criteria require PaO₂/FiO₂ < 50 mmHg for more than 12 hours
ESICM 2023 recommends VV-ECMO only for COVID-19 ARDS
questions.expl: EOLIA: pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h at RR 35/min (Pplat ≤ 32) – one criterion is enough. ESICM: VV-ECMO strong, moderate certainty; ECCO₂R outside RCTs strongly against. ([W10/D5](#W10-D5))

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS develops acute cor pulmonale. Which measures are physiologically appropriate?
options: Avoiding hyperinflation, since PVR is lowest at functional residual capacity.
Prone positioning, which unloads the right ventricle.
Liberal permissive hypercapnia, because hypercapnia lowers PVR.
Considering VV-ECMO for refractory ACP to allow ultra-protective ventilation and correct hypercapnia.
questions.expl: B: ↓ ΔP and PaCO₂, recruitment. A: the PVR–lung volume relationship is "U"-shaped. C: hypercapnia and acidosis ↑ PVR; target PaCO₂ < 48 mmHg. ([W07/D5](#W07-D5), [W10/D2](#W10-D2), [W10/D4](#W10-D4))

questions.stem: Comparing ESICM 2023 and ATS 2024 ARDS guidelines:
options: ESICM 2023 strongly recommends ECCO₂R to facilitate ultra-protective ventilation.
Both ESICM and ATS guidance support prone positioning for prolonged daily sessions in severe ARDS.
ESICM 2023 includes a recommendation on corticosteroids.
ATS 2024 suggests VV-ECMO in selected patients with severe ARDS (conditional recommendation).
questions.expl: D: conditional, low certainty; ESICM strong, moderate. A: strongly against outside RCTs. C: ESICM does not address corticosteroids; ATS 2024 conditionally suggests them. B: ESICM ≥ 16 h (strong, high); ATS 2017 > 12 h/day (prone was not re-addressed in the 2024 update). ([W10/D5](#W10-D5))

title: W10 · Saturday – weekly review: Respiratory I – ARDS

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with acute pancreatitis is on high-flow nasal oxygen at 25 L/min, FiO₂ 0.6, PaO₂ 66 mmHg. Lung ultrasound shows bilateral B-lines; echocardiography is normal. ABG and ventilators are readily available. Which statement is correct?
options: She meets the Berlin definition of moderate ARDS
She meets the global definition of ARDS for non-intubated patients
She does not meet the global definition because the HFNO flow is below 30 L/min
She cannot have ARDS because the cause is extrapulmonary
Lung ultrasound is not acceptable imaging in any ARDS definition
questions.expl: The global definition requires HFNO ≥ 30 L/min (or NIV/CPAP with PEEP ≥ 5); the exception without flow/PEEP requirements applies only to resource-limited settings. Berlin does not allow HFNO at all. Pancreatitis is a typical indirect risk factor.

questions.stem: A 172-cm man (actual weight 110 kg) with ARDS is ventilated with VT 550 mL, PEEP 12 cmH₂O, plateau pressure 32 cmH₂O.
options: His predicted body weight is approximately 68 kg.
His current VT is approximately 8 mL/kg PBW.
A VT of about 410 mL (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) would be appropriate.
His driving pressure is 20 cmH₂O.
questions.expl: A: 50 + 0.91 × 19.6 = 67.8 kg. B: 550/67.8 = 8.1 mL/kg. C: 6 × 67.8 ≈ 407 mL – actual weight is irrelevant. D: 32 − 12.

questions.stem: A 172-cm man (actual weight 110 kg, predicted body weight ~68 kg) with ARDS is ventilated with VT 550 mL, PEEP 12 cmH₂O and plateau pressure 32 cmH₂O; SpO₂ is 93 %. The most appropriate change is:
options: Leave settings unchanged because SpO₂ is 93 %
Perform a recruitment manoeuvre at 45 cmH₂O for 2 minutes
Increase PEEP to 18 cmH₂O
Switch to pressure support with no VT limit
Reduce VT to about 400 mL and increase respiratory rate, accepting some hypercapnia
questions.expl: Pplat > 30, ΔP 20, VT ~8 mL/kg PBW → reduce VT to ~6 mL/kg PBW, permissive hypercapnia.

questions.stem: Match the trials with their findings:
options: ALVEOLI – lower mortality with higher PEEP.
ARMA – mortality 31.0 % vs 39.8 % with 6 vs 12 mL/kg PBW.
EXPRESS – more ventilator-free days with PEEP set to plateau pressure 28–30 cmH₂O, without a significant mortality difference.
ART – lower 28-day mortality with maximal recruitment and PEEP titration.
questions.expl: A: ALVEOLI showed no mortality difference. D: higher mortality, 55.3 vs 49.3%.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with severe pneumonia–related ARDS has been intubated for 18 hours. After stabilisation on VT 6 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 12 cmH₂O and FiO₂ 0.7, PaO₂ is 84 mmHg. Haemodynamics are stable, ICP is not a concern. The next step with the strongest evidence for a mortality benefit is:
options: Recruitment manoeuvre at 40 cmH₂O for 40 s every 4 hours
Inhaled nitric oxide
Immediate VV-ECMO
Routine 48-hour cisatracurium infusion
Prone positioning for at least 16 hours per session
questions.expl: P/F = 84/0.7 = 120 (< 150, FiO₂ ≥ 0.6, PEEP ≥ 5) → PROSEVA criteria; ESICM strong, high certainty. EOLIA criteria not yet met.

questions.stem: Regarding neuromuscular blockade in ARDS:
options: ESICM 2023 recommends routine continuous NMBA infusion in moderate–severe non-COVID ARDS.
In ACURASYS, the control group received light sedation without placebo.
ROSE confirmed the mortality benefit seen in ACURASYS.
In ROSE, the control group received deep sedation with routine neuromuscular blockade.
questions.expl: A: ESICM recommends against it (strong, moderate certainty). B: ACURASYS controls received deep sedation with placebo. C: 42.5 vs 42.8%. D: ROSE controls received light sedation without routine NMBA.

questions.stem: A patient in the ICU for 16 days with persistent ARDS is still ventilated. A colleague suggests starting high-dose methylprednisolone now. Based on LaSRS, the most accurate statement is:
options: LaSRS used dexamethasone 6 mg for 10 days
LaSRS showed benefit only in COVID-19
Corticosteroids started ≥ 14 days after ARDS onset were associated with increased mortality
Late corticosteroids reduced 60-day mortality by half
Late corticosteroids had no adverse effects
questions.expl: LaSRS used methylprednisolone; overall 60-d mortality did not differ, with more neuromuscular weakness.

questions.stem: Regarding the Berlin definition and the new global definition of ARDS:
options: Only the global definition allows SpO₂/FiO₂ in place of PaO₂/FiO₂.
The global definition grades non-intubated patients as mild, moderate or severe.
Both require a minimum PEEP of 5 cmH₂O in intubated patients.
Both require onset within 72 hours of a known insult.
questions.expl: B: non-intubated patients are not stratified. D: both use onset within 1 week.

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS has PEEP increased from 8 to 14 cmH₂O at constant VT 400 mL. Plateau pressure changes from 26 to 28 cmH₂O, PaO₂/FiO₂ improves and blood pressure is unchanged. The best interpretation is:
options: Recruitment predominates: driving pressure fell from 18 to 14 cmH₂O and compliance rose
Overdistension predominates; return PEEP to 8
A pneumothorax has developed
Airway resistance has increased
Driving pressure is unchanged
questions.expl: ΔP 18 → 14; Crs 22 → 29 mL/cmH₂O.

questions.stem: Regarding the DEXA-ARDS trial:
options: It enrolled patients with mild ARDS (PaO₂/FiO₂ 200–300).
It was open-label and stopped early for low enrolment.
60-day mortality was higher with dexamethasone.
Dexamethasone did not change the number of ventilator-free days.
questions.expl: A: P/F ≤ 200 on PEEP ≥ 10, FiO₂ ≥ 0.5 at 24 h. C: 21 % vs 36 % – lower with dexamethasone. D: about 4.8 more ventilator-free days.

questions.stem: Which statement about driving pressure is most accurate?
options: A target of < 15 cmH₂O is a strong ESICM 2023 recommendation
It equals tidal volume divided by respiratory system compliance and was the ventilation variable most strongly associated with survival in a pooled analysis of nine RCTs
It is independent of tidal volume
It equals peak pressure minus PEEP
Its association with mortality disappears when plateau pressure is ≤ 30 cmH₂O
questions.expl: ΔP = Pplat − PEEP = VT/Crs; ESICM does not recommend it as a target (research question); the association held even with "protective" Pplat.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with influenza pneumonia–related ARDS has PaO₂/FiO₂ 65 mmHg for 4 hours despite VT 6 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 14 and prone positioning.
options: ESICM 2023 recommends VV-ECMO for such patients in an ECMO centre meeting organisational standards.
He already meets the EOLIA criterion PaO₂/FiO₂ < 50 mmHg for > 3 h.
If PaO₂/FiO₂ stays < 80 mmHg for > 6 h, he will meet an EOLIA criterion.
ESICM 2023 suggests ECCO₂R as an alternative to ECMO.
questions.expl: B: P/F 65 > 50. A: strong, moderate. D: strongly against ECCO₂R outside RCTs.

questions.stem: In the LUNG SAFE study, which finding illustrates that ARDS is "under-recognised"?
options: Clinician recognition ranged from about 51 % in mild to 79 % in severe ARDS
Hospital mortality of severe ARDS was 46 %
ARDS accounted for 10.4 % of ICU admissions
Plateau pressure was measured in about 40 % of patients
Most patients had PEEP < 12 cmH₂O
questions.expl: D and E illustrate rather "undertreatment" (insufficient measurement/treatment).

questions.stem: Regarding recruitment manoeuvres and PEEP in current guidelines:
options: ATS 2024 suggests higher PEEP without recruitment manoeuvres in moderate–severe ARDS.
The Briel meta-analysis found that higher PEEP reduced mortality most clearly in patients with PaO₂/FiO₂ > 200.
ESICM 2023 suggests against routine brief high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres.
ESICM 2023 strongly recommends against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres (≥ 35 cmH₂O for ≥ 1 min).
questions.expl: B: benefit at P/F ≤ 200; at > 200 a trend towards harm.

questions.stem: A patient with severe ARDS and a raised intracranial pressure after traumatic brain injury requires ventilation. Which strategy element must be applied most cautiously?
options: Monitoring driving pressure
Measuring plateau pressure
Head-of-bed elevation
Using predicted body weight to set VT
Permissive hypercapnia
questions.expl: Hypercapnia → cerebral vasodilatation → ↑ ICP. (Note: ↑ ICP is also a relative contraindication to prone positioning.)

title: W11 · D1 – VV-ECMO in ARDS: CESAR, EOLIA and the Bayesian reanalysis

questions.stem: Which of the following was an inclusion criterion of the EOLIA trial (despite optimised ventilation)?
options: PaO₂/FiO₂ < 80 mmHg for > 6 hours
Murray lung injury score ≥ 2.5
Mechanical ventilation for more than 7 days
PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg for > 12 hours
pH < 7.35 with PaCO₂ > 50 mmHg for > 1 hour
questions.expl: EOLIA criteria: P/F < 50 for > 3 h, P/F < 80 for > 6 h, or pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥ 60 for > 6 h. MV > 7 days was an exclusion criterion; the Murray score belongs to CESAR (≥ 3).

questions.stem: Regarding the CESAR trial:
options: Patients were randomised to referral to an ECMO centre or to conventional management.
All patients in the intervention arm received ECMO.
The control arm followed a mandatory lung-protective ventilation protocol.
The primary outcome was 28-day mortality.
questions.expl: B: only ~75 % (68/90) received ECMO. C: no protocol; lung-protective ventilation 70 vs 93 %. D: death or severe disability at 6 months.

questions.stem: In EOLIA, 60-day mortality was 35 % with ECMO vs 46 % in the control group (RR 0.76; 95 % CI 0.55–1.04). The most accurate interpretation is:
options: ECMO is harmful in severe ARDS
The trial proved equivalence of ECMO and conventional ventilation
The trial was stopped early because of excess bleeding
ECMO significantly reduces mortality in severe ARDS
The primary outcome was not statistically significant, and crossover to rescue ECMO in 28 % of controls diluted the comparison
questions.expl: The trial was stopped for futility (not for harm). "Non-significant" does not mean equivalence.

questions.stem: Regarding the Bayesian reanalysis of EOLIA (Goligher, JAMA 2018):
options: The probability of a large absolute risk reduction of ≥ 20 % was high.
It was a pre-specified primary analysis of EOLIA.
With most of the priors used, the posterior probability of any mortality benefit (RR < 1) was below 50 %.
Even with a strongly sceptical prior, the probability of benefit exceeded 85 %.
questions.expl: D: 88 %. C: P(RR < 1) was high across all priors, about 88–99 %. A: only 0–4 %. B: post hoc.

questions.stem: A patient on VV-ECMO for severe ARDS has adequate oxygenation but PaCO₂ is rising. The most direct way to increase CO₂ removal is to:
options: Start inhaled nitric oxide
Increase the sweep gas flow through the oxygenator
Increase the ventilator FiO₂
Increase PEEP to 20 cmH₂O
Reduce the extracorporeal blood flow
questions.expl: CO₂ elimination on ECMO is driven mainly by gas flow through the oxygenator (sweep); oxygenation mainly by blood flow.

questions.stem: Regarding the physiology of VV-ECMO:
options: Recirculation increases the effective oxygen delivery of the circuit.
Arterial oxygenation depends largely on extracorporeal blood flow relative to the patient's cardiac output.
It provides direct circulatory support to a failing left ventricle.
In the presence of severe cardiogenic shock, VA configuration is usually needed instead.
questions.expl: A: recirculated (already oxygenated) blood is drained back into the circuit – effective oxygen delivery falls. C: VV replaces the lungs, not the heart.

questions.stem: According to the 2023 ESICM ARDS guidelines, VV-ECMO in severe ARDS not due to COVID-19:
options: Is suggested only after 14 days of mechanical ventilation
Is recommended against because EOLIA was negative
Has no recommendation because there are no RCTs
Is recommended for patients meeting EOLIA criteria, with moderate certainty of evidence
Is recommended for all patients with PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg
questions.expl: Strong recommendation, moderate certainty; meta-analysis of CESAR + EOLIA RR 0.72.

questions.stem: In the ECMO arm of EOLIA, compared with controls:
options: Ischaemic stroke was less frequent.
Treatment failure (death, or crossover to ECMO in controls) was significantly lower.
Bleeding requiring transfusion was more frequent.
Severe thrombocytopenia was more frequent.

questions.stem: Which ventilator strategy corresponds to the ECMO-arm protocol of EOLIA?
options: Tidal volume 8 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 5 cmH₂O, FiO₂ 1.0
Plateau pressure ≤ 35 cmH₂O, PEEP 0, RR 35/min
Plateau pressure ≤ 24 cmH₂O, PEEP ≥ 10 cmH₂O, RR 10–30/min, FiO₂ 0.3–0.5
High-frequency oscillatory ventilation
Immediate extubation once ECMO is running
questions.expl: Ultra-protective ventilation – "lung rest".

questions.stem: Regarding the selection of patients for VV-ECMO:
options: ECMO should be considered before prone positioning has been tried.
Early referral to an experienced ECMO centre is a key lesson from CESAR.
In EOLIA, patients ventilated for more than 7 days were excluded.
ECMO is a treatment that reverses the underlying lung injury.
questions.expl: A: prone positioning and lung-protective ventilation should be optimised first. D: ECMO buys time and allows "lung rest"; it does not treat ARDS.

open.q: Explain why CESAR and EOLIA, despite both being cited in support of VV-ECMO, actually tested different questions, and why EOLIA is formally "negative".
open.model:
Key points expected:
- CESAR randomised to **referral to an ECMO centre** vs conventional care in the referring hospital – it tested a referral strategy, not ECMO itself.
- In CESAR only ~75 % (68/90) of the intervention arm received ECMO, and the control arm had no ventilation protocol (lung-protective ventilation 70 vs 93 %).
- EOLIA randomised to **early ECMO** vs conventional management, with rescue ECMO allowed: 28 % of controls crossed over.
- EOLIA 60-day mortality 35 vs 46 %, RR 0.76 (0.55–1.04), p = 0.09 – primary endpoint not met; stopped for futility.
- It was powered for an unrealistic 20 % absolute mortality reduction; the observed ARR was ~11 %, and crossover diluted the ITT effect.
- The post hoc Bayesian reanalysis showed an 88–99 % probability of some benefit, but uncertainty about its size.
- ESICM 2023 meta-analysis (CESAR + EOLIA) RR 0.72 (0.57–0.91) underpins a strong recommendation with moderate certainty for patients meeting EOLIA criteria.

open.q: A patient with severe non-COVID ARDS has had PaO₂/FiO₂ < 80 mmHg for 7 hours despite optimised ventilation. Outline your approach to VV-ECMO and to ventilation once ECMO is running.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Confirm that lung-protective ventilation, PEEP optimisation, prone positioning and NMB have been used; ECMO is part of a stepwise algorithm.
- The patient meets an EOLIA criterion (P/F < 80 mmHg for > 6 h); check exclusions (MV > 7 days, indication for VA-ECMO, irreversible disease, contraindication to anticoagulation).
- Refer early to an experienced ECMO centre (lesson from CESAR); ESICM 2023 recommends VV-ECMO in this setting.
- Typical cannulation: femoral drainage, internal jugular return; oxygenation driven by blood flow, CO₂ removal by sweep gas.
- Ultra-protective ventilation: Pplat ≤ 24 cmH₂O, PEEP ≥ 10 cmH₂O, RR 10–30/min, FiO₂ 0.3–0.5; targets PaO₂ 65–90 mmHg or SaO₂ > 90 %, PaCO₂ < 45 mmHg.
- Heparin anticoagulation (aPTT 40–55 s or anti-Xa 0.2–0.3 IU/mL); monitor for bleeding, thrombocytopenia, circuit thrombosis, haemolysis and recirculation.
- Wean by reducing circuit FiO₂, then sweep gas, with an off-sweep trial.

title: W11 · D2 – Oxygenation targets: HOT-ICU, ICU-ROX, LOCO2, UK-ROX and the harm of hyperoxia

questions.stem: In the HOT-ICU trial of adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, a PaO₂ target of 8 kPa compared with 12 kPa:
options: Increased 90-day mortality
Was only tested in patients with COPD
Increased the incidence of mesenteric ischaemia
Did not significantly change 90-day mortality
Reduced 90-day mortality
questions.expl: 42.9 vs 42.4 %, HR 1.02. Serious ischaemic events did not differ either.

questions.stem: Regarding the LOCO2 trial:
options: It enrolled patients with ARDS.
Mesenteric ischaemia occurred more often in the liberal arm.
The conservative arm targeted PaO₂ 90–105 mmHg.
It was stopped early because of safety concerns in the conservative arm.
questions.expl: B: 5 vs 0 % in the conservative arm. C: conservative = PaO₂ 55–70 mmHg (SpO₂ 88–92 %); 90–105 mmHg was the liberal arm.

questions.stem: The IOTA meta-analysis (Lancet 2018) concluded that in acutely ill adults:
options: Liberal oxygen reduces mortality in sepsis
Liberal oxygen therapy is associated with increased in-hospital and 30-day mortality
Conservative oxygen increases myocardial infarction
Oxygen should be titrated to SpO₂ 100 %
There is no relationship between SpO₂ and mortality
questions.expl: RR 1.21 (in-hospital) and 1.14 (30-day). Risk increased with higher SpO₂.

questions.stem: Regarding ICU-ROX:
options: The conservative arm used an upper SpO₂ limit of 97 %.
It enrolled mechanically ventilated adults in Australia and New Zealand.
Subgroup findings (e.g. hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy) should be considered hypothesis-generating.
Conservative oxygen significantly increased ventilator-free days.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old ventilated patient with pneumonia has SpO₂ 100 % on FiO₂ 0.7, and PaO₂ is 22 kPa. The most appropriate action is:
options: Titrate FiO₂ down, aiming for SpO₂ around 92–96 %
Target PaO₂ of 6 kPa to minimise oxidative stress
Increase PEEP to further improve oxygenation
Reduce FiO₂ to 0.21 immediately regardless of SpO₂
Keep FiO₂ unchanged; hyperoxia is protective in pneumonia
questions.expl: Hyperoxia has no benefit (IOTA). An abrupt fall in FiO₂ or an extremely low target is not safe (LOCO2).

questions.stem: Mechanisms by which hyperoxia may be harmful include:
options: Systemic vasodilatation with increased cardiac output.
Worsening hypercapnia in some patients with COPD.
Absorption atelectasis.
Generation of reactive oxygen species.
questions.expl: A: vasoconstriction and ↓ cardiac output.

questions.stem: In the UK-ROX trial (JAMA 2025) of 16 500 mechanically ventilated adults, a conservative oxygen strategy targeting SpO₂ 88–92 %:
options: Was stopped early because of mesenteric ischaemia
Did not significantly change 90-day mortality compared with usual care
Significantly increased 90-day mortality
Significantly reduced 90-day mortality
Was restricted to patients with ARDS
questions.expl: 35.4 vs 34.9 %. The difference in achieved oxygenation was only modest.

questions.stem: Which statements comparing oxygen-target trials are correct?
options: All of HOT-ICU, ICU-ROX and UK-ROX showed lower mortality with conservative oxygen.
HOT-ICU enrolled only invasively ventilated patients.
LOCO2 is the only one of these trials restricted to ARDS.
HOT-ICU used SpO₂-based targets.
questions.expl: B: HOT-ICU included non-ventilated patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. D: PaO₂ targets (8 vs 12 kPa).

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS is ventilated with FiO₂ 0.6. Based on LOCO2, which oxygenation target should be avoided?
options: SpO₂ 92–96 %
PaO₂ 9–10 kPa
Targeting PaO₂ 55–70 mmHg / SpO₂ 88–92 %
PaO₂ 75–90 mmHg
SpO₂ 94 %
questions.expl: In LOCO2 this conservative target was associated with higher 90-day mortality and mesenteric ischaemia.

questions.stem: Regarding pulse oximetry and oxygen targets:
options: Pulse oximetry tends to underestimate arterial saturation, particularly in patients with darker skin.
In hypercapnic COPD, an SpO₂ target of 88–92 % is commonly used.
Occult hypoxaemia is more relevant when low SpO₂ targets are used.
Arterial blood gas analysis is unnecessary when SpO₂ is in range.
questions.expl: A: it may overestimate saturation (occult hypoxaemia), especially in darker skin.

open.q: IOTA showed harm from liberal oxygen, yet HOT-ICU, ICU-ROX and UK-ROX found no mortality benefit from conservative targets. Explain this apparent discrepancy.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- IOTA (25 RCTs, 16 037 patients) showed harm from liberal O₂: in-hospital RR 1.21, 30-day RR 1.14, with risk rising with higher SpO₂.
- Harm from hyperoxia is not the same as benefit from a low target.
- IOTA included very liberal strategies (high FiO₂ regardless of saturation); ICU trials compared "low-normal" vs "high-normal" oxygenation.
- Small separation between arms: relatively low O₂ in the ICU-ROX control group; only ~2 % difference in mean SpO₂ in UK-ROX.
- Heterogeneous populations may hide opposite subgroup effects (ICU-ROX signals for HIE vs sepsis, not confirmed in UK-ROX).
- Different target metrics (SpO₂ vs PaO₂), with SpO₂ targets affected by oximetry inaccuracy.
- Conclusion: within the usual range the target probably matters little; the extremes are harmful.

open.q: Outline your oxygen-titration strategy for (a) a ventilated patient with ARDS and (b) a patient with hypercapnic COPD, including the role of pulse oximetry.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- General corridor: SpO₂ ~92–96 % or PaO₂ ~8–12 kPa (60–90 mmHg); avoid both extremes.
- Actively titrate FiO₂ down; SpO₂ persistently 98–100 % on FiO₂ > 0.4 means unnecessary FiO₂.
- ARDS: do not go below PaO₂ ~55–60 mmHg / SpO₂ ~88 % – in LOCO2 the 55–70 mmHg target was associated with higher 90-day mortality (44.4 vs 30.4 %) and mesenteric ischaemia (5 vs 0 %).
- Hypercapnic COPD: SpO₂ 88–92 % to avoid oxygen-induced hypercapnia (V/Q worsening, Haldane effect).
- Pulse oximetry may overestimate SaO₂ (occult hypoxaemia), especially with darker skin pigmentation and poor perfusion – more relevant at low targets.
- Verify with arterial blood gas analysis when in doubt.

title: W11 · D3 – HFNO and NIV in hypoxaemic respiratory failure

questions.stem: In the FLORALI trial, the primary outcome (intubation by day 28) was:
options: Significantly lower with HFNO in the whole population
Significantly lower with standard oxygen
Not significantly different between HFNO, standard oxygen and NIV
Significantly lower with NIV than with HFNO
Not measured; mortality was the primary outcome
questions.expl: 38 vs 47 vs 50 %, p = 0.18. A difference was seen only in the P/F ≤ 200 subgroup (post hoc).

questions.stem: Regarding FLORALI:
options: NIV was delivered via helmet.
90-day mortality was lowest in the HFNO group.
Patients with cardiogenic pulmonary oedema were excluded.
Patients with hypercapnia (PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg) were excluded.
questions.expl: B: 12 vs 23 vs 28 %. A: face mask.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia on HFNO (FiO₂ 0.8, 60 L/min) has SpO₂ 90 % and RR 38/min after 6 hours. The ROX index and its interpretation are:
options: ≈ 4.2 – low risk of failure
≈ 2.96 – high risk of HFNO failure; consider intubation
≈ 0.03 – cannot be interpreted
≈ 6.0 – HFNO success
≈ 27 – low risk of failure
questions.expl: (90/0.8)/38 = 112.5/38 ≈ 2.96. This is < 3.47 at 6 h, i.e. high risk of failure.

questions.stem: Patient self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI):
options: Is related to high respiratory drive and large swings in transpulmonary pressure.
Pendelluft may cause regional overdistension without a change in global tidal volume.
Strongly negative alveolar pressure may increase pulmonary oedema.
Is a definitively proven entity based on large RCTs.
questions.expl: D: a concept/hypothesis.

questions.stem: According to the 2017 ERS/ATS guideline, for NIV in de novo acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure:
options: NIV is recommended only via helmet
Strong recommendation against NIV
Conditional recommendation for NIV with high certainty
No recommendation was made
Strong recommendation for NIV
questions.expl: Unlike COPD with acidosis and cardiogenic oedema (strong recommendations).

questions.stem: Regarding helmet NIV trials:
options: Patel et al. was a large multicentre trial that completed its planned enrolment.
In HENIVOT, days free of respiratory support at 28 days were significantly higher with helmet NIV.
In Patel et al. (JAMA 2016), helmet NIV reduced intubation compared with face mask NIV.
In HENIVOT, intubation was more frequent with helmet NIV than with HFNO.
questions.expl: C: 18.2 vs 61.5 %. A: 83 patients, single centre, stopped early. B: 20 vs 18 days, NS. D: 30 vs 51 % – less frequent with helmet.

questions.stem: According to the ESICM 2023 ARDS guidelines, in non-ventilated patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure (not cardiogenic oedema or COPD exacerbation):
options: NIV is recommended over HFNO
HFNO is recommended to reduce mortality
Conventional oxygen is preferred over HFNO
HFNO is recommended over conventional oxygen to reduce intubation (strong, moderate certainty)
Immediate intubation is recommended
questions.expl: There is no recommendation for mortality. HFNO vs NIV: no recommendation.

questions.stem: Physiological effects of HFNO include:
options: Washout of nasopharyngeal dead space.
Only a low, flow-dependent positive airway pressure that is not precisely controlled.
Heated and humidified gas improving comfort and secretion clearance.
A delivered FiO₂ that is more stable than with a standard face mask.
questions.expl: B: a few cmH₂O, depending on flow and mouth closure – not a controlled PEEP as with NIV.

questions.stem: A patient with de novo hypoxaemic respiratory failure (P/F 140) on face-mask NIV has an expired tidal volume of 12 mL/kg PBW. This finding:
options: Requires increasing pressure support further
Indicates successful NIV and allows reduction of monitoring
Is irrelevant in hypoxaemic patients
Indicates the need for ECMO
Has been associated with NIV failure (threshold > 9.5 mL/kg PBW)
questions.expl: Carteaux (CCM 2016). It is also a possible mechanism of P-SILI. Consider timely intubation.

questions.stem: Regarding the HACOR score:
options: Among patients failing NIV, earlier intubation was associated with lower mortality.
It was developed for patients on HFNO rather than NIV.
It includes heart rate, acidosis, consciousness, oxygenation and respiratory rate.
A score > 5 after 1 hour of NIV predicts NIV success.
questions.expl: B: NIV; ROX is used for HFNO. D: > 5 at 1 h predicts NIV failure.

open.q: A patient with pneumonia has been on HFNO (FiO₂ 0.6, 60 L/min) for 12 hours with SpO₂ 93 % and RR 32/min. Calculate the ROX index, interpret it, and outline your next steps.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ROX = (SpO₂/FiO₂)/RR = (93/0.6)/32 = 155/32 ≈ 4.84.
- At 12 h this is above the high-risk threshold (< 3.85) but below the 4.88 threshold associated with a lower risk of intubation – an intermediate, "grey zone" value.
- Continue HFNO with close reassessment of ROX over time (predictive power increases with time).
- Look for signs of excessive respiratory drive/effort (P-SILI concept: large transpulmonary pressure swings, pendelluft, oedema).
- Do not delay intubation if the trajectory worsens – failure of non-invasive support with late intubation is associated with worse outcome.
- ROX is validated for HFNO in pneumonia; for NIV, use HACOR (> 5 after 1 h predicts failure).

open.q: Explain why NIV is not routinely recommended in de novo acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, whereas it is strongly recommended in COPD exacerbation with acidosis.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ERS/ATS 2017: NIV in hypercapnic COPD exacerbation (pH ≤ 7.35) – strong recommendation, high certainty; cardiogenic oedema – strong, moderate; de novo ARF – no recommendation.
- FLORALI: face-mask NIV had the highest 90-day mortality (28 % vs 12 % HFNO; HR 2.50 vs HFNO) and fewest ventilator-free days.
- Large tidal volumes on NIV (expired V_T > 9.5 mL/kg PBW) predict failure (Carteaux 2016).
- P-SILI concept: high drive → large transpulmonary swings, pendelluft, increased transmural vascular pressure and oedema.
- Delayed intubation after NIV failure worsens outcome (HACOR cohort: lower mortality with intubation < 12 h).
- Helmet NIV may perform better (higher sustained PEEP; Patel, HENIVOT), but evidence is limited/hypothesis-generating.
- ESICM 2023: HFNO over conventional O₂ (strong, moderate certainty); HFNO vs NIV – no recommendation.

title: W11 · D4 – Weaning and SBT: ATS/ACCP, PSV vs T-piece, weaning classification, RSBI

questions.stem: According to the 2007 international consensus (Boles), "difficult weaning" is defined as:
options: Failure of the initial SBT, with success requiring up to three SBTs or up to 7 days from the first SBT
Successful extubation after the first SBT
Reintubation within 7 days
Need for tracheostomy
Requiring more than three SBTs or more than 7 days of weaning
questions.expl: B = simple, E = prolonged.

questions.stem: Regarding the trial by Subirà et al. (JAMA 2019):
options: Successful extubation was more frequent in the pressure-support group.
90-day mortality was higher in the pressure-support group.
It compared a 30-minute SBT with pressure support 8 cmH₂O vs a 2-hour T-piece SBT.
Reintubation was significantly higher in the pressure-support group.

questions.stem: During a spontaneous breathing trial, a patient breathes at 30 breaths/min with a tidal volume of 250 mL. The RSBI is:
options: 1200 breaths/min/L – cannot be interpreted
75 breaths/min/L – predicts success
8.3 breaths/min/L – predicts failure
120 breaths/min/L – predicts failure
7.5 breaths/min/L – predicts success

questions.stem: Regarding the WIND classification:
options: It could classify only about half of ventilated patients.
Weaning starts at the first separation attempt (SBT or extubation without SBT).
Short weaning is defined as termination within 7 days of the first attempt.
ICU mortality increases from short to prolonged weaning.
questions.expl: D: 6 → 17 → 29 %. A: 99 %; it was the Boles classification that could not classify half. C: short < 1 day; difficult 1–7 days; prolonged > 7 days.

questions.stem: Which is the only strong recommendation in the 2017 ATS/ACCP guideline on liberation from mechanical ventilation?
options: Cuff leak test for all patients before extubation
Extubation to preventive NIV in high-risk patients ventilated > 24 h who passed an SBT
Use of a T-piece for the initial SBT
Computer-driven weaning protocols
Protocolised early mobilisation
questions.expl: Strong, moderate certainty. The others are conditional.

questions.stem: According to Boles et al. (2007):
options: Death within 48 hours after extubation counts as weaning failure.
SIMV is the preferred mode after a failed SBT.
Weaning success is defined as absence of ventilatory support 7 days after extubation.
The initial SBT should last at least 4 hours.
questions.expl: B: prefer PSV or AC, not SIMV. C: 48 hours. D: about 30 minutes (30–120 min).

questions.stem: A patient ventilated for 4 days for pneumonia is awake, on FiO₂ 0.35 and PEEP 5 cmH₂O, haemodynamically stable. According to the ATS/ACCP 2017 guideline, the preferred initial SBT is:
options: 2-hour T-piece trial
SIMV with stepwise rate reduction
SBT with inspiratory pressure augmentation of 5–8 cmH₂O
No SBT; extubate directly if RSBI < 105
CPAP 10 cmH₂O for 8 hours
questions.expl: Conditional recommendation, moderate certainty.

questions.stem: Regarding the rapid shallow breathing index (Yang & Tobin, 1991):
options: A value > 60 breaths/min/L predicted weaning failure.
It is calculated as tidal volume in litres divided by respiratory rate.
It should replace the spontaneous breathing trial.
It has high specificity, so a low RSBI guarantees successful extubation.
questions.expl: A: the threshold was > 105 breaths/min/L. B: RSBI = RR / VT (L). C: it does not replace the SBT. D: specificity 0.64.

questions.stem: A patient fails an SBT after 15 minutes with tachypnoea and diaphoresis. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Repeat the SBT every 2 hours until success
Perform an immediate tracheostomy
Return to comfortable ventilatory support, look for reversible causes, and repeat the SBT in about 24 hours
Switch to SIMV and wean the rate daily
Extubate anyway and apply HFNO
questions.expl: Look for the cause (e.g. weaning-induced pulmonary oedema, secretions, diaphragm weakness); SBT once daily.

questions.stem: Potential causes of weaning failure include:
options: Hypophosphataemia.
Weaning-induced pulmonary oedema.
Diaphragm dysfunction and ICU-acquired weakness.
Metabolic acidosis being the typical cause of hypoventilation.
questions.expl: D: hypoventilation is typically caused by metabolic alkalosis; acidosis ↑ load via ↑ ventilation.

open.q: Compare the Boles (2007) and WIND (2017) weaning classifications and explain why WIND was developed.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Boles: simple (extubated after the 1st SBT, ~69 %, ICU mortality < 5 %), difficult (≤ 3 SBTs or ≤ 7 days from 1st SBT), prolonged (> 3 SBTs or > 7 days).
- Boles counts from the first SBT and by the number of SBTs; it assumes every patient undergoes a formal SBT.
- Patients extubated without a formal SBT or dying before one cannot be classified – ~half of patients in WIND were unclassifiable by Boles.
- WIND (2729 patients, 36 ICUs) starts at the first separation attempt (SBT or extubation without SBT) and counts days.
- WIND groups: no weaning (24 %), short < 1 d (57 %, ICU mortality 6 %), difficult 1–7 d (10 %, 17 %), prolonged ≥ 7 d (9 %, 29 %).
- WIND classified 99 % of patients; mortality, MV duration and ICU stay increase from group 1 to 3.

open.q: A patient ventilated for 5 days meets readiness criteria. Outline how you would conduct the SBT and what you would do if it fails.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Readiness: improved cause, adequate oxygenation on low FiO₂/PEEP, haemodynamic stability without high-dose vasopressors, respiratory drive, cooperation, no severe acidosis; coordinate with sedation interruption.
- Initial SBT of ~30 min with PS 5–8 cmH₂O (ATS/ACCP, conditional, moderate certainty); Subirà: PSV 8/30 min vs T-piece 2 h → successful extubation 82.3 vs 74.0 % without more reintubation.
- Monitor failure criteria: tachypnoea, tachycardia/arrhythmia, BP changes, desaturation, accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, sweating, agitation, altered consciousness.
- RSBI (f/V_T) > 105 predicts failure but is only an aid, not a replacement for the SBT.
- If the SBT fails: return to comfortable ventilation (PSV/AC), avoid SIMV, repeat the SBT in ~24 h.
- Search for causes: weaning-induced pulmonary oedema, secretions/bronchospasm, diaphragm dysfunction/ICU-AW, delirium, hypophosphataemia/hypomagnesaemia, hypothyroidism, metabolic alkalosis.
- If high risk after a successful SBT, extubate to preventive NIV (the only strong ATS/ACCP recommendation).

title: W11 · D5 – Extubation failure and post-extubation support: HFNO vs NIV, stridor, corticosteroids

questions.stem: In the trial by Hernández et al. in low-risk patients (JAMA 2016), 24 hours of postextubation HFNO compared with conventional oxygen:
options: Had no effect on reintubation but reduced mortality
Was inferior to NIV
Reduced reintubation within 72 hours (4.9 % vs 12.2 %)
Was applied for 7 days
Increased reintubation
questions.expl: Reintubation within 72 h 4.9 vs 12.2 % (p = 0.004).

questions.stem: Regarding the HIGH-WEAN trial:
options: It compared HFNO alternating with NIV vs NIV alone.
Reintubation at day 7 was lower with HFNO plus NIV.
It enrolled patients at high risk of extubation failure (age > 65 years or underlying cardiac or respiratory disease).
ICU mortality was significantly lower with HFNO plus NIV.
questions.expl: A: the comparator was HFNO alone. B: 11.8 vs 18.2 %. D: 6 vs 9 %, NS.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops respiratory distress 10 hours after a planned extubation (RR 34/min, SpO₂ 88 % on 6 L/min, no stridor). Based on the Esteban trial (NEJM 2004), what is the main concern with starting NIV as rescue therapy?
options: NIV is contraindicated in women
NIV increases the risk of laryngeal oedema
NIV delays reintubation and was associated with higher ICU mortality
NIV is only effective via helmet
NIV reduces reintubation but increases pneumothorax
questions.expl: Reintubation 48 % in both arms, ICU mortality 25 vs 14 %, time to reintubation 12 vs 2.5 h.

questions.stem: Risk factors for postextubation stridor listed in the ATS/ACCP 2017 guideline include:
options: Female sex.
Traumatic intubation.
Reintubation after unplanned extubation.
Intubation for more than 6 days.
questions.expl: All four are listed. A large tube is a further risk factor.

questions.stem: A patient intubated for 9 days after a traumatic intubation passes an SBT, but the cuff leak test shows no audible leak. According to ATS/ACCP 2017, the best approach is:
options: Perform a tracheostomy
Postpone extubation for 7 days
Give nebulised adrenaline and extubate only after a positive repeat cuff leak test
Extubate immediately without further measures
Give systemic corticosteroids at least 4 hours before extubation; repeating the cuff leak test is not required
questions.expl: Conditional recommendation, moderate certainty.

questions.stem: Regarding the trial by Hernández et al. in high-risk patients (JAMA 2016):
options: HFNO was non-inferior to NIV for reintubation within 72 hours.
Postextubation respiratory failure was less frequent with HFNO.
Adverse events leading to withdrawal of therapy were more frequent with HFNO.
HFNO was shown to be superior to NIV for reintubation.
questions.expl: A: 22.8 vs 19.1 %, margin 10 %. B: 26.9 vs 39.8 %. C: 43 % with NIV vs 0 % with HFNO.

questions.stem: In the trial by François et al. (Lancet 2007), methylprednisolone 20 mg given 12, 8 and 4 hours before extubation and at extubation:
options: Reduced postextubation laryngeal oedema from 22 % to 3 %
Was given as a single 4 mg dose of dexamethasone
Was given only to patients failing a cuff leak test
Increased reintubation
Had no effect on laryngeal oedema
questions.expl: Reintubation fell from 8 to 4 %. It was given to all patients intubated ≥ 36 h.

questions.stem: Regarding the cuff leak test:
options: A single universally accepted volume threshold exists.
ATS/ACCP suggests performing it only in patients at high risk of postextubation stridor.
Routine testing of all patients may delay extubation because of false-positive results.
A small or absent leak suggests laryngeal oedema.
questions.expl: A: thresholds differed between studies.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with chronic heart failure, ventilated for 5 days for pneumonia, passes an SBT. Which postextubation strategy is best supported by evidence?
options: Rescue NIV only if respiratory failure develops
No oxygen; observe
Conventional oxygen via nasal cannula
HFNO alternating with prophylactic NIV
Immediate tracheostomy
questions.expl: High risk (> 65 y, cardiac disease). HIGH-WEAN and ATS/ACCP (preventive NIV, strong recommendation).

questions.stem: According to the ERS/ATS 2017 NIV guideline and the ERS 2022 HFNC guideline:
options: HFNC is suggested over conventional oxygen in non-surgical patients at low or moderate risk.
NIV is suggested against in established postextubation respiratory failure.
Prophylactic NIV is suggested for all extubated patients regardless of risk.
Prophylactic NIV is suggested in high-risk patients after extubation.
questions.expl: C: conditional recommendation against in non-high-risk patients.

open.q: Outline your post-extubation support strategy according to the patient's risk of extubation failure, citing the key trials.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Stratify risk (Hernández/HIGH-WEAN): high risk e.g. age > 65 y, cardiac or respiratory disease, APACHE II > 12, BMI > 30, poor secretion management, difficult/prolonged weaning, MV > 7 days.
- Low risk: HFNO over conventional O₂ – reintubation within 72 h 4.9 vs 12.2 % (Hernández I); ERS HFNC 2022 conditional recommendation.
- High risk: preventive NIV – ATS/ACCP 2017 strong recommendation (moderate certainty); ERS/ATS 2017 conditional.
- HIGH-WEAN: HFNO alternating with NIV reduced reintubation by day 7 (11.8 vs 18.2 %) vs HFNO alone; ICU mortality NS.
- HFNO alone is a reasonable alternative if NIV is not tolerated/contraindicated – non-inferior to NIV (22.8 vs 19.1 %, Hernández II).
- No preventive NIV in non-high-risk patients (ERS/ATS conditional against).
- Note different definition windows (48 h / 72 h / 7 days) when comparing trials.

open.q: Explain why NIV is appropriate to prevent but not to treat post-extubation respiratory failure, and how you would manage established post-extubation stridor.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Esteban 2004: NIV in established failure within 48 h of extubation – reintubation 48 % in both arms, but ICU mortality 25 vs 14 % (RR 1.78).
- Time to reintubation 12 h vs 2.5 h – delayed reintubation is the likely mechanism of harm; the trial was stopped early.
- ERS/ATS 2017: conditional recommendation against NIV in established post-extubation failure; preventive NIV in high-risk patients is recommended.
- Stridor risk factors: traumatic intubation, intubation > 6 days, large tube, female sex, reintubation after unplanned extubation.
- Prevention: cuff leak test in high-risk patients; if failed, systemic corticosteroids ≥ 4 h before extubation without repeating the test (meta-analysis: reintubation 5.8 vs 17.0 %, stridor 10.8 vs 31.9 %).
- Established stridor: positioning, nebulised adrenaline, systemic corticosteroids.
- With progression or fatigue, timely reintubation, prepared for a difficult airway and a smaller tube; do not rely on NIV.

title: W11 · Saturday – weekly review: Respiratory II

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with influenza pneumonia and ARDS has been ventilated for 2 days. He is proned and paralysed, on PEEP 14 cmH₂O, FiO₂ 1.0, with PaO₂ 6.0 kPa (45 mmHg) for the last 4 hours. Plateau pressure is 30 cmH₂O. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reduce the oxygenation target to PaO₂ 5 kPa
Switch to NIV
Continue current management; ECMO is not supported by evidence
Contact an ECMO centre to consider VV-ECMO, as he meets EOLIA-type criteria
Start VA-ECMO
questions.expl: P/F = 45 < 50 mmHg for > 3 h despite optimisation. ESICM 2023 recommends VV-ECMO according to EOLIA criteria (strong, moderate certainty). VA is not indicated without cardiac failure.

questions.stem: Regarding EOLIA and its Bayesian reanalysis:
options: The Bayesian reanalysis showed a high probability that ECMO reduces mortality by at least 20 % in absolute terms.
The trial was powered for a 20 % absolute reduction in mortality.
60-day mortality was 35 % with ECMO vs 46 % in controls.
28 % of control patients crossed over to rescue ECMO.
questions.expl: B: 60 → 40 %. A: P(ARR ≥ 20 %) only 0–4 %; P(any benefit) 88–99 %.

questions.stem: A patient on VV-ECMO (blood flow 4.5 L/min, sweep 4 L/min) has PaO₂ 7.5 kPa and PaCO₂ 4.8 kPa. The ventilator is set to plateau 24 cmH₂O, PEEP 12, FiO₂ 0.4. Which change will most directly improve arterial oxygenation?
options: Increase ventilator respiratory rate to 35/min
Increase sweep gas flow
Decrease PEEP to 5 cmH₂O
Increase extracorporeal blood flow
Increase plateau pressure to 35 cmH₂O
questions.expl: Oxygenation on VV-ECMO is determined mainly by circuit blood flow (relative to cardiac output). Sweep mainly affects CO₂.

questions.stem: Regarding oxygen-target trials in critically ill adults:
options: HOT-ICU compared SpO₂ targets of 88–92 % vs ≥ 96 %.
LOCO2 showed higher 90-day mortality with a conservative target in ARDS.
UK-ROX showed lower 90-day mortality with SpO₂ 88–92 %.
The IOTA meta-analysis found increased mortality with liberal oxygen therapy.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with severe COPD and acute hypercapnic exacerbation (pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 9 kPa) arrives on 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask with SpO₂ 99 %. The best immediate management is:
options: Keep oxygen unchanged and start HFNO at 60 L/min as first-line
Start CPAP only
Stop oxygen completely
Titrate oxygen to SpO₂ 88–92 % and start bilevel NIV
Immediately intubate
questions.expl: ERS/ATS 2017: NIV in COPD exacerbation with acidosis (strong, high certainty). ERS 2022: NIV first, before HFNC. Hyperoxia in COPD worsens hypercapnia.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with community-acquired pneumonia (P/F 150, PaCO₂ 4.5 kPa, no cardiac disease) is in the ICU and not intubated. Which statements are correct?
options: ESICM 2023 recommends HFNO over conventional oxygen to reduce intubation.
An expired tidal volume > 9.5 mL/kg PBW during NIV would be reassuring.
ERS/ATS 2017 strongly recommends NIV for de novo acute respiratory failure.
In FLORALI, 90-day mortality was lowest with NIV.
questions.expl: C: no recommendation. B: a predictor of NIV failure. D: lowest with HFNO (12 vs 23 vs 28 %).

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with community-acquired pneumonia and hypoxaemic respiratory failure (not intubated) is on HFNO (FiO₂ 0.7). After 12 hours, SpO₂ is 92 % and RR 36/min. What is the ROX index and its implication?
options: ROX ≈ 3.65; below 3.85 at 12 h – high risk of failure, consider intubation
ROX ≈ 5.1; low risk of failure
ROX ≈ 47; low risk
ROX ≈ 0.36; uninterpretable
ROX ≈ 4.9; continue unchanged

questions.stem: Regarding helmet NIV:
options: The helmet allows higher sustained PEEP than a face mask.
In HENIVOT, intubation was lower with helmet than with HFNO.
HENIVOT met its primary outcome (days free of respiratory support).
Patel et al. (JAMA 2016) reported higher intubation with helmet vs face mask in ARDS.
questions.expl: C: 20 vs 18 days, NS. B: 30 vs 51 %. D: lower – 18.2 vs 61.5 %.

questions.stem: A patient ventilated for 6 days for sepsis passes a 30-minute SBT on pressure support 8 cmH₂O. Which trial supports this SBT technique over a 2-hour T-piece trial?
options: Subirà et al. (JAMA 2019)
WIND
HIGH-WEAN
FLORALI
Esteban et al. (NEJM 2004)
questions.expl: Successful extubation 82.3 vs 74.0 %, with no difference in reintubation.

questions.stem: A patient failed his first SBT on day 3, failed again on day 5, and was extubated successfully on day 12 after the first SBT (four SBTs in total). Which statements are correct?
options: By the Boles classification, this is prolonged weaning.
By the WIND classification, this is prolonged weaning (≥ 7 days).
Successful weaning requires no ventilatory support for 48 hours after extubation.
ICU mortality in the WIND prolonged group was lower than in the short-weaning group.
questions.expl: A: > 3 SBTs, > 7 days. D: 29 vs 6 %.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with an RSBI of 115 breaths/min/L at the start of an SBT. The most accurate interpretation is:
options: Extubation will certainly succeed
An RSBI > 105 mandates tracheostomy
RSBI is calculated as tidal volume divided by respiratory rate
An RSBI > 105 is associated with weaning failure; assess carefully and look for reversible causes
RSBI is not related to weaning outcome
questions.expl: RSBI = f/V_T (L). Threshold 105 (Yang & Tobin). It is an aid, not a replacement for the SBT.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with COPD and heart failure, ventilated for 8 days, passed an SBT. Which postextubation strategies are supported?
options: If NIV is not tolerated, HFNO is a reasonable alternative (non-inferior in Hernández 2016).
Conventional oxygen alone as the preferred strategy.
Prophylactic NIV should be avoided in this high-risk patient (ATS/ACCP 2017).
HFNO alternating with NIV, which reduced reintubation compared with HFNO alone in HIGH-WEAN.
questions.expl: C: ATS/ACCP 2017 strongly recommends preventive NIV in high-risk patients. D: 11.8 vs 18.2 %.

questions.stem: Twelve hours after extubation, a patient develops respiratory distress without stridor (RR 35/min, accessory muscle use). NIV is started. Six hours later, there is no improvement. Based on the evidence, what is the main risk?
options: Pneumothorax from HFNO
Hyperoxia
None; NIV is recommended for established postextubation failure
Laryngeal oedema from NIV
Delayed reintubation, associated with increased mortality
questions.expl: Esteban 2004: ICU mortality 25 vs 14 %, time to reintubation 12 vs 2.5 h. ERS/ATS 2017: conditional recommendation against NIV in established failure.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman was intubated with difficulty (traumatic intubation) 7 days ago. She passes an SBT, but the cuff leak test shows no leak. Which statements are correct?
options: In the trial by François et al., methylprednisolone started 12 hours before extubation reduced laryngeal oedema from 22 % to 3 %.
The cuff leak test must be repeated after steroids before extubation.
Systemic corticosteroids at least 4 hours before extubation are suggested.
She has risk factors for postextubation stridor.
questions.expl: D: traumatic intubation, > 6 days, female sex.
