questions.stem: A 30-year-old with no comorbidities, APACHE II 8 and BMI 24 is extubated after 2 days of ventilation for a drug overdose (simple weaning). Which postextubation strategy has shown reduced reintubation compared with conventional oxygen in this type of patient?
options: HFNO for 24 hours
Heliox
Prophylactic NIV for 48 hours
Prophylactic dexamethasone
HFNO alternating with NIV
questions.expl: Hernández 2016 (low risk): reintubation 4.9 vs 12.2 %. ERS/ATS 2017 does not recommend preventive NIV in non-high-risk patients.

title: W12 · D1 – COPD exacerbation and severe asthma in the ICU

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with a COPD exacerbation has pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 68 mmHg and RR 28/min despite bronchodilators and controlled oxygen. According to ERS/ATS 2017, the best next step is:
options: High-flow nasal oxygen as first-line therapy
Bilevel non-invasive ventilation
Immediate intubation because pH is below 7.35
CPAP 10 cmH₂O
Increase FiO₂ to achieve SpO₂ ≥ 96 %
questions.expl: pH ≤ 7.35 with hypercapnia → bilevel NIV (strong, high certainty). HFNO only after a trial of NIV; hyperoxia worsens hypercapnia.

questions.stem: Regarding the ERS/ATS 2017 NIV guideline:
options: There is a strong recommendation to use NIV in acute asthma.
NIV is recommended as a trial in COPD patients considered to need intubation, unless rapidly deteriorating.
NIV is suggested against in COPD patients with hypercapnia but normal pH.
NIV is suggested against for weaning hypercapnic patients from invasive ventilation.
questions.expl: A: no recommendation in asthma. D: NIV is suggested to facilitate weaning in hypercapnic patients.

questions.stem: In the REDUCE trial in acute exacerbations of COPD, 5 days of prednisone 40 mg compared with 14 days:
options: Increased the rate of re-exacerbation within 6 months
Reduced mortality
Required intravenous administration throughout
Was only tested in ventilated patients
Was non-inferior for re-exacerbation and halved the cumulative steroid dose

questions.stem: Regarding dynamic hyperinflation in mechanically ventilated patients with severe airflow obstruction:
options: Increasing the respiratory rate is an effective way to correct rising PaCO₂ in this setting.
Intrinsic PEEP can be measured with an end-inspiratory occlusion in a passive patient.
Expiratory flow returning to zero before the next breath suggests significant air trapping.
Intrinsic PEEP imposes a threshold load that the patient must overcome to trigger the ventilator.
questions.expl: B: intrinsic PEEP requires an end-expiratory occlusion (end-inspiratory occlusion gives plateau pressure). C: air trapping = flow does NOT return to zero. A: it shortens expiration and worsens hyperinflation.

questions.stem: Shortly after intubation, a 24-year-old with life-threatening asthma becomes profoundly hypotensive; peak pressure is high and breath sounds are bilaterally present but quiet. The most appropriate immediate action is:
options: Increase PEEP to 15 cmH₂O
Start adrenaline infusion before any other step
Give a bolus of propofol
Increase respiratory rate to 30/min
Disconnect the patient from the ventilator briefly to allow full exhalation
questions.expl: Dynamic hyperinflation is most likely; disconnection is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Tension pneumothorax must be excluded.

questions.stem: According to the Rome proposal for COPD exacerbations:
options: Symptoms worsen over ≤ 28 days.
CRP ≥ 10 mg/L is one of the parameters used to define a moderate exacerbation.
Severity is primarily defined by where the patient is treated (home, ward, ICU).
A severe exacerbation includes hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis.
questions.expl: A: ≤ 14 days. C: objective parameters.

questions.stem: Which ventilator strategy is most appropriate for an intubated patient with status asthmaticus?
options: VT 10 mL/kg, RR 20/min, I:E 1:1
Target normal PaCO₂ at all costs
Pressure control with inspiratory time 2 s and RR 25/min
High PEEP of 15–20 cmH₂O to open airways
VT 6–8 mL/kg PBW, low RR, high inspiratory flow, accept pH > 7.20
questions.expl: Long expiration, low minute ventilation, permissive hypercapnia.

questions.stem: Regarding oxygen and high-flow therapy in hypercapnic COPD exacerbation:
options: The target SpO₂ is 94–98 %.
HFNC has been shown to be superior to NIV in reducing mortality in this population.
ERS 2022 suggests a trial of HFNC before NIV.
Excess oxygen does not affect PaCO₂ in hypercapnic COPD.
questions.expl: A: 88–92 %. B: neither equivalence nor superiority has been demonstrated. C: NIV first, HFNC only if NIV is not tolerated. D: excess oxygen may raise PaCO₂ through V/Q worsening and the Haldane effect.

questions.stem: Which finding in a patient with acute asthma is most concerning for impending respiratory failure?
options: Expiratory wheeze throughout both lungs
PaCO₂ 45 mmHg in a tachypnoeic, exhausted patient
Serum potassium 3.4 mmol/L after salbutamol
SpO₂ 94 % on 2 L/min oxygen
Heart rate 110/min after salbutamol
questions.expl: Normocapnia in a tachypnoeic asthmatic = exhaustion, impending failure.

questions.stem: In severe acute asthma (GINA 2025):
options: Oxygen should be titrated to SpO₂ 93–95 % in adults.
IV magnesium sulphate 2 g may be given for severe exacerbations not responding to initial treatment.
Routine antibiotics are recommended.
A "silent chest" is a sign of life-threatening asthma.

open.q: A 70-year-old with COPD presents with pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 72 mmHg, RR 30/min and SpO₂ 97 % on 10 L/min via a face mask. Outline your initial management in the first 2 hours.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Look for mimics/aggravating conditions: PE, acute heart failure, pneumonia, pneumothorax.
- Controlled oxygen titrated down to SpO₂ 88–92 % (Venturi mask) – excess O₂ worsens V/Q and Haldane effect → ↑ PaCO₂.
- Short-acting bronchodilators (SABA ± SAMA); prednisone 40 mg/d for 5 days (REDUCE: non-inferior to 14 days, half the dose).
- Antibiotics (~5 days) – indicated when NIV/MV is needed or with purulent sputum plus another cardinal symptom; no methylxanthines.
- Bilevel NIV for pH ≤ 7.35 with hypercapnia (strong, high certainty): oronasal mask, IPAP ~10–12 titrated towards ~20 cmH₂O, EPAP ~4–6 cmH₂O.
- Check contraindications (arrest, unable to protect airway, non-cooperation, haemodynamic instability, excessive secretions, untreated pneumothorax).
- ABG after 1–2 h; failure to improve pH/PaCO₂ predicts failure – ICU monitoring with intubation immediately available. HFNO only if NIV is not tolerated.

open.q: Explain the physiology of dynamic hyperinflation and how it guides ventilator settings and the management of hypotension after intubation in status asthmaticus.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ↑ airway resistance and expiratory flow limitation → incomplete expiration → air trapping → dynamic hyperinflation → intrinsic PEEP.
- Consequences: ↑ work of breathing, inspiratory threshold load, ↑ dead space, ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return, ↑ PVR → hypotension, even PEA.
- Settings: VT 6–8 mL/kg PBW, low RR 10–14/min, high inspiratory flow 60–100 L/min, I:E 1:3–1:5, low external PEEP in asthma, permissive hypercapnia (pH > 7.20), Pplat < 30 cmH₂O.
- Monitor auto-PEEP: end-expiratory occlusion in a passive patient; flow not returning to zero on the flow curve.
- High Ppeak with normal Pplat = ↑ resistance; both ↑ = ↓ compliance or hyperinflation.
- Hypotension after intubation: disconnect from the ventilator for 30–60 s, give fluids, exclude tension pneumothorax.
- Increasing RR for rising PaCO₂ worsens hyperinflation; ketamine is a useful bronchodilating sedative; ECCO₂R/VV-ECMO in refractory cases.

title: W12 · D2 – Severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP)

questions.stem: Which of the following is a MAJOR criterion for severe community-acquired pneumonia according to ATS/IDSA 2019?
options: Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min
Multilobar infiltrates
Confusion
Septic shock requiring vasopressors
PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 250
questions.expl: Major criteria: septic shock requiring vasopressors and MV; the others are minor.

questions.stem: Regarding the CAPE COD trial:
options: Patients with influenza were included and benefited most.
Patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors at inclusion were excluded.
Hydrocortisone 400 mg/day was used initially.
28-day mortality was approximately 6 % vs 12 %.
questions.expl: A: influenza was excluded. C: 200 mg/day for 4 or 8 days, then tapered.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old returns from a hotel stay with high fever, diarrhoea, confusion, sodium 126 mmol/L and bilateral consolidation. The Legionella urinary antigen is negative. The most appropriate statement is:
options: Legionella cannot cause severe pneumonia
The urinary antigen detects mainly serogroup 1, so Legionella is not excluded
Legionella is excluded; stop macrolide
β-lactam monotherapy is sufficient for Legionella
Hyponatraemia argues against Legionella
questions.expl: PCR/culture from the lower respiratory tract is needed; continue the macrolide/fluoroquinolone.

questions.stem: According to the ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT 2023 sCAP guidelines:
options: Procalcitonin is suggested to guide reduction of antibiotic duration.
Fluoroquinolones are preferred over macrolides when added to a β-lactam.
Empirical oseltamivir is suggested during influenza season when PCR is unavailable.
High-flow nasal oxygen is suggested over conventional oxygen in hypoxaemic patients not requiring immediate intubation.
questions.expl: B: macrolide, not fluoroquinolone.

questions.stem: The REMAP-CAP corticosteroid domain in severe CAP (2025) showed:
options: Benefit restricted to influenza pneumonia
Stopping for futility, with a large mortality reduction considered unlikely
That fludrocortisone is required for benefit
Clear mortality benefit from hydrocortisone in all subgroups
Superiority of methylprednisolone over hydrocortisone
questions.expl: 90-day mortality 15 % vs 9.8 %; a small benefit or harm was not excluded.

questions.stem: Regarding empirical antibiotic therapy for severe CAP:
options: Anaerobic coverage is routinely required in suspected aspiration pneumonia without abscess or empyema.
Prior isolation of MRSA or Pseudomonas in the respiratory tract is a relevant risk factor for resistant pathogens.
ATS/IDSA 2019 recommends β-lactam monotherapy for severe CAP.
Anti-MRSA therapy should be given to all patients admitted to ICU.
questions.expl: C: β-lactam plus macrolide or β-lactam plus respiratory fluoroquinolone. D: only with individual risk factors. A: no routine anaerobic coverage (good practice statement).

questions.stem: The 2025 ATS CAP guideline on corticosteroids states:
options: Corticosteroids are strongly recommended for influenza pneumonia
Corticosteroids are recommended for all hospitalised CAP
Corticosteroids are conditionally recommended for severe CAP, but not for influenza pneumonia
Corticosteroids should only be given with septic shock refractory to vasopressin
No recommendation can be made
questions.expl: In non-severe CAP there is a strong recommendation against.

questions.stem: Regarding corticosteroid trials in severe CAP:
options: ESCAPe used methylprednisolone 40 mg/day and found no significant difference in 60-day mortality.
In CAPE COD, insulin requirements were higher with hydrocortisone.
CAPE COD reduced the need for intubation among patients not intubated at baseline.
REMAP-CAP used a Bayesian adaptive platform design.

questions.stem: The main reason a macrolide (rather than β-lactam alone) is added in severe CAP is:
options: Coverage of atypical pathogens such as Legionella and Mycoplasma, plus possible immunomodulation
Anaerobic coverage
Reduction of QT interval
Activity against Pseudomonas
Better activity against MRSA
questions.expl: Atypical pathogens lack a cell wall accessible to β-lactams; macrolides may also act through immunomodulation.

questions.stem: Microbiological work-up in severe CAP (ATS/IDSA 2019):
options: Blood cultures are not required in severe CAP.
Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens should be tested.
Procalcitonin should be used to decide whether to start empirical antibiotics.
Sputum Gram stain and culture should be obtained.
questions.expl: A: blood cultures are recommended before antibiotics in severe CAP. C: procalcitonin is used to shorten duration, not to decide on starting antibiotics.

open.q: A 62-year-old is admitted to the ICU with severe CAP (no MRSA/Pseudomonas risk factors), P/F 180 on HFNO, no vasopressors, influenza PCR negative. Outline your diagnostic and therapeutic plan.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Severity: ATS/IDSA criteria (1 major or ≥ 3 minor); ICU admission without delay.
- Microbiology: blood cultures and sputum Gram stain/culture before antibiotics; pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens (remember Legionella antigen detects only serogroup 1); influenza PCR in season.
- Empirical β-lactam + macrolide (ERS/ESICM prefer macrolide over fluoroquinolone; ATS/IDSA allows either); no routine MRSA/Pseudomonas or anaerobic coverage.
- HFNO over standard oxygen; NIV only in selected patients given the risk of delayed intubation.
- Consider hydrocortisone (CAPE COD: 200 mg/d for 4 days then taper to 8 or 14 days; 28-day mortality 6.2 vs 11.9 %) – patient resembles the CAPE COD population (ICU, P/F < 300, no shock, no influenza); ATS 2025 conditional recommendation, best within 24 h; monitor glucose/insulin requirements.
- Use procalcitonin to shorten (not start) antibiotics; treat for at least 5 days and until clinical stability.

open.q: Explain why CAPE COD, ESCAPe and REMAP-CAP reached different conclusions about corticosteroids in severe CAP.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- CAPE COD (n = 800): hydrocortisone 200 mg/d → 28-day mortality 6.2 vs 11.9 % (p = 0.006), fewer intubations and vasopressor initiations.
- ESCAPe (n = 586): methylprednisolone 40 mg/d for 7 days → 60-day mortality 16 vs 18 %, NS; did not reach planned enrolment.
- REMAP-CAP (n = 658): hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 h for 7 days → 90-day mortality 15 vs 9.8 %, stopped for futility; small benefit or harm not excluded.
- Differences in corticosteroid type and dose, and timing (CAPE COD within 24 h of meeting criteria).
- Population: CAPE COD excluded septic shock and influenza; REMAP-CAP included both.
- Low mortality in CAPE COD; in REMAP-CAP unequal randomisation (536:122) and a small control group gave wide intervals.
- Resulting guidance: ATS 2025 conditional recommendation for severe CAP but not influenza; ERS/ESICM 2023 (pre-CAPE COD) only with shock.

title: W12 · D3 – Airway management in the ICU

questions.stem: In the INTUBE study, the most frequent major peri-intubation adverse event in critically ill patients was:
options: Cardiac arrest
Cardiovascular instability
Aspiration
Oesophageal intubation
Severe hypoxaemia
questions.expl: 42.6 %; hypoxaemia 9.3 %, cardiac arrest 3.1 %.

questions.stem: Regarding the DEVICE trial:
options: Video laryngoscopy increased first-attempt success compared with direct laryngoscopy.
Video laryngoscopy significantly reduced severe complications.
The trial was stopped early for efficacy.
It was conducted in operating theatres.
questions.expl: A: 85.1 vs 70.8 %. B: 21.4 vs 20.9 %. D: emergency departments and ICUs.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with pneumonia and SpO₂ 88 % on a non-rebreather mask requires intubation. Based on PREOXI, the best preoxygenation strategy is:
options: No preoxygenation to avoid delay
Bag-valve mask without a PEEP valve only during apnoea
Non-invasive ventilation for at least 3 minutes
Nasal cannula 4 L/min
Non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min for 3 minutes
questions.expl: Hypoxaemia 9.1 % vs 18.5 %.

questions.stem: According to the DAS 2018 guideline for tracheal intubation in critically ill adults:
options: Unlimited laryngoscopy attempts are acceptable as long as SpO₂ remains > 90 %.
Capnography should be used to confirm tube placement.
If a second-generation supraglottic device succeeds, the team should stop and think about the next step.
The recommended front-of-neck technique is needle cricothyroidotomy with jet ventilation.
questions.expl: A: max. 3 attempts plus one by a more experienced operator. D: scalpel–bougie–tube.

questions.stem: The BOUGIE trial (JAMA 2021) showed that routine use of a bougie compared with an endotracheal tube with stylet:
options: Did not significantly increase first-attempt success
Was only tested with direct laryngoscopy in operating rooms
Reduced severe hypoxaemia by half
Significantly increased first-attempt success
Increased oesophageal intubation tenfold

questions.stem: Regarding the RSI trial comparing ketamine with etomidate (NEJM 2025):
options: Cardiovascular collapse was less frequent with ketamine.
28-day in-hospital mortality was significantly lower with ketamine.
Etomidate significantly increased mortality due to adrenal suppression.
It enrolled patients in both emergency departments and ICUs.
questions.expl: A: more frequent with ketamine – 22.1 vs 17.0 %. B: 28.1 vs 29.1 %, NS.

questions.stem: A patient has the following: Mallampati IV, obstructive sleep apnoea, and SpO₂ 78 % despite preoxygenation. The intubating doctor is an anaesthetist. The MACOCHA score is:
questions.expl: 5 + 2 + 1 = 8 → high risk.

questions.stem: Regarding bag-mask ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy (PreVent):
options: It significantly increased aspiration.
Severe hypoxaemia occurred in about 11 % vs 23 %.
It reduced the incidence of severe hypoxaemia.
It was conducted in critically ill adults in ICUs.
questions.expl: A: aspiration 2.5 vs 4.0 %, no difference.

questions.stem: A patient with severe diabetic ketoacidosis (pH 6.95, PaCO₂ 15 mmHg) requires intubation for decreased consciousness. The most important ventilator consideration immediately after intubation is:
options: Allow permissive hypercapnia
Use a high PEEP of 15 cmH₂O
Set a standard minute ventilation of 6 L/min
Use a low respiratory rate of 10/min
Match or exceed the pre-intubation minute ventilation
questions.expl: A sudden fall in MV → loss of respiratory compensation → precipitous fall in pH.

questions.stem: Suxamethonium is relatively or absolutely contraindicated in:
options: Major burns several days old
Hyperkalaemia
History of malignant hyperthermia
Denervation injury (e.g. spinal cord injury) more than 72 hours old
questions.expl: A, D: upregulated extrajunctional receptors – risk of severe hyperkalaemia. C: absolute contraindication.

open.q: A hypotensive (MAP 58 mmHg), hypoxaemic (SpO₂ 86 % on a non-rebreather) patient with pneumonia needs intubation in the ICU. Outline your plan, justifying each step with evidence from the lesson.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Recognise a physiologically difficult airway; cardiovascular instability is the most common major event (INTUBE: 42.6 %; any major event 45.2 %).
- Checklist, team roles, plans A–D verbalised, capnography; assess MACOCHA (≥ 3 = high risk).
- Haemodynamics: IV/IO access, fluids if hypovolaemic, vasopressor ready (noradrenaline/push-dose); reduced dose of induction agent; ketamine vs etomidate – same mortality but more collapse with ketamine (22.1 vs 17.0 %, RSI 2025); avoid propofol.
- Oxygenation: NIV preoxygenation (PREOXI: hypoxaemia 9.1 vs 18.5 %), apnoeic oxygenation, bag-mask ventilation during apnoea (PreVent: 10.9 vs 22.8 %).
- Videolaryngoscope first (DEVICE: first-attempt success 85.1 vs 70.8 %); bougie as rescue only (BOUGIE NS).
- RSI with rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg or suxamethonium (check contraindications).
- DAS: max 3+1 attempts → 2nd-gen SAD → mask → CICO: scalpel–bougie–tube; expect post-intubation hypotension.

title: W12 · D4 – Tracheostomy: indications, timing, technique, complications

questions.stem: In the TracMan trial, early tracheostomy (within 4 days) compared with late tracheostomy (day 10 or later):
options: Reduced 30-day mortality significantly
Increased ventilator-associated pneumonia
Reduced ICU length of stay by 7 days
Increased 2-year mortality
Did not reduce 30-day mortality

questions.stem: Regarding percutaneous versus surgical tracheostomy (meta-analysis, Crit Care 2014):
options: Unstable cervical spine favours the percutaneous approach.
Percutaneous tracheostomy was associated with fewer stoma infections.
Technical difficulties were more frequent with percutaneous tracheostomy.
Percutaneous tracheostomy took longer to perform.
questions.expl: A: unstable cervical spine favours the surgical approach. D: shorter procedure.

questions.stem: A patient with a tracheostomy formed 2 days ago becomes acutely hypoxic; a suction catheter cannot be passed through the tube after removal of the inner cannula. The next step according to the NTSP algorithm is:
options: Change the tube over a guidewire under fluoroscopy
Vigorous bag ventilation through the tracheostomy tube
Deflate the cuff
Give nebulised salbutamol
Immediate surgical cricothyroidotomy
questions.expl: If there is no improvement → remove the tube and oxygenate via the mouth/stoma.

questions.stem: Regarding a patient with a total laryngectomy:
options: Face mask ventilation over the mouth and nose will oxygenate the lungs.
The upper airway remains connected to the trachea.
Oral intubation is a reasonable secondary rescue option.
Oxygen should be applied to the stoma.
questions.expl: A, B: after laryngectomy the trachea ends in the stoma – the upper airway is disconnected. C: in laryngectomy, never attempt orotracheal intubation.

questions.stem: Three weeks after tracheostomy, a patient has a small episode of bright red bleeding from the stoma that stops spontaneously. The most important concern is:
options: Granulation tissue requiring no action
Thyroid isthmus bleeding
Tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Stomal infection
Tracheo-innominate artery fistula with risk of massive haemorrhage
questions.expl: "Sentinel bleed" – immediate investigation and a surgeon.

questions.stem: Regarding the TracMan trial:
options: It was conducted in UK ICUs.
Early tracheostomy increased sedation days.
Most procedures were percutaneous.
Fewer than half of patients in the late group actually received a tracheostomy.
questions.expl: C: 89 %. B: less sedation.

questions.stem: The recommended tracheostomy cuff pressure is approximately:
options: 60–80 cmH₂O
40–50 cmH₂O
5–10 cmH₂O
Cuff should always be deflated in ventilated patients
20–30 cmH₂O
questions.expl: Prevents mucosal ischaemia, stenosis and microaspiration.

questions.stem: Regarding SETPOINT2 (severe stroke):
options: Early tracheostomy significantly improved functional outcome at 6 months.
The primary outcome was 30-day mortality.
Early tracheostomy was performed within 5 days of intubation.
Six-month mortality was significantly lower with early tracheostomy.
questions.expl: A: 43.5 vs 47.1 %. B: mRS 0–4 at 6 months. D: no significant difference.

questions.stem: Which complication is most dangerous in the first days after percutaneous tracheostomy?
options: Accidental decannulation
Voice change
Tracheomalacia
Granuloma formation
Tracheal stenosis
questions.expl: Immature tract – reinsertion is difficult, risk of false passage.

questions.stem: Measures that increase the safety of percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy include:
options: Routine use in patients with non-palpable landmarks and large goitre
Bronchoscopic guidance
Pre-procedural ultrasound of the neck
Multiple or single-step dilation rather than guidewire dilating forceps to reduce major intraprocedural bleeding
questions.expl: A: surgical tracheostomy is preferable.

open.q: A patient's tracheostomy (performed percutaneously 3 days ago) appears blocked, with acute desaturation. Outline your step-by-step management, and explain how it would differ if the patient had a total laryngectomy.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Call for help; look, listen, feel at the mouth and the stoma; use capnography.
- High-flow oxygen to both the face and the stoma.
- Remove speaking valve/cap/inner cannula; try to pass a suction catheter – do not bag vigorously through a possibly displaced/blocked tube (risk of subcutaneous emphysema).
- If the catheter does not pass → deflate the cuff; if no improvement → remove the tracheostomy tube.
- Primary oxygenation: via mouth (mask, SAD) with the stoma covered, or via the stoma (paediatric mask/SAD).
- Secondary: orotracheal intubation with the tube advanced distal to the stoma, or intubation of the stoma (smaller tube/6.0 over bougie or fibrescope); the tract is immature at 3 days, so reinsertion is hazardous.
- Laryngectomy: mouth/nose are not connected to the lungs – oxygenate and intubate only via the stoma; never attempt orotracheal intubation.

open.q: A colleague wants to perform a tracheostomy on day 3 in a ventilated patient "to improve survival". Discuss the evidence on timing.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- TracMan (909 patients, 70 UK ICUs): early (≤ 4 days) vs late (≥ 10 days) – 30-day mortality 30.8 vs 31.5 %, no difference; no difference at 2 years.
- Fewer than half of the late group ever received a tracheostomy – clinicians predict poorly who will need prolonged ventilation, so early tracheostomy exposes many patients to an unnecessary procedure.
- Procedural complications 6.3 % in TracMan.
- Early tracheostomy reduced sedation days (5 vs 8 in survivors).
- SETPOINT2 (severe stroke, 382 patients): tracheostomy within 5 days did not improve mRS 0–4 at 6 months (43.5 vs 47.1 %), mortality NS.
- Decision should be individual, typically after ~10 days if extubation is not realistic.

title: W12 · D5 – Pleural disease, pneumothorax, massive haemoptysis

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has a moderate pleural effusion. Diagnostic tap: pH 7.15, no frank pus. According to BTS 2023, the most appropriate action is:
options: Insert a small-bore intercostal drain
Antibiotics alone and repeat tap in 1 week
Intrapleural streptokinase
Measure pleural LDH before deciding
Immediate surgical decortication
questions.expl: pH ≤ 7.2 = high risk → drain (≤ 14 F). LDH is used when pH is 7.2–7.4.

questions.stem: Regarding the MIST2 trial:
options: Combination tPA and DNase improved radiographic pleural opacity compared with placebo.
DNase alone was associated with more surgical referrals.
tPA alone was as effective as the combination.
Surgical referral at 3 months was higher with combination therapy.
questions.expl: B: 39 %. D: lower – 4 vs 16 %.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with a first, large primary spontaneous pneumothorax is minimally breathless with normal vital signs. Based on BTS 2023 and Brown et al. (NEJM 2020), a reasonable option is:
options: Immediate VATS pleurodesis
Mandatory large-bore chest drain because of the size
Conservative management with follow-up
Intubation and positive-pressure ventilation
Talc slurry via drain
questions.expl: Symptoms, not size, determine management.

questions.stem: Regarding lung ultrasound for pneumothorax:
options: Absent lung sliding is specific for pneumothorax.
A lung point has low specificity for pneumothorax.
Absent lung sliding may occur after right mainstem intubation (left lung).
The presence of B-lines at a given site excludes pneumothorax at that site.
questions.expl: A: absent sliding also occurs with one-lung intubation, pleurodesis, apnoea, ARDS. B: a lung point is virtually 100 % specific.

questions.stem: In a mechanically ventilated patient with a bronchopleural fistula and a large air leak, which ventilator change is most appropriate?
options: Increase chest drain suction to −40 cmH₂O
Increase tidal volume to compensate for leak
Add a long inspiratory pause
Increase PEEP to 15 cmH₂O
Reduce tidal volume, PEEP and inspiratory time, accepting hypercapnia
questions.expl: Reduce the transpulmonary pressure across the fistula; minimise drain suction.

questions.stem: In life-threatening haemoptysis from the right lung:
options: Bronchial artery embolisation is the first-line definitive therapy.
A large single-lumen tube (≥ 8.0) facilitates therapeutic bronchoscopy.
Most bleeding originates from the pulmonary arteries.
The patient should be positioned left side down.
questions.expl: C: bronchial arteries. D: bleeding side (right) down to protect the healthy lung.

questions.stem: In the MIST1 trial, intrapleural streptokinase for pleural infection:
options: Was only tested in malignant effusions
Showed no benefit on mortality or need for surgery
Reduced the need for surgery
Was superior to tPA plus DNase
Reduced mortality
questions.expl: 454 patients, no benefit vs placebo.

questions.stem: Regarding pleural infection (BTS 2023):
options: Pleural fluid glucose < 3.3 mmol/L suggests a high likelihood of needing drainage when pH is unavailable.
Single-agent DNase is recommended for residual collections.
Pleural fluid pH should be measured with a blood gas analyser.
Initial drainage should use a small-bore drain (≤ 14 F).
questions.expl: B: only in combination with tPA.

questions.stem: A ventilated ARDS patient suddenly develops hypotension, SpO₂ 75 % and rising airway pressures with absent breath sounds on the left. The most appropriate immediate step is:
options: Bronchoscopy
Increase PEEP
CT scan of the chest
Immediate decompression (finger thoracostomy or needle) followed by chest drain
Chest X-ray before any intervention
questions.expl: Tension PTX is a clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: Regarding Brown et al. (NEJM 2020) on primary spontaneous pneumothorax:
options: Conservative management met the non-inferiority criterion in the primary analysis.
Conservative management was associated with a lower risk of recurrence.
The result was robust to all sensitivity analyses for missing data.
About 15 % of the conservative group required intervention.

questions.stem: Two hours after extubation following surgery that involved the right hemidiaphragm, a patient with a right chest drain becomes acutely breathless, hypotensive and hypoxaemic. The drain is not swinging or bubbling. The erect CXR shows a large right pneumothorax, a depressed right hemidiaphragm and mediastinal shift to the left. The most appropriate immediate action is:
options: Increase suction on the existing drain and repeat the CXR in 1 hour
Re-intubate and start positive-pressure ventilation before decompression
Clamp the existing drain to prevent re-expansion pulmonary oedema
Request a CT chest to confirm drain position before any intervention
Decompress the right chest immediately (needle or finger thoracostomy), then insert a second drain and check/clear or replace the non-functioning one
questions.expl: A drain that neither swings nor bubbles is blocked, kinked or misplaced; the patient has a tension pneumothorax (clinical deterioration + mediastinal shift + depressed hemidiaphragm). Decompress first, then place a new drain and deal with the failed one. Suction on a blocked drain is useless (A), clamping worsens tension (C), CT delays life-saving treatment (D), and positive pressure before decompression worsens tension physiology (B).

open.q: A patient with pneumonia has a pleural effusion with pH 7.30 and LDH 1200 IU/L. Interpret these results and outline management, including what to do if a residual collection persists after the drain stops draining.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- pH 7.2–7.4 = intermediate risk; LDH > 900 IU/L with clinical features → consider a chest drain (BTS 2023).
- pH should be measured anaerobically in a blood gas analyser, without lidocaine/heparin contamination; glucose < 3.3 mmol/L supports drainage if pH unavailable; pus or positive Gram/culture = empyema → drain.
- Small-bore drain (≤ 14 F) under US guidance; antibiotics covering anaerobes; RAPID score for risk stratification.
- Residual collection with a non-draining tube: intrapleural tPA 10 mg + DNase 5 mg twice daily for 3 days (MIST2: better CXR, surgical referral 4 vs 16 %); consider tPA 5 mg with bleeding risk, informed consent.
- Not tPA alone, DNase alone (more surgical referrals, 39 %) or streptokinase (MIST1: no benefit).
- VATS decortication if drainage and intrapleural therapy fail or with ongoing sepsis.

open.q: Outline the immediate management of life-threatening haemoptysis in the ICU.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- The threat is asphyxia, not exsanguination; source mostly bronchial arteries.
- Position bleeding side down to protect the healthy lung.
- Secure the airway with a large single-lumen tube (≥ 8.0) for bronchoscopy/suction; isolate the lung if needed (selective intubation of the healthy main bronchus, bronchial blocker or double-lumen tube); blind advancement usually enters the right bronchus.
- Correct coagulopathy, stop anticoagulants/antiplatelets; tranexamic acid (IV or inhaled) as support.
- CT angiography if stable enough; bronchoscopy for localisation, cold saline, topical vasoconstrictors, blockade.
- Bronchial artery embolisation as first-line definitive therapy (risk of recurrence, rare spinal cord ischaemia).
- Surgical resection when BAE fails or with a localised source (aspergilloma, trauma, PA injury).

title: W12 · Saturday – weekly review: Respiratory III

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with COPD arrives with increased breathlessness and purulent sputum. On 4 L/min oxygen via nasal prongs SpO₂ is 97 %, pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 75 mmHg, RR 26/min. Besides bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics, the best management is:
options: Immediate intubation
Increase oxygen to 6 L/min and repeat gas in 4 hours
Start high-flow nasal oxygen at FiO₂ 0.6 instead of NIV
Reduce oxygen to target SpO₂ 88–92 % and start bilevel NIV
Intravenous aminophylline infusion
questions.expl: Hyperoxia worsens hypercapnia; pH ≤ 7.35 → NIV (strong, high certainty).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old intubated for status asthmaticus is ventilated with VT 450 mL, RR 12/min, inspiratory flow 80 L/min. Peak pressure is 48 cmH₂O, plateau pressure 24 cmH₂O.
options: Increasing RR to 24/min would worsen dynamic hyperinflation.
Plateau pressure is within a safe range.
The large peak–plateau difference indicates high airway resistance.
An end-expiratory hold can quantify intrinsic PEEP if the patient is passive.
questions.expl: A: increasing RR shortens expiration and worsens hyperinflation – PaCO₂ is managed by permissive hypercapnia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old is admitted to ICU with pneumococcal pneumonia, P/F 180 on HFNO FiO₂ 0.6, no vasopressors and negative influenza PCR. Which adjunct has RCT evidence of reduced 28-day mortality in this population?
options: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day started early
Inhaled nitric oxide
Intravenous immunoglobulin
Methylprednisolone 40 mg/day for 7 days
Empirical oseltamivir
questions.expl: CAPE COD: 6.2 % vs 11.9 %. ESCAPe (methylprednisolone) was negative.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with severe CAP after a cruise has hyponatraemia, diarrhoea and raised CK.
options: β-lactam monotherapy adequately covers Legionella.
Legionella is a likely pathogen.
A negative urinary antigen excludes Legionella.
Lower respiratory tract PCR detects only serogroup 1 Legionella.
questions.expl: C: the urinary antigen detects only serogroup 1. D: PCR detects all serogroups and species. A: a macrolide or fluoroquinolone is needed.

questions.stem: A hypoxaemic patient (SpO₂ 86 % on a non-rebreather mask) with septic shock requires emergency intubation in the ICU. Which combination is best supported by RCT evidence?
options: Awake fibreoptic intubation as first choice
Routine bougie, nasal cannula preoxygenation, propofol 2 mg/kg
Direct laryngoscopy, mask preoxygenation, no bag ventilation during apnoea
Ketamine 2 mg/kg because it reduces mortality compared with etomidate
Video laryngoscopy, NIV preoxygenation, bag-mask ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy
questions.expl: DEVICE, PREOXI, PreVent. RSI trial: ketamine did not reduce mortality and caused more collapse.

questions.stem: During an ICU intubation, three laryngoscopy attempts by the registrar and one by the consultant have failed. Oxygenation is falling.
options: Full neuromuscular blockade should be ensured before front-of-neck access.
Further laryngoscopy attempts should continue until success.
Supraglottic airway insertion should be skipped; front-of-neck access is the next step.
If SAD and face-mask ventilation fail, scalpel–bougie–tube cricothyroidotomy is indicated.
questions.expl: B: DAS 2018 allows max. 3 + 1 attempts. C: Plan B is a second-generation SAD.

questions.stem: Which statement about tracheostomy timing is supported by the TracMan trial?
options: Tracheostomy within 4 days reduces 30-day mortality
All late-group patients eventually received tracheostomy
Late tracheostomy increases 2-year mortality
Early tracheostomy does not improve survival but reduces sedation exposure
Clinicians accurately predict which patients will need prolonged ventilation
questions.expl: 30-day mortality 30.8 vs 31.5 %; fewer sedation days; fewer than half of the late group received a tracheostomy.

questions.stem: A patient 4 days after percutaneous tracheostomy develops sudden respiratory distress and the ventilator alarms for high pressure.
options: If a suction catheter passes easily, the tube is likely patent.
Forceful bag ventilation via the tube should be attempted before checking patency.
High-flow oxygen should be applied to the face and the stoma.
The inner cannula should be removed.
questions.expl: B: risk of subcutaneous emphysema.

questions.stem: A patient with a total laryngectomy is apnoeic. The correct route for oxygenation is:
options: Laryngeal mask airway via the mouth
Face mask over mouth and nose
Via the neck stoma (e.g. paediatric face mask or tube in the stoma)
Nasal high-flow
Orotracheal intubation
questions.expl: After laryngectomy the mouth and nose are not connected to the lungs.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with pneumonia has a loculated pleural effusion; pleural pH 7.05, a 12 F drain was inserted but drainage stopped with residual collection on ultrasound.
options: DNase alone is a suitable alternative to the combination.
Intrapleural tPA 10 mg plus DNase 5 mg once daily for 7 days is the standard regimen.
Surgical referral should be considered if sepsis persists despite drainage and intrapleural therapy.
Intrapleural streptokinase is recommended.
questions.expl: B: twice daily for 3 days (MIST2). D: MIST1. A: MIST2.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient with ARDS has inspired VT 450 mL and expired VT 250 mL after a chest drain for pneumothorax, with continuous bubbling. Which intervention is LEAST appropriate?
options: Reduce PEEP to the lowest acceptable level
Accept permissive hypercapnia
Increase chest drain suction to maximum
Encourage spontaneous breathing modes when feasible
Shorten inspiratory time
questions.expl: Suction increases flow through the fistula. Leak = 200 mL.

questions.stem: A patient with cavitary tuberculosis sequelae has massive haemoptysis from the left lung and is deteriorating.
options: Death is usually due to exsanguination rather than asphyxia.
Bronchial artery embolisation is the preferred definitive treatment.
Blind advancement of a single-lumen tube usually enters the right main bronchus, isolating the healthy lung.
Position the patient left side down.
questions.expl: A: death is usually from asphyxia.

questions.stem: Which feature is NOT part of the ATS/IDSA 2019 minor criteria for severe CAP?
options: Multilobar infiltrates
Need for invasive mechanical ventilation
Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min
Platelets < 100 × 10⁹/L
Temperature < 36 °C
questions.expl: MV is a major criterion.

questions.stem: Concerning severe asthma and COPD in the ICU:
options: In COPD with acute hypercapnic failure, ERS suggests trying NIV before HFNC.
NIV in acute asthma carries a strong ERS/ATS recommendation.
Five days of systemic corticosteroids is sufficient in most COPD exacerbations.
IV magnesium sulphate is contraindicated in severe asthma.
questions.expl: B: no recommendation. C: REDUCE. D: IV magnesium 2 g may be used in severe asthma not responding to initial therapy.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with an ICU intubation planned has Mallampati III, limited mouth opening (2.5 cm) and GCS 7; the operator is an anaesthetist and SpO₂ is 95 %. Which is correct?
options: MACOCHA 12 – maximum risk
MACOCHA 3 – low risk
MACOCHA does not apply to ICU patients
MACOCHA 7 – high risk of difficult intubation
MACOCHA 2 – low risk
questions.expl: 5 + 1 + 1 = 7; ≥ 3 = high risk.

title: W13 · D1 – Ventilation modes: VCV, PCV, PRVC, PSV, SIMV, APRV, NAVA, PAV

questions.stem: A patient on volume-controlled ventilation with constant inspiratory flow of 60 L/min, VT 500 mL and PEEP 5 cmH₂O has a respiratory system compliance of 25 mL/cmH₂O and an airway resistance of 10 cmH₂O/L/s. The expected peak and plateau pressures are:
options: Ppeak 25, Pplat 20 cmH₂O
Ppeak 45, Pplat 35 cmH₂O
Ppeak 35, Pplat 25 cmH₂O
Ppeak 35, Pplat 30 cmH₂O
Ppeak 30, Pplat 25 cmH₂O

questions.stem: Regarding pressure support ventilation (PSV):
options: In a patient with COPD, increasing the cycle-off threshold (% of peak flow) shortens inspiration and can reduce delayed cycling.
A backup respiratory rate is delivered only if the patient stops triggering (apnoea backup).
Breaths are patient-triggered and flow-cycled.
Ineffective triggering is associated with excessive levels of pressure support.
questions.expl: B: there is no mandatory rate – only an apnoea backup. D: Thille 2006.

questions.stem: In the trial by Esteban et al. (NEJM 1995) comparing four weaning methods, which approach was associated with the slowest weaning?
options: Non-invasive ventilation after early extubation
Synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation
Once-daily spontaneous breathing trial
Multiple daily spontaneous breathing trials
Pressure support with gradual reduction
questions.expl: IMV median 5 days; a once-daily SBT was 2.83× faster than IMV.

questions.stem: A patient is ventilated in pressure control with an inspiratory pressure of 15 cmH₂O above PEEP; respiratory system compliance is 40 mL/cmH₂O and inspiratory time is long enough for pressure equilibration.
options: A fall in compliance in this mode results primarily in a fall in tidal volume.
When fully passive, the expected VT is about 400 mL.
The displayed airway pressure rises to 25 cmH₂O when the patient makes this effort.
If the patient generates a muscle pressure of 10 cmH₂O, VT may approach 1000 mL.
questions.expl: B: 15 × 40 = 600 mL. C: the ventilator holds the set pressure; effort increases VT, not P_aw.

questions.stem: In pressure-regulated volume control (PRVC), a patient with high respiratory drive starts to generate large inspiratory efforts. The most likely ventilator response is:
options: It increases the backup rate
It decreases inspiratory pressure because the measured VT exceeds the target
It cycles off on Edi decrease
It increases inspiratory pressure to maintain target VT
It switches automatically to volume control with constant flow
questions.expl: The patient "delivers" the volume himself → the ventilator reduces support and work of breathing rises.

questions.stem: Regarding neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA):
options: The trial by Demoule et al. showed a higher asynchrony index with NAVA than with PSV.
The diaphragmatic electrical activity is recorded with surface electrodes on the chest wall.
The delivered pressure is proportional to Edi multiplied by the NAVA level.
In the multicentre trial by Demoule et al., NAVA significantly increased the proportion of patients remaining in a partial ventilatory mode at 48 h.
questions.expl: A: lower with NAVA – 14.7 vs 26.7 %. B: Edi is recorded with electrodes on an oesophageal (nasogastric) catheter. D: 67.2 vs 63.3 %, NS.

questions.stem: Which statement about airway pressure release ventilation (APRV) is correct?
options: It is recommended as first-line ventilation in all ARDS patients
It is a flow-cycled, patient-triggered pressure mode without spontaneous breathing
In the trial by Zhou et al., APRV significantly reduced ICU mortality
CO₂ removal occurs mainly during brief releases from a high continuous pressure
Its tidal volume during releases is fixed by the ventilator
questions.expl: Zhou 2017: ↑ ventilator-free days (19 vs 2), mortality 19.7 vs 34.3 % NS (p = 0.053).

questions.stem: Regarding proportional assist ventilation (PAV+):
options: PAV+ estimates resistance and compliance automatically using short inspiratory pauses.
Support decreases as patient effort increases.
Runaway can occur if the delivered assistance exceeds the actual respiratory load.
In the study by Xirouchaki et al., PAV+ had a higher failure rate than pressure support.
questions.expl: B: support is proportional to effort – it increases as effort increases. D: 11.1 vs 22.0 % in favour of PAV+.

questions.stem: On volume-controlled ventilation with constant flow, the pressure–time curve of a patient with strong inspiratory effort shows a concave "scooped" inspiratory limb. The most likely problem and solution are:
options: Endotracheal tube obstruction – suction
Pneumothorax – chest drain
Delayed cycling – increase cycle-off threshold
Auto-triggering – make trigger less sensitive
Flow starvation – increase inspiratory flow or switch to a pressure-targeted mode
questions.expl: The fixed flow does not meet patient demand → the pressure curve is "scooped" downwards.

questions.stem: Regarding classification of ventilator breaths:
options: In volume control, airway pressure depends on respiratory system compliance and resistance.
A breath that is time-triggered is a mandatory breath.
In PSV, the breath ends when a set inspiratory time has elapsed.
A ventilator can control either volume/flow or pressure during a given inspiration, but not both simultaneously.
questions.expl: C: PSV is flow-cycled.

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS is on APRV (P-high 28 cmH₂O, T-high 5 s, P-low 0 cmH₂O, T-low 0.8 s). On the flow–time curve the expiratory flow during each release peaks at 60 L/min and decays to 20 L/min before pressure returns to P-high. According to the approach described in BJA Education (2020), the most appropriate adjustment is:
options: Add pressure support of 10 cmH₂O to spontaneous breaths
Shorten T-low (in 0.1-s steps) until the release ends at about 45 L/min
Lengthen T-low to 1.2 s so that expiratory flow reaches zero
Shorten T-high to 2 s to increase the number of releases
Increase P-low to 10 cmH₂O and leave T-low unchanged
questions.expl: The release should be terminated at ~75 % of peak expiratory flow (0.75 × 60 = 45 L/min). Flow falling to 20 L/min (33 %) means T-low is too long → risk of derecruitment; shorten T-low by 0.1 s at a time. Allowing flow to reach zero (C) defeats the intended auto-PEEP; added PS (A) may over-distend recruited lung.

questions.stem: Regarding airway pressure release ventilation (APRV):
options: Severe bronchospasm is a relative contraindication because a short T-low cannot adequately empty slow lung units.
Spontaneous inspiratory efforts taken at P-high may generate high transpulmonary pressures, particularly in heterogeneous lungs.
APRV is recommended in preference to prone positioning for severe ARDS.
In the trial by Zhou et al. (2017), patients on APRV were less often successfully extubated than those on low tidal volume ventilation.
questions.expl: D: more often – 66.2 % vs 38.8 %. C: prone positioning has robust mortality evidence and should come first; APRV is considered if prone is contraindicated or fails (Swindin, BJA Educ 2020).

open.q: A patient with recovering ARDS is switched from VCV to pressure control (Pinsp 15 cmH₂O above PEEP, C 40 mL/cmH₂O) and starts making strong inspiratory efforts (estimated P_mus ≈ 10 cmH₂O). Calculate the expected tidal volume with and without effort, and explain why a "low" displayed pressure may be misleading. How would you monitor this patient?
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Equation of motion: in pressure-targeted modes VT = (Pinsp + P_mus) × C.
- Passive: VT ≈ 15 × 40 = 600 mL; with effort: (15 + 10) × 40 ≈ 1000 mL.
- The displayed airway pressure stays at 15 cmH₂O – the ventilator holds the set pressure; effort increases VT, not P_aw.
- Transpulmonary pressure = ventilator pressure + P_mus → hidden volutrauma / P-SILI risk.
- Monitor VT (not just pressure) and estimates of effort/drive: P0.1, Pocc, Pes (Brochard 2017).
- Also note: a fall in compliance in PCV causes a fall in VT → low VE alarm is mandatory.
- If Ti < ~3τ, pressure does not equilibrate and VT is smaller than Pinsp × C.

open.q: Compare the evidence for SIMV, PSV and a daily spontaneous breathing trial as weaning strategies, and explain the physiological reason SIMV performs poorly.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Esteban (NEJM 1995): 546 patients, 130 randomised after failing a 2-h SBT.
- Median weaning duration: IMV 5 d, PSV 4 d, multiple SBTs 3 d, once-daily SBT 3 d.
- Once-daily SBT weaned patients 2.83× faster than IMV and 2.05× faster than PSV.
- SIMV mixes supported mandatory and unsupported/partially supported spontaneous breaths.
- Respiratory muscles cannot adapt breath by breath → effort remains high even during mandatory breaths.
- Conclusion: SIMV is the slowest weaning method; the preferred approach is a daily SBT (T-piece or low PS).

title: W13 · D2 – Waveforms, loops and respiratory mechanics: compliance, resistance, τ, pauses, oesophageal pressure

questions.stem: A sedated, paralysed patient on volume control (constant flow 60 L/min, VT 450 mL, PEEP 8 cmH₂O, total PEEP 8 cmH₂O) has Ppeak 38 cmH₂O and Pplat 26 cmH₂O. Which pair of values is correct?
options: Static compliance 25 mL/cmH₂O; airway resistance 12 cmH₂O/L/s
Static compliance 17 mL/cmH₂O; airway resistance 12 cmH₂O/L/s
Static compliance 25 mL/cmH₂O; airway resistance 0.2 cmH₂O/L/s
Static compliance 15 mL/cmH₂O; airway resistance 26 cmH₂O/L/s
Static compliance 30 mL/cmH₂O; airway resistance 6 cmH₂O/L/s
questions.expl: C_stat = 450/(26 − 8) = 450/18 = 25 mL/cmH₂O; R = (38 − 26)/1 L/s = 12 cmH₂O/L/s. A value of 15 mL/cmH₂O would be C_dyn = 450/(38 − 8).

questions.stem: A ventilated patient's peak pressure rises suddenly from 28 to 42 cmH₂O while the plateau pressure stays at 22 cmH₂O. Possible causes include:
options: Tension pneumothorax
Endobronchial (right main bronchus) intubation
Kinked or bitten endotracheal tube
Abdominal distension
questions.expl: Unchanged Pplat = a resistance problem (tube kinking, secretions, bronchospasm). Pneumothorax, endobronchial intubation and abdominal distension reduce compliance and raise Pplat.

questions.stem: A patient has airway resistance of 20 cmH₂O/L/s and respiratory system compliance of 50 mL/cmH₂O. Approximately how long an expiratory time is needed to exhale about 95 % of the tidal volume?
Regarding ventilator waveforms:
options: A "scooped-out" expiratory limb of the flow–volume loop suggests restrictive lung disease.
Saw-tooth oscillations on the flow trace may indicate secretions or water in the circuit.
Expiratory flow that returns to zero before the next breath suggests dynamic hyperinflation.
A volume–time curve whose expiratory limb does not return to baseline suggests a leak.
questions.expl: A: it suggests obstruction. C: dynamic hyperinflation = expiratory flow does not return to zero.

questions.stem: Dynamic compliance is lower than static compliance in a patient because:
options: Dynamic compliance uses plateau pressure in the denominator
Dynamic compliance includes the pressure needed to overcome airway resistance
Static compliance is measured during spontaneous breathing
Dynamic compliance excludes PEEP
Static compliance includes the chest wall but dynamic compliance does not
questions.expl: C_dyn = VT/(Ppeak − PEEP); Ppeak contains the resistive component.

questions.stem: Regarding oesophageal pressure measurement:
options: The balloon should be positioned in the lower third of the oesophagus.
During an occlusion test, a ratio ΔPes/ΔPaw close to 1 confirms adequate positioning.
In EPVent-2, oesophageal pressure–guided PEEP reduced 28-day mortality.
Transpulmonary pressure equals oesophageal pressure minus airway pressure.
questions.expl: C: 32.4 vs 30.6 %, no difference. D: P_L = P_aw − P_es.

questions.stem: A patient with BMI 48 is ventilated with PEEP 10 cmH₂O. End-expiratory oesophageal pressure is 16 cmH₂O. The end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure and its implication are:
options: +6 cmH₂O – adequate; no change
+26 cmH₂O – overdistension; reduce PEEP
−16 cmH₂O – pneumothorax likely
−6 cmH₂O – dependent lung regions are likely collapsing; consider increasing PEEP
0 cmH₂O – oesophageal balloon is misplaced
questions.expl: P_L,ee = 10 − 16 = −6 cmH₂O.

questions.stem: VT 500 mL, Pplat 30 cmH₂O, PEEP 10 cmH₂O; tidal swing in oesophageal pressure is 5 cmH₂O.
options: Respiratory system elastance is 60 cmH₂O/L.
Chest wall elastance is 20 cmH₂O/L.
Lung elastance is 50 cmH₂O/L.
The lung (transpulmonary) driving pressure is 15 cmH₂O.

questions.stem: In the study by Chiumello et al. (AJRCCM 2008), the ratio of lung elastance to respiratory system elastance:
options: Was constant at about 0.5 in all patients
Varied widely (approximately 0.33–0.95), so plateau pressure is an imperfect surrogate of lung stress
Was always above 0.9 in ARDS
Was lower in healthy than in ARDS patients by a fixed amount
Could be predicted from tidal volume per kg PBW
questions.expl: E_L/E_rs ranged 0.33–0.95, so the same Pplat can mean very different lung stress.

questions.stem: Regarding inspiratory and expiratory hold manoeuvres:
options: An end-inspiratory hold in a passive patient allows measurement of plateau pressure.
Airway resistance can be calculated from Ppeak − Pplat during volume-controlled ventilation with constant inspiratory flow.
Active inspiratory effort during the hold falsely lowers the measured plateau pressure.
Intrinsic PEEP = total PEEP measured during an end-expiratory hold minus set PEEP.
questions.expl: B: R = (Ppeak − Pplat)/flow – valid only with constant flow in VCV, not with decelerating flow.

open.q: A paralysed patient on VCV (VT 500 mL, constant flow 60 L/min, PEEP_set 5) has Ppeak 35, Pplat 25 and PEEP_tot 5 cmH₂O. Calculate static and dynamic compliance, driving pressure, airway resistance and the time constant, and interpret whether expiratory time is adequate. Then explain how you would distinguish a resistance problem from a compliance problem if Ppeak suddenly rose.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- C_stat = 500/(25 − 5) = 25 mL/cmH₂O; C_dyn = 500/(35 − 5) = 16.7 mL/cmH₂O (C_dyn ≤ C_stat because it includes resistance).
- ΔP = 25 − 5 = 20 cmH₂O.
- R_aw = (35 − 25)/1 L/s = 10 cmH₂O/L/s – valid only with constant flow; flow converted to L/s.
- τ = 10 × 0.025 = 0.25 s; 3τ = 0.75 s (~95 % exhaled) → a 2-s expiration is sufficient.
- Use PEEP_tot (end-expiratory hold) rather than set PEEP; measurements require a passive patient.
- If Ppeak rises with unchanged Pplat → ↑ resistance (bronchospasm, secretions, kinked/bitten tube).
- If Ppeak and Pplat both rise → ↓ compliance (pneumothorax, endobronchial intubation, atelectasis, oedema, ↑ IAP, dynamic hyperinflation).

open.q: An obese patient (PEEP 12 cmH₂O) has an end-expiratory oesophageal pressure of 17 cmH₂O and Pplat 32 cmH₂O. Interpret these values and discuss the role of oesophageal pressure monitoring in light of Talmor (2008) and EPVent-2 (2019).
open.model:
Key points expected:
- P_L = P_aw − P_es; P_L,ee = 12 − 17 = −5 cmH₂O → dependent regions collapse at end-expiration (atelectrauma).
- Increasing PEEP to achieve P_L,ee ≥ 0 is physiologically justified.
- With a stiff chest wall a Pplat of 32 does not necessarily mean excessive lung stress (E_L/E_rs varies 0.33–0.95, Chiumello).
- Correct balloon position: lower third of oesophagus, occlusion test ΔP_es/ΔP_aw ≈ 0.8–1.2, cardiac oscillations.
- Talmor (EPVent, 61 patients): P/F 88 mmHg higher at 72 h, better compliance; not powered for mortality.
- EPVent-2 (200 patients): no difference in death + ventilator-free days; 28-d mortality 32.4 vs 30.6 %.
- Conclusion: not routine; useful physiologically in obesity, ↑ IAP, stiff chest wall, high patient effort.

title: W13 · D3 – Patient–ventilator asynchronies

questions.stem: During a 30-minute recording, the ventilator delivers 450 cycles. You count 50 ineffective efforts and 25 double-triggered cycles. The asynchrony index is:
Regarding the study by Thille et al. (ICM 2006):
options: About a quarter of patients had an asynchrony index above 10 %.
Ineffective triggering and double triggering were the two main patterns.
Double triggering was more frequent in pressure support than in assist-control ventilation.
A high asynchrony index was associated with a longer duration of mechanical ventilation.
questions.expl: A: 24 %. C: more frequent in ACV.

questions.stem: A COPD patient on pressure support 20 cmH₂O, PEEP 5 cmH₂O, VT 9 mL/kg PBW shows frequent small dips in airway pressure with transient increases in expiratory flow that are not followed by a ventilator breath. The best initial change is:
options: Switch to SIMV
Decrease pressure support
Decrease the cycle-off threshold from 25 % to 5 %
Increase pressure support to 25 cmH₂O
Make the trigger less sensitive
questions.expl: Ineffective efforts from excessive support (Thille 2008); a higher cycle-off and external PEEP against PEEPi also help.

questions.stem: Regarding Blanch et al. (ICM 2015):
options: Asynchronies were recorded continuously in 50 patients, totalling several million breaths.
The most common asynchrony was double triggering.
An asynchrony index above 10 % was associated with higher ICU and hospital mortality.
The study proved that asynchrony causes death.
questions.expl: A: ~8.7 million. B: ineffective inspiratory efforts during expiration were the most common. D: observational – marker vs cause.

questions.stem: A deeply sedated ARDS patient on volume assist-control (no spontaneous triggering) shows, after several machine-triggered breaths, a negative deflection of airway pressure late in inspiration followed by a second stacked breath. This is:
options: Auto-triggering
Delayed cycling
Ineffective effort due to auto-PEEP
Flow starvation from high flow
Reverse triggering
questions.expl: The ventilator triggers the breath and the diaphragm contracts only afterwards (entrainment); breath stacking may result.

questions.stem: Auto-triggering:
options: May falsely suggest absent respiratory drive during brain-death assessment.
Is associated with a ventilator rate lower than the patient's neural rate.
Is not caused by cardiac oscillations.
Can be caused by a circuit leak.
questions.expl: A: it may falsely suggest preserved drive (breaths delivered without effort). B: the ventilator rate is higher. C: cardiac oscillations are a classic cause.

questions.stem: In pressure support, the pressure–time curve shows a pressure spike at the end of inspiration and a slowly decaying inspiratory flow in a COPD patient. The appropriate adjustment is:
options: Decrease PEEP to zero
Raise the cycle-off threshold (e.g. 25 % → 45 %)
Lower the cycle-off threshold (e.g. 25 % → 10 %)
Increase pressure support
Increase inspiratory rise time to the maximum
questions.expl: Delayed cycling – a higher % cycle-off shortens inspiration.

questions.stem: Regarding double triggering:
options: It is more frequent with assist-control than with pressure support.
It occurs when the patient's neural inspiratory time is longer than the ventilator inspiratory time.
It can result in a delivered volume close to twice the set tidal volume.
The appropriate correction is always to shorten inspiratory time further.
questions.expl: A: Thille 2006. D: Ti/VT should rather be lengthened and drive treated.

questions.stem: In the study by Vaporidi et al. (ICM 2017), which measure of ineffective efforts was associated with mortality?
options: Ineffective effort index > 10 %
No measure was associated with outcome
Ineffective efforts only during sleep
Overall ineffective effort index
Clusters of ineffective efforts (> 30 within 3 minutes)
questions.expl: Neither the overall IE index nor IE index > 10 % correlated with outcome.

questions.stem: A patient on PSV 10 cmH₂O has intrinsic PEEP of 8 cmH₂O, set PEEP 0 and a pressure trigger of −2 cmH₂O.
options: Applying external PEEP may reduce the effort needed to trigger.
The ventilator-displayed rate may underestimate the patient's true respiratory rate.
The patient must lower alveolar pressure by about 10 cmH₂O before a breath is triggered.
Increasing pressure support to 20 cmH₂O is the most effective way to eliminate ineffective efforts.
questions.expl: C: 8 + 2. D: larger VT → more PEEPi and IE.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia (respiratory system compliance 28 mL/cmH₂O) is on PSV 8 cmH₂O, PEEP 8 cmH₂O, cycle-off 40 %, rate 32/min. The flow–time curve shows, immediately after the peak expiratory flow, a small positive bump with an abrupt slowing of expiratory flow; some breaths are followed within 0.3 s by a second triggered breath. The most appropriate adjustment is:
options: Raise cycle-off to 60 %
Increase PEEP to 14 cmH₂O to reduce the time constant
Make the trigger less sensitive
Lower cycle-off to about 20–25 % (and consider more pressure support)
Reduce pressure support to 4 cmH₂O
questions.expl: Early (premature) cycling – the ventilator ends inspiration while the patient is still inhaling (short τ of a stiff lung reaches a high cycle-off threshold quickly, low PS), leading to double triggering. Lower cycle-off prolongs inspiration; this is a "high drive / under-assistance" asynchrony, so reducing support (E) would worsen it.

questions.stem: Regarding classifications of patient–ventilator asynchrony:
options: Ineffective efforts, delayed cycling and reverse triggering are typically associated with low respiratory drive and/or excessive assistance.
Delayed triggering is classified as a major asynchrony.
Early cycling and double triggering are typically associated with high respiratory drive and/or insufficient assistance.
Ineffective effort is a major asynchrony because the patient's effort receives no ventilator support.
questions.expl: B: the breath is delivered, only late → minor asynchrony. A, C: aetiological classification (Murias 2016) – it tells you whether to decrease or increase support.

questions.stem: A patient with COPD on non-invasive pressure support (IPAP 16, EPAP 5 cmH₂O, ETS 25 %) with a moderate mask leak has long inspirations, an end-inspiratory pressure spike and visible ineffective efforts during expiration. The most appropriate cycling adjustment is:
options: Increase the rise time to the slowest setting and leave ETS unchanged
Lower ETS to 10 %
Switch to a pressure trigger of −5 cmH₂O
Raise ETS (e.g. to 40–50 %) and set a maximum inspiratory time
Increase IPAP to 22 cmH₂O
questions.expl: Long τ (COPD) plus leak delay the fall of inspiratory flow to 25 % of peak → late cycling → shortened expiration, dynamic hyperinflation and ineffective efforts. A higher ETS ends inspiration earlier; Ti max is a back-up when leak prevents flow cycling. Lowering ETS (B) or raising IPAP (E) prolongs inspiration and worsens hyperinflation; a less sensitive trigger (C) increases ineffective efforts.

questions.stem: Regarding double triggering and ineffective efforts:
options: Setting external PEEP at about 75 % of measured intrinsic PEEP can reduce the inspiratory load needed to trigger.
Increasing pressure support is the first-line response to frequent ineffective efforts.
In reverse triggering, the first breath of a stacked pair is initiated by the patient.
Double triggering due to high drive is usually improved by lowering the expiratory trigger sensitivity (cycle-off %) in pressure support.
questions.expl: C: the first breath is ventilator-initiated – the insufflation itself elicits the muscle contraction (De Oliveira 2021). D: a lower cycle-off lengthens mechanical Ti to match the longer neural Ti. B: over-assistance is a main cause – reduce PS/VT. A: counterbalances PEEPi; PEEP set above PEEPi raises end-inspiratory pressure (volume modes) or reduces VT (pressure modes).

open.q: A COPD patient on PSV 20 cmH₂O (PEEP 5, VT 9 mL/kg PBW) has frequent ineffective efforts and a pressure spike at end-inspiration. Outline your stepwise management of this asynchrony and explain the mechanisms involved.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Look at the patient and the pressure–time and flow–time waveforms together; exclude technical causes (leak, water, secretions, kinked tube).
- Ineffective efforts: PEEPi must be overcome before triggering (e.g. PEEPi 8 + trigger −2 → ~10 cmH₂O effort needed).
- Excessive support is the most common correctable cause → reduce PS/VT (Thille 2008: PS 20 → 13 cmH₂O, IE 45 % → 0 %, VT 10.2 → 5.9 mL/kg).
- Do not increase PS – larger VT → more PEEPi → more IE.
- End-inspiratory pressure spike with slow flow decay = delayed cycling (long τ) → raise cycle-off to 40–50 %.
- Apply external PEEP to partly counterbalance PEEPi; consider a more sensitive trigger and less sedation.
- Consider NAVA/PAV+ for persistent asynchrony (better synchrony, hard outcomes not proven).

open.q: Explain why Thille (2006), Blanch (2015) and Vaporidi (2017) reach different conclusions about the clinical significance of asynchronies.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Thille 2006: 62 patients, 30-min recordings; 24 % had AI > 10 %; associated with longer ventilation (median 25.5 vs 7.5 d).
- Blanch 2015: 50 patients, continuous automated recording of ~8.7 million breaths; median AI 3.41 %; AI > 10 % associated with higher ICU and hospital mortality.
- Vaporidi 2017: 110 patients, 24-h recordings on PSV/PAV; IE index (even > 10 %) did not correlate with outcome, but IE clusters (> 30 in 3 min, 38 % of patients) did (ventilation ≥ 8 d, hospital mortality).
- Differences in recording duration (snapshot vs continuous) and the metric used (overall index vs clusters).
- All are observational – asynchrony may be a marker of severity rather than a cause.

title: W13 · D4 – VILI, P-SILI, mechanical power, P0.1 and Pocc

questions.stem: A patient on volume control has VT 500 mL, RR 24/min, Ppeak 32 cmH₂O, Pplat 26 cmH₂O, PEEP 10 cmH₂O. Using the simplified formula MP = 0.098 × RR × VT(L) × (Ppeak − ½ΔP), the mechanical power is approximately:
options: 56.4 J/min
37.6 J/min
17.6 J/min
28.2 J/min
11.8 J/min

questions.stem: According to Gattinoni et al. (ICM 2016), mechanical power:
options: Increases exponentially with tidal volume (exponent 2).
Increases linearly with PEEP.
Increases with respiratory rate with an exponent of about 0.5.
Has an established safe threshold of 12 J/min in patients with ARDS.
questions.expl: C: exponent ~1.4. D: ~12 J/min in healthy pigs; no threshold established for ARDS.

questions.stem: Atelectrauma is best described as:
options: Release of inflammatory mediators into the circulation
Diaphragm injury from excessive assistance
Injury caused by high FiO₂
Injury from cyclic opening and closing of unstable alveoli
Injury from excessive end-inspiratory transpulmonary pressure causing air leak
questions.expl: Cyclic opening/closing of alveoli with shear stress at the interface of open and collapsed regions.

questions.stem: Regarding patient self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI) as described by Brochard et al. (AJRCCM 2017):
options: Strong inspiratory efforts can cause pendelluft, shifting gas between lung regions.
Monitoring of P0.1, tidal volume or oesophageal pressure is discouraged in spontaneously breathing patients at risk.
Its existence and clinical relevance have been proven by large randomised trials.
Negative intrathoracic pressure swings decrease pulmonary vascular transmural pressure and protect against oedema.
questions.expl: B: monitoring of drive/effort is suggested. C: it is a concept. D: they increase transmural vascular pressure and promote oedema.

questions.stem: A patient on PSV 10 cmH₂O, PEEP 6 cmH₂O (Ppeak 16 cmH₂O) has a ΔPocc of −15 cmH₂O during an end-expiratory occlusion. The estimated dynamic transpulmonary driving pressure (ΔPL,dyn = ΔPaw − ⅔ × ΔPocc) is:
options: 20 cmH₂O
10 cmH₂O
0 cmH₂O
26 cmH₂O
5 cmH₂O

questions.stem: Regarding P0.1:
options: In Telias et al. (AJRCCM 2020), a P0.1 > 3.5 cmH₂O detected potentially high effort.
It is the airway pressure drop 100 ms after the onset of an inspiratory effort against an occluded airway.
A P0.1 ≤ 1.0 cmH₂O suggests excessive inspiratory effort.
P0.1 is unreliable because patients consciously react to the 100-ms occlusion.
questions.expl: C: ≤ 1.0 cmH₂O suggests low effort, possibly over-assistance. D: the patient does not perceive a 100-ms occlusion.

questions.stem: In the analysis by Serpa Neto et al. (ICM 2018) of MIMIC-III and eICU, mechanical power:
options: Was not associated with mortality once tidal volume was low
Was associated with higher in-hospital mortality, with risk rising consistently above about 17 J/min
Was protective above 20 J/min
Was tested as a randomised titration target
Was associated with mortality only in patients with ARDS on ECMO
questions.expl: Even with low VT, high MP was associated with mortality (OR 1.70).

questions.stem: In the study by Chiumello et al. (AJRCCM 2008) on lung stress and strain:
options: The authors concluded that plateau pressure and tidal volume are inadequate surrogates of lung stress and strain.
Specific lung elastance was about 13.5 cmH₂O and similar across patient groups.
A VT of 500 mL in a patient with an FRC of 300 mL produces a strain of about 1.7.
Lung stress can be estimated as specific lung elastance × strain.
questions.expl: A: chest wall elastance and lung size vary widely. C: 500/300 = 1.67.

questions.stem: A patient in pressure control has RR 25/min, VT 0.4 L, PEEP 10 cmH₂O and inspiratory pressure 15 cmH₂O above PEEP. Mechanical power by the formula 0.098 × RR × VT × (PEEP + ΔPinsp) is approximately:
options: 49.0 J/min
9.8 J/min
24.5 J/min
36.8 J/min
14.7 J/min

questions.stem: Regarding the occlusion pressure (Pocc) method of Bertoni et al. (Crit Care 2019):
options: Excessive effort (Pmus > 10 cmH₂O) was rare in the studied patients.
Muscle pressure can be estimated as approximately −2 × ΔPocc.
ΔPocc is the maximal airway pressure deflection during an end-expiratory occlusion.
The method requires an oesophageal balloon at the bedside.
questions.expl: A: 84 % of patient-days. B: Pmus ≈ −¾ × ΔPocc. D: non-invasive method.

open.q: An ARDS patient on VCV has VT 0.5 L, RR 20, Ppeak 30, Pplat 25 and PEEP 10 cmH₂O. Calculate mechanical power using the simplified bedside formula, propose ventilator changes to reduce it, and discuss the limitations of using MP as a target.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ΔP = 25 − 10 = 15; MP ≈ 0.098 × RR × VT × (Ppeak − ½ΔP) = 0.098 × 20 × 0.5 × 22.5 ≈ 22 J/min.
- Component check: resistive 2.5 + elastic 3.75 + PEEP 5 = 11.25 cmH₂O·L/breath × 20 × 0.098 = 22.05 J/min.
- MP rises with VT, ΔP and flow (exponent 2), RR (exponent 1.4) and PEEP (linearly) → reduce VT, ΔP, RR and flow (e.g. VT 0.4 L, RR 14 → ~10.7 J/min).
- Increasing RR to compensate for low VT increases MP.
- Serpa Neto 2018: risk rose above ~17 J/min; +5 J/min → OR 1.06/1.10; association even with low VT (OR 1.70) – observational.
- No safe threshold for ARDS (12 J/min only in healthy pigs); no RCT has titrated MP; not a guideline target.
- MP does not indicate whether energy goes to healthy or collapsed regions; PEEP raises MP but may reduce ΔP and atelectrauma.

open.q: A patient on PSV 12 cmH₂O, PEEP 8 cmH₂O has ΔPocc −18 cmH₂O and a high P0.1. Estimate muscle pressure and dynamic transpulmonary driving pressure, interpret the findings in the context of P-SILI, and outline your management.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ΔP_aw = Ppeak − PEEP = 12 cmH₂O.
- P_mus ≈ −¾ × ΔPocc = 13.5 cmH₂O (> 10 → high effort).
- ΔP_L,dyn ≈ ΔP_aw − ⅔ × ΔPocc = 12 + 12 = 24 cmH₂O (> 20 → potentially injurious).
- P0.1 > 3.5 cmH₂O indicates high effort (Telias 2020: sens 80 %, spec 77 %).
- P-SILI mechanisms: large P_L swings, pendelluft (local strain), ↑ pulmonary vascular transmural pressure → oedema.
- Treat causes of high drive (acidosis, anxiety, delirium, hypoxaemia, fever); adjust support/sedation (more PS may reduce effort but not ΔP_L).
- Consider intubation with protective ventilation, ECCO₂R/ECMO if excessive drive persists; P-SILI remains a concept, beware premature intubation.

title: W13 · D5 – Ventilation in obstruction: auto-PEEP, external PEEP, permissive hypercapnia, status asthmaticus

questions.stem: A paralysed patient with COPD is ventilated with VT 500 mL, set PEEP 5 cmH₂O, Pplat 27 cmH₂O. An end-expiratory hold shows total PEEP of 15 cmH₂O. The intrinsic PEEP and the correct static compliance are:
options: 10 cmH₂O; 41.7 mL/cmH₂O
10 cmH₂O; 22.7 mL/cmH₂O
15 cmH₂O; 22.7 mL/cmH₂O
20 cmH₂O; 50 mL/cmH₂O
5 cmH₂O; 41.7 mL/cmH₂O
questions.expl: PEEPi = 15 − 5 = 10; C_stat = 500/(27 − 15) = 500/12 = 41.7 mL/cmH₂O. (22.7 = erroneous calculation with set PEEP: 500/22.)

questions.stem: Consequences of dynamic hyperinflation in a ventilated patient include:
options: Reduced venous return and hypotension
Reduced risk of barotrauma
Reduced work of triggering in assisted modes
Falsely elevated pulmonary artery occlusion pressure
questions.expl: B: hyperinflation increases the risk of barotrauma. C: work of triggering increases.

questions.stem: A patient with severe asthma becomes profoundly hypotensive shortly after intubation and manual bag ventilation at a high rate. The most appropriate immediate action is:
options: Increase PEEP to 15 cmH₂O
Give sodium bicarbonate
Start high-dose adrenaline infusion
Increase the respiratory rate to clear CO₂
Disconnect from the ventilator/bag for 30–60 s and reassess blood pressure
questions.expl: Dynamic hyperinflation; if BP does not rise, exclude tension pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Regarding measurement of intrinsic PEEP:
options: Expiratory flow failing to reach zero before the next breath suggests its presence.
Static PEEPi is measured by an end-expiratory occlusion in a passive patient.
Active expiratory muscle contraction can falsely increase measured PEEPi.
Dynamic PEEPi usually overestimates static PEEPi.
questions.expl: D: it underestimates.

questions.stem: In a ventilated patient with severe asthma, which single change most effectively reduces dynamic hyperinflation?
options: Increasing tidal volume while reducing the rate
Reducing minute ventilation by lowering the respiratory rate
Decreasing inspiratory flow
Increasing PEEP
Adding an end-inspiratory pause of 1 s
questions.expl: Tuxen 1987 – V_EI increased with minute ventilation; lower flow (C) and a pause (E) shorten Te.

questions.stem: In the study by Caramez et al. (CCM 2005) on PEEP in airway obstruction during controlled ventilation:
options: Paradoxical responses occurred only in COPD and never in asthma.
A paradoxical response with decreased plateau pressure and total PEEP was observed in some patients.
Routine external PEEP set at twice the measured PEEPi was proposed.
Baseline variables reliably predicted which patients would respond paradoxically.
questions.expl: B: 5/8. A: also in asthma. C: an empirical PEEP trial monitoring plateau pressure was proposed.

questions.stem: In Williams et al. (1992), the variable predictive of complications (hypotension, barotrauma) in ventilated asthmatics was:
options: Peak airway pressure > 50 cmH₂O
PaCO₂ > 80 mmHg
End-inspiratory lung volume above FRC ≥ 1.4 L
Respiratory rate > 20/min
Arterial pH < 7.20
questions.expl: Complications in 65 % with V_EI ≥ 1.4 L vs 0 % below this threshold.

questions.stem: Permissive hypercapnia:
options: Is a deliberate acceptance of elevated PaCO₂ to limit hyperinflation and lung stress.
Is relatively contraindicated in raised intracranial pressure.
May worsen pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular function.
Requires routine sodium bicarbonate to keep pH above 7.35.
questions.expl: D: bicarbonate is not routine; pH ≥ ~7.15–7.20 is commonly accepted.

questions.stem: A patient has a time constant of 1.5 s. Ventilator settings: RR 12/min, VT 500 mL, constant flow 60 L/min. The expiratory time and approximate fraction of VT exhaled are:
According to ERS/ATS 2017 guidelines on non-invasive ventilation:
options: The COPD recommendation is conditional with low certainty of evidence.
A recommendation for NIV in acute asthma was not made because of uncertain evidence.
Bilevel NIV is recommended for COPD exacerbation with pH ≤ 7.35.
NIV is suggested for hypercapnic COPD exacerbation without acidosis.
questions.expl: A: strong recommendation, high certainty. D: conditional recommendation against.

open.q: A patient with status asthmaticus is intubated and ventilated at RR 20/min, VT 500 mL, Ti 1 s; estimated τ is 1.5 s. Shortly afterwards BP falls to 70/40 mmHg. Outline your immediate management and how you would reset the ventilator, with calculations.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Suspect dynamic hyperinflation: ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → hypotension/PEA (Pepe & Marini).
- Disconnect from the ventilator for 30–60 s; if BP improves, DHI was the cause; if not, exclude tension pneumothorax and tube obstruction.
- Current Te = 3 − 1 = 2 s = 1.33τ → only ~74 % of VT exhaled.
- Reconnect with low RR (e.g. 12/min), high flow (60 L/min → Ti 0.5 s): Te 4.5 s = 3τ → ~95 % exhaled; minute ventilation 10 → 6 L/min.
- Reducing RR helps more than increasing flow; low VT (~6–8 mL/kg PBW), I:E ≥ 1:3.
- Monitor Pplat (< 30, ideally < 25), PEEPi (end-expiratory hold), BP; Ppeak reflects resistance.
- Accept permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥ ~7.15–7.20) unless raised ICP or RV failure; deep sedation ± NMB; fluids for hypovolaemia.
- Williams 1992: V_EI ≥ 1.4 L → complications in 65 %.

open.q: Explain why the effect of external PEEP differs between an assisted COPD patient with flow limitation and a patient with obstruction on controlled ventilation, and describe how you would titrate PEEP in each.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Expiratory flow limitation: collapsing airways behave like a "waterfall" – external PEEP below the critical closing pressure does not reduce expiratory flow or increase hyperinflation.
- In assisted modes external PEEP counterbalances PEEPi → less effort to trigger, ↓ work of breathing, fewer ineffective efforts.
- Practical: set external PEEP below measured PEEPi (~⅔–80 %) and check that Pplat/volume do not rise.
- Controlled ventilation: response unpredictable (Caramez 2005, 8 patients) – biphasic, classic overinflation or paradoxical (↓ FRC, ↓ Pplat, ↓ PEEP_tot in 5/8).
- No baseline variable predicted the response → empirical PEEP trial: keep PEEP if Pplat falls or is unchanged, withdraw if it rises.
- Measure PEEPi by end-expiratory hold in a passive patient; external PEEP is not contraindicated in asthma.

title: W13 · Saturday – weekly review: Mechanical ventilation – physics

questions.stem: A paralysed patient on volume control (constant flow 30 L/min, VT 400 mL, PEEP 10 cmH₂O, no intrinsic PEEP) has Ppeak 34 cmH₂O and Pplat 30 cmH₂O. Which is correct?
options: Static compliance 20 mL/cmH₂O; resistance 4 cmH₂O/L/s; driving pressure 20 cmH₂O
Static compliance 13.3 mL/cmH₂O; resistance 8 cmH₂O/L/s; driving pressure 30 cmH₂O
Static compliance 20 mL/cmH₂O; resistance 8 cmH₂O/L/s; driving pressure 20 cmH₂O
Static compliance 16.7 mL/cmH₂O; resistance 4 cmH₂O/L/s; driving pressure 24 cmH₂O
Static compliance 40 mL/cmH₂O; resistance 0.13 cmH₂O/L/s; driving pressure 10 cmH₂O

questions.stem: Regarding ventilation modes:
options: In PSV, breaths are patient-triggered, pressure-targeted and time-cycled.
