The usual aciclovir dose with normal renal function is 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Delay in aciclovir is the main modifiable determinant of poor outcome; start it empirically within hours of presentation, before MRI or LP results.
- B (True) – CSF HSV PCR in the first 72 h may be falsely negative; repeat 3–7 days later if HSE remains likely, continuing aciclovir meanwhile.
- C (False) – **MRI** (FLAIR/DWI hyperintensity of the medial temporal lobes and insula) is far more sensitive than CT, which is often normal early.
- D (True) – 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly for 14–21 days, reduced in renal impairment; ensure hydration to avoid crystal nephropathy.

**EDIC trap:** A negative day-1 PCR never justifies stopping aciclovir when the clinical picture fits.

**Ref:** Solomon et al., ABN/BIA viral encephalitis guidelines, J Infect 2012; Tunkel et al., IDSA encephalitis guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2008.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with a renal transplant, on tacrolimus and prednisolone, presents with 3 days of fever, headache, unsteadiness and new diplopia with a right facial palsy. CSF: WBC 450/µL (60 % neutrophils), protein 1.4 g/L, CSF/serum glucose ratio 0.35; Gram stain shows no organisms. Which empirical regimen should be started, together with dexamethasone?
options: Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin
Ceftriaxone plus ciprofloxacin
Ceftriaxone alone
Ceftriaxone plus high-dose amoxicillin
Liposomal amphotericin plus flucytosine
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Immunosuppression (and age > 50) is a risk factor for *Listeria monocytogenes*, which typically causes rhombencephalitis – brainstem signs, cranial nerve palsies, ataxia – and the Gram stain is often negative or misread. Cephalosporins have no activity against *Listeria*, so high-dose amoxicillin/ampicillin must be added to a third-generation cephalosporin (co-trimoxazole if severe penicillin allergy).

**Why not the others:**

- A – Vancomycin covers penicillin-resistant pneumococci but not *Listeria*.
- B – Ciprofloxacin is not a recommended anti-*Listeria* agent for meningitis.
- C – Ceftriaxone alone leaves *Listeria* uncovered.
- E – Amphotericin + flucytosine fits cryptococcal meningitis (lymphocytic CSF, raised opening pressure), not this neutrophilic picture.

**EDIC trap:** *Listeria* meningitis is treated for ≥ 21 days.

**Ref:** van de Beek et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016; Charlier et al., MONALISA, Lancet Infect Dis 2017.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 90 cells/µL) has a 3-week history of headache, night sweats and weight loss, and now a left sixth nerve palsy. Sodium is 127 mmol/L. CSF: lymphocytes 220/µL, protein 2.1 g/L, CSF/serum glucose ratio 0.3; Gram stain and cryptococcal antigen are negative. MRI shows basal meningeal enhancement and mild hydrocephalus. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis rapidly?
options: CSF India ink stain
Serum Toxoplasma IgG
CSF VDRL
CSF cytology for lymphoma
Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra on a large-volume CSF sample
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Subacute lymphocytic meningitis with very high protein, low glucose, basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, sixth nerve palsy and hyponatraemia in advanced HIV points to tuberculous meningitis. WHO recommends Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra as the initial CSF test (sensitivity improves with ≥ 6 mL of CSF); a negative result does not exclude TBM.

**Why not the others:**

- A – India ink is less sensitive than cryptococcal antigen, which is already negative.
- B – Serum *Toxoplasma* IgG shows prior exposure and does not diagnose meningitis; toxoplasmosis causes ring-enhancing lesions.
- C – CSF VDRL tests for neurosyphilis, which does not explain this subacute basal picture with hydrocephalus.
- D – CSF cytology for lymphoma has low sensitivity and is not the most likely diagnosis.

**EDIC trap:** In TBM, ART is deferred ~4–8 weeks (early ART increased severe adverse events), and adjunctive dexamethasone did not improve survival in HIV-positive adults (ACT HIV).

**Ref:** WHO consolidated TB guidelines, Module 3: diagnosis, 2024; Donovan et al., ACT HIV, N Engl J Med 2023.

title: Case-style practice · W03-D3 · Necrotising soft-tissue infection and toxic shock

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with diabetes presents with severe thigh pain, fever and hypotension 2 days after a minor abrasion. The overlying skin shows only mild erythema. Regarding suspected necrotising fasciitis:
options: Surgical exploration should not wait for cross-sectional imaging when clinical suspicion is high.
Crepitus is present in most patients at presentation.
Clindamycin is added to broad-spectrum therapy mainly for suppression of toxin production.
Near-normal overlying skin makes necrotising fasciitis unlikely.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Delay to debridement is the strongest modifiable predictor of death; imaging must not delay surgery in an unstable patient.
- B (False) – Crepitus and gas are **late** signs present in a minority – specific but insensitive.
- C (True) – Clindamycin inhibits ribosomal toxin synthesis and is unaffected by the inoculum (Eagle) effect; it is combined with a broad-spectrum β-lactam (piperacillin–tazobactam or a carbapenem) ± MRSA cover.
- D (False) – Infection spreads along the fascia beneath initially normal-looking skin; **pain out of proportion** to findings is the classic early clue.

**EDIC trap:** Hypotension plus disproportionate pain after minor trauma = NSTI until surgical exploration proves otherwise.

**Ref:** Stevens et al., IDSA SSTI guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2014; Sartelli et al., WSES/SIS-E consensus, World J Emerg Surg 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding toxic shock syndromes (TSS):
options: Blood cultures are positive more often in streptococcal than in staphylococcal TSS.
Desquamation, particularly of the palms and soles, typically appears 1–2 weeks after onset.
TSST-1 acts as a superantigen, cross-linking MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors outside the antigen-binding groove.
Positive blood cultures for S. aureus are required for the diagnosis of staphylococcal TSS.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Streptococcal TSS is bacteraemic in ~60% of cases, staphylococcal TSS in < 5%.
- B (True) – Late desquamation (palms and soles, 1–2 weeks after onset) is a CDC criterion for confirmed staphylococcal TSS.
- C (True) – TSST-1 is a superantigen that cross-links MHC class II and the TCR Vβ chain outside the antigen-binding groove, activating up to 20% of T cells non-specifically and producing a cytokine storm.
- D (False) – Staphylococcal TSS is toxin-mediated; the CDC definition requires fever, rash, hypotension, ≥ 3 organ systems and negative tests for alternatives – **not** positive *S. aureus* blood cultures.

**EDIC trap:** Negative blood cultures in a shocked woman with erythroderma favour staphylococcal TSS.

**Ref:** Lappin & Ferguson, Lancet Infect Dis 2009; CDC TSS (other than streptococcal) case definition 2011.

questions.stem: Regarding the classification and assessment of necrotising soft-tissue infection (NSTI):
options: Type 1 NSTI is polymicrobial with anaerobes and is typical of perineal (Fournier's) infection in diabetic patients.
Type 2 NSTI is most commonly caused by Clostridium perfringens.
A LRINEC score below 6 reliably excludes NSTI.
NSTI due to Vibrio vulnificus is associated with seawater exposure and chronic liver disease.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Type 1 (the most common) is polymicrobial – anaerobes, Enterobacterales, streptococci – and typical of Fournier's gangrene in diabetics.
- B (False) – Type 2 is monomicrobial, usually **group A streptococcus** (± *S. aureus*); clostridial myonecrosis is classed separately as gas gangrene (or with type 1).
- C (False) – LRINEC has poor sensitivity (~68% in meta-analysis) and must **not** be used to rule out NSTI.
- D (True) – *Vibrio vulnificus* (type 3, with *Aeromonas*) is linked to marine wounds, raw shellfish and cirrhosis; type 4 is fungal.

**EDIC trap:** Type 2 GAS NSTI affects healthy people of any age, often without a portal of entry.

**Ref:** Fernando et al., Ann Surg 2019; Stevens & Bryant, N Engl J Med 2017.

questions.stem: Concerning the diagnosis and treatment of necrotising fasciitis:
options: Gas in the soft tissues on CT is required to make the diagnosis.
Antibiotics alone are adequate for early type 1 infection in a haemodynamically stable patient.
Pain is usually proportionate to the visible skin changes.
Necrosis of muscle with intact fascia is the defining lesion.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Gas is absent in many cases; CT findings (fascial thickening, fluid) support but cannot exclude the diagnosis. Surgical exploration ("finger test": easy dissection, dishwater fluid, no bleeding) is diagnostic.
- B (False) – Surgical debridement is the cornerstone regardless of type or stability; antibiotics are adjunctive.
- C (False) – Pain is classically **out of proportion** to the visible skin changes.
- D (False) – Necrotising fasciitis is defined by necrosis of the superficial/deep **fascia**; myonecrosis may coexist but does not define it.

**EDIC trap:** Plan a second-look operation within 24 h.

**Ref:** Stevens & Bryant, N Engl J Med 2017; Sartelli et al., WSES/SIS-E consensus, World J Emerg Surg 2022.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents 3 days after septorhinoplasty with nasal packing in situ. She has a temperature of 39.6 °C, diffuse macular erythroderma, BP 78/40 mmHg, diarrhoea, confusion, creatine kinase 2400 U/L, creatinine 190 µmol/L and platelets 85 × 10⁹/L. Her conjunctivae are injected. Alongside fluid resuscitation, which is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: IV immunoglobulin as the sole specific treatment
Ceftriaxone, leaving the packing in place to protect the surgical result
CT of the sinuses before any antibiotic is given
Remove the nasal packing and give an anti-staphylococcal β-lactam plus clindamycin
Meropenem monotherapy
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Fever, erythroderma, shock and multi-organ involvement (GI, CNS, muscle, platelets, kidney) after nasal packing is staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome. Priorities: remove the toxin source and give a bactericidal anti-staphylococcal agent (flucloxacillin/cefazolin; vancomycin or linezolid if MRSA risk) plus a protein-synthesis inhibitor (clindamycin or linezolid) to suppress toxin production.

**Why not the others:**

- A – IVIG is an adjunct in refractory cases, not a substitute for source control and antibiotics.
- B – Leaving the packing leaves the toxin source in place; ceftriaxone also lacks an antitoxin effect.
- C – Delaying antibiotics for imaging is wrong in shock.
- E – Meropenem alone lacks an antitoxin effect and is unnecessarily broad.

**EDIC trap:** Non-menstrual TSS follows nasal packing, surgical wounds, burns.

**Ref:** Lappin & Ferguson, Lancet Infect Dis 2009; Stevens et al., IDSA SSTI guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2014.

title: Case-style practice · W03-D4 · Immunocompromised patient: neutropenia and HIV

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman on chemotherapy for breast cancer presents with a temperature of 38.6 °C, BP 84/50 mmHg and a neutrophil count of 0.2 × 10⁹/L. She has a tunnelled central venous catheter without signs of exit-site infection. Regarding her initial management:
options: An empirical antipseudomonal β-lactam should be given within 1 hour.
Febrile neutropenia is defined using a neutrophil count < 0.5 × 10⁹/L, or one expected to fall below this.
Vancomycin should be added routinely because she has a central venous catheter.
Given her septic shock, adding an aminoglycoside (or escalating to a carbapenem, depending on local resistance) is reasonable.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – An antipseudomonal β-lactam (piperacillin–tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem) within 1 h; delays increase mortality.
- B (True) – Standard ESMO/IDSA definition: ANC < 0.5 × 10⁹/L or expected to fall below this within 48 h, with fever ≥ 38.3 °C (or ≥ 38.0 °C for 1 h).
- C (False) – Glycopeptides are added only for specific indications (suspected serious catheter-related infection, skin/soft-tissue infection, pneumonia, MRSA colonisation, haemodynamic instability) – not for the mere presence of a CVC.
- D (True) – Septic shock is a complicated presentation: ECIL-4 recommends a **de-escalation** approach (carbapenem, or β-lactam + aminoglycoside, ± anti-MRSA cover), narrowing at 72–96 h.

**EDIC trap:** The line need not be removed immediately unless tunnel/pocket infection or *S. aureus*, *Pseudomonas* or *Candida* bacteraemia.

**Ref:** Averbuch et al., ECIL-4, Haematologica 2013; Klastersky et al., ESMO guideline, Ann Oncol 2016.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with HIV infection after presenting with weight loss and painful swallowing; her CD4 count is 260 cells/µL and HIV viral load 85 000 copies/mL. She has not yet started antiretroviral therapy, and further investigations are under way. Which one of the following conditions, if present, would by itself establish a diagnosis of AIDS?
options: Multidermatomal herpes zoster
Oral hairy leukoplakia
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2
Oesophageal candidiasis
Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura
questions.expl:
**Why D:** With a CD4 count > 200 cells/µL, AIDS (CDC stage 3) is defined by an AIDS-defining illness. Candidiasis of the oesophagus, trachea, bronchi or lungs is AIDS-defining; oral candidiasis is not. Odynophagia and weight loss fit oesophageal candidiasis.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Multidermatomal herpes zoster is a "category B" indicator condition, not AIDS-defining.
- B – Oral hairy leukoplakia is a category B condition.
- C – Cervical dysplasia/carcinoma in situ is category B; only invasive cervical carcinoma is AIDS-defining.
- E – ITP is an HIV-associated condition but not AIDS-defining.

**EDIC trap:** AIDS-defining conditions relevant to ICU include *Pneumocystis* pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, tuberculosis, recurrent bacterial pneumonia and CMV retinitis.

**Ref:** Selik et al., CDC revised surveillance case definition, MMWR Recomm Rep 2014.

title: Case-style practice · W03-D5 · Infection prevention and control

questions.stem: Regarding selective digestive decontamination (SDD) in ventilated ICU patients:
options: It aims to eradicate carriage of aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, S. aureus and yeasts while preserving the anaerobic flora.
It uses non-absorbable antimicrobials applied as an oropharyngeal paste and an enteral suspension.
SuDDICU (JAMA 2022) showed a significant reduction in hospital mortality.
Enteral vancomycin is a routine component in all ICUs.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SDD targets aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, *S. aureus* and yeasts while sparing anaerobes, which maintain colonisation resistance.
- B (True) – Non-absorbable topical agents (classically colistin, tobramycin and amphotericin B/nystatin) are given as oropharyngeal paste and enteral suspension throughout ventilation, plus a short IV cephalosporin course.
- C (False) – SuDDICU (5982 patients, 19 Australian ICUs) found hospital mortality 27.0% vs 29.1%, OR 0.91 (0.82–1.02) – **not significant**.
- D (False) – Enteral vancomycin is added only in units with endemic MRSA, not routinely.

**EDIC trap:** The pooled evidence (Hammond 2022) suggests a small benefit that depends on the IV component.

**Ref:** Myburgh et al., SuDDICU, JAMA 2022; Hammond et al., JAMA 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding hand hygiene, decontamination of equipment and central-line infection programmes:
options: "Before an aseptic procedure" and "after body fluid exposure risk" are two of the WHO five moments for hand hygiene.
In the Spaulding classification, items that enter sterile tissue or the vascular system require sterilisation.
An alcohol-based hand rub is preferred to soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.
The Matching Michigan programme in English ICUs targeted central venous catheter–associated bloodstream infection.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – The WHO five moments: before touching a patient, before a clean/aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, after touching patient surroundings.
- B (True) – Spaulding: critical items (sterile tissue, vascular system) → sterilisation; semi-critical (mucous membranes, e.g. laryngoscope blades, bronchoscopes) → high-level disinfection; non-critical (intact skin) → low-level disinfection/cleaning.
- C (False) – Visibly soiled hands (and *C. difficile*/norovirus exposure) require **soap and water**; alcohol rub is preferred otherwise.
- D (True) – Matching Michigan adapted the Keystone CVC bundle to 215 English ICUs; CVC-BSI rates fell, partly in line with a pre-existing downward trend.

**EDIC trap:** Alcohol does not kill *C. difficile* spores.

**Ref:** WHO guidelines on hand hygiene in health care, 2009; Bion et al., Matching Michigan, BMJ Qual Saf 2013.

questions.stem: Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 in England, which of the following must be notified by the attending clinician on clinical suspicion?
options: Legionnaires' disease
Botulism
Uncomplicated seasonal influenza A in an adult
Invasive group A streptococcal disease
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Legionnaires' disease is listed in Schedule 1.
- B (True) – Botulism is listed in Schedule 1.
- C (False) – Seasonal influenza is monitored through laboratory surveillance and is **not** clinician-notifiable.
- D (True) – Invasive group A streptococcal disease (and scarlet fever) is notifiable.

Schedule 1 also includes acute meningitis, acute encephalitis, meningococcal septicaemia, tuberculosis, tetanus, HUS, measles, diphtheria and viral haemorrhagic fevers. Notification is on **clinical suspicion**, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. Other European countries have analogous national lists under the EU decision on communicable disease surveillance.

**Ref:** Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, SI 2010/659 (as amended); UKHSA, Notifiable diseases and causative organisms: how to report, 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding prevention of device-associated infection in the ICU:
options: 2 % chlorhexidine in 70 % alcohol is preferred to povidone-iodine for skin antisepsis before CVC insertion.
The subclavian site is associated with a lower risk of catheter-related bloodstream infection than the femoral site.
Routine replacement of CVCs every 7 days reduces catheter-related bloodstream infection.
The risk of bacteriuria with an indwelling urinary catheter is roughly 3–7 % per day of catheterisation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – In CLEAN, chlorhexidine–alcohol reduced CRBSI by about 80% vs povidone iodine–alcohol (0.28 vs 1.32/1000 catheter-days, HR 0.21).
- B (True) – In 3SITES the subclavian site had the lowest rate of CRBSI + symptomatic DVT (1.5 vs 4.6/1000 catheter-days for femoral), at the cost of more pneumothorax.
- C (False) – Scheduled replacement (over a guidewire or at a new site) does **not** reduce infection and adds mechanical risk; remove catheters when no longer needed.
- D (True) – Bacteriuria risk is roughly 3–7% per catheter-day, which is why daily review and early removal are the key CAUTI-prevention measures.

**EDIC trap:** Keystone's fifth bundle element is removal of unnecessary lines, not routine replacement.

**Ref:** Mimoz et al., CLEAN, Lancet 2015; Parienti et al., 3SITES, N Engl J Med 2015; Gould et al., CDC CAUTI guideline 2009 (updated 2019).

questions.stem: Regarding the evidence on selective decontamination strategies:
options: SDD is primarily intended for patients expected to require mechanical ventilation for more than 48 hours.
Selective oropharyngeal decontamination (SOD) omits the enteral component of SDD.
A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis found SDD to be associated with lower hospital mortality in ventilated patients.
SDD markedly increases the incidence of Clostridioides difficile infection.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Trials enrolled patients expected to be ventilated beyond the next day or two (SuDDICU: > 48 h).
- B (True) – SOD uses only the oropharyngeal paste, without the enteral suspension or IV component; de Smet (NEJM 2009) compared SDD, SOD and standard care.
- C (True) – Hammond et al. (32 RCTs, 24,389 patients) estimated hospital mortality RR 0.91 (95% CrI 0.82–0.99), moderate certainty.
- D (False) – *C. difficile* infection is not increased; SuDDICU's ecological analysis showed non-inferiority for *C. difficile*.

**EDIC trap:** SuDDICU itself was neutral, unit-level non-inferiority for resistant organisms was not confirmed, and data from high-resistance settings (R-GNOSIS) are not reassuring.

**Ref:** Hammond et al., JAMA 2022; Myburgh et al., SuDDICU, JAMA 2022; de Smet et al., N Engl J Med 2009.

title: Case-style practice · W04-D2 · Fluid responsiveness

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man on day 2 after laparotomy for faecal peritonitis is ventilated on pressure support 10 cmH2O and PEEP 6 cmH2O, triggering every breath at 24/min. He is in sinus rhythm with MAP 61 mmHg on low-dose noradrenaline. Which finding best indicates that he will increase his cardiac output with a fluid bolus?
options: Pulse pressure variation of 16 % on the radial arterial line
Central venous pressure of 4 mmHg
Inferior vena cava collapsibility of 50 % on ultrasound
A small left-ventricular end-diastolic area on transthoracic echocardiography
A 15 % rise in left-ventricular outflow tract VTI during passive leg raising
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Passive leg raising transfers ~300 mL of venous blood from the legs and splanchnic bed and, when measured with real-time CO or LVOT VTI (threshold ≈ 10 %), predicts fluid responsiveness regardless of spontaneous breathing, arrhythmia or tidal volume (pooled AUROC 0.95). A 15 % rise in VTI is well above the threshold and above the ~12 % precision limit of echo VTI.

**Why not the others:**

- A – PPV is valid only with fully controlled ventilation, VT ≥ 8 mL/kg, sinus rhythm and a closed chest; triggering every breath invalidates it.
- B – CVP is a static measure and predicts responsiveness poorly, even when low.
- C – IVC collapsibility during spontaneous or assisted breathing has only modest accuracy and is confounded by inspiratory effort.
- D – LV end-diastolic area is a static preload index with poor predictive value.

**Ref:** Monnet X, et al. Passive leg raising for predicting fluid responsiveness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1935–1947. Monnet X, Shi R, Teboul JL. Prediction of fluid responsiveness. What's new? *Ann Intensive Care* 2022;12:46.

title: Case-style practice · W04-D3 · Haemodynamic monitoring

questions.stem: Regarding interpretation of the arterial pressure waveform in an ICU patient:
options: The maximum slope of the systolic upstroke (dP/dt max) from a peripheral line is a rough index of LV contractility but is influenced by arterial compliance.
A pulse pressure variation of 18 % in a patient ventilated with a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg who is triggering breaths reliably indicates preload responsiveness.
Systolic pressure measured in the radial artery is normally lower than in the ascending aorta.
A dicrotic notch positioned low on the descending limb suggests a high systemic vascular resistance.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Peripheral dP/dt max tracks LV contractility directionally but is affected by vascular tone, compliance and pulse amplification.
- B (False) – With triggering and VT 6 mL/kg PPV is uninterpretable – irregular efforts can create false positives and low VT false negatives; use PLR or EEO.
- C (False) – Distal pulse amplification by reflected waves makes radial systolic pressure **higher** than aortic; MAP is similar.
- D (False) – A low dicrotic notch suggests vasodilatation and low SVR; a high notch suggests vasoconstriction.

**Ref:** Saugel B, et al. Cardiac output estimation using pulse wave analysis. *Br J Anaesth* 2021;126:67–76. Michard F, et al. Applicability of pulse pressure variation. *Crit Care* 2015;19:144.

questions.stem: Concerning variables obtained with a pulmonary artery catheter:
options: Thermodilution cardiac output is a measured variable, calculated from the area under the temperature–time curve (Stewart–Hamilton equation).
Pulmonary vascular resistance is calculated from mean pulmonary artery pressure, PAOP and cardiac output.
Mixed venous oxygen saturation is measured from blood sampled at the catheter tip in the pulmonary artery.
Oxygen consumption can be derived (reverse Fick) from cardiac output and the arterial and mixed venous oxygen contents.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Thermodilution CO is measured with the Stewart–Hamilton equation (CO inversely proportional to the area under the curve); accuracy falls with severe TR, shunts and very low output.
- B (True) – PVR = 80 × (mPAP − PAOP) / CO in dyn·s·cm⁻⁵, or without the factor 80 in Wood units.
- C (True) – SvO2 comes from blood sampled at the PA tip or from fibreoptic oximetry – true mixed venous blood.
- D (True) – Reverse Fick: VO2 = CO × (CaO2 − CvO2) × 10; likewise DO2 = CO × CaO2 × 10.

**EDIC trap:** Measured: pressures, PAOP, thermodilution CO, SvO2. Derived: CI, SV, SVR, PVR, DO2, VO2.

**Ref:** Rajaram SS, et al. Pulmonary artery catheters for adult patients in intensive care. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2013;(2):CD003408. Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: Regarding oesophageal Doppler monitoring:
options: It measures blood flow velocity in the descending thoracic aorta and estimates stroke volume using a nomogram-derived aortic cross-sectional area.
A corrected flow time (FTc) below 330 ms is specific for hypovolaemia.
Its velocity measurement is accurate regardless of the angle between the beam and the direction of flow.
It is poorly tolerated by awake patients and is used mainly in sedated, intubated patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Only descending aortic flow (~70 % of CO) is measured and scaled by a nomogram; altered flow distribution (cross-clamp, pregnancy) causes error.
- B (False) – A short FTc reflects low preload but also high afterload (vasoconstriction, mitral stenosis); interpret it with the SV response to fluid.
- C (False) – The Doppler equation contains cos θ; angles > 20° underestimate velocity, so probe position matters.
- D (True) – It is poorly tolerated awake and suits theatre and sedated, intubated ICU patients.

**Ref:** Singer M. Oesophageal Doppler. *Curr Opin Crit Care* 2009;15:244–248. Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with septic shock is ventilated and triggering the ventilator. She is in permanent atrial fibrillation (ventricular rate 110–140/min) and echocardiography shows severe tricuspid regurgitation with a dilated right ventricle. She has received 2 L of crystalloid and remains on noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min. You want to track her response to fluid and dobutamine. Which method is most appropriate?
options: Serial transthoracic echocardiographic LVOT VTI averaged over several beats
Pulse pressure variation from the radial arterial line
Bolus thermodilution via a pulmonary artery catheter
Trend of central venous pressure
Uncalibrated pulse-contour analysis of beat-to-beat stroke volume variation
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Echocardiographic LVOT VTI (× LVOT area = SV), **averaged over 5–10 cardiac cycles**, copes with the irregular rhythm and can be repeated after each fluid bolus or dobutamine change. Because LVOT area is constant, changes in VTI alone track changes in stroke volume.

**Why not the others:**

- B – PPV requires sinus rhythm and controlled ventilation; both conditions fail here.
- C – Severe TR recirculates the cold indicator and makes PAC thermodilution unreliable.
- D – CVP is not a measure of flow and is raised by TR.
- E – SVV has the same limitations as PPV, and uncalibrated pulse contour is unreliable with high-dose vasopressors.

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815. Vieillard-Baron A, et al. A decade of progress in critical care echocardiography. *Intensive Care Med* 2019;45:770–788.

questions.stem: Regarding the physics of invasive arterial pressure measurement:
options: An underdamped system overestimates systolic and underestimates diastolic pressure.
Long, compliant tubing lowers the natural frequency of the system.
If the transducer is raised 10 cm above the phlebostatic axis, the displayed pressure will be about 7 mmHg lower than the true value.
A fast-flush test producing one or two oscillations before returning to baseline indicates appropriate damping.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Resonance (ringing) exaggerates systolic peaks and lowers diastolic pressure; MAP is relatively preserved.
- B (True) – Natural frequency falls with long, compliant tubing, air bubbles and extra stopcocks, and rises with short, stiff, wide-bore tubing.
- C (True) – 10 cmH2O ≈ 7.4 mmHg; levelling to the phlebostatic axis is distinct from zeroing to atmosphere.
- D (True) – 1.5–2 oscillations indicate optimal damping; none suggests overdamping, many suggest underdamping.

**Ref:** Saugel B, et al. How to measure blood pressure using an arterial catheter: a systematic 5-step approach. *Crit Care* 2020;24:172.

questions.stem: Which of the following typically raise the pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP)?
options: Severe idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension with a normal left heart
Acute massive pulmonary embolism
Acute severe mitral regurgitation
Aggressive diuresis in a patient with normal cardiac function
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Pulmonary arterial hypertension is pre-capillary: high mPAP and PVR with PAOP ≤ 15 mmHg.
- B (False) – PE is a pre-capillary obstruction; PAOP is normal or low because LV filling falls.
- C (True) – Acute severe MR produces large v waves and a raised PAOP.
- D (False) – Diuresis lowers PAOP.

**EDIC trap:** High PEEP or a catheter tip outside West zone 3 can falsely elevate PAOP.

**Ref:** Humbert M, et al. 2022 ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guidelines. *Eur Heart J* 2022;43:3618–3731. Magder S. *Chest* 2017;151:908–916.

title: Case-style practice · W04-D4 · Lactate

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin presents with vomiting, AKI (creatinine 520 µmol/L), pH 6.98 and lactate 18 mmol/L, with normal blood pressure. Regarding lactate and lactic acidosis:
options: Hyperlactataemia in sepsis always indicates tissue hypoxia.
Metformin accumulation can cause type B lactic acidosis.
The kidney is the main organ of lactate clearance.
D-lactate (e.g. in short-bowel syndrome) is detected by standard blood gas lactate analysers.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Much septic hyperlactataemia comes from β2-stimulated aerobic glycolysis and reduced hepatic clearance; lactate marks severity, not proof of anaerobiosis.
- B (True) – Metformin inhibits mitochondrial respiration and hepatic gluconeogenesis from lactate; accumulation in AKI causes MALA, and EXTRIP recommends dialysis in severe cases (e.g. lactate > 20 mmol/L, pH ≤ 7.0).
- C (False) – The liver clears ~60–70 % (Cori cycle); the kidneys ~20–30 %.
- D (False) – Analysers use L-lactate oxidase; D-lactic acidosis causes a raised anion gap and encephalopathy with a normal measured lactate.

**Ref:** Garcia-Alvarez M, Marik P, Bellomo R. Sepsis-associated hyperlactatemia. *Crit Care* 2014;18:503. Calello DP, et al. EXTRIP metformin. *Crit Care Med* 2015;43:1716–1730. Kraut JA, Madias NE. Lactic acidosis. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:2309–2319.

title: Case-style practice · W05-D1 · Acid–base: anion gap and blood gas analysis

questions.stem: Which of the following typically cause a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis?
options: Ureterosigmoidostomy
Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis
Toluene inhalation (glue sniffing)
Moderate chronic kidney disease (GFR 20–50 mL/min)
questions.expl:
- A (True) – with urine in the colon, Cl⁻ is absorbed in exchange for HCO₃⁻ (and NH₄⁺ is reabsorbed), causing a hyperchloraemic acidosis.
- B (True) – impaired distal H⁺ secretion gives a urine pH > 5.5 and a positive urinary anion gap, often with hypokalaemia.
- C (True) – toluene is metabolised to hippuric acid; hippurate is rapidly excreted in urine with Na⁺/K⁺, so the AG is often normal and hypokalaemia is prominent.
- D (True) – moderate CKD reduces ammoniagenesis, causing a hyperchloraemic acidosis. The gap rises only when GFR falls further and phosphate and sulphate accumulate.

**EDIC trap:** CKD moves from a normal-AG to a high-AG acidosis as GFR declines.

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Madias NE, Metabolic acidosis: pathophysiology, diagnosis and management, Nat Rev Nephrol 2010;6:274–285; Berend K, de Vries AP, Gans RO, N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445.

questions.stem: A patient is cooled to 32 °C. Blood gases are analysed in a standard analyser. Regarding blood gas analysis:
options: The PaO2 reported at 37 °C is higher than the true in vivo value at 32 °C.
Alpha-stat management uses temperature-corrected values.
pH-stat management requires increasing minute ventilation to remove CO2.
A sample with a very high leucocyte count left at room temperature for an hour will show a falsely high PaO2.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – when blood is warmed to 37 °C in the analyser, gas solubility falls and partial pressures rise, so uncorrected PO₂ and PCO₂ overestimate in vivo values in hypothermia.
- B (False) – alpha-stat uses values measured at 37 °C (**uncorrected**), preserving the ionisation state of histidine imidazole groups.
- C (False) – pH-stat targets a temperature-corrected PaCO₂ of ~5.3 kPa, i.e. relative hypercapnia, achieved by adding CO₂ or **reducing** ventilation.
- D (False) – metabolising leucocytes (and platelets) consume O₂ in the syringe ("leucocyte larceny"), so PaO₂ is falsely **low**.

**EDIC trap:** alpha-stat = uncorrected (37 °C) values; pH-stat = temperature-corrected values.

**Ref:** Ashwood ER, Kost G, Kenny M, Clin Chem 1983;29:1877–1885; Fox MJ, Brody JS, Weintraub LR, Am J Med 1979;67:742–746.

questions.stem: Regarding causes and interpretation of a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis:
options: Pyroglutamic acidosis (5-oxoprolinuria) may occur with regular paracetamol in malnourished patients, especially when combined with flucloxacillin.
Propylene glycol, a solvent in high-dose IV lorazepam infusions, can cause a raised anion gap and osmolar gap.
Hypoalbuminaemia lowers the anion gap and can mask a raised-gap acidosis unless the gap is corrected.
Large-volume 0.9 % saline administration causes a raised anion gap acidosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – glutathione depletion leads to 5-oxoproline accumulation, and flucloxacillin inhibits 5-oxoprolinase; malnutrition, sepsis and CKD increase the risk.
- B (True) – propylene glycol is metabolised to L- and D-lactate, causing a raised anion gap together with a raised osmolar gap.
- C (True) – albumin is the main unmeasured anion; corrected AG ≈ AG + 0.25 × (40 − albumin g/L).
- D (False) – saline lowers the SID through hyperchloraemia, causing a **normal** anion gap acidosis.

**Ref:** Berend K et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445; Emmett M, Acetaminophen toxicity and 5-oxoproline (pyroglutamic acid): a tale of two cycles, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2014;9:191–200.

title: Case-style practice · W05-D2 · Stewart approach to acid–base

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis has: pH 7.40, PaCO2 5.3 kPa, HCO3⁻ 24 mmol/L, Na⁺ 138, K⁺ 4.0, Cl⁻ 110, lactate 1.0 mmol/L, albumin 18 g/L. Regarding her acid–base status:
options: Her apparent strong ion difference is about 31 mEq/L, which is reduced.
Her low albumin produces a metabolic alkalosis that offsets an acidifying process.
The normal pH and bicarbonate exclude a metabolic acid–base disorder.
Infusing 20 % albumin is the appropriate treatment for this acid–base disturbance.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SIDa = (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + lactate) = 142 − 111 = 31 mEq/L (normal ~40–42, ignoring Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺): a hyperchloraemic (low-SID) acidosis.
- B (True) – albumin is the main component of ATOT; a low ATOT is alkalinising (~+6–7 mmol/L BE at 18 g/L), which is why her pH is normal.
- C (False) – two opposing metabolic disorders cancel out; Stewart or albumin-corrected anion gap analysis reveals them.
- D (False) – acid–base values are not a target for albumin; treat the cause (chloride load, underlying illness).

**EDIC trap:** a normal pH and HCO₃⁻ ≠ normal acid–base status in hypoalbuminaemia (Fencl: ~1/6 of ICU patients).

**Ref:** Kellum JA, Determinants of blood pH in health and disease, Crit Care 2000;4:6–14; Fencl V et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2000;162:2246–2251.

questions.stem: In the Stewart (physicochemical) approach:
options: Bicarbonate concentration is an independent variable.
The total concentration of weak acids (ATOT), mainly albumin and phosphate, is an independent variable.
Lactate is a dependent variable.
The hydroxide ion concentration is an independent variable.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – bicarbonate is a **dependent** variable, determined by PaCO₂, SID and ATOT.
- B (True) – ATOT (mainly albumin and phosphate) is one of the three independent variables, with PaCO₂ and SID.
- C (False) – lactate is a strong (fully dissociated) anion and therefore a component of the SID: it changes the independent variables rather than being determined by them.
- D (False) – OH⁻, like H⁺, HCO₃⁻, A⁻ and CO₃²⁻, is a dependent variable.

**Ref:** Stewart PA, Modern quantitative acid–base chemistry, Can J Physiol Pharmacol 1983;61:1444–1461; Kellum JA, Crit Care 2000;4:6–14.

title: Case-style practice · W06-D1 · Hyponatraemia

questions.stem: Which of the following typically produce hyponatraemia with a normal or raised (not low) serum osmolality?
options: Hyperglycaemia of 40 mmol/L
Repeated doses of IV mannitol
Severe hypertriglyceridaemia measured by an indirect ion-selective electrode
Primary (psychogenic) polydipsia
questions.expl:
- A (True) – without insulin, glucose is an effective osmole that draws water out of cells (translocational, hypertonic hyponatraemia). Na⁺ falls by ~1.6–2.4 mmol/L for each 5.5 mmol/L rise in glucose, i.e. by ~10–15 mmol/L at 40 mmol/L.
- B (True) – mannitol is also an effective osmole. It causes hyponatraemia with normal or high measured osmolality and a raised osmolar gap.
- C (True) – this is pseudohyponatraemia: lipids or paraproteins reduce the plasma water fraction, so an indirect ISE (laboratory analyser) underestimates Na⁺. A direct ISE (blood gas analyser) gives the true value, and osmolality is normal.
- D (False) – primary polydipsia causes **hypotonic** hyponatraemia with maximally dilute urine (U-osm ≤ 100 mOsm/kg).

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (and Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47).

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman collapses with a generalised seizure after a marathon. Serum sodium is 118 mmol/L and she remains drowsy (GCS 11). Regarding her immediate treatment:
options: 150 mL of 3 % saline over 20 minutes is appropriate, repeated (up to twice) until sodium has risen by about 5 mmol/L.
Fluid restriction alone is the appropriate first-line treatment.
Tolvaptan is recommended for severe symptoms.
1 L of 0.9 % saline over an hour is the preferred initial therapy.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – exercise-associated hyponatraemia with a seizure and reduced consciousness is an emergency. Give 150 mL of 3 % saline over 20 min (100 mL boluses in some EAH protocols), recheck Na⁺ and repeat until it has risen by ~5 mmol/L, which usually improves symptoms.
- B (False) – fluid restriction is far too slow with severe symptoms; it suits asymptomatic EAH or chronic SIAD.
- C (False) – vaptans act slowly and unpredictably and are not recommended for severe symptoms.
- D (False) – isotonic saline barely raises Na⁺ and, while non-osmotic ADH release persists (as in EAH), it can even lower it.

**EDIC trap:** SALSA showed that rapid intermittent boluses are as safe as a slow continuous infusion, with less need for re-lowering.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (and Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47); Baek SH et al. (SALSA), JAMA Intern Med 2021;181:81–92; Hew-Butler T et al., Clin J Sport Med 2015;25:303–320.

questions.stem: Regarding definitions and safe correction of hyponatraemia (European guideline):
options: Profound hyponatraemia is defined as a serum sodium below 130 mmol/L.
Hyponatraemia is classified as chronic if documented to have lasted ≥ 48 hours or if the duration is unknown.
Hypokalaemia, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition and liver disease increase the risk of osmotic demyelination.
If sodium has been overcorrected, re-lowering with desmopressin and 5 % dextrose is contraindicated.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – mild is 130–135, moderate 125–129 and profound < 125 mmol/L.
- B (True) – hyponatraemia is chronic if it has lasted ≥ 48 h, and when the duration is unknown it is treated as chronic.
- C (True) – hypokalaemia, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition and liver disease (and Na⁺ ≤ 105 mmol/L) lower the threshold for osmotic demyelination. The usual limits are ≤ 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h and ≤ 8 mmol/L per further 24 h; aim for ~8 mmol/L/24 h in high-risk patients.
- D (False) – active re-lowering is recommended if the limit is exceeded: stop active treatment and give 10 mL/kg of electrolyte-free water (5 % glucose) over 1 h ± desmopressin 2 µg IV.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (and Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47); Sterns RH, Disorders of plasma sodium, N Engl J Med 2015;372:55–65.

title: Case-style practice · W06-D2 · Magnesium disorders

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman who has taken omeprazole 40 mg daily for 6 years is admitted with muscle cramps and carpopedal spasm. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L despite a week of oral supplements, corrected calcium is 1.85 mmol/L, QTc is 560 ms, and the monitor shows self-terminating runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: IV calcium gluconate 10 %, repeated until the QTc normalises
IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10–15 minutes
IV potassium chloride 40 mmol over 1 hour as the sole treatment
IV amiodarone 300 mg
Oral alfacalcidol
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Long-term PPI therapy impairs active intestinal magnesium absorption (TRPM6/7) and causes severe hypomagnesaemia. This in turn causes refractory hypokalaemia (ROMK-mediated renal K⁺ wasting) and hypocalcaemia (reduced PTH secretion and end-organ resistance). Torsades-type polymorphic VT with a long QT is treated with MgSO₄ 2 g (≈ 8 mmol) IV, whatever the serum Mg²⁺; potassium and calcium will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

**Why not the others:**
- A – calcium does not treat torsades, and the hypocalcaemia will not correct while Mg²⁺ is low.
- C – KCl alone will not correct the K⁺ while magnesium depletion keeps the kidney wasting K⁺, and it does not stop torsades.
- D – amiodarone prolongs the QT and is contraindicated in torsades de pointes.
- E – alfacalcidol acts over days and does not address the magnesium-driven hypocalcaemia or the arrhythmia.

**Ref:** Soar J, Böttiger BW, Carli P, et al. ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110769; Hess MW, et al., Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2012;36:405–413.

title: Case-style practice · W06-D3 · Refeeding, phosphate and calcium

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa (BMI 13 kg/m²) was admitted to ICU after a collapse. Nasogastric feeding was started at 25 kcal/kg/day. On day 3 she is tachycardic and weak with new ankle oedema; phosphate is 0.28 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L and magnesium 0.50 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Reduce the feed to about 10 kcal/kg/day, give IV phosphate, potassium and magnesium with thiamine, then increase feeding slowly
Stop all feeding for 48 hours until the electrolytes have normalised
Switch to parenteral nutrition at the same caloric target
Continue the current feed and give oral phosphate supplements only
Give furosemide for the oedema and continue the current feed
questions.expl:
**Why A:** This is refeeding syndrome: an insulin-driven intracellular shift of phosphate, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ with Na⁺ and water retention (oedema, tachycardia). A BMI of 13 alone puts her at high risk by NICE (which suggests even 5 kcal/kg/day if BMI < 14). Reduce energy delivery rather than stopping it, replace electrolytes IV with cardiac monitoring, give thiamine and B vitamins, then advance feeding gradually over 4–7 days. In the Doig trial, protocolised caloric restriction improved 60-day survival (a secondary outcome).

**Why not the others:**
- B – stopping all feeding prolongs starvation; the evidence supports restricting energy, not stopping it.
- C – parenteral nutrition at the same target causes the same insulin-driven shift.
- D – oral phosphate alone is inadequate for a level < 0.3 mmol/L, and the feed rate perpetuates the problem.
- E – furosemide worsens the hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, and continuing the feed sustains the refeeding.

**Ref:** da Silva JSV, et al. ASPEN consensus recommendations for refeeding syndrome, Nutr Clin Pract 2020;35:178–195; Doig GS, et al., Lancet Respir Med 2015;3:943–952; NICE CG32 (2006, updated 2017).

questions.stem: Which of the following can cause hypercalcaemia?
options: Long-term lithium therapy
Vitamin A toxicity
Sarcoidosis
Milk-alkali syndrome
questions.expl:
- A (True) – lithium raises the set-point of the calcium-sensing receptor and causes PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia.
- B (True) – vitamin A and other retinoids stimulate osteoclastic bone resorption.
- C (True) – granulomas express 1α-hydroxylase and produce calcitriol, which causes PTH-suppressed hypercalcaemia that responds to glucocorticoids.
- D (True) – excess calcium with absorbable alkali (e.g. calcium carbonate) causes hypercalcaemia, metabolic alkalosis and AKI.

**EDIC trap:** primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy cause ~90 % of cases. Thiazides, thyrotoxicosis, immobilisation and adrenal insufficiency are other causes.

**Ref:** Minisola S, et al. The diagnosis and management of hypercalcaemia, BMJ 2015;350:h2723; Walker MD, Shane E. Hypercalcemia: a review, JAMA 2022;328:1624–1636.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with squamous cell lung carcinoma presents with confusion and polyuria. Corrected calcium is 3.6 mmol/L, PTH suppressed, PTH-related peptide raised, eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m². After 24 hours and 4 L of IV 0.9 % saline his calcium is 3.3 mmol/L and he remains drowsy. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Furosemide 80 mg IV 6-hourly
Prednisolone 40 mg daily
Urgent haemodialysis
Subcutaneous calcitonin as the sole long-term therapy
IV zoledronic acid
questions.expl:
**Why E:** This is PTHrP-mediated humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy that remains symptomatic after rehydration, so it needs an IV bisphosphonate. Zoledronic acid 4 mg is the most potent; adjust the dose or avoid it in severe renal impairment. The Endocrine Society 2023 guideline suggests an IV bisphosphonate or denosumab, and denosumab is preferred when the disease is bisphosphonate-refractory or renal impairment is severe.

**Why not the others:**
- A – loop diuretics are used only for volume overload after rehydration, not to lower calcium.
- B – glucocorticoids are for calcitriol-mediated causes (lymphoma, granulomatous disease), not PTHrP.
- C – dialysis is reserved for severe hypercalcaemia with renal failure or neurological compromise that does not respond to treatment.
- D – calcitonin acts within hours but tachyphylaxis develops within 48 h, so it is a bridge, not long-term therapy.

**Ref:** El-Hajj Fuleihan G, et al. Treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy in adults: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108:507–528; Walker MD, Shane E, JAMA 2022;328:1624–1636.

title: Case-style practice · W07-D2 · Mechanical circulatory support

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a continuous-flow left ventricular assist device (LVAD), implanted as destination therapy, is admitted with dizziness. Regarding LVAD patients:
options: A palpable pulse may be weak or absent, and blood pressure is best measured with a Doppler probe or arterial line.
Right ventricular failure is a major early complication after LVAD implantation.
Hypovolaemia can cause "suction events", in which the LV collapses onto the inflow cannula and provokes ventricular arrhythmias.
Chest compressions are absolutely contraindicated if the patient is unresponsive with no evidence of device flow.
questions.expl: A – continuous flow reduces pulsatility; a Doppler opening pressure approximates MAP (target ~70–80 mmHg). B – increased venous return and septal shift after LV unloading can unmask RV failure (up to 20–40 %), requiring inotropes, pulmonary vasodilators or temporary RVAD. C – suction events: low flow, arrhythmias; treat with fluid and speed reduction. D – ERC 2025 and the AHA advise that if the patient is unresponsive and the device cannot be restarted or there is no flow, chest compressions should be started; the risk of cannula dislodgement is outweighed by the need for perfusion. Reference: Lott C, et al. European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2025 Special Circumstances in Resuscitation. **Resuscitation** 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753; Peberdy MA, et al. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults and children with mechanical circulatory support: a scientific statement from the AHA. **Circulation** 2017;135:e1115–e1134.

questions.stem: Regarding the principles of the intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP):
options: The balloon should inflate on the R wave of the ECG.
Significant aortic regurgitation is a contraindication.
Helium is used because it is more soluble in blood than carbon dioxide.
Balloon size is selected primarily according to the patient's body weight.
questions.expl: A – inflation occurs at the dicrotic notch (aortic valve closure, around the middle of the T wave); deflation is timed just before the next systole (R wave). B – diastolic inflation would increase regurgitant volume; aortic dissection and severe peripheral vascular disease are other contraindications. C – helium is chosen for its low density (rapid shuttling); CO2 is more soluble and was used earlier for safety in case of rupture. D – balloon size (e.g. 30–50 mL) is chosen by patient height. Reference: Krishna M, Zacharowski K. Principles of intra-aortic balloon pump counterpulsation. **Contin Educ Anaesth Crit Care Pain** 2009;9:24–28; Thiele H, et al. IABP-SHOCK II. **N Engl J Med** 2012;367:1287–1296.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man develops acute severe mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture 3 days after an inferior myocardial infarction. He is in cardiogenic shock and an IABP is inserted via the femoral artery as a bridge to emergency surgery; BP before insertion was 82/50 mmHg with pulmonary oedema. Each of the following is an expected effect of correctly timed counterpulsation EXCEPT:
options: A reduction in regurgitant fraction
An increase in diastolic aortic pressure
A reduction in left-ventricular afterload
An increase in left-ventricular end-diastolic pressure
A modest increase in forward cardiac output
questions.expl: Deflation just before systole lowers aortic end-diastolic pressure and afterload, which increases forward stroke volume and reduces the regurgitant fraction in MR (and shunt in post-infarct VSD); LV wall stress, end-diastolic pressure and myocardial O2 demand fall. Inflation in diastole augments diastolic (coronary) perfusion pressure. IABP is still used as a bridge in mechanical complications of MI, but IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit in AMI cardiogenic shock without mechanical complications, and ESC 2023 does not recommend its routine use there. Reference: Byrne RA, et al. 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes. **Eur Heart J** 2023;44:3720–3826; Thiele H, et al. IABP-SHOCK II. **N Engl J Med** 2012;367:1287–1296.

questions.stem: Regarding IABP timing, position and evidence:
options: On chest X-ray, the radio-opaque tip should lie about 2–3 cm below the origin of the left subclavian artery, roughly at the level of the carina.
Late deflation increases left-ventricular afterload and workload.
Early inflation, before aortic valve closure, improves stroke volume.
ESC 2023 guidelines recommend routine IABP insertion in acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock.
questions.expl: A – too high risks occluding the left subclavian/carotid; too low risks renal and mesenteric artery occlusion. B – a balloon still inflated during early systole forces the LV to eject against it. C – early inflation causes premature aortic valve closure, reduced stroke volume and increased LVEDV/afterload. D – routine IABP is not recommended (class III) in AMI-CS without mechanical complications, based on IABP-SHOCK II (no difference in 30-day, 1-year or 6-year mortality). Reference: Byrne RA, et al. 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines. **Eur Heart J** 2023;44:3720–3826; Thiele H, et al. Intraaortic balloon pump in cardiogenic shock complicating acute myocardial infarction: long-term 6-year outcome of IABP-SHOCK II. **Circulation** 2019;139:395–403.

title: Case-style practice · W07-D3 · Acute coronary syndromes in ICU

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has just undergone primary PCI to an occluded proximal right coronary artery. In the coronary care unit his BP is 78/45 mmHg and HR 38/min with complete heart block. JVP is raised, lungs are clear, and echocardiography shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle with good LV function. He has already received 500 mL of crystalloid. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start a glyceryl trinitrate infusion
Insert a temporary pacing wire, ideally achieving AV-synchronous pacing
Give IV furosemide 40 mg
Give a further 2 L of crystalloid rapidly
Insert an intra-aortic balloon pump
questions.expl: RV infarction makes cardiac output highly dependent on heart rate, preload and atrial contribution; bradycardia/AV block (common with proximal RCA occlusion) should be treated with temporary pacing, ideally dual-chamber to restore AV synchrony. Nitrates and diuretics (A, C) reduce preload and are harmful. A modest fluid challenge is reasonable, but large volumes (D) overdistend the RV, shift the septum and reduce LV filling. IABP (E) mainly supports the LV. Inotropes (dobutamine) or mechanical RV support are considered if shock persists. Reference: Byrne RA, et al. 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes. **Eur Heart J** 2023;44:3720–3826; Harjola VP, et al. Contemporary management of acute right ventricular failure: a statement from the Heart Failure Association and the Working Group on Pulmonary Circulation and Right Ventricular Function of the ESC. **Eur J Heart Fail** 2016;18:226–241.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with known stable coronary disease is on day 3 after hip fracture fixation. She develops melaena; haemoglobin falls to 62 g/L, HR is 125/min and BP 92/55 mmHg. She complains of central chest tightness, the ECG shows new 1.5 mm horizontal ST depression in V4–V6, and high-sensitivity troponin rises from 30 to 900 ng/L. According to the Fourth Universal Definition, this is best classified as:
options: Type 1 myocardial infarction
Type 4a myocardial infarction
Non-ischaemic (acute) myocardial injury
Type 2 myocardial infarction
Type 5 myocardial infarction
questions.expl: A rise and fall of troponin above the 99th centile together with evidence of ischaemia (symptoms, new ischaemic ECG changes) caused by an oxygen supply–demand imbalance (anaemia, tachycardia, hypotension) – not acute atherothrombosis – is type 2 MI. Non-ischaemic myocardial injury (C) is a troponin rise without clinical evidence of ischaemia (e.g. sepsis, myocarditis, PE). Type 1 is plaque rupture/erosion with thrombus; type 4a is PCI-related; type 5 CABG-related. Management targets the cause (transfusion, endoscopic haemostasis), not antithrombotic escalation. Reference: Thygesen K, et al. Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018). **Eur Heart J** 2019;40:237–269.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man presents 1 hour after insufflating cocaine with central chest pain, agitation, HR 130/min and BP 195/115 mmHg. He is sweating and tremulous with dilated pupils. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with 1 mm ST depression in the lateral leads, and the first troponin is pending. Which initial treatment is LEAST appropriate?
options: Aspirin 300 mg orally
IV benzodiazepine titrated to sedation
IV propranolol
Sublingual or IV glyceryl trinitrate
IV phentolamine if hypertension persists despite benzodiazepines and nitrates
questions.expl: In acute cocaine toxicity, non-selective β-blockade may leave α-adrenergic vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening coronary spasm and hypertension; guidelines advise avoiding β-blockers in the acute phase. Benzodiazepines reduce the central sympathetic drive and are first-line, combined with aspirin and nitrates; an α-antagonist (phentolamine) or calcium channel blocker is used for persistent hypertension. Thrombolysis is relatively contraindicated by uncontrolled hypertension, and primary PCI is preferred if STEMI develops. Reference: McCord J, et al. Management of cocaine-associated chest pain and myocardial infarction: a scientific statement from the AHA. **Circulation** 2008;117:1897–1907; Byrne RA, et al. 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines. **Eur Heart J** 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Regarding reperfusion and antithrombotic therapy in STEMI (ESC 2023):
options: Primary PCI is preferred if the anticipated time from STEMI diagnosis to wire crossing is ≤ 120 minutes; otherwise fibrinolysis should be given within 10 minutes of diagnosis.
After successful fibrinolysis, routine angiography within 2–24 hours is recommended.
A resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patient with persistent ST elevation should undergo emergency angiography, even if comatose.
Ticagrelor is preferred over prasugrel in patients proceeding to PCI.
questions.expl: A – the 120-minute threshold defines the pharmaco-invasive alternative. B – a pharmaco-invasive strategy (angiography 2–24 h after successful lysis; immediate rescue PCI if failed) is recommended. C – primary PCI is recommended for resuscitated patients with persistent ST elevation (in contrast, routine immediate angiography is not recommended without ST elevation – COACT, TOMAHAWK). D – prasugrel should be considered in preference to ticagrelor for patients proceeding to PCI (class IIa, ISAR-REACT 5). Reference: Byrne RA, et al. 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes. **Eur Heart J** 2023;44:3720–3826; Schüpke S, et al. ISAR-REACT 5. **N Engl J Med** 2019;381:1524–1534.

title: Case-style practice · W07-D4 · Inotropes, acute heart failure and stress cardiomyopathy

questions.stem: Regarding levosimendan:
options: It sensitises the myofilaments to calcium by binding cardiac troponin C in a calcium-dependent manner.
In LeoPARDS, adding levosimendan reduced organ dysfunction in septic shock.
Its active metabolite OR-1896 has a half-life of about 80 hours, so effects persist for days after a 24-hour infusion.
Its principal adverse haemodynamic effect is hypertension.
questions.expl: A – calcium sensitisation (troponin C) plus vasodilatation via K-ATP channel opening; it does not raise intracellular calcium, so myocardial O2 consumption rises little and diastolic relaxation is not impaired. B – LeoPARDS found no reduction in mean SOFA score, more supraventricular tachyarrhythmias and lower likelihood of weaning from ventilation; SSC suggests against levosimendan. C – OR-1896 explains prolonged action; a loading dose is often omitted to avoid hypotension. D – vasodilatation and hypotension (and tachyarrhythmia, hypokalaemia) are the main adverse effects. Reference: Gordon AC, et al. LeoPARDS. **N Engl J Med** 2016;375:1638–1648; Papp Z, et al. Levosimendan: molecular mechanisms and clinical implications – consensus of experts. **Int J Cardiol** 2012;159:82–87.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman is 3 hours out of theatre after mitral valve replacement and tricuspid annuloplasty for longstanding mitral regurgitation. HR 118/min (sinus), MAP 68 mmHg on noradrenaline 0.08 µg/kg/min, CVP 18 mmHg, mean PAP 45 mmHg, PAOP 14 mmHg, cardiac index 1.8 L/min/m², SvO2 52 %, lactate 3.4 mmol/L. Echocardiography shows a dilated, poorly contracting right ventricle and a well-seated prosthesis. Which is the most appropriate addition?
options: Dobutamine 10 µg/kg/min
Milrinone infusion (without a bolus), maintaining MAP with noradrenaline
Levosimendan 12 µg/kg loading bolus followed by infusion
Intra-aortic balloon pump
A further increase in noradrenaline alone to a MAP of 85 mmHg
questions.expl: This is low cardiac output from RV failure with raised pulmonary vascular resistance after mitral surgery. A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor (inodilator) increases RV contractility and lowers PVR with less chronotropy than dobutamine, which would further increase an already high heart rate (A). The bolus of milrinone or levosimendan (C) is omitted to avoid hypotension. IABP (D) supports the LV and does little for RV failure. Raising noradrenaline alone (E) does not improve output. Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (NO, epoprostenol) are reasonable adjuncts. In DOREMI, milrinone and dobutamine had similar outcomes in cardiogenic shock. Reference: Mathew R, et al. Milrinone as compared with dobutamine in the treatment of cardiogenic shock (DOREMI). **N Engl J Med** 2021;385:516–525; Harjola VP, et al. Contemporary management of acute right ventricular failure: a statement from the HFA and ESC WG on Pulmonary Circulation. **Eur J Heart Fail** 2016;18:226–241.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought in with acute breathlessness. BP 205/120 mmHg, HR 115/min, RR 36/min, SpO2 82 % on a 15 L/min non-rebreathe mask, widespread crackles. She is alert and able to follow commands. ABG: pH 7.28, PaCO2 6.5 kPa. ECG shows LV hypertrophy without ST elevation. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Immediate rapid sequence induction and intubation
IV morphine 10 mg and furosemide
CPAP or NIV together with a titrated IV nitrate infusion
High-flow nasal oxygen and IV furosemide only
Fibrinolysis
questions.expl: This is hypertensive acute heart failure with pulmonary oedema. Non-invasive positive pressure (CPAP/NIV) rapidly improves oxygenation, work of breathing and acidosis and reduces LV afterload; IV nitrates reduce preload and afterload and are the key drug when SBP is high. ESC HF guidelines recommend NIV in respiratory distress (RR > 25, SpO2 < 90 %); 3CPO showed faster physiological improvement (no mortality difference). Intubation is for failure of NIV, coma or exhaustion; morphine is not routinely recommended (associated with harm); fibrinolysis has no role without STEMI. Reference: McDonagh TA, et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure. **Eur Heart J** 2021;42:3599–3726; Gray A, et al. 3CPO. **N Engl J Med** 2008;359:142–151.

questions.stem: Regarding Takotsubo (stress) syndrome:
options: Mid-ventricular and basal ("inverted") patterns of wall-motion abnormality occur, as well as apical ballooning.
In shock with dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction, inotropes such as dobutamine are the first-line treatment.
Recurrence does not occur.
In-hospital mortality is negligible, similar to that of the general population.
questions.expl: A – apical ballooning is commonest, but mid-ventricular, basal and focal types are recognised. B – catecholamines worsen LVOTO (and may perpetuate the syndrome); treat with fluids, cautious β-blockade, and levosimendan or mechanical support if cardiogenic shock without obstruction. C – recurrence occurs in ~2 % per year. D – in-hospital mortality (~4–5 %) and complications (cardiogenic shock, LV thrombus, arrhythmia) are comparable to ACS; physical triggers (e.g. critical illness) carry a worse prognosis than emotional ones. Reference: Ghadri JR, et al. International expert consensus document on Takotsubo syndrome (Parts I and II). **Eur Heart J** 2018;39:2032–2046 and 2047–2062; Templin C, et al. **N Engl J Med** 2015;373:929–938.

title: Case-style practice · W07-D5 · Pulmonary hypertension

questions.stem: Regarding pulmonary hypertension (PH), according to the 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines:
options: PH is defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure > 20 mmHg at rest, measured by right-heart catheterisation.
Pre-capillary PH requires a PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg and a pulmonary vascular resistance > 2 Wood units.
Left heart disease (group 2) is the most common cause of PH.
Pulmonary arterial vasodilators (e.g. PDE-5 inhibitors, endothelin antagonists) are recommended for PH due to left heart disease.
questions.expl: A, B – the 2022 definition lowered the threshold from mPAP ≥ 25 to > 20 mmHg and PVR from > 3 to > 2 WU; post-capillary PH has PAWP > 15 mmHg. C – group 2 is commonest, followed by group 3 (lung disease/hypoxia). D – PAH-specific drugs are not recommended in group 2 PH (no benefit, possible harm from pulmonary oedema); treat the underlying left heart disease. Reference: Humbert M, et al. 2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension. **Eur Heart J** 2022;43:3618–3731.

title: Case-style practice · W08-D1 · Atrial fibrillation in the critically ill

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with an irregular broad-complex tachycardia at 240/min with varying QRS morphology; a previous ECG showed a short PR interval and delta waves. Regarding his management:
options: If he is haemodynamically stable, IV procainamide or ibutilide may be used for pharmacological cardioversion.
Synchronised DC cardioversion is indicated if he becomes haemodynamically unstable.
IV amiodarone is the drug of choice.
Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is recommended after this episode.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in stable pre-excited AF, IV procainamide or ibutilide (or flecainide/propafenone) slow conduction over the accessory pathway and can restore sinus rhythm.
- B (True) – electrical cardioversion is the treatment if he becomes unstable, or if in doubt, because pre-excited AF at 240/min can degenerate to VF.
- C (False) – the ESC advises against IV amiodarone in pre-excited AF; like other AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin) it can increase conduction over the accessory pathway.
- D (True) – catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is recommended after pre-excited AF, as this is a high-risk pathway.

**EDIC trap:** An irregular, very fast broad-complex tachycardia with changing QRS shape is pre-excited AF until proven otherwise – do not block the AV node.

**Ref:** Brugada J et al., 2019 ESC SVT Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:655–720; Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation (5 years, left atrium 58 mm, on apixaban) and heart failure with LVEF 30 % is admitted with pneumonia. Ventricular rate is 150/min, BP 112/70 mmHg, and she has bibasal crackles with SpO2 92 % on 4 L/min oxygen. Which is the most appropriate rate-control strategy?
options: Synchronised DC cardioversion
IV verapamil
IV flecainide
Repeated IV metoprolol boluses targeting a heart rate below 80/min
IV digoxin loading, treating the pneumonia and optimising volume status
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Her AF is permanent with a 58-mm left atrium, so the goal is rate control, not rhythm. In HFrEF with acute congestion, IV digoxin (or IV amiodarone) controls the rate without depressing contractility or BP. Treating the trigger (pneumonia, hypoxaemia, volume status) is essential, and lenient rate control (< 110/min) is acceptable at first (ESC 2024).

**Why not the others:**
- A – she is not in shock, and cardioversion of long-standing permanent AF with a large atrium is unlikely to last.
- B – verapamil is negatively inotropic and contraindicated with LVEF ≤ 40%.
- C – flecainide is contraindicated in structural heart disease and HFrEF.
- D – repeated beta-blocker boluses during acute pulmonary congestion can cause decompensation, and < 80/min is a strict, not initial, target.

**Ref:** Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man presents with 2 hours of palpitations and chest pain. ECG shows an irregular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180/min. BP is 72/40 mmHg, he is clammy and confused. He has no previous cardiac history. A defibrillator and an anaesthetist for sedation are available, and his potassium is 4.2 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Synchronised cardioversion, starting at the maximum biphasic energy
Unsynchronised shock at 150 J
Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV bolus
Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20 minutes before any shock
Anticoagulation with heparin and transoesophageal echocardiography before cardioversion
questions.expl:
**Why A:** This tachyarrhythmia has adverse features (shock, myocardial ischaemia, reduced consciousness), so it needs immediate synchronised cardioversion under sedation or anaesthesia. ERC 2025 recommends that for AF the first synchronised shock is delivered at maximum defibrillator output rather than escalating. If it fails, give amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 min and repeat the shock.

**Why not the others:**
- B – an unsynchronised shock may fall on the T wave (R-on-T) and cause VF.
- C – adenosine is for regular narrow-complex tachycardia; this rhythm is irregular.
- D – amiodarone is given after a failed shock or in stable patients; it would delay treatment of shock.
- E – instability overrides the usual anticoagulation/TOE requirements, although heparin should be started as soon as possible.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult ALS, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110769; Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

title: Case-style practice · W08-D2 · Pulmonary embolism

questions.stem: Regarding risk stratification of acute pulmonary embolism (ESC 2019):
options: A normotensive patient with sPESI ≥ 1, RV dysfunction on CT and an elevated troponin is classified as intermediate-high risk.
A patient with systolic BP 85 mmHg for 20 minutes and RV dilatation is classified as intermediate-high risk.
Full-dose systemic thrombolysis is recommended routinely for intermediate-high-risk PE.
An RV/LV diameter ratio ≥ 1.0 on CT pulmonary angiography indicates RV dysfunction.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – evidence of RV strain on both imaging and biomarkers in a normotensive patient with sPESI ≥ 1 means intermediate-high risk; one or none is intermediate-low.
- B (False) – persistent hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg for > 15 min, not explained by another cause) is haemodynamic instability, which makes this **high risk**.
- C (False) – routine primary thrombolysis is not recommended; in PEITHO it reduced decompensation but increased major and intracranial bleeding. Rescue thrombolysis (or catheter-directed therapy) is used if the patient deteriorates.
- D (True) – an RV/LV diameter ratio ≥ 1.0 on CTPA (or > 1.0 on echo) indicates RV dysfunction.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman develops dyspnoea and pleuritic pain 10 days after a knee replacement; CT confirms bilateral pulmonary emboli with an RV/LV ratio of 1.2. She is normotensive with HR 112/min and SpO2 91 % on air, and a 12-lead ECG is recorded. Each of the following ECG findings is recognised in acute pulmonary embolism EXCEPT:
options: T-wave inversion in leads V1–V4
New right bundle branch block
An S1Q3T3 pattern
New-onset atrial fibrillation
Left ventricular hypertrophy with lateral strain pattern
questions.expl:
**Why E:** LVH with a lateral strain pattern reflects chronic LV pressure overload (e.g. hypertension, aortic stenosis) and is not a sign of acute PE. Acute PE loads the right ventricle, so the ECG may show sinus tachycardia (most common), anterior T-wave inversion, QR in V1, S1Q3T3, RBBB, right axis deviation or atrial arrhythmias. Overall, the ECG is neither sensitive nor specific for PE.

**Why not the others:**
- A – T-wave inversion in V1–V4 reflects RV strain and is linked to RV dysfunction and worse outcome.
- B – new RBBB (complete or incomplete) is a sign of acute RV dilatation.
- C – the S1Q3T3 pattern is a recognised, though uncommon, sign of acute RV strain.
- D – atrial arrhythmias, including new AF, occur in acute PE.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603; Shopp JD et al., Acad Emerg Med 2015;22:1127–1137.

questions.stem: Which of the following increase the risk of venous thromboembolism?
options: Heterozygous factor V Leiden
Haemophilia A
Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria
Vitamin K deficiency
questions.expl:
- A (True) – factor V Leiden causes resistance to activated protein C; it is the most common inherited thrombophilia in Europeans (~5-fold VTE risk when heterozygous).
- B (False) – haemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency and causes bleeding, not thrombosis.
- C (True) – in PNH, complement-mediated haemolysis and platelet activation cause thrombosis at unusual sites (hepatic, cerebral, mesenteric veins); thrombosis is the main cause of death.
- D (False) – vitamin K deficiency lowers factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C/S), and the net effect is a bleeding tendency.

**EDIC trap:** Low protein C and S in vitamin K deficiency does not make it prothrombotic overall – the procoagulant factors fall too.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603; Hill A et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17028.

questions.stem: Regarding reperfusion therapy in acute pulmonary embolism:
options: The standard systemic regimen of alteplase is 100 mg over 2 hours (or an accelerated 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes).
In PEITHO, tenecteplase in intermediate-high-risk PE reduced death or haemodynamic decompensation but increased major bleeding, including haemorrhagic stroke.
When thrombolysis is given during cardiac arrest from suspected PE, resuscitation should be continued for 60–90 minutes before stopping.
Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment is an alternative in high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESC 2019: alteplase 100 mg over 2 h is standard; the accelerated regimen of 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min (max 50 mg) is used mainly in cardiac arrest or extreme instability.
- B (True) – in PEITHO (1006 patients) the primary outcome fell from 5.6% to 2.6%, but major extracranial bleeding (6.3% vs 1.2%) and stroke (2.4% vs 0.2%, mostly haemorrhagic) rose; 30-day mortality did not differ.
- C (True) – ERC guidance: consider continuing CPR for 60–90 min after giving a thrombolytic for PE.
- D (True) – surgical embolectomy (I C) or catheter-directed treatment (IIa C) is an alternative when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed.

**EDIC trap:** In intermediate-high-risk PE, HI-PEITHO and PRAGUE-26 (2026) showed that catheter-directed thrombolysis reduced early decompensation, but not mortality.

**Ref:** Meyer G et al. (PEITHO), N Engl J Med 2014;370:1402–1411; Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603; Lott C et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Special Circumstances, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

title: Case-style practice · W08-D3 · Aortic dissection and tamponade

questions.stem: Regarding the chest X-ray in acute aortic dissection:
options: A normal chest X-ray excludes aortic dissection.
Mediastinal widening is present in nearly all cases.
Pleural effusions associated with dissection are typically right-sided.
The "calcium sign" requires a separation of less than 2 mm between intimal calcification and the outer aortic wall.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the chest X-ray is normal in about 10–20% of dissections, so it cannot exclude the diagnosis.
- B (False) – mediastinal widening is seen in only about 60% of cases.
- C (False) – effusions from dissection (haemothorax or reactive) are usually **left-sided**.
- D (False) – the calcium sign is displacement of intimal calcification by **> 6–10 mm** from the outer aortic contour, not < 2 mm.

**EDIC trap:** Other CXR clues are an abnormal aortic contour, apical cap, tracheal deviation to the right and a depressed left main bronchus – but CT angiography (or TOE if unstable) is the diagnostic test.

**Ref:** Erbel R et al., 2014 ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2014;35:2873–2926; Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700; Hagan PG et al. (IRAD), JAMA 2000;283:897–903.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is 4 hours out of theatre after aortic valve replacement. His chest drains, which had drained 150 mL/h, have abruptly stopped. Cardiac index has fallen from 2.4 to 1.5 L/min/m², CVP risen from 8 to 17 mmHg and PAOP from 10 to 18 mmHg, HR is 125/min and noradrenaline requirements are rising. Transthoracic windows are poor, and transoesophageal echocardiography shows a posterior clot compressing the right atrium. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Subxiphoid needle pericardiocentesis
Emergency re-exploration (resternotomy)
Increase inotropic support and observe
IV furosemide to reduce filling pressures
Milk and strip the drains and repeat imaging in 1 hour
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Drains that suddenly stop after heavy output, with rising CVP and PAOP, falling cardiac index and rising vasopressor need, mean postoperative tamponade. TOE confirms a localised posterior clot compressing the right atrium. After cardiac surgery, tamponade is often due to localised clot, so classic signs (equal pressures, pulsus paradoxus) may be missing. The treatment is surgical re-exploration; emergency resternotomy on the ICU is part of the CALS protocol if arrest occurs.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a needle cannot remove clot, and pericardiocentesis is dangerous after sternotomy.
- C – more inotropes do not relieve the compression and only delay treatment.
- D – the patient is preload-dependent, so furosemide would worsen output.
- E – waiting an hour in worsening tamponade risks cardiac arrest.

**Ref:** STS Task Force on Resuscitation After Cardiac Surgery, Ann Thorac Surg 2017;103:1005–1020; Adler Y et al., 2015 ESC Pericardial Diseases Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921–2964.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension develops sudden severe chest pain followed 20 minutes later by left-sided weakness. On arrival (onset 90 min ago), BP is 170/90 mmHg in the right arm and 115/70 mmHg in the left arm, and there is a new early diastolic murmur. CT head shows no haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: IV alteplase for acute ischaemic stroke
Aspirin and ticagrelor loading
CT angiography of the thoracic and abdominal aorta
Coronary angiography
IV unfractionated heparin
