questions.expl:
**Why C:** Chest pain followed by a neurological deficit, a 55-mmHg inter-arm BP difference and a new early diastolic (AR) murmur strongly suggest type A dissection extending into the supra-aortic vessels. About 5–10% of dissections present with stroke. The aorta must be imaged before any antithrombotic treatment – CT angiography, or bedside TOE/TTE if unstable. If confirmed: IV beta-blocker (HR < 60/min, SBP 100–120 mmHg) and emergency surgery.

**Why not the others:**
- A – alteplase in dissection can cause fatal bleeding or tamponade.
- B – dual antiplatelet loading for presumed ACS increases bleeding at surgery.
- D – coronary angiography delays diagnosis and catheter manipulation in a dissected aorta is hazardous.
- E – heparin may extend the dissection or haemopericardium.

**EDIC trap:** Always look for dissection "red flags" before thrombolysis for stroke or STEMI.

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700; Isselbacher EM et al., 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, Circulation 2022;146:e334–e482.

title: Case-style practice · W08-D4 · Hypertensive emergencies

questions.stem: Regarding hypertensive emergencies and urgencies:
options: A hypertensive emergency is defined by severe BP elevation associated with acute hypertension-mediated organ damage.
In a hypertensive emergency without a compelling condition, BP should be normalised within the first hour.
In acute aortic dissection, systolic BP should be lowered rapidly to ≤ 120 mmHg (with heart rate ≤ 60/min).
Severe asymptomatic hypertension without organ damage should be treated with IV labetalol in the emergency department.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – acute organ damage (encephalopathy, retinopathy, AKI, acute HF, ACS, dissection, eclampsia, TMA) defines an emergency, not the absolute BP value.
- B (False) – without a compelling condition, MAP is lowered by no more than ~20–25% over several hours, to avoid cerebral, renal and coronary hypoperfusion (autoregulation shifted right).
- C (True) – aortic dissection is the exception: SBP ≤ 120 mmHg and HR ≤ 60/min immediately, with a beta-blocker first and then a vasodilator.
- D (False) – severe hypertension without acute organ damage is an urgency, managed by starting or intensifying oral therapy and lowering BP gradually; IV treatment is unnecessary and risky.

**EDIC trap:** Pulmonary oedema and ACS also need an immediate reduction (SBP < 140 mmHg).

**Ref:** van den Born BJH et al., ESC Council on Hypertension position document, Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Pharmacother 2019;5:37–46; McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018.

title: Case-style practice · W08-D5 · Valvular disease, endocarditis and cardiomyopathy

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman who injects heroin presents with fever, cough and haemoptysis. CT shows multiple peripheral cavitating nodules, and echocardiography shows a 15 mm vegetation on the tricuspid valve with moderate regurgitation. Blood cultures have been taken and she is haemodynamically stable on the ward. Which statement about her condition is correct?
options: Her prognosis is worse than that of left-sided native-valve endocarditis.
Most patients with this condition require valve surgery.
Candida species are the most likely cause.
Staphylococcus aureus is the most likely cause.
Septic pulmonary emboli are an uncommon complication.
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Tricuspid endocarditis in people who inject drugs is caused by *S. aureus* in 60–90% of cases (MRSA in some regions). The clinical picture is typical: fever, cough and haemoptysis from septic pulmonary emboli, with cavitating nodules on CT. Other causes are streptococci, *Pseudomonas* and *Candida*.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the prognosis is relatively good (in-hospital mortality < 10%), better than left-sided NVE.
- B – most patients are treated medically; ESC 2023 surgery is for right HF from severe TR not responding to diuretics, persistent bacteraemia or difficult organisms, or vegetations > 20 mm with recurrent PE.
- C – *Candida* is an uncommon cause.
- E – septic pulmonary emboli are common, as here.

**EDIC trap:** Her 15-mm vegetation does not meet the > 20 mm threshold for right-sided surgery.

**Ref:** Delgado V et al., 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948–4042.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old man with known severe aortic stenosis (valve area 0.6 cm², mean gradient 52 mmHg, preserved LV function) undergoes hip fracture fixation under spinal anaesthesia. Shortly after the block his BP falls to 70/40 mmHg with HR 105/min (sinus) and he becomes nauseated and pale. The surgeons are waiting to start. Which drug is most appropriate?
options: Ephedrine 6 mg boluses
Phenylephrine (or metaraminol) boluses followed by an infusion
Glyceryl trinitrate infusion
Dobutamine infusion
Adrenaline 1 mg IV bolus
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In severe AS the hypertrophied LV has a fixed stroke volume and depends on diastolic pressure for coronary perfusion. Spinal anaesthesia causes vasodilation, and hypotension then leads to ischaemia and a downward spiral; tachycardia shortens diastole and makes it worse. A pure α-agonist (phenylephrine, metaraminol) or noradrenaline restores coronary perfusion pressure without raising heart rate. Keep sinus rhythm and treat AF promptly.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ephedrine raises heart rate (β effect), which is unwanted at HR 105/min.
- C – glyceryl trinitrate is a vasodilator and can cause cardiovascular collapse.
- D – dobutamine causes tachycardia and vasodilation.
- E – 1 mg of adrenaline is an arrest dose and would cause severe tachycardia and hypertension.

**Ref:** Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2025; Halvorsen S et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines on non-cardiac surgery, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3826–3924.

questions.stem: Regarding hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM):
options: Dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction is worsened by hypovolaemia, vasodilators and positive inotropes.
Digoxin is useful to relieve symptoms of obstructive HCM.
Mavacamten, a cardiac myosin inhibitor, may be used for symptomatic obstructive HCM.
In shock caused by dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction, dobutamine is the first-line drug.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – a smaller LV cavity (hypovolaemia, vasodilators) or stronger contraction (inotropes) increases systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and the LVOT gradient.
- B (False) – digoxin is a positive inotrope and is avoided in obstructive HCM, as are vasodilators.
- C (True) – ESC 2023: beta-blockers first-line, then (or added) the myosin inhibitor mavacamten or disopyramide; septal reduction therapy for refractory symptoms.
- D (False) – shock from dynamic LVOT obstruction is treated with fluids, a pure vasoconstrictor (phenylephrine/noradrenaline), beta-blockade and stopping inotropes; dobutamine worsens the obstruction.

**EDIC trap:** Dynamic LVOT obstruction can also occur without HCM in hypovolaemic, catecholamine-treated septic patients – look for SAM on echo.

**Ref:** Arbelo E et al., 2023 ESC Cardiomyopathy Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503–3626.

title: Case-style practice · W09-D1 · Advanced life support: drugs and access

questions.stem: Regarding drug therapy during adult advanced life support (ERC 2025):
options: In a shockable rhythm, adrenaline 1 mg is given after the third shock and then every 3–5 minutes.
Amiodarone 300 mg is given after three shocks, with a further 150 mg after the fifth shock.
Lidocaine 100 mg is an acceptable alternative if amiodarone is unavailable.
In a non-shockable rhythm, adrenaline should be withheld until two cycles of CPR have been completed.
questions.expl: A, B – unchanged since ERC 2015/2021: adrenaline and amiodarone after the third shock. C – lidocaine 1 mg/kg (100 mg), further 50 mg after the fifth shock, is the alternative (ALPS trial). D – in PEA/asystole, give adrenaline 1 mg as soon as IV/IO access is obtained (earlier adrenaline is associated with better outcomes in non-shockable rhythms). Reference: Soar J, Böttiger BW, Carli P, et al. European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support. **Resuscitation** 2025;215(Suppl 1):110769; Kudenchuk PJ, et al. ALPS. **N Engl J Med** 2016;374:1711–1722.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is in refractory VF after an out-of-hospital arrest. Paramedics have failed two attempts at peripheral IV cannulation over 2 minutes; three shocks have been delivered and high-quality CPR with mechanical compressions is ongoing; an i-gel is in place with a capnography trace. Which is the most appropriate action?
options: Give adrenaline 3 mg via the tracheal tube
Give adrenaline 1 mg intramuscularly
Interrupt CPR to insert a femoral central venous catheter
Insert an intraosseous needle and give double the IV dose of adrenaline
Insert an intraosseous needle (proximal humerus or tibia) and give the standard IV doses
questions.expl: ERC 2025 recommends attempting IV access first and using the intraosseous route if IV access is not rapidly achievable. IO doses are the same as IV doses. PARAMEDIC-3 and IVIO found no improvement in survival with an IO-first strategy, but IO remains the standard fallback. Tracheal drug administration is no longer recommended (unpredictable absorption); IM adrenaline is not used in arrest; central venous cannulation interrupts CPR and takes too long. Reference: Soar J, et al. ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support. **Resuscitation** 2025;215(Suppl 1):110769; Couper K, et al. A randomized trial of drug route in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (PARAMEDIC-3). **N Engl J Med** 2025;392:336–348.

questions.stem: Regarding vascular access during cardiac arrest:
options: In PARAMEDIC-3, an intraosseous-first strategy improved 30-day survival compared with an IV-first strategy.
Drugs given via a peripheral vein should be followed by a flush of about 20 mL.
If neither IV nor IO access is available, the tracheal route is recommended for adrenaline.
Proximal humeral IO sites generally achieve higher flow rates than proximal tibial sites.
questions.expl: A – PARAMEDIC-3 (n = 6082) found no difference in 30-day survival (4.5 % vs 5.1 %), and IVIO (Denmark) likewise found no benefit. B – a 20 mL flush (and limb elevation) speeds delivery to the central circulation. C – the tracheal route is no longer recommended. D – the humerus is closer to the central circulation and allows higher flows, although no outcome benefit by site has been shown. Reference: Couper K, et al. PARAMEDIC-3. **N Engl J Med** 2025;392:336–348; Vallentin MF, et al. IVIO. **N Engl J Med** 2025;392:349–360; Soar J, et al. ERC 2025 ALS. **Resuscitation** 2025;215(Suppl 1):110769.

title: Case-style practice · W09-D2 · Post-resuscitation care

questions.stem: Regarding the evidence base for post-cardiac arrest care:
options: In TTM2, targeted hypothermia at 33 °C improved 6-month survival compared with normothermia and early treatment of fever.
In BOX, a restrictive oxygen target reduced death or severe disability compared with a liberal target.
In TOMAHAWK, immediate coronary angiography in resuscitated patients without ST elevation did not reduce 30-day mortality.
ERC–ESICM 2025 recommends routine prophylactic antibiotics after ROSC.
questions.expl: A – TTM2 (n = 1900): no difference in mortality or functional outcome; hypothermia caused more arrhythmias; ERC–ESICM recommends active fever prevention (≤ 37.5 °C) for at least 72 h. B – BOX: PaO2 targets of 9–10 vs 13–14 kPa (and MAP 63 vs 77 mmHg) showed no difference. C – TOMAHAWK and COACT were neutral (TOMAHAWK showed a trend towards harm); delayed/selective angiography is appropriate without STE. D – prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely recommended despite a lower early pneumonia rate in ANTHARTIC. Reference: Nolan JP, Sandroni C, Cariou A, et al. ERC–ESICM Guidelines 2025: Post-Resuscitation Care. **Resuscitation** 2025;215(Suppl 1):110809; Desch S, et al. TOMAHAWK. **N Engl J Med** 2021;385:2544–2553; Schmidt H, et al. BOX (oxygen). **N Engl J Med** 2022;387:1467–1476.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has ROSC after 12 minutes of in-hospital VF arrest due to hyperkalaemia, which has been corrected. She is intubated, ventilated with FiO2 0.6 and remains comatose. SpO2 100 %, PaO2 35 kPa, PaCO2 3.8 kPa, MAP 72 mmHg, temperature 36.9 °C. The ECG shows no ST elevation. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reduce FiO2 to target SpO2 94–98 % and adjust ventilation to normocapnia
Maintain FiO2 0.6 for 24 hours to protect the brain from hypoxia
Increase minute ventilation to a PaCO2 of 3.5 kPa to reduce intracranial pressure
Actively cool to 33 °C for 24 hours
Arrange immediate coronary angiography
questions.expl: ERC–ESICM 2025 recommends avoiding both hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia after ROSC – titrate FiO2 to SpO2 94–98 % (PaO2 10–13 kPa) once SpO2 can be measured reliably – and targeting normocapnia (PaCO2 4.5–6.0 kPa); hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction. Temperature management means preventing fever (≤ 37.5 °C) rather than cooling to 33 °C (TTM2). Immediate angiography is reserved for ST elevation or high suspicion of ongoing coronary occlusion – here there is a non-coronary cause. Reference: Nolan JP, et al. ERC–ESICM Guidelines 2025: Post-Resuscitation Care. **Resuscitation** 2025;215(Suppl 1):110809; Dankiewicz J, et al. TTM2. **N Engl J Med** 2021;384:2283–2294.

title: Case-style practice · W09-D3 · Temperature control after cardiac arrest

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is being cooled to 33 °C (for example in a trial or local protocol). Regarding the physiological effects of mild induced hypothermia:
options: Potassium shifts into cells during cooling and may rebound to hyperkalaemia during rewarming.
Reduced hepatic clearance increases plasma concentrations of sedatives and opioids, which can delay awakening.
Shivering increases metabolic rate and oxygen consumption and should be controlled.
Hypothermia typically causes sinus tachycardia and QT shortening.
questions.expl: A – intracellular shift and cold diuresis cause hypokalaemia; rewarm slowly (0.25–0.5 °C/h). B – cytochrome P450 activity falls ~7–20 % per °C below 37 °C (propofol, fentanyl, midazolam accumulate), confounding neuroprognostication. C – shivering is treated with sedation, opioids, magnesium, surface counter-warming and, if needed, neuromuscular blockade. D – hypothermia causes bradycardia, PR/QT prolongation and J (Osborn) waves. Other complications: infection (pneumonia), coagulopathy/bleeding, hyperglycaemia and diuresis. TTM2 showed no benefit of 33 °C over fever prevention. Reference: Polderman KH. Mechanisms of action, physiological effects, and complications of hypothermia. **Crit Care Med** 2009;37(7 Suppl):S186–S202; Dankiewicz J, et al. TTM2. **N Engl J Med** 2021;384:2283–2294.

title: Case-style practice · W09-D4 · Neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman remains comatose after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Regarding prognostication of poor neurological outcome (ERC–ESICM 2025):
options: Bilaterally absent N20 waves on somatosensory evoked potentials (≥ 24 h after ROSC) predict poor outcome.
A neuron-specific enolase above 60 µg/L at 48 and/or 72 hours supports a poor outcome.
Multimodal prognostication may be performed as early as 12 hours after ROSC.
An absent motor response to pain at 24 hours is sufficient on its own to predict poor outcome.
questions.expl: The algorithm applies to patients who are comatose (motor score ≤ 3) ≥ 72 h after ROSC, after exclusion of confounders (sedation, hypothermia, metabolic causes). Poor outcome is likely when ≥ 2 of: no pupillary and corneal reflexes, bilaterally absent N20, highly malignant EEG (suppressed background ± periodic discharges, burst-suppression), NSE > 60 µg/L at 48/72 h, status myoclonus ≤ 72 h, diffuse anoxic injury on CT/MRI. A single sign such as motor response alone is not sufficient, and early assessment risks self-fulfilling prophecies. Reference: Nolan JP, et al. ERC–ESICM Guidelines 2025: Post-Resuscitation Care. **Resuscitation** 2025;215(Suppl 1):110809; Sandroni C, et al. Prognostication after cardiac arrest. **Crit Care** 2018;22:150.

title: Case-style practice · W10-D1 · ARDS definition and transfusion-related lung injury

questions.stem: Regarding the 2023 Global definition of ARDS:
options: Non-intubated patients receiving high-flow nasal oxygen at ≥ 30 L/min can be diagnosed with ARDS.
An SpO2/FiO2 ratio ≤ 315 (with SpO2 ≤ 97 %) can be used instead of PaO2/FiO2.
Bilateral opacities may be identified with lung ultrasound by a trained operator.
A pulmonary artery occlusion pressure < 18 mmHg is required to exclude cardiogenic oedema.
questions.expl: The Global definition keeps the Berlin timing (≤ 1 week) and the requirement that oedema is not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload, but extends to non-intubated patients (HFNO ≥ 30 L/min or NIV/CPAP ≥ 5 cmH2O), accepts SpO2/FiO2 and lung ultrasound, and adds a resource-limited variant without PEEP/flow requirements. The PAOP criterion was abandoned with the Berlin definition (2012); ARDS may coexist with raised hydrostatic pressure. Reference: Matthay MA, et al. A new global definition of acute respiratory distress syndrome. **Am J Respir Crit Care Med** 2024;209:37–47; ARDS Definition Task Force. Berlin definition. **JAMA** 2012;307:2526–2533.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a postpartum haemorrhage receives 4 units of red cells and 4 units of fresh frozen plasma over 2 hours with a neutral fluid balance. Ninety minutes after the last unit she develops fever, hypotension and hypoxaemia (PaO2/FiO2 120 mmHg) with bilateral infiltrates. Echocardiography shows normal LV function and a small, collapsing IVC; BNP is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)
Anaphylactic transfusion reaction
Aspiration pneumonitis
Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction
questions.expl: TRALI = new acute hypoxaemia with bilateral infiltrates within 6 h of transfusion without evidence of left atrial hypertension; it is often accompanied by fever and hypotension and is associated with plasma-rich products (donor anti-HLA/HNA antibodies). TACO (B) presents with hypertension, raised BNP and fluid overload. Anaphylaxis (C) causes bronchospasm, urticaria and angio-oedema; haemolytic reactions (E) cause haemoglobinuria and DIC rather than isolated lung injury. Management is supportive (lung-protective ventilation, no diuretics) and reporting to haemovigilance. If the hypoxaemia occurred later or with another risk factor, it would be classified as ARDS ("TRALI type II" if ARDS risk factor present). Reference: Vlaar APJ, et al. A consensus redefinition of transfusion-related acute lung injury. **Transfusion** 2019;59:2465–2476; Vlaar APJ, et al. Transfusion strategies in non-bleeding critically ill adults: ESICM clinical practice guideline. **Intensive Care Med** 2020;46:673–696.

title: Case-style practice · W10-D4 · Rescue therapies in severe ARDS

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has influenza A pneumonia complicated by ARDS, intubated 30 hours ago. He is ventilated with VT 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, PEEP 14 cmH2O, FiO2 0.8; plateau pressure 29 cmH2O, PaO2/FiO2 85 mmHg, pH 7.27, PaCO2 7.9 kPa. He is deeply sedated, haemodynamically stable on low-dose noradrenaline, and has not yet been turned prone. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: High-frequency oscillatory ventilation
Inhaled nitric oxide as a definitive therapy
Immediate referral for VV-ECMO without other changes
Prone positioning for at least 16 hours per day
A staircase recruitment manoeuvre to PEEP 35 cmH2O followed by decremental PEEP titration
questions.expl: In moderate–severe ARDS (P/F < 150 mmHg), prone positioning for ≥ 16 h/day reduces mortality (PROSEVA) and is strongly recommended by ESICM 2023. He does not yet meet EOLIA criteria after optimisation (e.g. P/F < 50 for > 3 h, < 80 for > 6 h, or pH < 7.25 with PaCO2 ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h); ECMO should be considered if he fails proning. HFOV increased mortality (OSCILLATE) or had no effect (OSCAR); iNO improves oxygenation transiently without survival benefit; prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres increased mortality in ART and are recommended against. Reference: Guérin C, et al. PROSEVA. **N Engl J Med** 2013;368:2159–2168; Grasselli G, et al. ESICM guidelines on ARDS. **Intensive Care Med** 2023;49:727–759; Combes A, et al. EOLIA. **N Engl J Med** 2018;378:1965–1975.

questions.stem: According to the ESICM 2023 ARDS guidelines:
options: Prone positioning is recommended for patients with moderate–severe ARDS.
Prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres are recommended against.
Inhaled nitric oxide is recommended because it improves survival.
Routine continuous infusion of neuromuscular blocking agents is recommended in moderate–severe ARDS.
questions.expl: A – strong recommendation (PROSEVA, meta-analyses). B – ART (Brazil) showed higher 28-day mortality with high-pressure recruitment and titrated PEEP; brief recruitment manoeuvres are not recommended either way. C – iNO is not recommended to improve survival; it improves oxygenation transiently but does not reduce mortality and may cause AKI. D – after ROSE (no mortality benefit of early cisatracurium with lighter sedation), ESICM recommends against routine continuous NMBA infusion; NMBA may still be used for specific indications (e.g. refractory asynchrony). Reference: Grasselli G, Calfee CS, Camporota L, et al. ESICM guidelines on acute respiratory distress syndrome: definition, phenotyping and respiratory support strategies. **Intensive Care Med** 2023;49:727–759; NHLBI PETAL Network. ROSE. **N Engl J Med** 2019;380:1997–2008; ART Investigators. **JAMA** 2017;318:1335–1345.

title: Case-style practice · W11-D1 · ECMO for respiratory failure

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man (BMI 38 kg/m²) with severe ARDS after influenza pneumonia has been mechanically ventilated for 12 days, with plateau pressures of 32–34 cmH2O for most of that time. Despite prone positioning, his PaO2/FiO2 is 55 mmHg and pH 7.22 with PaCO2 9 kPa. Echocardiography shows normal biventricular function, and he has no other organ failure. Which feature most argues against VV-ECMO in this patient?
options: His age
A PaO2/FiO2 of 55 mmHg despite prone positioning
Twelve days of high-pressure mechanical ventilation before referral
Hypercapnic acidosis with pH 7.22
Obesity with a BMI of 38 kg/m²
questions.expl: Duration of high-pressure/high-FiO2 ventilation before ECMO (> 7 days) is associated with poor outcome (a component of the RESP score) because established fibroproliferative lung injury is less reversible; ELSO lists mechanical ventilation at high settings for > 7–10 days as a relative contraindication. Severe hypoxaemia and hypercapnic acidosis despite optimisation (B, D) are indications (EOLIA criteria). Age 52 and obesity (A, E) are not contraindications; obesity is not associated with worse ECMO outcomes. Reference: Tonna JE, et al. Management of adult patients supported with VV-ECMO: guideline from the ELSO. **ASAIO J** 2021;67:601–610; Schmidt M, et al. Predicting survival after ECMO for severe acute respiratory failure: the RESP score. **Am J Respir Crit Care Med** 2014;189:1374–1382; Combes A, et al. EOLIA. **N Engl J Med** 2018;378:1965–1975.

title: Case-style practice · W11-D2 · Pulse oximetry

questions.stem: Regarding sources of error in pulse oximetry:
options: In patients with darker skin pigmentation, pulse oximetry more often overestimates arterial saturation, missing occult hypoxaemia.
IV methylene blue causes a transient falsely low SpO2.
Severe anaemia (haemoglobin 70 g/L) alone causes large SpO2 errors at normal saturations.
Fetal haemoglobin causes major errors in SpO2.
questions.expl: A – occult hypoxaemia (SaO2 < 88 % with SpO2 92–96 %) was about three times more frequent in Black than in White patients (Sjoding 2020); regulators (FDA 2025 draft guidance) now require more diverse validation. B – methylene blue absorbs strongly at 660 nm. C – oximetry measures the ratio of oxy- to total haemoglobin, so moderate anaemia causes little error at normal saturations (accuracy worsens with severe anaemia and hypoxaemia). D – HbF has similar absorption spectra to HbA and causes negligible error. Reference: Sjoding MW, et al. Racial bias in pulse oximetry measurement. **N Engl J Med** 2020;383:2477–2478; Jubran A. Pulse oximetry. **Crit Care** 2015;19:272.

questions.stem: Regarding the principles of pulse oximetry:
options: It uses light at about 660 nm (red) and 940 nm (infrared).
Deoxyhaemoglobin absorbs more red light (660 nm) than oxyhaemoglobin.
Its calibration is empirical, derived from healthy volunteers desaturated to about 70–80 %, so accuracy declines below this range.
Venous pulsations (e.g. severe tricuspid regurgitation) can produce falsely low readings.
questions.expl: A, B – the ratio of pulsatile (AC) to non-pulsatile (DC) absorbance at the two wavelengths ("ratio of ratios") is converted to SpO2 via a calibration curve; deoxyhaemoglobin absorbs more red, oxyhaemoglobin more infrared light. C – values below ~70–80 % are extrapolated and less accurate. D – the device assumes all pulsatile absorbance is arterial; venous pulsation, tourniquets or probe position below heart level with congestion lower the reading. Carboxyhaemoglobin is read as oxyhaemoglobin; methaemoglobin drives readings towards ~85 %. Reference: Jubran A. Pulse oximetry. **Crit Care** 2015;19:272; Chan ED, Chan MM, Chan MM. Pulse oximetry: understanding its basic principles facilitates appreciation of its limitations. **Respir Med** 2013;107:789–799.

title: Case-style practice · W11-D3 · Non-invasive ventilation

questions.stem: Regarding non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in acute respiratory failure (ERS/ATS 2017):
options: In acute hypercapnic exacerbations of COPD (pH ≤ 7.35), NIV reduces the need for intubation and mortality.
NIV is contraindicated in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
NIV is recommended to treat established respiratory failure after extubation.
NIV is recommended as first-line therapy for de novo hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
questions.expl: A – strong recommendation, high certainty. B – bilevel NIV or CPAP is recommended in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (strong). C – NIV for established post-extubation failure may delay reintubation and increase mortality (Esteban 2004); it is suggested only to prevent failure in high-risk patients (with HFNO as an alternative). D – no recommendation was made for de novo hypoxaemic failure; HFNO is suggested over NIV in this setting by the 2022 ERS guideline. Reference: Rochwerg B, et al. Official ERS/ATS clinical practice guidelines: noninvasive ventilation for acute respiratory failure. **Eur Respir J** 2017;50:1602426; Oczkowski S, et al. ERS clinical practice guidelines: high-flow nasal cannula in acute respiratory failure. **Eur Respir J** 2022;59:2101574.

title: Case-style practice · W11-D4 · Weaning from mechanical ventilation

questions.stem: Regarding predictors of successful weaning from mechanical ventilation:
options: The rapid shallow breathing index (respiratory rate divided by tidal volume in litres) is measured during unassisted breathing, with a threshold of about 105 breaths/min/L.
A maximal inspiratory pressure more negative than −20 to −30 cmH2O is associated with weaning success.
A spontaneous breathing trial is a better predictor of successful extubation than indices measured beforehand.
A low RSBI has high specificity, so it guarantees successful extubation.
questions.expl: A – Yang & Tobin (1991) described RSBI < 105 as predicting success. B – MIP reflects inspiratory muscle strength but alone has poor specificity. C – guidelines recommend proceeding directly to an SBT (PS 5–8 cmH2O or T-piece, 30–120 min) in patients meeting readiness criteria, rather than relying on predictors. D – RSBI is sensitive but not specific; extubation can still fail from upper-airway, secretion or cardiac causes. Reference: Yang KL, Tobin MJ. A prospective study of indexes predicting the outcome of trials of weaning from mechanical ventilation. **N Engl J Med** 1991;324:1445–1450; Boles JM, et al. Weaning from mechanical ventilation. **Eur Respir J** 2007;29:1033–1056.

title: Case-style practice · W12-D1 · Acute asthma and COPD exacerbation

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with acute asthma. Which of the following are features of life-threatening asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN)?
options: Cardiac arrhythmia
Heart rate > 110/min
Respiratory rate ≥ 25/min
questions.expl: Life-threatening features: PEF < 33 % best/predicted, SpO2 < 92 %, PaO2 < 8 kPa, "normal" PaCO2 (4.6–6.0 kPa), silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, arrhythmia, exhaustion, altered consciousness, hypotension. HR ≥ 110/min, RR ≥ 25/min, PEF 33–50 % and inability to complete sentences define acute severe asthma. A raised PaCO2 or need for ventilation with raised pressures defines near-fatal asthma. Reference: British Thoracic Society/SIGN. British guideline on the management of asthma (SIGN 158), 2019; BTS/NICE/SIGN. Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management (NG245), 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding the treatment of acute severe asthma in adults:
options: Nebulised salbutamol should be driven by air rather than oxygen in hypoxaemic patients.
Oral prednisolone is less effective than IV hydrocortisone.
Antibiotics should be given routinely.
Benzodiazepines are useful on the ward to relieve anxiety and dyspnoea.
questions.expl: A – oxygen-driven nebulisers are used in hypoxaemic patients (target SpO2 94–98 %). B – oral prednisolone 40–50 mg is as effective as IV steroids if it can be swallowed and retained. C – most exacerbations are viral; antibiotics only with evidence of bacterial infection. D – sedatives are contraindicated outside a critical care setting because they depress respiratory drive. Reference: SIGN 158 British guideline on the management of asthma, 2019; Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) report 2024.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with asthma has received three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol doses, nebulised ipratropium and oral prednisolone 50 mg over the last hour. She can speak in short sentences, HR 120/min, RR 28/min, SpO2 95 % on oxygen, PEF 45 % of best, PaCO2 4.4 kPa. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Intubation and mechanical ventilation
IV aminophylline loading dose
Heliox-driven nebulisers as the next routine step
Chest X-ray before any further treatment
IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 20 minutes
questions.expl: She has acute severe asthma that has not responded adequately to initial bronchodilator therapy. A single dose of IV magnesium sulphate (1.2–2 g over 20 min) is recommended for acute severe asthma with a poor initial response (reduces admissions in some studies; 3MG found no benefit of nebulised magnesium). Aminophylline (B) is reserved for life-threatening/near-fatal asthma after senior review. She has no indications for intubation (exhaustion, rising PaCO2, altered consciousness). Heliox is not routinely recommended; chest X-ray should not delay treatment. Reference: SIGN 158 British guideline on the management of asthma, 2019; Kew KM, et al. Intravenous magnesium sulfate for treating adults with acute asthma in the emergency department. **Cochrane Database Syst Rev** 2014;(5):CD010909.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with a history of two previous ICU admissions is assessed in the emergency department during an asthma attack after running out of his inhalers. He is receiving oxygen and nebulised salbutamol while arterial blood gases are being obtained. Each of the following findings indicates life-threatening asthma EXCEPT:
options: PaCO2 5.4 kPa
SpO2 90 % on air
New confusion
Heart rate 125/min
PEF 30 % of predicted
questions.expl: Tachycardia ≥ 110/min is a feature of acute severe (not life-threatening) asthma. A "normal" PaCO2 (4.6–6.0 kPa) in a tachypnoeic asthmatic indicates fatigue and is life-threatening; SpO2 < 92 %, altered consciousness and PEF < 33 % are also life-threatening features. Bradycardia or hypotension are pre-terminal signs. Reference: SIGN 158 British guideline on the management of asthma, 2019; GINA 2024.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 35 % predicted) is admitted with an infective exacerbation. After 1 hour of nebulised bronchodilators, prednisolone, antibiotics and controlled oxygen: RR 28/min, alert, SpO2 91 % on 28 % Venturi, pH 7.31, PaCO2 8.4 kPa, HCO3⁻ 31 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start bilevel NIV in a monitored setting, targeting SpO2 88–92 %
High-flow nasal oxygen at 60 L/min and FiO2 0.6
Immediate intubation and invasive ventilation
Doxapram infusion
Increase to 60 % Venturi mask oxygen
questions.expl: Persistent respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35, PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa) despite optimal medical therapy is the indication for NIV (strong recommendation, ERS/ATS 2017; BTS/ICS 2016). Target SpO2 88–92 % to avoid oxygen-induced hypercapnia (E is harmful). ERS 2022 suggests trying NIV before HFNO in hypercapnic COPD; HFNO with a high FiO2 (B) is inappropriate. Intubation is for NIV failure or contraindications; doxapram is only used when NIV is unavailable or inappropriate. Reference: Davidson AC, et al. BTS/ICS guideline for the ventilatory management of acute hypercapnic respiratory failure in adults. **Thorax** 2016;71(Suppl 2):ii1–ii35; Rochwerg B, et al. ERS/ATS NIV guidelines. **Eur Respir J** 2017;50:1602426.

title: Case-style practice · W12-D2 · Severe pneumonia and influenza

questions.stem: Regarding severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP):
options: In CAPE COD, hydrocortisone reduced 28-day mortality in severe CAP.
Need for vasopressors is a major criterion of the ATS/IDSA definition of severe CAP.
A parapneumonic effusion with a pleural fluid pH below 7.2 requires chest tube drainage.
Combination therapy with a macrolide is not recommended in severe CAP.
questions.expl: A – CAPE COD (n = 800, France): 28-day mortality 6.2 % vs 11.9 % with hydrocortisone 200 mg/day; ERS/ESICM 2023 suggests hydrocortisone in severe CAP with shock (SCCM 2024 recommends corticosteroids in severe CAP); avoid in influenza or uncontrolled fungal infection. B – the two major criteria are septic shock requiring vasopressors and invasive ventilation. C – pH < 7.2 (or frank pus, positive Gram stain/culture) indicates a complicated effusion/empyema needing drainage. D – β-lactam plus macrolide is recommended for severe CAP (ERS/ESICM 2023; ATS/IDSA 2019). Reference: Dequin PF, et al. CAPE COD. **N Engl J Med** 2023;388:1931–1941; Martin-Loeches I, et al. ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines for the management of severe community-acquired pneumonia. **Intensive Care Med** 2023;49:615–632; Metlay JP, et al. ATS/IDSA CAP guideline. **Am J Respir Crit Care Med** 2019;200:e45–e67.

questions.stem: A previously well 19-year-old man has had an influenza-like illness for 4 days. He now presents with haemoptysis, hypotension, a white cell count of 1.8 × 10⁹/L and rapidly progressive multilobar consolidation with early cavitation. Sputum Gram stain shows abundant Gram-positive cocci in clusters, and Panton–Valentine leukocidin (PVL)–producing Staphylococcus aureus is suspected; susceptibilities are not yet available. Which is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial regimen?
options: Flucloxacillin alone
Vancomycin alone
Co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin
Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline
Linezolid plus clindamycin plus rifampicin, with IV immunoglobulin considered
questions.expl: PVL-associated necrotising pneumonia (young, post-influenza, haemoptysis, leucopenia, cavitation) has high mortality. UK guidance recommends toxin-suppressing agents: linezolid plus clindamycin and rifampicin (covering MRSA until susceptibilities are known), and considering IVIG to neutralise toxin. Flucloxacillin alone (A) lacks toxin suppression and misses MRSA; vancomycin (B) has poor lung penetration and does not suppress toxin production. Standard CAP regimens (C, D) do not reliably cover PVL-MRSA. Reference: Health Protection Agency (UKHSA). Guidance on the diagnosis and management of PVL-associated Staphylococcus aureus infections in England, 2nd ed., 2008 (updated); Gillet Y, et al. Factors predicting mortality in necrotizing community-acquired pneumonia caused by S. aureus containing PVL. **Clin Infect Dis** 2007;45:315–321.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation presents with 4 days of fever, myalgia and cough, now breathless with SpO2 90 % on air. She is not vaccinated this season. RR is 30/min and chest X-ray shows bilateral patchy infiltrates. Nasopharyngeal PCR is positive for influenza A. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Withhold oseltamivir because symptoms began more than 48 hours ago
Start oseltamivir immediately and arrange early critical care review
Give high-dose methylprednisolone
Avoid chest imaging because of the pregnancy
Defer ICU review until PaO2/FiO2 falls below 100 mmHg
questions.expl: Pregnancy (especially the third trimester) and obesity were the leading risk factors for critical illness and death in the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, and pregnant women remain a high-risk group for seasonal influenza. Neuraminidase inhibitors should be started as soon as possible in any hospitalised or high-risk patient, regardless of symptom duration (benefit is still seen > 48 h). Corticosteroids are associated with higher mortality in influenza pneumonia. Imaging must not be withheld (shielded CXR/CT dose is low). The threshold for ICU review should be low. Reference: Uyeki TM, et al. Clinical practice guidelines by the IDSA: 2018 update on diagnosis, treatment, chemoprophylaxis and institutional outbreak management of seasonal influenza. **Clin Infect Dis** 2019;68:e1–e47; Siston AM, et al. Pandemic 2009 influenza A(H1N1) virus illness among pregnant women in the United States. **JAMA** 2010;303:1517–1525.

title: Case-style practice · W12-D4 · Tracheostomy emergencies

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is on day 5 after a percutaneous tracheostomy (patent upper airway, not a laryngectomy). He becomes acutely hypoxic and agitated with no capnography trace. Oxygen has been applied to face and stoma, the inner cannula removed, a suction catheter will not pass, and the cuff has been deflated without improvement. The tracheostomy tube has now been removed. He has a pulse but is not breathing adequately. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Blindly reinsert a new tracheostomy tube through the stoma
Perform a needle cricothyroidotomy
Oxygenate via the upper airway with bag–mask ventilation while occluding the stoma
Perform fibreoptic bronchoscopy through the stoma
Wait for the ENT team before any further airway intervention
questions.expl: In the NTSP algorithm, once a non-patent tube has been removed, primary emergency oxygenation in a patient with a patent upper airway is via the mouth/nose (bag–mask, oral airway or supraglottic device) with the stoma covered; alternatively via the stoma (paediatric face mask or LMA over the stoma). Secondary manoeuvres are oral intubation or, by an experienced operator, stoma intubation (ideally fibreoptic-guided). Blind reinsertion through an immature (< 7–10 days) percutaneous tract risks false passage. Reference: McGrath BA, Bates L, Atkinson D, Moore JA; National Tracheostomy Safety Project. Multidisciplinary guidelines for the management of tracheostomy and laryngectomy airway emergencies. **Anaesthesia** 2012;67:1025–1041.

questions.stem: Regarding tracheostomy airway emergencies (NTSP):
options: Waveform capnography is the best indicator of a patent tracheostomy airway in a ventilated patient.
In a patient with a patent upper airway, oxygen should be applied to both the face and the stoma.
A patient with a laryngectomy can be oxygenated via the mouth.
A percutaneous tracheostomy tract less than 7 days old allows safe blind reinsertion.
questions.expl: A – capnography is mandatory for ventilated tracheostomy patients; absence of a trace indicates obstruction or displacement. B – this is the first step in the algorithm. C – after laryngectomy, the trachea is disconnected from the upper airway: oxygenate only via the stoma (and bedside signage must state this). D – immature tracts (particularly percutaneous) can close or allow false passage; reinsertion should be by an experienced operator with a fibreoptic scope or bougie, or the patient intubated orally. Reference: McGrath BA, et al. NTSP guidelines. **Anaesthesia** 2012;67:1025–1041.

title: Case-style practice · W12-D5 · Pleural disease

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with severe COPD presents with sudden breathlessness. SpO2 is 88 % on air, RR 26/min, BP 132/80 mmHg. Chest X-ray shows a left pneumothorax with a 2.5 cm rim at the level of the hilum and no mediastinal shift. She lives alone. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Observation and discharge with review in 48 hours
Small-bore (≤ 14 F) Seldinger chest drain and hospital admission
Needle aspiration and discharge if successful
Large-bore (28 F) surgical chest drain
Immediate video-assisted thoracoscopic pleurodesis
questions.expl: She has a symptomatic secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (underlying lung disease, age > 50) of > 2 cm. BTS guidance favours intervention with a small-bore drain and admission; aspiration is reserved for smaller (1–2 cm), minimally symptomatic SSP, and observation alone or discharge is unsafe with significant symptoms and poor reserve. Small-bore drains are as effective as large-bore drains and better tolerated. Definitive surgery is considered for a persistent air leak (> 3–5 days) or recurrence. Reference: Roberts ME, et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease. **Thorax** 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1–s42; MacDuff A, et al. Management of spontaneous pneumothorax: BTS pleural disease guideline 2010. **Thorax** 2010;65(Suppl 2):ii18–ii31.

questions.stem: Regarding pleural fluid analysis:
options: A pleural fluid/serum protein ratio > 0.5 indicates an exudate.
A pleural fluid LDH greater than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH indicates an exudate.
In patients on diuretics, Light's criteria may misclassify transudates as exudates; a serum–pleural albumin gradient > 12 g/L then favours a transudate.
Pleural fluid pH should be measured in frankly purulent fluid.
questions.expl: A, B – Light's criteria (any one = exudate): protein ratio > 0.5, LDH ratio > 0.6, or pleural LDH > 2/3 ULN serum LDH. C – diuresis concentrates pleural protein and LDH, so ~25 % of cardiac transudates are misclassified; the albumin gradient (or NT-proBNP) helps. D – frank pus indicates empyema needing drainage regardless of pH, and pus can damage the blood gas analyser; pH is measured in non-purulent fluid when infection is suspected (< 7.2 → drain). Reference: Light RW, et al. Pleural effusions: the diagnostic separation of transudates and exudates. **Ann Intern Med** 1972;77:507–513; Roberts ME, et al. BTS Guideline for pleural disease. **Thorax** 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1–s42.

title: Case-style practice · W13-D1 · Humidification and aerosol therapy

questions.stem: Regarding humidification and nebulisation in ventilated patients:
options: In a normal spontaneously breathing adult, the isothermic saturation boundary lies a few centimetres below the carina.
Heat and moisture exchangers are preferred in patients with copious, bloody secretions.
A jet nebuliser driven by an external gas source does not affect the delivered tidal volume or triggering.
Placing a nebuliser between the heat and moisture exchanger and the endotracheal tube is the recommended arrangement.
questions.expl: A – at the ISB inspired gas reaches 37 °C and 100 % relative humidity (44 mg/L); intubation bypasses the upper airway and moves the ISB distally. B – HMEs are contraindicated with copious or bloody secretions (risk of occlusion), large leaks, hypothermia and very high minute ventilation; use a heated humidifier. C – extra flow from an external jet nebuliser adds to the delivered volume, alters FiO2 and can impair triggering; vibrating-mesh nebulisers add no gas. D – an HME must not be placed between the nebuliser and the patient (it filters the aerosol), and placing the nebuliser proximal to the HME wets it; remove the HME during nebulisation or use a heated humidifier. Reference: Restrepo RD, Walsh BK. Humidification during invasive and noninvasive mechanical ventilation: 2012 AARC clinical practice guideline. **Respir Care** 2012;57:782–788; Dhand R. Aerosol delivery during mechanical ventilation: from basic techniques to new devices. **J Aerosol Med Pulm Drug Deliv** 2008;21:45–60.

title: Case-style practice · W13-D2 · Respiratory mechanics and PEEP

questions.stem: Regarding respiratory mechanics during mechanical ventilation:
options: During volume control with constant flow, the difference between peak and plateau pressure reflects airway (including tube) resistance.
Static compliance is calculated as tidal volume divided by (peak pressure − PEEP).
In a patient with expiratory flow limitation, setting external PEEP well above intrinsic PEEP reduces hyperinflation.
Pressure-controlled ventilation produces a constant (square-wave) inspiratory flow.
questions.expl: A – Ppeak − Pplat = flow × resistance. B – static compliance = VT / (Pplat − total PEEP); using peak pressure gives "dynamic" compliance, which includes resistance. C – external PEEP up to ~80 % of PEEPi reduces the inspiratory threshold load without worsening hyperinflation; PEEP exceeding PEEPi adds to end-expiratory volume. D – PCV produces a decelerating flow pattern; volume control is usually constant flow. Reference: Hess DR. Respiratory mechanics in mechanically ventilated patients. **Respir Care** 2014;59:1773–1794; Marini JJ. Dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP: two concepts that should be distinguished. **Am J Respir Crit Care Med** 2011;184:756–762.

questions.stem: Regarding the physiological effects of PEEP:
options: PEEP reduces left-ventricular afterload by decreasing LV transmural pressure.
PEEP that overdistends alveoli increases right-ventricular afterload.
PEEP reduces the pressure gradient for venous return.
PEEP improves oxygenation partly by recruiting alveoli and increasing functional residual capacity.
questions.expl: Raised intrathoracic pressure lowers LV transmural (afterload) pressure – beneficial in LV failure and cardiogenic pulmonary oedema – but reduces venous return by raising right atrial pressure. Overdistension compresses alveolar vessels and increases PVR, potentially causing acute cor pulmonale. Recruitment increases FRC and reduces shunt. The net effect on cardiac output depends on volume status and ventricular function. Reference: Mahmood SS, Pinsky MR. Heart–lung interactions during mechanical ventilation: the basics. **Ann Transl Med** 2018;6:349; Vieillard-Baron A, et al. Experts' opinion on management of hemodynamics in ARDS patients: focus on the effects of mechanical ventilation. **Intensive Care Med** 2016;42:739–749.

questions.stem: Regarding gas exchange and respiratory mechanics:
options: An increase in physiological dead space fraction raises PaCO2 if minute ventilation is unchanged.
Doubling respiratory rate while halving tidal volume keeps alveolar ventilation constant.
In the upright, spontaneously breathing lung, ventilation per unit volume is greater at the bases than at the apices.
The compliance of the respiratory system equals the sum of lung compliance and chest wall compliance.
questions.expl: A – PaCO2 ∝ VCO2 / [VE × (1 − VD/VT)]. B – alveolar ventilation = RR × (VT − VD); with a fixed dead space, halving VT reduces alveolar ventilation even though minute ventilation is unchanged. C – basal alveoli start smaller, on a steeper part of the pressure–volume curve. D – elastances add (1/Crs = 1/CL + 1/Ccw), so respiratory system compliance is lower than either component. Reference: West JB, Luks AM. *West's Respiratory Physiology: The Essentials*, 11th ed. Wolters Kluwer 2021; Hess DR. **Respir Care** 2014;59:1773–1794.

title: Case-style practice · W15-D1 · Traumatic brain injury

questions.stem: A 34-year-old motorcyclist is admitted with an isolated severe traumatic brain injury. The team wants to quote a 6-month outcome estimate to the family using the CRASH and IMPACT prognostic models. Regarding the variables in these models:
options: The GCS motor score (not the total GCS) is one of the three variables of the IMPACT core model.
Traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage on the admission CT is a variable of the IMPACT extended model.
Serum sodium is one of the laboratory variables of the IMPACT lab model.
Intracranial pressure values recorded during the first 24 h are part of the IMPACT extended model.
questions.expl: IMPACT core = age, GCS motor score and pupillary reactivity. The extended model adds pre-hospital hypoxia and hypotension, Marshall CT class, traumatic SAH and epidural haematoma; the lab model adds glucose and haemoglobin (not sodium). Neither IMPACT nor CRASH uses ICU-phase data such as ICP – both are admission models built for baseline risk stratification. CRASH uses age, GCS, pupils, major extracranial injury and CT findings, with country-income adjustment. Ref: Steyerberg EW et al. *PLoS Med* 2008; MRC CRASH Trial Collaborators. *BMJ* 2008.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with a severe diffuse TBI (GCS 6, Marshall III) is ventilated in a neuro-ICU. Regarding interventions according to the Brain Trauma Foundation 4th edition guideline and later trials:
options: Early prophylactic hypothermia (33–35 °C) is recommended to improve outcome in diffuse injury.
Prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation to a PaCO2 ≤ 3.3 kPa (25 mmHg) is not recommended.
High-dose methylprednisolone is not recommended because it increased mortality.
Phenytoin prophylaxis in the first week reduces the incidence of late (post-traumatic) epilepsy.
questions.expl: BTF 4th ed. (2016) does not recommend prophylactic hypothermia (POLAR 2018 found no benefit; Eurotherm3235 showed harm when used for ICP control). Prolonged hyperventilation ≤ 25 mmHg is a Level IIB "not recommended". Steroids are Level I contraindicated after CRASH-1 (increased mortality). Phenytoin (or levetiracetam) reduces early (< 7 days) seizures only – it does not prevent late post-traumatic epilepsy. Ref: Carney N et al. *Neurosurgery* 2017; Cooper DJ et al. *JAMA* 2018 (POLAR).

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with diffuse TBI has an intraparenchymal ICP monitor. He is sedated with propofol and fentanyl, head-up 30°, normothermic, PaCO2 4.9 kPa, Na 141 mmol/L and MAP 90 mmHg. Over 15 min the ICP rises to 28 mmHg and stays there; CPP is 62 mmHg. A repeat CT shows diffuse swelling with no surgical lesion. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Bolus of 20 % human albumin to expand plasma volume
Thiopental infusion titrated to burst suppression
Therapeutic hypothermia to 33 °C
Bolus of hyperosmolar therapy (hypertonic saline or mannitol)
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV followed by 4 mg 6-hourly
questions.expl: Sustained ICP > 22 mmHg despite basic measures (sedation, positioning, normocapnia, normothermia) should be treated next with intermittent hyperosmolar boluses – a tier 1 SIBICC intervention. Barbiturate coma and hypothermia are tier 3 rescue options with significant harms (Eurotherm3235 showed worse outcome with hypothermia for ICP). Albumin was associated with higher mortality in TBI (SAFE-TBI) and steroids are harmful (CRASH-1). Ref: Hawryluk GWJ et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2019 (SIBICC); Andrews PJD et al. *N Engl J Med* 2015.

title: Case-style practice · W15-D2 · Subarachnoid haemorrhage

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with WFNS grade 3 aneurysmal SAH had her anterior communicating artery aneurysm coiled on day 1. Regarding prevention and detection of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI):
options: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 h for 21 days reduces the risk of poor outcome.
Prophylactic induced hypertension in an asymptomatic patient is recommended once the aneurysm is secured.
Prophylactic hypervolaemia improves cerebral blood flow and outcome.
A mean MCA flow velocity > 200 cm/s with a Lindegaard ratio > 6 on transcranial Doppler suggests severe vasospasm.
questions.expl: Nimodipine is the only drug with proven outcome benefit (it reduces DCI rather than angiographic spasm). Prophylactic hypertension and hypervolaemia ("triple H") are not recommended; the aim is euvolaemia and avoidance of hypotension. TCD MCA velocity > 200 cm/s with Lindegaard (MCA/ICA) > 6 indicates severe vasospasm; a ratio < 3 suggests hyperaemia. Ref: Hoh BL et al. *Stroke* 2023 (AHA/ASA aSAH guideline); Treggiari MM et al. *Neurocrit Care* 2023.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man asks about his own risk of aneurysmal SAH after his sister died from one. Regarding risk factors for aneurysmal SAH:
options: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease increases the risk of intracranial aneurysm and SAH.
Moderate regular alcohol intake is protective against aneurysmal SAH.
Diabetes mellitus roughly doubles the risk of aneurysmal SAH.
Screening for unruptured aneurysms is routinely recommended for anyone with a single affected first-degree relative.
questions.expl: ADPKD (and other connective-tissue disorders) carries a several-fold higher aneurysm prevalence. Alcohol intake shows a dose-dependent increase in risk, not protection; the main modifiable factors are smoking, hypertension and heavy alcohol. Diabetes and hypercholesterolaemia are not positively associated (some studies even show an inverse association). Screening is usually advised when ≥ 2 first-degree relatives are affected or in ADPKD, not for a single affected relative. Ref: Feigin VL et al. *Stroke* 2005; Claassen J, Park S. *Lancet* 2022.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with WFNS grade 2 SAH had a basilar tip aneurysm coiled on admission. Twenty hours later she becomes progressively drowsy (GCS 15 → 11) with impaired upward gaze. Pupils are equal and reactive. Na 138 mmol/L, glucose 7 mmol/L, temperature 37.2 °C. TCD velocities are normal. CT shows enlarged temporal horns and a rounded third ventricle with periventricular lucency, without new blood. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Switch nimodipine to the intravenous route
Start noradrenaline to raise MAP by 20 %
Give 3 % hypertonic saline 250 ml
Repeat cerebral angiography to exclude rebleeding
Insert an external ventricular drain
questions.expl: Early decline in consciousness with upgaze palsy and ventriculomegaly with transependymal oedema is acute obstructive/communicating hydrocephalus, which occurs in ~20–30 % of SAH and is treated with CSF diversion (EVD). DCI is unusual before day 3 and TCD is normal; no new blood argues against rebleeding; sodium and glucose are normal. Ref: Hoh BL et al. *Stroke* 2023; Claassen J, Park S. *Lancet* 2022.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with a clipped middle cerebral artery aneurysm develops new expressive aphasia and right arm drift on day 7 after SAH. CT shows no hydrocephalus, rebleeding or established infarct. He is euvolaemic, Na 139 mmol/L, glucose 6.8 mmol/L, and MAP 84 mmHg on oral nimodipine. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: 2 L of colloid to achieve a CVP > 12 mmHg
Noradrenaline to raise MAP stepwise, reassessing the neurological deficit
Mannitol 1 g/kg
Simvastatin 80 mg via nasogastric tube
Switch to high-dose intravenous nimodipine
questions.expl: Symptomatic DCI after the aneurysm is secured is usually treated with a trial of induced hypertension (stepwise MAP increase while assessing neurological response), with endovascular rescue (angioplasty/intra-arterial vasodilators) if refractory. The evidence is weak (HIMALAIA stopped early), but hypervolaemia and haemodilution are harmful, high-dose statin (STASH) showed no benefit, and IV nimodipine causes hypotension without proven advantage over oral. Ref: Gathier CS et al. *Stroke* 2018 (HIMALAIA); Treggiari MM et al. *Neurocrit Care* 2023.

title: Case-style practice · W15-D4 · Acute stroke

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is found by his wife at 08:00 with left hemiparesis, left neglect and dysarthria; he was last seen well at 23:00. NIHSS is 14, glucose 6.1 mmol/L, BP 172/94 mmHg. Non-contrast CT shows no haemorrhage (ASPECTS 8); CT angiography shows a right M1 occlusion and CT perfusion a small ischaemic core with a large penumbra. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Aspirin 300 mg and admission to the stroke unit
Lower BP to < 140/90 mmHg and repeat imaging in 24 h
Endovascular thrombectomy
Unfractionated heparin infusion
Early decompressive hemicraniectomy
questions.expl: In unknown-onset/wake-up stroke with a proximal anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion and a favourable imaging profile, thrombectomy improves functional outcome up to 24 h from last seen well (DAWN, DEFUSE-3), and more recent trials extend benefit to larger cores. IV thrombolysis can also be considered with imaging selection (WAKE-UP, EXTEND), but thrombectomy is the key intervention here. BP needs only to be kept ≤ 185/110 mmHg peri-procedure; heparin and hemicraniectomy are not indicated. Ref: Nogueira RG et al. *N Engl J Med* 2018; Albers GW et al. *N Engl J Med* 2018; Turc G et al. *Eur Stroke J* 2023 (ESO).

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with a left MCA infarct (> 50 % of the territory) was independent before the stroke. She becomes drowsy (GCS 15 → 11) 30 h after onset despite head elevation and normoglycaemia; repeat CT shows space-occupying oedema with 6 mm midline shift. The family asks about decompressive hemicraniectomy. All of the following statements are consistent with current evidence EXCEPT:
options: Surgery within 48 h reduces mortality in patients aged ≤ 60 years.
In patients > 60 years surgery increases survival, but most survivors have moderately severe or severe disability.
Dominant-hemisphere infarction is not by itself a contraindication to surgery.
Osmotherapy may temporise but has not been shown to improve outcome.
Sustained ICP > 20 mmHg on an invasive monitor should be documented before surgery is offered.
questions.expl: The decision for hemicraniectomy in malignant MCA infarction is clinical and radiological (infarct volume, midline shift, decreasing consciousness); ICP monitoring is not required and ICP may be normal despite life-threatening shift. Pooled DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET data show a large mortality reduction in ≤ 60 years when done within 48 h; DESTINY II showed survival benefit in > 60 years at the cost of more disability, so shared decision-making is essential. Aphasia is not an exclusion. Ref: Vahedi K et al. *Lancet Neurol* 2007; Jüttler E et al. *N Engl J Med* 2014; van der Worp HB et al. *Eur Stroke J* 2021.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man presents with vertigo, vomiting, dysarthria and fluctuating consciousness. Regarding posterior circulation stroke:
options: Thrombectomy for acute basilar artery occlusion improves functional outcome compared with best medical treatment in selected patients up to 12–24 h.
In an acute vestibular syndrome, a normal head-impulse test is reassuring for a peripheral cause.
Early diffusion-weighted MRI can be falsely negative in brainstem infarction.
For a space-occupying cerebellar infarct with brainstem compression, an EVD alone is preferred to suboccipital decompressive craniectomy.
questions.expl: ATTENTION and BAOCHE (2022) showed better functional outcome with thrombectomy for basilar occlusion. In HINTS, a normal head-impulse test in a patient with acute continuous vertigo suggests a central (stroke) cause. DWI is falsely negative in up to ~20 % of small posterior-fossa infarcts within 24–48 h. Space-occupying cerebellar infarction is treated with suboccipital decompression (± EVD); EVD alone risks upward herniation and does not relieve brainstem compression. Ref: Tao C et al. *N Engl J Med* 2022; Jovin TG et al. *N Engl J Med* 2022; Wijdicks EFM et al. *Stroke* 2014.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman presents 2 h after onset of a right hemiparesis due to an ischaemic stroke; she has known atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation. Regarding early management:
options: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is an accepted alternative to alteplase for IV thrombolysis.
BP should be lowered to ≤ 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis is started.
Prophylactic-dose LMWH started within 24 h reduces mortality and is preferred to intermittent pneumatic compression.
For minor-to-moderate stroke, starting a DOAC within 48 h is as safe as delaying it to 6–14 days.
questions.expl: ESO 2023 recommends tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as an alternative to alteplase. BP must be ≤ 185/110 before and < 180/105 for 24 h after lysis. In immobile stroke patients, IPC reduced DVT (CLOTS 3); early LMWH has no mortality benefit and increases bleeding. ELAN (2023) and OPTIMAS (2024) showed early DOAC initiation is non-inferior and not associated with more bleeding. Ref: Alamowitch S et al. *Eur Stroke J* 2023; Fischer U et al. *N Engl J Med* 2023 (ELAN); CLOTS 3 Collaboration. *Lancet* 2013.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man presents 90 min after the sudden onset of a right homonymous hemianopia, expressive and receptive dysphasia, and weakness of the right face, arm and leg. He is right-handed, takes no anticoagulants and his glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. CT shows no haemorrhage. According to the Oxfordshire (Bamford) classification, which category fits best?
options: Lacunar syndrome (LACS)
Partial anterior circulation syndrome (PACS)
Posterior circulation syndrome (POCS)
Total anterior circulation syndrome (TACS)
Transient ischaemic attack
questions.expl: TACS requires all three: higher cerebral dysfunction (dysphasia, neglect), homonymous visual field defect and motor/sensory deficit in ≥ 2 of face, arm, leg. PACS = two of the three or isolated cortical deficit; LACS = pure motor/sensory without cortical signs; POCS = brainstem/cerebellar or isolated hemianopia. TACS has the worst prognosis (~40 % 30-day mortality) and usually reflects a proximal MCA/ICA occlusion – a thrombectomy candidate. Ref: Bamford J et al. *Lancet* 1991.

title: Case-style practice · W15-D5 · Status epilepticus

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has been having a generalised convulsive seizure for 7 minutes on arrival of the ambulance; no IV access can be obtained. Regarding drug treatment of convulsive status epilepticus:
options: Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg is an effective first-line alternative to IV lorazepam when venous access is not available.
After failure of benzodiazepines, levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate have similar efficacy.
Status epilepticus is termed refractory when seizures continue after a benzodiazepine and one second-line antiseizure drug.
Rocuronium terminates electrographic seizure activity and facilitates ventilation.
questions.expl: RAMPART showed IM midazolam (autoinjector) was at least as effective as IV lorazepam pre-hospital. ESETT found levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg and valproate 40 mg/kg each stopped seizures in ~50 %. Refractory SE = failure of first- and second-line therapy, requiring anaesthetic agents (midazolam, propofol, thiopental) with EEG monitoring. Neuromuscular blockers abolish the motor signs only – seizures continue electrographically, so EEG is mandatory if they are used. Ref: Silbergleit R et al. *N Engl J Med* 2012; Kapur J et al. *N Engl J Med* 2019; Trinka E et al. *Epilepsia* 2015.

title: Case-style practice · W16-D1 · Analgesia and sedation

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with Child–Pugh C alcohol-related cirrhosis is intubated for severe community-acquired pneumonia. He has oliguric AKI (creatinine 310 µmol/L) and is not yet on renal replacement therapy. He needs an opioid infusion for analgesia-based sedation to tolerate the ventilator. Which opioid has pharmacokinetics least affected by his hepatic and renal dysfunction?
options: Remifentanil
Morphine
Oxycodone
Pethidine (meperidine)
Codeine
questions.expl: Remifentanil is hydrolysed by non-specific blood and tissue esterases, so its context-sensitive half-time (~3–4 min) is unchanged by liver or kidney failure. Morphine-6-glucuronide (active) and morphine-3-glucuronide accumulate in renal failure; oxycodone depends on hepatic CYP metabolism and renal excretion; norpethidine accumulates and causes seizures; codeine is a prodrug with unpredictable CYP2D6 activation. Note that the remifentanil metabolite (remifentanil acid) accumulates in renal failure but has negligible activity. Ref: Devlin JW et al. *Crit Care Med* 2018 (PADIS); Breen D et al. *Crit Care* 2004.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man on long-term oxycodone for chronic back pain is in ICU after an emergency laparotomy. His thoracic epidural fell out on day 1. Despite escalating IV morphine PCA his pain score remains 8/10, limiting coughing. He is on low-dose noradrenaline, creatinine is rising, and he has a prolonged ileus. Which is the most appropriate additional analgesic strategy?
options: IV ketorolac 30 mg 8-hourly
IV clonidine infusion
Gabapentin via nasogastric tube
Double the morphine PCA bolus dose
Low-dose IV ketamine infusion
questions.expl: Low-dose ketamine (e.g. 0.1–0.3 mg/kg/h) is an effective opioid-sparing adjunct, especially in opioid-tolerant patients and after major abdominal surgery; PADIS suggests it in post-surgical ICU patients. NSAIDs are inadvisable with AKI and vasopressor need; clonidine worsens hypotension; gabapentinoids require enteral absorption (ileus) and act slowly; further opioid escalation worsens ileus without solving tolerance. Ref: Devlin JW et al. *Crit Care Med* 2018 (PADIS); Brinck ECV et al. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2018.

title: Case-style practice · W16-D2 · Delirium

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman is on day 5 of mechanical ventilation for pneumonia. Sedation has been stopped for a spontaneous breathing trial, but she is RASS +3, CAM-ICU positive and repeatedly tries to pull out her tube despite reorientation, family presence and pain control. She has no history of alcohol use. QTc is 520 ms. Which drug is the most appropriate choice?
options: Lorazepam IV bolus
Dexmedetomidine infusion
Haloperidol 5 mg IV 6-hourly
Quetiapine via nasogastric tube
Propofol infusion to RASS −4
questions.expl: For agitated delirium that prevents weaning/extubation, PADIS suggests dexmedetomidine; DahLIA showed more ventilator-free hours with dexmedetomidine than placebo in agitated delirium. With QTc 520 ms, haloperidol and quetiapine add arrhythmic risk, and neither shortens delirium (MIND-USA, AID-ICU). Benzodiazepines are a risk factor for delirium; deep propofol sedation delays weaning. Ref: Reade MC et al. *JAMA* 2016 (DahLIA); Devlin JW et al. *Crit Care Med* 2018 (PADIS); Andersen-Ranberg NC et al. *N Engl J Med* 2022.

questions.stem: A surgical ICU wants to reduce delirium among its elderly ventilated patients. Regarding delirium prevention:
options: Higher compliance with the ABCDEF bundle is associated with less delirium and coma.
Prophylactic low-dose haloperidol in high-risk patients reduced 28-day mortality in the REDUCE trial.
Non-pharmacological sleep promotion (earplugs, eye masks, noise reduction) is suggested by PADIS.
Rivastigmine added to haloperidol shortens delirium duration.
questions.expl: In >15 000 patients, ABCDEF bundle compliance was associated with less delirium, coma, restraint use and mortality. REDUCE (haloperidol 1–2 mg 8-hourly in 1789 patients) showed no effect on 28-day survival or delirium. PADIS suggests a multicomponent sleep-promoting strategy. The rivastigmine trial was stopped early because of higher mortality and longer delirium. Ref: Pun BT et al. *Crit Care Med* 2019; van den Boogaard M et al. *JAMA* 2018; van Eijk MM et al. *Lancet* 2010.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a 66-year-old ventilated patient with the CAM-ICU. Regarding this tool:
options: A patient with a RASS of −4 cannot be assessed and is considered comatose.
Inattention (feature 2) is tested with the Mini-Mental State Examination.
A positive result requires all four features to be present.
A known diagnosis of dementia precludes the use of CAM-ICU.
questions.expl: Assessment starts with the RASS: at −4/−5 the patient is comatose and is reassessed later. Inattention is tested with the letters test (squeeze on "A") or pictures. CAM-ICU is positive with features 1 (acute change/fluctuation) + 2 (inattention) + either 3 (altered level of consciousness, RASS ≠ 0) or 4 (disorganised thinking). It remains valid in patients with dementia (it detects acute change from baseline). Ref: Ely EW et al. *JAMA* 2001; Devlin JW et al. *Crit Care Med* 2018.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man has a 6-day episode of ICU delirium after septic shock. Regarding the epidemiology and consequences of ICU delirium:
options: Longer duration of delirium is independently associated with worse long-term cognitive impairment.
Hyperactive delirium is the most common subtype in ventilated patients.
An Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC) score ≥ 4 indicates delirium.
Haloperidol or ziprasidone shortened delirium duration compared with placebo in MIND-USA.
questions.expl: BRAIN-ICU showed delirium duration predicted global cognition at 3 and 12 months. Hypoactive and mixed forms predominate and are often missed. ICDSC (8 items) ≥ 4 indicates delirium. MIND-USA found no difference in days alive without delirium or coma with haloperidol or ziprasidone versus placebo. Ref: Pandharipande PP et al. *N Engl J Med* 2013; Girard TD et al. *N Engl J Med* 2018; Bergeron N et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2001.

title: Case-style practice · W16-D3 · Neuromuscular disorders

questions.stem: A 26-year-old student develops progressive limb weakness 10 days after a diarrhoeal illness. Regarding the epidemiology and immunology of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS):
options: About two-thirds of patients report an infection in the weeks before onset.
Anti-GQ1b antibodies are characteristic of the pure motor axonal (AMAN) variant.
The annual incidence is about 20 per 100 000 population.
Weakness typically continues to progress for more than 8 weeks before reaching its nadir.
questions.expl: Around two-thirds have a preceding respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (Campylobacter jejuni most often; also CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, Zika, SARS-CoV-2). Anti-GQ1b is associated with Miller Fisher syndrome and Bickerstaff encephalitis; AMAN is associated with anti-GM1/GD1a. Incidence is ~1–2 per 100 000/year. Nadir is reached within 4 weeks (usually 2); progression > 8 weeks suggests CIDP. Ref: Shahrizaila N et al. *Lancet* 2021; Leonhard SE et al. *Nat Rev Neurol* 2019.

questions.stem: Several patients with neuromuscular disease need emergency intubation. Regarding the use of neuromuscular blocking drugs:
options: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, suxamethonium can cause hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest.
In myotonic dystrophy, suxamethonium can cause generalised myotonic contracture that makes ventilation difficult.
Patients with myasthenia gravis are less sensitive than normal to non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers.
Sugammadex can reverse rocuronium-induced block in myasthenia gravis.
questions.expl: Dystrophic and denervated muscle can release large amounts of potassium (rhabdomyolysis/upregulated receptors) after suxamethonium. Myotonic patients may develop sustained contracture. Myasthenic patients are resistant to suxamethonium but very sensitive to non-depolarising agents – use reduced doses with quantitative monitoring. Sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium independently of acetylcholinesterase and has been used successfully in MG. Ref: Martyn JAJ, Richtsfeld M. *Anesthesiology* 2006; Blichfeldt-Lauridsen L, Hansen BD. *Acta Anaesthesiol Scand* 2012.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis is admitted to ICU with pneumonia and hypomagnesaemia. Which of the following drugs are recognised to precipitate or worsen myasthenic weakness?
options: Intravenous magnesium sulphate
Azithromycin
Ceftriaxone
Paracetamol
questions.expl: Magnesium reduces presynaptic acetylcholine release and can provoke crisis. Macrolides, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides impair neuromuscular transmission (FDA warnings for macrolides and quinolones). Others include beta-blockers, immune checkpoint inhibitors, quinine and botulinum toxin. Third-generation cephalosporins and paracetamol are considered safe choices. Ref: Sheikh S et al. *Muscle Nerve* 2021; Narayanaswami P et al. *Neurology* 2021.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with 4 days of ascending weakness and areflexia is in a high-dependency unit receiving IVIg. He now has a weak cough, difficulty swallowing saliva and bifacial weakness. SpO2 is 97 % on air and PaCO2 5.1 kPa. Bedside vital capacity has fallen from 32 to 17 ml/kg over 12 h, and maximal inspiratory pressure is −25 cmH2O. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Elective endotracheal intubation in the ICU
Non-invasive ventilation via a face mask
Continue observation until PaCO2 rises above 6.5 kPa
Switch from IVIg to plasma exchange and repeat vital capacity in 6 h
Start pyridostigmine
questions.expl: The "20/30/40 rule" (VC < 20 ml/kg, MIP weaker than −30 cmH2O, MEP < 40 cmH2O), rapid decline and bulbar dysfunction predict respiratory failure; intubation should be elective before hypoxaemia or hypercapnia, which are late signs. NIV is unsafe with bulbar weakness and aspiration risk. Changing immunotherapy does not address the imminent airway problem (and PE after IVIg is not beneficial); pyridostigmine has no role in GBS. Ref: Lawn ND et al. *Arch Neurol* 2001; Shahrizaila N et al. *Lancet* 2021.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman reports 3 weeks of drooping eyelids and double vision that are worse in the evening, and tiredness of her jaw towards the end of meals. Neck flexion weakens after repeated testing. Reflexes, sensation and CK are normal. CT chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Polymyositis
Myasthenia gravis
Miller Fisher syndrome
Myotonic dystrophy
questions.expl: Fatigable ocular, bulbar and proximal weakness without sensory signs, normal reflexes and CK, plus a thymic mass (thymoma or hyperplasia), is typical of acetylcholine-receptor antibody myasthenia gravis. LEMS has proximal leg weakness, areflexia that improves after exercise, autonomic features and is associated with small-cell lung cancer. Polymyositis raises CK; Miller Fisher gives ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia; myotonic dystrophy has myotonia and distal weakness. Ref: Gilhus NE. *N Engl J Med* 2016.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with suspected GBS has a lumbar puncture on day 3 of symptoms. Regarding CSF findings:
options: CSF protein may still be normal in the first week of illness.
A CSF white cell count > 50 cells/µl should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis.
A low CSF glucose is typical of GBS.
Albuminocytological dissociation is specific to GBS.
questions.expl: Protein is raised in only ~50 % in the first week (~90 % by week 3), so a normal early result does not exclude GBS. Mild pleocytosis (5–50/µl) is compatible, but > 50/µl suggests infection (HIV, Lyme, CMV polyradiculitis), leptomeningeal malignancy or sarcoid. Glucose is normal. Raised protein with normal cells is also seen in CIDP, spinal block, diabetes and other conditions. Ref: Leonhard SE et al. *Nat Rev Neurol* 2019; Fokke C et al. *Brain* 2014.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man who injects black-tar heroin into his thigh presents with 2 days of double vision, slurred speech and difficulty swallowing. He is alert and afebrile, has bilateral ptosis, poorly reactive dilated pupils, a dry mouth and symmetrical weakness of the neck and arms; sensation is normal. There is an indurated abscess on his thigh. In addition to supportive care and wound debridement, which treatment is most important?
options: Intravenous immunoglobulin
Plasma exchange
Pyridostigmine
Benzylpenicillin alone
Botulinum antitoxin
questions.expl: Descending symmetrical paralysis starting with cranial nerves, autonomic signs (dilated pupils, dry mouth), normal sensation and preserved consciousness in an injecting drug user = wound botulism. Antitoxin should be given as early as possible on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmation, because it only neutralises circulating toxin. Antibiotics are given after antitoxin with debridement; IVIg/plasma exchange are GBS treatments; pyridostigmine is ineffective. Ref: Rao AK et al. *MMWR Recomm Rep* 2021 (CDC botulism guidelines).

title: Case-style practice · W16-D4 · Brain death and confirmation of death

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man with a massive intracerebral haemorrhage is being tested for death by neurological criteria according to the UK Code of Practice. Regarding the brainstem reflex tests:
options: The vestibulo-ocular reflex is tested with at least 50 ml of ice-cold water instilled into each external auditory meatus over 1 minute.
Absent gag and cough reflexes indicate loss of glossopharyngeal and vagal (medullary) function.
The pupils need not be dilated, but must be fixed and unresponsive to bright light.
Preserved deep tendon reflexes in the legs preclude the diagnosis.
questions.expl: The tests assess the cranial-nerve reflex arcs: pupils (II/III), corneal (V/VII), vestibulo-ocular (VIII/III/VI, ≥ 50 ml ice-cold water over 1 min with tympanic membranes visible), motor response in cranial nerve distribution to central pain, gag and cough (IX/X), then apnoea. Mid-sized fixed pupils are compatible. Spinal reflexes – tendon reflexes, triple flexion, even Lazarus sign – may persist and do not preclude diagnosis. Ref: Academy of Medical Royal Colleges. *Code of Practice for the Diagnosis and Confirmation of Death* 2008 (rev. 2025); Greer DM et al. *JAMA* 2020 (World Brain Death Project).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with hypoxic brain injury after cardiac arrest is being considered for brainstem death testing in the UK. Which of the following are correct preconditions or apnoea-test requirements?
options: Before the apnoea test PaCO2 should be ≥ 6.0 kPa with pH < 7.40, and it must rise by > 0.5 kPa with no respiratory effort.
Blood glucose should be between 3.0 and 20 mmol/L.
Serum sodium must be between 135 and 145 mmol/L.
Core temperature must be ≥ 36 °C.
questions.expl: UK guidance requires reversible causes to be excluded: core temperature > 34 °C, sodium 115–160 mmol/L, potassium > 2 mmol/L, phosphate and magnesium 0.5–3.0 mmol/L, glucose 3.0–20 mmol/L, and no residual sedative or neuromuscular blocking effect. In the apnoea test, starting PaCO2 ≥ 6.0 kPa (pH < 7.40) and a rise ≥ 0.5 kPa without respiratory effort over 5 min confirm apnoea (higher starting values in chronic CO2 retainers). Ref: Academy of Medical Royal Colleges. *Code of Practice for the Diagnosis and Confirmation of Death* 2008 (rev. 2025); Greer DM et al. *JAMA* 2020.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old man with metastatic cancer, on a palliative pathway in a monitored ward bed, has a cardiorespiratory arrest. Regarding confirmation of death after circulatory arrest (UK practice):
options: Death should be confirmed only after a minimum of 5 minutes of observed continuous cardiorespiratory arrest.
