options: A perfusion pressure (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) < 30 mmHg supports the diagnosis.
Tibial shaft fractures are the commonest cause of acute compartment syndrome.
The limb should be elevated well above heart level to reduce swelling.
Continuous compartment pressure monitoring is useful in sedated patients at risk.
questions.expl: ΔP = diastolic pressure − compartment pressure < 30 mmHg (McQueen) is the most used threshold, especially valuable in obtunded patients where pain (the key early clinical sign, particularly on passive stretch) cannot be assessed – continuous pressure monitoring is advised. Tibial fractures account for ~40 % of cases. Elevation reduces arterial inflow; the limb should be kept at heart level, with circumferential dressings removed and urgent fasciotomy if confirmed. Ref: McQueen MM, Court-Brown CM. *J Bone Joint Surg Br* 1996; von Keudell AG et al. *Lancet* 2015.

title: Case-style practice · W24-D1 · Poisoning: general principles and antidotes

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman (50 kg) took about 60 tablets of ferrous sulphate (65 mg elemental iron each) 3 hours ago. She has vomited twice and has abdominal pain. Regarding iron poisoning:
options: Ingestion of more than 60 mg/kg of elemental iron is potentially severe.
Serum iron is most informative when measured 1 hour after ingestion.
Desferrioxamine–iron complexes can colour the urine reddish ("vin rosé").
Prolonged desferrioxamine infusion (> 24 h) has been associated with ARDS.
questions.expl: She has ingested ~78 mg/kg elemental iron (3900 mg/50 kg): < 20 mg/kg rarely causes toxicity, 20–60 mg/kg moderate, > 60 mg/kg potentially severe. Serum iron should be measured at ~4 h (peak 4–6 h; later for modified-release). Desferrioxamine is given for severe toxicity (shock, acidosis, altered consciousness) or high levels; ferrioxamine is renally excreted and colours the urine. Infusions beyond 24 h are linked to pulmonary toxicity. Activated charcoal does not bind iron; whole-bowel irrigation is considered if many tablets are visible on X-ray. Ref: Chang TP, Rangan C. *Pediatr Emerg Care* 2011; Manoguerra AS et al. *Clin Toxicol* 2005.

questions.stem: Regarding specific antidotes in poisoning:
options: Methylene blue is the first-line antidote for cyanide poisoning.
In patients with G6PD deficiency, methylene blue is the preferred treatment for methaemoglobinaemia.
Flumazenil should be given routinely to comatose patients after an unknown mixed overdose.
Naloxone reverses tramadol-induced seizures.
questions.expl: Hydroxocobalamin is first-line for cyanide (with sodium thiosulfate as adjunct). Methylene blue treats methaemoglobinaemia but is ineffective and can cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency – exchange transfusion or ascorbic acid are alternatives. Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in mixed overdoses (TCA, benzodiazepine dependence) and is not used routinely. Tramadol seizures are serotonergic/monoaminergic; naloxone does not prevent them – use benzodiazepines. Ref: Dart RC et al. *Ann Emerg Med* 2018 (antidote stocking consensus); Jang DH, Hoffman RS. *Ann Emerg Med* 2011 (methylene blue).

title: Case-style practice · W24-D2 · Paracetamol poisoning

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents 9 hours after taking 40 × 500 mg paracetamol tablets. Regarding management in current UK practice:
options: A single treatment line starting at 100 mg/L at 4 hours is used irrespective of individual risk factors.
The 12-hour SNAP acetylcysteine regimen causes fewer anaphylactoid reactions and less vomiting than the traditional 21-hour regimen.
After a staggered overdose the nomogram cannot be used and acetylcysteine should be given.
Acetylcysteine has no benefit when started more than 24 hours after ingestion.
questions.expl: Since 2012 the MHRA uses a single 100 mg/L line because "high-risk" factors (enzyme inducers, alcohol, malnutrition) are poorly predictive. SNAP showed fewer adverse reactions with a 12-h regimen, now widely adopted. Staggered or unknown-time ingestion invalidates the nomogram. Late acetylcysteine still reduces mortality in established liver failure (improved haemodynamics and oxygen delivery), so it should be given at any time with evidence of toxicity. Ref: Bateman DN et al. *Lancet* 2014 (SNAP); Keays R et al. *BMJ* 1991; MHRA. *Drug Safety Update* 2012.

title: Case-style practice · W24-D3 · Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is intubated after an amitriptyline overdose with a QRS of 150 ms. Regarding treatment of TCA cardiotoxicity:
options: Flecainide is appropriate for broad-complex tachycardia.
Sodium bicarbonate is given to a target arterial pH of about 7.45–7.55.
Physostigmine is recommended to reverse anticholinergic toxicity.
Class IA antiarrhythmics such as procainamide are contraindicated.
questions.expl: TCAs block fast sodium channels; sodium bicarbonate (1–2 mmol/kg boluses) provides a sodium load and alkalinisation that reduce drug binding, aiming for pH 7.45–7.55. Class IA and IC drugs (procainamide, flecainide) block sodium channels and worsen toxicity; lidocaine (IB) is a second-line option. Physostigmine may cause bradycardia, asystole and seizures in TCA poisoning. Lipid emulsion and ECMO are rescue options. Ref: Body R et al. *Emerg Med J* 2011; Bruccoleri RE, Burns MM. *J Med Toxicol* 2016.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought in 2 hours after taking her mother's amitriptyline. Which of the following are typical clinical features of TCA toxicity?
options: Sinus tachycardia
Pinpoint pupils
Hyperactive bowel sounds and diarrhoea
Profuse sweating
questions.expl: TCAs have anticholinergic effects: tachycardia (the most common ECG finding), dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, ileus, urinary retention and agitation/delirium, plus sodium-channel blockade (wide QRS, R in aVR > 3 mm), alpha-blockade (hypotension), seizures and coma. Miosis, increased bowel activity and sweating suggest cholinergic (organophosphate) or opioid toxicity. Ref: Kerr GW et al. *Emerg Med J* 2001; Body R et al. *Emerg Med J* 2011.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman is found drowsy with an empty pack of dosulepin. GCS is 10, HR 128/min, BP 84/50 mmHg and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS of 140 ms and a terminal R wave of 4 mm in aVR. Venous pH is 7.30. She has not had seizures. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Amiodarone 300 mg IV
Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV
Physostigmine 1 mg IV
Flumazenil 0.5 mg IV
Sodium bicarbonate 8.4 % 1–2 mmol/kg IV
questions.expl: QRS > 100 ms (seizure risk) and > 160 ms (ventricular arrhythmia risk), a prominent terminal R in aVR, hypotension and acidosis indicate sodium-channel cardiotoxicity – treat with hypertonic sodium bicarbonate boluses, repeated to narrow the QRS and maintain pH 7.45–7.55, together with airway protection and fluids/vasopressors. Amiodarone prolongs QT and worsens hypotension; magnesium is for torsades; physostigmine and flumazenil can precipitate arrhythmias and seizures. Ref: Bruccoleri RE, Burns MM. *J Med Toxicol* 2016; Body R et al. *Emerg Med J* 2011.

title: Case-style practice · W24-D4 · Toxic alcohols and smoke inhalation

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man is admitted 18 hours after drinking illicit spirits with friends. He complains of blurred vision "like a snowstorm" and abdominal pain. pH 7.05, PaCO2 2.6 kPa, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, anion gap 32 mmol/L, lactate 3 mmol/L, measured osmolality 330 mOsm/kg (calculated 295). Ethanol is undetectable. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Fomepizole and haemodialysis
Intravenous ethanol alone
Sodium bicarbonate alone
Thiamine and pyridoxine alone
Acetylcysteine
questions.expl: Visual disturbance, severe high-anion-gap acidosis and an osmolar gap of 35 suggest methanol poisoning (formic acid toxicity to the retina and basal ganglia). Fomepizole (or ethanol) blocks alcohol dehydrogenase to stop formation of toxic metabolites; EXTRIP recommends haemodialysis for methanol poisoning with severe acidosis (pH ≤ 7.15), visual or neurological signs, or high levels, as it removes both parent alcohol and formate. Bicarbonate and folinic acid are adjuncts; thiamine/pyridoxine are adjuncts for ethylene glycol. Ref: Roberts DM et al. *Crit Care Med* 2015 (EXTRIP); McMartin K et al. *Br J Clin Pharmacol* 2016.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old firefighter is rescued unconscious from an enclosed-space fire. He is intubated, BP 82/40 mmHg, PaO2 32 kPa on FiO2 1.0, lactate 11 mmol/L, COHb 18 % and central venous saturation 88 %. There are no external burns. Carbon monoxide and cyanide toxicity are both suspected. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV
Continue 100 % oxygen
Sodium thiosulfate as an adjunct
Sodium nitrite as first-line antidote
Vasopressor support
questions.expl: In smoke inhalation, combined CO and cyanide toxicity is common; coma, shock and lactate > 8–10 mmol/L despite high PaO2 and a raised ScvO2 (impaired cellular O2 extraction) suggest cyanide. Hydroxocobalamin is first-line because it does not impair oxygen transport. Nitrites induce methaemoglobinaemia, which further reduces oxygen-carrying capacity already compromised by carboxyhaemoglobin, so they are avoided in fire victims. Thiosulfate (rhodanese substrate) is an acceptable adjunct. Ref: Anseeuw K et al. *Eur J Emerg Med* 2013; Baud FJ et al. *N Engl J Med* 1991.

title: Case-style practice · W25-D1 · Liver disease in pregnancy

questions.stem: A 34-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks presents with a week of nausea, vomiting, polydipsia and malaise. She is mildly jaundiced and confused. BP 138/86 mmHg, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, ALT 320 U/L, bilirubin 95 µmol/L, INR 2.1, fibrinogen 1.1 g/L, platelets 110 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 175 µmol/L, urate high, ammonia raised. Ultrasound shows no haematoma. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: HELLP syndrome
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Acute hepatitis E infection
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
questions.expl: Third-trimester hepatic failure with hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy with low fibrinogen, encephalopathy, AKI, raised urate and ammonia, polydipsia and only modest transaminase rise fulfils the Swansea criteria (≥ 6) for AFLP. Treatment is prompt delivery after stabilisation (glucose, blood products) with intensive care. HELLP typically has marked hypertension, haemolysis and severe thrombocytopenia with preserved glucose and fibrinogen; cholestasis has pruritus and raised bile acids without liver failure; hepatitis E gives much higher transaminases; TTP has severe thrombocytopenia and MAHA. Ref: Ch'ng CL et al. *Gut* 2002; Knight M et al. *Gut* 2008.

title: Case-style practice · W25-D2 · Obstetric emergencies

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman is having a caesarean section at term under spinal anaesthesia. Immediately after delivery of the placenta she becomes acutely dyspnoeic, SpO2 falls to 78 %, BP drops to 60/30 mmHg and she becomes unresponsive. Echocardiography shows a dilated, poorly contracting right ventricle. Thirty minutes later she is oozing from all puncture sites with fibrinogen 0.6 g/L. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pulmonary thromboembolism
Amniotic fluid embolism
Anaphylaxis to oxytocin
High spinal block
Placental abruption
questions.expl: Sudden cardiorespiratory collapse during labour or delivery (or within 30 min of placental delivery) with acute RV failure, hypoxaemia and early overt DIC (fibrinogen often < 2 g/L) in the absence of fever meets the SMFM diagnostic criteria for amniotic fluid embolism. Diagnosis is clinical; there is no confirmatory laboratory test. PE rarely causes early consumptive coagulopathy; anaphylaxis has bronchospasm/urticaria and no DIC; high spinal causes bradycardia and weakness without DIC; abruption precedes delivery with pain and bleeding. Management is supportive: CPR, RV support, early aggressive correction of coagulopathy and, if needed, ECMO. Ref: Clark SL et al. *Am J Obstet Gynecol* 2016; Pacheco LD et al. *Am J Obstet Gynecol* 2016 (SMFM).

title: Case-style practice · W25-D3 · Maternal sepsis

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman, 3 days after an emergency caesarean section, presents with fever 39.4 °C, severe abdominal pain out of proportion to signs, offensive lochia; her toddler has had a sore throat this week. HR 132/min, BP 82/45 mmHg, RR 28/min, lactate 4.6 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Oral co-amoxiclav and review in 6 hours
CT abdomen and pelvis before starting antibiotics
Await blood culture results to target therapy
Immediate laparotomy and hysterectomy before resuscitation
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin within 1 hour, with fluids and critical care referral
questions.expl: This is septic shock, most likely from invasive group A streptococcal endometritis (household contact with pharyngitis, pain out of proportion). Antimicrobials should be given within 1 hour (after cultures, without delaying), with fluid resuscitation and early critical care input. Clindamycin is added to suppress toxin production in suspected GAS. Imaging and source control (which may include surgery) follow resuscitation; oral therapy and waiting for cultures are inappropriate. Ref: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists. *Green-top Guideline 64b* 2012; Evans L et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign).

title: Case-style practice · W25-D4 · Oncological emergencies

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma starts chemotherapy. Regarding tumour lysis syndrome (TLS):
options: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
Allopurinol rapidly lowers an already raised serum uric acid.
Urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate is recommended to prevent TLS.
Hypercalcaemia is a typical laboratory feature of TLS.
questions.expl: Rasburicase converts uric acid to allantoin, producing hydrogen peroxide that causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in G6PD deficiency. Allopurinol only prevents new uric acid formation (and increases xanthine); rasburicase is preferred for high-risk or established hyperuricaemia. Alkalinisation is no longer recommended – it promotes calcium phosphate and xanthine precipitation. TLS causes hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and secondary hypocalcaemia; clinical TLS adds AKI, arrhythmia or seizures (Cairo–Bishop). Ref: Howard SC et al. *N Engl J Med* 2011; Cairo MS, Bishop M. *Br J Haematol* 2004.

title: Case-style practice · W26-D1 · Perioperative risk assessment

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man is referred for cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) before an elective open oesophagectomy. Regarding CPET and functional capacity:
options: Peak oxygen consumption is most reliably estimated from the peak heart rate achieved.
A ventilatory equivalent for CO2 (VE/VCO2) slope above about 34 at the anaerobic threshold is associated with increased postoperative risk.
The anaerobic threshold can be identified non-invasively using the V-slope method.
In the METS study, subjective clinician assessment of functional capacity accurately identified patients with poor fitness.
questions.expl: CPET measures VO2 directly from expired gas (heart rate–based estimates are unreliable). The anaerobic threshold is detected when VCO2 rises disproportionately to VO2 (V-slope); AT < ~10–11 ml/kg/min and high VE/VCO2 (ventilatory inefficiency) predict complications. METS (1401 patients) showed that subjective assessment had poor sensitivity for detecting low fitness, whereas DASI and NT-proBNP added predictive value. Ref: Levett DZH et al. *Br J Anaesth* 2018 (POETTS); Wijeysundera DN et al. *Lancet* 2018 (METS).

questions.stem: A surgical team is choosing a risk model to counsel a 78-year-old woman before an emergency laparotomy. Regarding perioperative risk scores:
options: P-POSSUM uses the same physiological and operative variables as POSSUM with a different equation to reduce overprediction of mortality.
The NELA risk model is designed for patients undergoing emergency laparotomy.
The ASA physical status classification incorporates the complexity of the planned surgery.
A preoperative creatinine > 177 µmol/L (2 mg/dl) is one of the six Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) predictors.
questions.expl: POSSUM (12 physiological + 6 operative variables) overpredicts mortality in low-risk patients; P-POSSUM recalibrated the equation. The NELA model (UK National Emergency Laparotomy Audit) is specific to emergency laparotomy. ASA grades the patient's pre-existing condition only. RCRI predictors: high-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes and creatinine > 177 µmol/L; age is not included. Ref: Prytherch DR et al. *Br J Surg* 1998; Lee TH et al. *Circulation* 1999; Eugene N et al. *Br J Anaesth* 2018 (NELA model).

title: Case-style practice · W26-D2 · Cardiac surgical ICU

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with diabetes and CKD stage 3 is scheduled for urgent CABG and aortic valve replacement. Regarding cardiac surgery-associated AKI (CSA-AKI):
options: Pre-existing CKD is one of the strongest risk factors.
Emergency surgery increases the risk.
Off-pump surgery eliminates the risk of AKI.
Perioperative high-dose atorvastatin prevented AKI in a randomised trial.
questions.expl: Risk factors include CKD, older age, diabetes, heart failure/low EF, emergency or combined surgery, long cardiopulmonary bypass and transfusion. Off-pump surgery reduced mild AKI in CORONARY but did not change dialysis or longer-term renal outcomes, and AKI still occurs. High-dose perioperative atorvastatin did not reduce AKI (Billings 2016). The KDIGO bundle in high-risk patients (biomarker-guided) reduced AKI in PrevAKI. Ref: Billings FT et al. *JAMA* 2016; Garg AX et al. *JAMA* 2014; Meersch M et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2017.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman is in the ICU 4 h after mitral valve repair, with epicardial ventricular wires connected to a temporary pacemaker set to VVI 80/min, output 5 mA, sensitivity 2 mV. Her own rhythm is now sinus at 95/min, but pacing spikes continue to appear at regular intervals, including one falling on a T wave. Which is the most appropriate adjustment?
options: Increase the sensitivity by lowering the mV setting
Increase the output to 10 mA
Increase the pacing rate to 100/min
Reverse the polarity of the pacing wires
Switch to asynchronous VOO mode
questions.expl: Pacing spikes despite an intrinsic rhythm faster than the set rate = undersensing; spikes on the T wave risk R-on-T ventricular fibrillation. Making the pacemaker more sensitive (lower mV number) allows it to detect native QRS complexes and inhibit. Increasing output treats failure to capture; asynchronous mode is used to avoid inappropriate inhibition from oversensing (e.g. diathermy) and would worsen the competition. If undersensing persists, the generator should be set to a rate below the intrinsic rate or switched off with wires kept ready. Ref: Reade MC. *Anaesthesia* 2007; Gammage MD. *Heart* 2000.

title: Case-style practice · W26-D3 · Organ donation

questions.stem: Regarding organ donation after circulatory (DCD) and brainstem (DBD) death:
options: In UK DCD practice, the functional warm ischaemic time begins when systolic BP falls below 50 mmHg (or SpO2 < 70 %).
Normothermic regional perfusion after DCD restores oxygenated blood flow to the brain as well as abdominal organs.
The heart tolerates a longer period of cold ischaemia than the kidney.
Lungs cannot be donated if the PaO2/FiO2 ratio is below 40 kPa at any time.
questions.expl: Functional WIT starts with significant hypotension/hypoxia after withdrawal; organ-specific limits apply. NRP (abdominal or thoracoabdominal) deliberately excludes cerebral circulation by clamping/occluding the aortic arch vessels. Cold ischaemia tolerance: kidney ~24–36 h, liver ~12 h, heart ~4–6 h (ex-situ perfusion extends this). Lungs with poor initial oxygenation can often be optimised with recruitment, bronchoscopy and protective ventilation (or ex-vivo lung perfusion), so a low ratio is not an absolute exclusion. Ref: Meyfroidt G et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2019; Thuong M et al. *Transpl Int* 2016 (DCD consensus).

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has been confirmed dead by neurological criteria and his family supports organ donation. Over 2 hours his urine output rises to 400 ml/h, serum sodium increases from 145 to 156 mmol/L and urine osmolality is 110 mOsm/kg. MAP is 72 mmHg on low-dose noradrenaline. Which is the most appropriate treatment for his polyuria?
options: Intravenous hydrocortisone
Insulin infusion
Desmopressin (DDAVP) IV
Triiodothyronine (T3) infusion
Replace urine output ml-for-ml with 0.9 % saline
questions.expl: Central diabetes insipidus develops in most DBD donors; untreated hypernatraemia (> 155 mmol/L) is associated with graft dysfunction, particularly of the liver. Desmopressin (V2-selective) treats DI without vasoconstriction; low-dose vasopressin is an alternative that also supports BP. Losses should be replaced with hypotonic fluid (e.g. 5 % glucose), not saline, which worsens hypernatraemia. Hydrocortisone is part of donor management (and for vasopressor-refractory shock) and T3 is no longer routinely recommended, but neither treats DI. Ref: Meyfroidt G et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2019; Kotloff RM et al. *Crit Care Med* 2015.

title: Case-style practice · W26-D4 · Transplant recipients in ICU

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man who had an orthotopic heart transplant 2 years ago is admitted with sepsis. Regarding the physiology of the denervated heart:
options: Atropine does not increase the heart rate.
Isoprenaline is an effective chronotrope.
The resting heart rate is typically higher than normal (about 90–110/min).
Indirect-acting sympathomimetics such as ephedrine have a reduced chronotropic effect.
questions.expl: The transplanted heart lacks autonomic innervation: vagal tone is absent (higher intrinsic rate, no response to atropine or vagal manoeuvres), and it relies on circulating catecholamines and the Frank–Starling mechanism to raise output. Direct-acting agents (isoprenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine) work normally (beta-receptors may even be upregulated), whereas indirect agents relying on neuronal noradrenaline release (ephedrine) are less effective. Neostigmine can still cause bradycardia (and has caused asystole) owing to direct cardiac muscarinic effects. Ref: Costanzo MR et al. *J Heart Lung Transplant* 2010 (ISHLT guidelines); Cheng DCH, Ong DD. *Can J Anaesth* 1993.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman received a kidney transplant 7 months ago; her co-trimoxazole prophylaxis was stopped at 6 months and she recently had pulsed methylprednisolone for rejection. She presents with 5 days of dry cough and breathlessness. SpO2 is 86 % on air; CT shows bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities with sparing of the periphery. LDH and serum beta-D-glucan are elevated. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Atovaquone suspension
High-dose intravenous trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole
Voriconazole
Ganciclovir
Amoxicillin plus clarithromycin
questions.expl: Recent augmented immunosuppression, stopped prophylaxis, hypoxaemia with diffuse ground glass, high LDH and beta-D-glucan point to Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; diagnosis is confirmed by BAL PCR/immunofluorescence but treatment should not be delayed. TMP-SMX (15–20 mg/kg/day of trimethoprim) is first-line; atovaquone is for mild disease or intolerance. Adjunctive steroids are standard in HIV with hypoxaemia but their benefit in non-HIV patients is uncertain. Voriconazole has no activity against Pneumocystis; ganciclovir is for CMV. Ref: Maschmeyer G et al. *J Antimicrob Chemother* 2016 (ECIL); Fishman JA, Gans H. *Clin Transplant* 2019 (AST).

title: Case-style practice · W28-D1 · Pharmacokinetics in critical illness

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with combined hepatic and renal failure needs several drugs whose elimination does not depend on these organs. Regarding organ-independent drug elimination:
options: Remifentanil is hydrolysed by non-specific blood and tissue esterases.
Cisatracurium is eliminated mainly by Hofmann degradation.
Suxamethonium is hydrolysed by plasma (butyryl)cholinesterase.
Clevidipine is cleared mainly by hepatic cytochrome P450 metabolism.
questions.expl: Remifentanil, esmolol and clevidipine are ester drugs hydrolysed by blood/tissue esterases, giving short, organ-independent half-lives (clevidipine t½ ~1 min). Cisatracurium undergoes temperature- and pH-dependent Hofmann elimination (producing laudanosine, less than atracurium). Suxamethonium and mivacurium are hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase – prolonged block occurs with genetic variants or severe liver disease. Ref: Egan TD. *Clin Pharmacokinet* 1995; Kisor DF, Schmith VD. *Clin Pharmacokinet* 1999; Varon J, Marik PE. *Crit Care* 2008.

title: Case-style practice · W28-D2 · Sedative drug toxicity

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with severe TBI has received propofol at 5 mg/kg/h for 3 days to control ICP, with noradrenaline for CPP. He develops new right bundle branch block with coved ST elevation in V1–V2, progressive bradycardia, rising noradrenaline requirement, lactate 6 mmol/L, CK 9000 U/L, triglycerides 6.5 mmol/L and dark urine. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Increase the propofol dose to suppress cerebral metabolism further
Start an amiodarone infusion
Give a 1 L crystalloid bolus and continue propofol
Stop propofol, switch to an alternative sedative and provide organ support (including RRT or ECMO if needed)
Add a ketamine infusion while continuing propofol
questions.expl: Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) – metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hypertriglyceridaemia, Brugada-like ECG, bradyarrhythmias progressing to asystole, AKI and cardiac failure – is associated with doses > 4 mg/kg/h for > 48 h, young age, TBI, catecholamines and steroids. Mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation is impaired. Management is immediate cessation of propofol, supportive care, pacing for bradycardia, and RRT or ECMO in refractory cases; carbohydrate supply may help. Amiodarone worsens bradycardia. Ref: Hemphill S et al. *Br J Anaesth* 2019; Kam PCA, Cardone D. *Anaesthesia* 2007.

title: Case-style practice · W28-D4 · Receptor pharmacology

questions.stem: A septic patient on noradrenaline and dobutamine is also given several antagonists. Regarding drug–receptor interactions:
options: An inverse agonist reduces the constitutive (baseline) activity of its receptor.
A non-competitive antagonist increases the maximal effect (Emax) of an agonist.
A partial agonist always has a lower affinity for its receptor than a full agonist.
A drug's potency is determined only by its intrinsic efficacy.
questions.expl: Inverse agonists stabilise the inactive receptor state and reduce constitutive activity. Competitive antagonists cause a parallel rightward shift (surmountable, Emax unchanged); non-competitive or irreversible antagonists decrease Emax. Partial agonists have submaximal intrinsic efficacy but may have high affinity (e.g. buprenorphine), so they can antagonise full agonists. Potency (EC50) depends on both affinity and efficacy (and on receptor reserve). Ref: Neubig RR et al. *Pharmacol Rev* 2003 (IUPHAR nomenclature); Rang HP. *Br J Pharmacol* 2006.

questions.stem: Regarding receptor types and second-messenger systems relevant to ICU drugs:
options: Beta-1 adrenoceptors couple to Gs, increasing intracellular cAMP.
Corticosteroids act mainly through membrane tyrosine-kinase receptors.
The GABA-A receptor is a ligand-gated chloride channel.
Muscarinic M2 receptors in the heart couple to Gq.
questions.expl: Beta-1 (and beta-2) → Gs → adenylate cyclase → cAMP (dobutamine; PDE3 inhibitors such as milrinone prevent cAMP breakdown). Steroids and thyroid hormones act on intracellular nuclear receptors that alter gene transcription; insulin acts via a tyrosine-kinase receptor. GABA-A (benzodiazepines, propofol) and nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels. Cardiac M2 receptors couple to Gi (reducing cAMP and opening K channels → bradycardia); M1/M3 and alpha-1 couple to Gq. Ref: Alexander SPH et al. *Br J Pharmacol* 2023 (Concise Guide to Pharmacology).

title: Case-style practice · W28-D5 · Anticoagulant pharmacology

questions.stem: Several ICU patients are receiving different anticoagulants. Regarding their mechanisms and reversal:
options: Argatroban is eliminated mainly by the kidneys and should be avoided in renal failure.
Idarucizumab reverses rivaroxaban.
Andexanet alfa reverses dabigatran.
Protamine fully reverses fondaparinux.
questions.expl: Argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor) is hepatically cleared and is therefore suitable in renal failure (dose-reduce in liver failure); bivalirudin is partly renally cleared. Idarucizumab is a humanised antibody fragment that binds dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor). Andexanet alfa is a decoy factor Xa that binds FXa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban). Fondaparinux (indirect, antithrombin-mediated FXa inhibitor) has no protamine binding; protamine fully reverses UFH and only partially LMWH. Ref: Pollack CV et al. *N Engl J Med* 2017 (RE-VERSE AD); Connolly SJ et al. *N Engl J Med* 2019 (ANNEXA-4); Cuker A et al. *Am J Hematol* 2019.

title: Case-style practice · W29-D1 · CVC, arterial line, complications; ultrasound guidance

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in the ICU needs invasive arterial monitoring and several limb vascular access sites are considered. Regarding the surface anatomy of peripheral arteries:
options: At the wrist, the radial artery is palpated lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis.
In the antecubital fossa, the brachial artery lies lateral to the biceps tendon.
At the inguinal ligament, the femoral artery lies at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.
On the dorsum of the foot, the dorsalis pedis artery runs just lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.
questions.expl: The radial artery lies between the brachioradialis and flexor carpi radialis tendons (lateral to FCR). The brachial artery lies MEDIAL to the biceps tendon, with the median nerve medial to the artery – hence the nerve-injury risk of brachial cannulation. The femoral artery is at the mid-inguinal point (the mid-point of the inguinal ligament is slightly more lateral). Dorsalis pedis runs lateral to EHL and is absent or impalpable in a minority of people. Ultrasound guidance improves first-pass success at all of these sites. Reference: Lamperti M et al. International evidence-based recommendations on ultrasound-guided vascular access. **Intensive Care Med** 2012;38:1105–17.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman requires an ultrasound-guided right internal jugular central venous catheter. Regarding the relevant neck anatomy:
options: In the lower neck the internal jugular vein usually lies lateral (often anterolateral) to the common carotid artery.
The anterior border of the posterior triangle of the neck is formed by the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
The external jugular vein runs deep to sternocleidomastoid throughout its course.
The vagus nerve lies outside the carotid sheath, anterior to the internal jugular vein.
questions.expl: The IJV lies lateral/anterolateral to the carotid within the carotid sheath; excessive head rotation increases arterial overlap, so a neutral or slightly rotated head is preferred with real-time ultrasound. The posterior triangle is bounded by SCM (anterior), trapezius (posterior) and clavicle (base). The external jugular vein is SUPERFICIAL, crossing over SCM beneath platysma. The vagus lies INSIDE the carotid sheath, posterior and between the artery and vein. Reference: Lamperti M et al. International evidence-based recommendations on ultrasound-guided vascular access. **Intensive Care Med** 2012;38:1105–17.

title: Case-style practice · W29-D2 · Chest drain, pericardiocentesis, paracentesis, lumbar puncture

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with suspected encephalitis in the ICU is being considered for lumbar puncture. Which statements about safety of the procedure are correct?
options: If he is on twice-daily therapeutic-dose enoxaparin, at least 24 h should elapse after the last dose before needle insertion.
If he had a GCS of 9 with a new unilateral fixed dilated pupil, brain imaging should precede the LP.
Cellulitis over the lumbar puncture site is a contraindication to puncture through that area.
A platelet count of 70 × 10⁹/L mandates platelet transfusion before LP.
questions.expl: ASRA guidance (adopted widely for neuraxial needle placement) recommends ≥24 h after therapeutic LMWH. Signs of brain shift (reduced consciousness, focal signs, pupillary abnormality) require CT first; empirical antimicrobials must not be delayed for imaging/LP. Local skin/soft-tissue infection is a contraindication at that site. Most guidance accepts LP with platelets ≥40–50 × 10⁹/L, so 70 × 10⁹/L needs no transfusion. Reference: Horlocker TT et al. Regional anesthesia in the patient receiving antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy (ASRA 4th ed.). **Reg Anesth Pain Med** 2018;43:263–309; van de Beek D et al. ESCMID guideline: diagnosis and treatment of acute bacterial meningitis. **Clin Microbiol Infect** 2016;22:S37–62.

questions.stem: In ICU bedside procedures, landmarks matter even when ultrasound is available. Regarding procedural anatomy:
options: For paracentesis, a left lower quadrant site lateral to the rectus sheath reduces the risk of injuring the inferior epigastric vessels.
In the femoral triangle the femoral nerve lies medial to the femoral vein.
Echocardiography-guided pericardiocentesis chooses the entry point where the effusion is largest and closest to the skin, which is not necessarily subxiphoid.
The inferior epigastric arteries run in the linea alba, so the midline infra-umbilical approach carries the greatest risk of abdominal wall bleeding.
questions.expl: The inferior epigastric vessels run deep to the rectus muscles (roughly at the junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral third of a line from umbilicus to mid-inguinal point), so the lateral LLQ (and the avascular linea alba) are the safer sites; ultrasound guidance is recommended. In the femoral triangle the order from lateral to medial is Nerve–Artery–Vein (NAVY). Echo-guided pericardiocentesis (apical, parasternal or subxiphoid) has a lower complication rate than blind subxiphoid puncture. Reference: Adler Y et al. 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases. **Eur Heart J** 2015;36:2921–64; Biggins SW et al. AASLD practice guidance on ascites. **Hepatology** 2021;74:1014–48.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has an LP for suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Regarding lumbar anatomy and CSF physiology in adults:
options: The line joining the iliac crests (Tuffier's line) usually crosses the L4 spinous process or L4–5 interspace.
Total CSF volume is about 150 mL, with production of roughly 500 mL/day.
Normal CSF glucose is about 60–70 % of the simultaneous plasma glucose.
Opening pressure should be measured with the patient sitting upright, where the normal range is 25–35 cmH₂O.
questions.expl: Tuffier's line is the usual landmark for L3–4/L4–5 (it may be higher in obesity, so ultrasound helps). CSF volume ~125–150 mL and turnover ~3–4 times/day. CSF:plasma glucose ratio normally ~0.6; <0.4 suggests bacterial/fungal/TB infection. Opening pressure must be measured in the LATERAL decubitus position with legs extended – sitting values are spuriously high and uninterpretable; normal adult values are up to ~20–25 cmH₂O. Reference: Sakka L, Coll G, Chazal J. Anatomy and physiology of cerebrospinal fluid. **Eur Ann Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Dis** 2011;128:309–16.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with a large parapneumonic effusion needs an intercostal drain. Regarding safe insertion:
options: The needle and drain should pass just above the upper border of a rib.
The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs along the upper border of each rib.
Thoracic ultrasound is recommended before (or during) drain insertion for pleural fluid.
Trocar insertion is recommended to facilitate placement of small-bore drains.
questions.expl: The vein–artery–nerve bundle lies in the costal groove on the INFERIOR border of each rib, so entry is over the upper border of the rib below. BTS guidance recommends image (ultrasound) guidance for all pleural procedures for fluid, and the safe triangle (lateral border of pectoralis major, anterior border of latissimus dorsi, line at the level of the 5th ICS, apex below the axilla). Small-bore drains are inserted by Seldinger technique; trocars should not be used because of visceral injury risk. Reference: Roberts ME et al. British Thoracic Society guideline for pleural disease. **Thorax** 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1–42.

title: Case-style practice · W29-D3 · Bronchoscopy, BAL; emergency/failed airway

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with a 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' situation requires emergency front-of-neck access. Regarding airway anatomy:
options: The thyroid isthmus overlies the cricothyroid membrane.
The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring of the airway.
The right main bronchus is longer and more horizontal than the left.
The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
questions.expl: The thyroid isthmus overlies the 2nd–4th tracheal rings, below the cricoid – the cricothyroid membrane is relatively avascular, which is why scalpel–bougie–tube cricothyroidotomy is the DAS technique. The cricoid is the only complete ring. The RIGHT main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical (hence right endobronchial intubation/aspiration). All intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid (external laryngeal nerve). Reference: Frerk C et al. Difficult Airway Society 2015 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult intubation in adults. **Br J Anaesth** 2015;115:827–48.

questions.stem: During rapid sequence induction in a 40-year-old ICU patient, two intubation attempts fail and a supraglottic airway (SGA) is considered. Which statements are correct?
options: A second-generation SGA (with gastric drain channel) is recommended for rescue oxygenation.
If cricoid pressure impedes SGA insertion, it should be released.
An SGA can be used as a conduit for flexible-scope-guided intubation.
Second-generation SGAs generally achieve higher oropharyngeal seal pressures than the classic LMA.
questions.expl: DAS/ICS-FICM guidance: after failed intubation, insert a second-generation SGA (maximum three attempts), releasing cricoid pressure if necessary. If oxygenation is achieved, options include waking the patient, intubating through the SGA with a flexible scope (often via an Aintree catheter), or proceeding with the SGA in rare circumstances. Second-generation devices have higher seal pressures and allow gastric drainage, although none fully protects against aspiration. Reference: Higgs A et al. Guidelines for the management of tracheal intubation in critically ill adults. **Br J Anaesth** 2018;120:323–52.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman is on the surgical ward 5 hours after a parathyroidectomy. Nursing staff note a rapidly enlarging anterior neck swelling. She is anxious, has inspiratory stridor and SpO₂ 89 % on 15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreather mask. Help, including an airway team, has been called and is on its way. Which is the MOST appropriate immediate step?
options: Nebulised adrenaline and IV dexamethasone, then reassess in 15 minutes
Urgent CT of the neck to delineate the collection before any intervention
Open the skin sutures and the deep (strap muscle) layer at the bedside to evacuate the clot
Inhalational induction of anaesthesia on the ward to preserve spontaneous breathing
Awake fibreoptic nasal intubation before any manipulation of the wound
questions.expl: Post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery haematoma compresses the airway and causes venous/lymphatic laryngeal oedema. The multidisciplinary consensus guideline uses the 'SCOOP' approach (Skin exposure, Cut sutures, Open skin, Open muscles, Pack) at the bedside as soon as airway compromise is recognised, in parallel with calling for help and giving oxygen. Imaging delays treatment; steroids/adrenaline do not decompress the haematoma; gas induction and awake techniques are hazardous in a distressed, obstructing patient. If tracheal intubation is then needed it should be performed by the most experienced operator with front-of-neck access prepared. Reference: Iliff HA et al. Management of haematoma after thyroid surgery: systematic review and multidisciplinary consensus guidelines. **Anaesthesia** 2022;77:82–95.

title: Case-style practice · W29-D5 · ICU imaging (CXR/CT) and ECG interpretation

questions.stem: A 72-year-old ICU patient on several drugs is found to have a QTc of 520 ms. Which of the following typically PROLONG the QT interval?
options: Hypomagnesaemia
Hypocalcaemia
Digoxin therapy
Hyperkalaemia
questions.expl: Hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia prolong QT (hypocalcaemia by lengthening the ST segment). Digoxin SHORTENS QT and causes 'reverse tick' ST depression. Hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves, PR/QRS widening and a normal or shortened QT; it is hypokalaemia that prolongs QT(U). Management of QT prolongation: stop offending drugs (e.g. haloperidol, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron), correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺, monitor. Reference: Drew BJ et al. Prevention of torsade de pointes in hospital settings: AHA/ACCF scientific statement. **J Am Coll Cardiol** 2010;55:934–47.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman with sudden dyspnoea and a CT-confirmed central pulmonary embolism has a 12-lead ECG. Regarding ECG findings of acute right ventricular pressure overload:
options: An S1Q3T3 pattern is present in only a minority of patients with acute PE.
Sinus bradycardia is the most common ECG abnormality in acute PE.
Left axis deviation is the typical axis change of acute RV strain.
A normal ECG makes haemodynamically significant PE unlikely enough to stop further investigation.
questions.expl: S1Q3T3 is specific but insensitive (~10–20 %). Sinus TACHYCARDIA is the commonest abnormality; other signs of RV strain include T-wave inversion in V1–V4, new RBBB, RIGHT axis deviation and P pulmonale. The ECG is neither sensitive nor specific; a normal ECG does not exclude PE, and diagnostic work-up follows clinical probability, D-dimer and CTPA/echo. Reference: Konstantinides SV et al. 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism. **Eur Heart J** 2020;41:543–603.

questions.stem: A post-operative cardiac surgical patient's chest X-ray is reviewed for device positions. Which statements are correct?
options: The ideal tip of a right internal jugular CVC is in the lower SVC or at the cavo-atrial junction.
A left-sided CVC whose tip abuts the lateral wall of the SVC at a steep angle carries a risk of vessel perforation.
A pulmonary artery catheter tip projecting over the peripheral lung field beyond the hilum should be withdrawn.
The radio-opaque tip of an intra-aortic balloon pump should lie at the level of the renal arteries (L1).
questions.expl: CVC tips should lie in the lower SVC/cavo-atrial junction (roughly at or just below the carina). Left-sided catheters may end perpendicular to the SVC wall – perforation/tamponade risk. A PAC tip should be within ~2 cm of the hilum; a peripheral position risks infarction and PA rupture. The IABP tip should be in the descending thoracic aorta ~2 cm distal to the left subclavian artery – radiologically at about the level of the carina / 2nd–3rd anterior intercostal space; a low balloon occludes visceral/renal arteries. Reference: Godoy MCB et al. Chest radiography in the ICU: Part 2, Evaluation of cardiovascular lines and other devices. **AJR Am J Roentgenol** 2012;198:572–81.

title: Case-style practice · W30-D1 · Hypothermia

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is found outdoors with a core temperature of 27 °C. Regarding his ECG:
options: The amplitude of the Osborn (J) wave tends to increase as core temperature falls.
Shivering artefact may obscure the baseline in mild hypothermia.
Sinus tachycardia is the typical rhythm in moderate hypothermia (28–32 °C).
The Osborn wave is pathognomonic of hypothermia.
questions.expl: J waves enlarge with falling temperature. Shivering (in mild hypothermia) causes artefact. Moderate hypothermia typically produces sinus bradycardia, AF with slow ventricular response and prolonged PR/QRS/QT; below ~28 °C the risk of VF and asystole rises sharply. J waves also occur with hypercalcaemia, brain injury/SAH and early repolarisation, so they are not pathognomonic. Reference: Brown DJA et al. Accidental hypothermia. **N Engl J Med** 2012;367:1930–8; Paal P et al. Accidental hypothermia: 2021 update. **Int J Environ Res Public Health** 2022;19:501.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old avalanche victim is being actively rewarmed on VA-ECMO and temperature is monitored continuously. Regarding temperature measurement sites:
options: Bladder temperature lags behind core temperature during rapid rewarming or cooling.
Axillary temperature overestimates core temperature.
An oesophageal probe in the upper third of the oesophagus is the most accurate site because it is closest to the larynx.
Rectal temperature responds faster than oesophageal temperature to rapid changes.
questions.expl: Bladder temperature is accurate at steady state with good urine flow but lags during rapid change (and in anuria). Axillary readings UNDERESTIMATE core temperature. The oesophageal probe should be in the LOWER third (behind the heart); the upper oesophagus is cooled by tracheal gas. Rectal temperature lags considerably; oesophageal (or pulmonary artery) temperature is the reference during rewarming. Reference: Paal P et al. Accidental hypothermia – an update. **Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med** 2016;24:111.

title: Case-style practice · W30-D2 · Heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, NMS, serotonin syndrome

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman taking sertraline is started on linezolid for MRSA pneumonia and develops agitation, sweating and tremor. Regarding serotonin toxicity:
options: Under the Hunter criteria, inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis after a serotonergic agent is diagnostic.
Linezolid, a weak non-selective MAO inhibitor, can precipitate serotonin toxicity with SSRIs.
Physical restraint without sedation is the recommended way to control agitation.
Antipyretics such as paracetamol are effective treatment for the hyperthermia.
questions.expl: The Hunter criteria (clonus – spontaneous, inducible or ocular – plus agitation/diaphoresis, or tremor plus hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature >38 °C and clonus) are more sensitive and specific than Sternbach's. Linezolid is a recognised precipitant. Restraint worsens isometric muscle contraction, hyperthermia and lactic acidosis – benzodiazepines are first-line, with cyproheptadine as an adjunct. Hyperthermia is due to muscle activity, so antipyretics do not work; severe cases need sedation, paralysis and intubation. Reference: Boyer EW, Shannon M. The serotonin syndrome. **N Engl J Med** 2005;352:1112–20.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old festival-goer is brought in after taking 'ecstasy' (MDMA). Which statements are correct?
options: MDMA-associated hyponatraemia is more often reported in young women.
Core temperature above 40 °C warrants rapid active cooling and, if needed, sedation and neuromuscular blockade.
Seizures due to acute severe hyponatraemia are treated with a bolus of hypertonic saline.
Beta-blockers are the first-line treatment for MDMA-induced tachycardia and hypertension.
questions.expl: MDMA causes SIADH-like ADH release plus excessive water intake; young women are over-represented among severe cases. Hyperthermia (with rhabdomyolysis, DIC, AKI and liver injury) is the main killer: rapid cooling, benzodiazepines, and paralysis/ventilation if temperature persists (dantrolene is not of proven benefit). Symptomatic acute hyponatraemia: hypertonic saline bolus (e.g. 150 mL 3 %). Sympathomimetic toxicity is treated with benzodiazepines first; beta-blockers risk unopposed alpha-stimulation. Reference: Hall AP, Henry JA. Acute toxic effects of 'Ecstasy' (MDMA) and related compounds. **Br J Anaesth** 2006;96:678–85; Spasovski G et al. Clinical practice guideline on hyponatraemia. **Eur J Endocrinol** 2014;170:G1–47.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is undergoing elective knee arthroscopy under sevoflurane anaesthesia with a laryngeal mask and spontaneous ventilation, later converted to controlled ventilation. Forty minutes into the case the anaesthetist suspects malignant hyperthermia. Each of the following is consistent with an EARLY malignant hyperthermia crisis EXCEPT:
options: End-tidal CO₂ rising despite a doubling of minute ventilation
Dark, cola-coloured urine as the presenting feature
Unexplained sinus tachycardia
Generalised muscle rigidity
Mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis on arterial blood gas
questions.expl: Early MH signs reflect hypermetabolism: unexplained rising ETCO₂ (the most sensitive early sign), tachycardia, tachypnoea (if breathing spontaneously), muscle rigidity (masseter or generalised) and a mixed respiratory/metabolic acidosis. Myoglobinuria, hyperkalaemia, rising CK, hyperthermia and arrhythmias are LATE features. Management: stop volatile, hyperventilate with high-flow O₂, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV repeated as needed, active cooling and treatment of hyperkalaemia. Reference: Glahn KPE et al. Recognizing and managing a malignant hyperthermia crisis: guidelines from the European Malignant Hyperthermia Group. **Br J Anaesth** 2020;125:133–40.

title: Case-style practice · W30-D5 · Electrical injury; CBRN and pandemic preparedness

questions.stem: A patient in the cardiac ICU has a temporary transvenous pacing wire and a saline-filled central line. Regarding electrical safety:
options: Microshock refers to current delivered directly to the myocardium, where around 100 µA may be enough to cause VF.
Class II equipment is double-insulated and has no protective earth.
Type BF equipment is suitable for direct electrical connection to the heart.
Direct current is more likely than 50 Hz mains alternating current to cause VF at the same current magnitude.
questions.expl: Because current is concentrated at the myocardium, very small currents (~50–150 µA) can induce VF via an intracardiac conductor (macroshock through the skin needs ~100 mA). Class I equipment has a protective earth; class II is double-insulated. Only Type CF ('cardiac floating', leakage <10 µA normal / <50 µA single fault) equipment is suitable for direct cardiac connection – B and BF are not. Mains-frequency AC (50–60 Hz) is particularly arrhythmogenic and causes tetany preventing release; DC is less likely to cause VF at the same current. Reference: Boumphrey S, Langton JA. Electrical safety in the operating theatre. **BJA CEPD Reviews** 2003;3:10–4.

title: Case-style practice · W31-D1 · Withholding and withdrawing treatment

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man without capacity has been ventilated for 3 weeks after a massive stroke; the team considers that continuing life-sustaining treatment is not in his interests. Regarding decision-making about withholding and withdrawing treatment:
options: Withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatment are generally regarded as ethically equivalent.
In England and Wales, a valid and applicable advance decision refusing ventilation is legally binding.
A family request to continue a treatment the team considers non-beneficial obliges clinicians to provide it.
Clinicians must obtain the family's consent before withdrawing treatment from an incapacitated adult.
questions.expl: International consensus treats withholding and withdrawing as morally equivalent, although clinicians often find withdrawal harder. A valid, applicable advance decision to refuse treatment (written, witnessed, with an explicit statement if life-sustaining) is binding under the Mental Capacity Act; requests for treatment are not. Families must be consulted about the patient's values and wishes, but they cannot demand non-beneficial treatment and (unless a legally appointed proxy) do not consent on the patient's behalf; persistent disagreement should be managed by second opinions, mediation and, ultimately, the courts. Reference: Cook D, Rocker G. Dying with dignity in the intensive care unit. **N Engl J Med** 2014;370:2506–14; Sprung CL et al. Changes in end-of-life practices in European intensive care units from 1999 to 2016. **JAMA** 2019;322:1692–1704.

title: Case-style practice · W31-D3 · Capacity, consent, research in the ICU

questions.stem: A 55-year-old ICU patient with full capacity asks that his diagnosis of HIV infection not be shared with anyone. Regarding medical confidentiality:
options: The duty of confidentiality ends when the patient dies.
His spouse is automatically entitled to the diagnosis despite his refusal.
Clinicians are obliged to disclose information to the police about any crime a patient reveals, without consent.
If he later loses capacity, information may be shared with anyone who states that they are next of kin.
questions.expl: Confidentiality persists after death. A capacitous patient's refusal must generally be respected; disclosure without consent is justified only by law, a court order, or a sufficiently serious public interest (e.g. to protect an identifiable person from serious harm such as transmission risk to a sexual partner, after encouraging the patient to disclose). There is no general duty to report every crime – only specific statutory duties (e.g. gunshot/knife wounds in UK guidance, notifiable diseases). After loss of capacity, sharing with those close to the patient is guided by best interests and the patient's known wishes, not by self-declared kinship; health data are 'special category' data under GDPR. Reference: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation). **Official Journal of the European Union** 2016;L119:1–88.

questions.stem: Regarding capacity and consent in the ICU, which statements are correct?
options: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific.
Under the Montgomery judgment, the materiality of a risk is judged by what a reasonable body of doctors would disclose.
Deferred consent can be ethically acceptable in emergency research when prior consent is impossible.
A health-and-welfare attorney can refuse life-sustaining treatment only if the lasting power of attorney explicitly grants that authority.
questions.expl: A patient may have capacity for one decision but not another, and capacity fluctuates (e.g. delirium). Montgomery (UK Supreme Court 2015) replaced the Bolam 'reasonable doctor' test with a patient-centred test: risks a reasonable person in the patient's position – or this particular patient – would consider significant. Deferred (or 'research without prior consent') models are accepted in emergency/ICU research under ethics approval and EU Clinical Trials Regulation 536/2014. Under the MCA, an LPA attorney can refuse life-sustaining treatment only when expressly authorised. Reference: Chan SW et al. Montgomery and informed consent: where are we now? **BMJ** 2017;357:j2224.

title: Case-style practice · W31-D4 · Donation after circulatory death (DCD)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with catastrophic hypoxic brain injury is being considered for controlled donation after circulatory death in a country with an opt-out (deemed consent) system. Which statements are correct?
options: The family is still approached and involved even when consent is deemed.
A registered objection to donation can be overridden by the family if they wish donation to proceed.
Members of the transplant team should not be involved in the decision to withdraw life-sustaining treatment.
Pre-mortem administration of heparin to a potential cDCD donor is legally permitted in every European country.
questions.expl: In opt-out systems families remain central – they provide information on the person's last known wishes and in practice their support is sought. A recorded decision NOT to donate must be respected. The decision to withdraw treatment must be made independently of, and before, any donation discussion, without transplant team involvement (separation of roles). Ante-mortem interventions (heparin, cannulation, NRP) vary considerably between countries and are not universally permitted. Reference: Lomero M et al. Donation after circulatory death today: an updated overview of the European landscape. **Transpl Int** 2020;33:76–88.

questions.stem: Regarding donation after circulatory death (DCD) classification and physiology:
options: Modified Maastricht category II describes donors after unsuccessful resuscitation (uncontrolled DCD).
During abdominal normothermic regional perfusion, cerebral circulation is deliberately restored.
Functional warm ischaemic time is usually longer in controlled than in uncontrolled DCD.
The 'no-touch' observation period after circulatory arrest is uniformly 5 minutes across Europe.
questions.expl: Madrid 2011 modified Maastricht: I found dead, II unsuccessful resuscitation (both uncontrolled), III awaiting arrest after withdrawal of treatment (controlled), IV arrest in a brain-dead donor; V (euthanasia) in some countries. NRP restores oxygenated flow to abdominal (or thoraco-abdominal) organs only – the aortic arch vessels are occluded/ligated to exclude cerebral perfusion. Uncontrolled DCD has much longer warm ischaemia (arrest, CPR, transfer). No-touch periods vary from 5 min (e.g. UK, Spain, France) to 20 min (Italy). Reference: Thuong M et al. New classification of donation after circulatory death donors definitions and terminology. **Transpl Int** 2016;29:749–59; Lomero M et al. **Transpl Int** 2020;33:76–88.

title: Case-style practice · W32-D1 · Scoring systems (APACHE, SAPS, SOFA)

questions.stem: Which of the following are correctly described?
options: SAPS 3 is a severity-of-illness score based on data collected around ICU admission.
The Child–Pugh score is a generic ICU mortality prediction model.
NEWS2 is a track-and-trigger system to detect deterioration in ward patients.
SOFA-2 (2025) was designed primarily as a mortality-prediction model rather than an organ dysfunction score.
questions.expl: SAPS 3 uses data from the first hour of ICU admission and has regional customisation equations. Child–Pugh (like MELD) is disease-specific for cirrhosis. NEWS2 (UK RCP 2017) aggregates physiological parameters to trigger escalation. SOFA-2, like the original SOFA, describes organ dysfunction (six systems, 0–4 each); its association with mortality was validated, but it is not a mortality model. Reference: Ranzani OT et al. Development and validation of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-2 score. **JAMA** 2025; Vincent JL, Moreno R. Clinical review: scoring systems in the critically ill. **Crit Care** 2010;14:207.

questions.stem: Regarding the statistical properties of ICU prognostic models:
options: A model with high discrimination (AUROC 0.90) is necessarily well calibrated.
Calibration can be assessed with calibration plots or the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test.
Over time, as care improves, older models tend to over-predict mortality and need recalibration.
A standardised mortality ratio (SMR) of 0.8 means observed mortality was 20 % higher than predicted.
questions.expl: Discrimination (ranking survivors vs non-survivors) and calibration (agreement between predicted and observed risk across strata) are independent; a model can rank perfectly yet systematically over- or under-estimate risk. 'Model drift' with improving care leads to over-prediction, hence periodic recalibration or new versions (APACHE IV, SAPS 3). SMR = observed/predicted deaths; 0.8 means 20 % FEWER deaths than predicted. Reference: Vincent JL, Moreno R. Clinical review: scoring systems in the critically ill. **Crit Care** 2010;14:207.

questions.stem: Regarding commonly used clinical scores:
options: The Injury Severity Score is the sum of the squares of the highest AIS grades in the three most severely injured body regions.
The Glasgow Coma Scale ranges from 3 to 15.
A qSOFA ≥2 is part of the Sepsis-3 definition of sepsis.
A RASS of 0 corresponds to an alert and calm patient.
questions.expl: ISS = sum of squares of the three highest AIS scores from different regions (range 1–75; any AIS 6 = 75). GCS 3–15. qSOFA is a bedside prompt to identify patients at risk outside the ICU; sepsis itself is defined as infection plus an acute SOFA increase ≥2 – and qSOFA is no longer recommended as a single screening tool (SSC 2021). RASS ranges from +4 (combative) to −5 (unrousable), 0 = alert and calm. Reference: Singer M et al. The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). **JAMA** 2016;315:801–10; Sessler CN et al. The Richmond Agitation–Sedation Scale. **Am J Respir Crit Care Med** 2002;166:1338–44.

questions.stem: A regional network wants to compare risk-adjusted mortality across its ICUs using a published admission score that had an AUROC of 0.86 in its derivation cohort. When applied to 4000 patients in your unit, it ranks patients well (AUROC 0.84), but mean predicted hospital mortality is 30 % whereas observed mortality is 18 %, with the gap present in every risk decile. Which is the BEST description of the problem?
options: Poor discrimination of the score in the local population
A type II error caused by an inadequate sample size
Lead-time bias due to earlier ICU admission
Poor calibration, with systematic over-prediction of risk in this population
Spectrum bias that invalidates the AUROC
questions.expl: Discrimination is preserved (AUROC 0.84), but predicted and observed risks disagree consistently across deciles – a calibration failure. Benchmarking with such a model would produce a flattering SMR (0.6) for every unit. Causes include case-mix differences, changes in care since derivation (model drift) and differences in data collection; remedies are first-level customisation (recalibration) or a newer model. A useful score must first be valid and well-calibrated for the population in which it is used. Reference: Vincent JL, Moreno R. Clinical review: scoring systems in the critically ill. **Crit Care** 2010;14:207.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with cirrhosis is admitted with pneumonia and his APACHE II score is calculated. Which of the following contribute points to the APACHE II score?
options: Glasgow Coma Scale
Serum creatinine, with double points in acute renal failure
A history of severe organ insufficiency or immunocompromise (chronic health points)
Arterial pH (or serum bicarbonate if no blood gas is available)
questions.expl: APACHE II = Acute Physiology Score (12 variables, worst value in the first 24 h: temperature, MAP, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygenation, arterial pH/HCO₃⁻, Na⁺, K⁺, creatinine – doubled in ARF – haematocrit, WBC and 15 − GCS) + age points + chronic health points (cirrhosis, NYHA IV, severe COPD, dialysis, immunocompromise), with more points for emergency surgery/non-operative admission. Bilirubin, albumin, lactate and sex are not included. Reference: Knaus WA et al. APACHE II: a severity of disease classification system. **Crit Care Med** 1985;13:818–29.

title: Case-style practice · W32-D2 · Triage, capacity, staffing; intra- and inter-hospital transport

questions.stem: Regarding ICU organisation, staffing and outcomes:
options: High-intensity intensivist staffing (closed units or mandatory intensivist consultation) was associated with lower hospital mortality in a systematic review of observational studies.
A randomised trial showed that adding overnight in-house intensivists to a unit with daytime intensivist coverage reduced mortality.
Discharge from ICU at night has been associated with higher post-ICU mortality in observational studies.
Higher nursing workload relative to staffing has been associated with increased ICU mortality.
questions.expl: Pronovost (2002) found lower ICU and hospital mortality with high-intensity staffing. Kerlin et al. (RCT, 2013) found no benefit of nighttime intensivists where daytime intensivist care was already present; observational data (Wallace 2012) suggested benefit only in low-intensity units. Night discharge and high patient-to-nurse ratios/workload are associated with worse outcomes, though data are observational. Reference: Pronovost PJ et al. **JAMA** 2002;288:2151–62; Kerlin MP et al. A randomized trial of nighttime physician staffing in an intensive care unit. **N Engl J Med** 2013;368:2201–9; Neuraz A et al. **Crit Care Med** 2015;43:1587–94.

questions.stem: A ventilated 52-year-old woman is transferred by fixed-wing air ambulance with a cabin altitude of 8000 ft (≈565 mmHg). Regarding the physics of altitude:
options: Gas trapped in a closed space (e.g. an ETT cuff) expands by roughly one-third at this cabin altitude.
Pressurised air-ambulance cabins are always maintained at sea-level pressure.
The volume increase of an ETT cuff on ascent is described by Charles' law.
If FiO₂ is unchanged, altitude has no effect on her PaO₂.
questions.expl: Boyle's law (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ at constant temperature): 760/565 ≈ 1.35 – a ~35 % volume increase in trapped gas (cuffs, pneumothorax, bowel, air in IV bags). Cabins are usually pressurised to 6000–8000 ft; sea-level cabins are possible only at reduced cruising altitude and cost. Charles' law relates volume to temperature. Although FiO₂ is unchanged, barometric pressure falls, so PiO₂ (Dalton's law) and PaO₂ fall – FiO₂/PEEP may need increasing; undrained pneumothorax should be drained before flight. Reference: Droogh JM et al. Transferring the critically ill patient: are we there yet? **Crit Care** 2015;19:62.

title: Case-style practice · W32-D3 · Quality indicators, errors and incidents

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman ventilated for 10 days develops skin damage over the sacrum and under her nasogastric tube fixation. According to the NPIAP/EPUAP staging system:
options: A stage 2 pressure injury is partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis.
A stage 4 pressure injury is full-thickness skin loss without exposed bone, tendon or muscle.
Medical device-related pressure injuries are excluded from staging.
Prone positioning for ARDS reduces the incidence of facial pressure injuries.
questions.expl: Stage 1 = non-blanchable erythema of intact skin; stage 2 = partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis; stage 3 = full-thickness skin loss (fat visible) without exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone; stage 4 = full-thickness skin AND tissue loss with these structures exposed; plus unstageable and deep tissue pressure injury. Device-related injuries are staged using the same system (mucosal ones are not). Prone positioning INCREASES pressure injuries (face, chest, knees). Reference: Edsberg LE et al. Revised National Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel pressure injury staging system. **J Wound Ostomy Continence Nurs** 2016;43:585–97; Guérin C et al. (PROSEVA). **N Engl J Med** 2013;368:2159–68.

questions.stem: A unit introduces a daily checklist inspired by care bundles such as FAST HUG and ABCDEF. Regarding the evidence behind individual elements:
options: Head-of-bed elevation to 30–45° is a component of ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundles.
Spontaneous awakening and breathing trials are part of the ABCDEF bundle.
Stress ulcer prophylaxis is indicated for every ICU patient regardless of bleeding risk.
Targeting blood glucose of 4.4–6.1 mmol/L reduces mortality in mixed ICU populations.
questions.expl: Head-up positioning is a standard VAP-prevention measure. ABCDEF = Assess/manage pain, Both SAT and SBT, Choice of sedation, Delirium, Early mobility, Family engagement. SUP should be reserved for patients at high risk of GI bleeding (SUP-ICU found no mortality benefit of pantoprazole; REVISE 2024 showed fewer bleeds in ventilated patients without mortality effect). NICE-SUGAR showed higher mortality with 4.5–6.0 mmol/L vs <10 mmol/L. Reference: Vincent JL. Give your patient a fast hug (at least) once a day. **Crit Care Med** 2005;33:1225–9; Krag M et al. (SUP-ICU). **N Engl J Med** 2018;379:2199–208; NICE-SUGAR Investigators. **N Engl J Med** 2009;360:1283–97.

title: Case-style practice · W32-D4 · PICS and long-term outcomes

questions.stem: A follow-up clinic assesses survivors 6 months after ICU discharge. Regarding instruments used to measure long-term outcomes:
options: EQ-5D-5L covers mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression.
The Impact of Event Scale-Revised (IES-R) screens for post-traumatic stress symptoms.
The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) is used to screen for cognitive impairment.
The SF-36 produces a single summary index that is used directly to calculate QALYs.
questions.expl: EQ-5D is a generic, patient-reported utility measure (five dimensions) whose index can be used to calculate QALYs. IES-R (22 items) screens for PTSD symptoms; HADS for anxiety/depression; MoCA for cognition – all recommended in PICS core outcome sets. SF-36 yields eight domains and two summary scores (physical and mental component); utilities require conversion to the SF-6D. Reference: Needham DM et al. Core outcome measures for clinical research in acute respiratory failure survivors. **Am J Respir Crit Care Med** 2017;196:1122–30.

title: Case-style practice · W33-D1 · Study design, bias

questions.stem: Regarding the interpretation of superiority RCTs in critical care:
options: ARISE did not show a mortality benefit of early goal-directed therapy, so the null hypothesis was not rejected.
NICE-SUGAR rejected the null hypothesis, finding higher mortality with intensive glucose control.
TTM2 found no significant difference in mortality between targeted hypothermia at 33 °C and normothermia after cardiac arrest.
A superiority trial with a non-significant result demonstrates that the two treatments are equivalent.
questions.expl: ARISE (2014) – like ProCESS and ProMISe – found no difference with EGDT. NICE-SUGAR (2009) found increased 90-day mortality with 4.5–6.0 mmol/L targets (the null can be rejected in the direction of harm). TTM2 (2021) found no difference in 6-month mortality. 'Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence': equivalence or non-inferiority must be tested with a pre-specified margin and appropriate design. Reference: ARISE Investigators. **N Engl J Med** 2014;371:1496–506; Dankiewicz J et al. (TTM2). **N Engl J Med** 2021;384:2283–94.

questions.stem: Regarding trial phases, certainty of evidence and inference:
options: Phase 1 trials are usually small studies assessing safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics, often in healthy volunteers.
In GRADE, a body of evidence from RCTs starts as moderate certainty.
Statistical power equals 1 − α.
A 95 % confidence interval for a risk ratio of 0.82–1.03 indicates a statistically significant benefit at the 5 % level.
questions.expl: Phase 1 = first-in-human safety/PK; phase 2 = dose-finding/preliminary efficacy; phase 3 = confirmatory efficacy; phase 4 = post-marketing. GRADE: RCT evidence starts HIGH and observational evidence LOW, then is rated down (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias) or up. Power = 1 − β (β = type II error probability); α is the type I error rate. A CI crossing 1 (no effect) is not significant at the 5 % level. Reference: Guyatt GH et al. GRADE: an emerging consensus on rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations. **BMJ** 2008;336:924–6.

title: Case-style practice · W33-D2 · Sensitivity, specificity, LR, ROC

questions.stem: A new point-of-care biomarker for bacterial infection has a sensitivity of 90 % and a specificity of 80 % at the manufacturer's cut-off. Which statements are correct?
options: The positive likelihood ratio is 4.5.
The negative likelihood ratio is 0.2.
In a population with 10 % prevalence, the positive predictive value is approximately 33 %.
Sensitivity will fall if the test is used in a population with lower prevalence.
questions.expl: LR+ = sens/(1 − spec) = 0.9/0.2 = 4.5. LR− = (1 − sens)/spec = 0.1/0.8 = 0.125. With 10 % prevalence per 1000: TP = 90, FP = 0.2 × 900 = 180, PPV = 90/270 ≈ 33 % (NPV = 720/730 ≈ 99 %). Sensitivity and specificity are (in principle) independent of prevalence, whereas predictive values change with prevalence (spectrum effects can still alter sensitivity in practice). Raising a cut-off moves along the ROC curve, trading sensitivity for specificity. Reference: Akobeng AK. Understanding diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity, specificity and predictive values. **Acta Paediatr** 2007;96:338–41; Akobeng AK. Understanding diagnostic tests 2: likelihood ratios, pre- and post-test probabilities and their use in clinical practice. **Acta Paediatr** 2007;96:487–91.

title: Case-style practice · W33-D3 · NNT, ARR, RR, OR

questions.stem: In an RCT, 90-day mortality is 25 % in the control group and 20 % in the intervention group. Which statements are correct?
options: The absolute risk reduction is 5 % and the number needed to treat is 20.
The relative risk is 0.80, corresponding to a relative risk reduction of 20 %.
The odds ratio is 0.75, further from 1 than the relative risk, as expected for a common outcome.
A type I error is concluding that a difference exists when in truth there is none.
questions.expl: ARR = 25 − 20 = 5 %; NNT = 1/0.05 = 20. RR = 0.20/0.25 = 0.80, RRR = 20 %. OR = (0.20/0.80)/(0.25/0.75) = 0.25/0.333 = 0.75; the OR exaggerates the RR when the outcome is common and approximates it only for rare outcomes (<~10 %). Type I error = false positive (α); type II = false negative (β). Reference: Schechtman E. Odds ratio, relative risk, absolute risk reduction, and the number needed to treat – which of these should we use? **Value Health** 2002;5:431–6.

title: Case-style practice · W34-D2 · Paediatric resuscitation (ERC 2025 PLS) and physiology

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child weighing 12 kg (measured) has a cardiac arrest with a shockable rhythm. According to ERC Paediatric Life Support guidance:
options: IV/IO adrenaline 10 µg/kg corresponds to 1.2 mL of 1:10 000 (100 µg/mL) adrenaline.
Each defibrillation shock should be approximately 4 J/kg, i.e. about 50 J.
A fluid bolus, if indicated, is 10 mL/kg of crystalloid (120 mL).
Amiodarone 5 mg/kg is given after the first shock.
questions.expl: Adrenaline 10 µg/kg = 120 µg = 1.2 mL of 100 µg/mL; in shockable rhythms it is given after the 3rd shock (then every 3–5 min). Defibrillation 4 J/kg (max 120–150 J in ERC guidance). Fluid boluses are 10 mL/kg (balanced crystalloid preferred) and reassessed. Amiodarone 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg) is given after the 3rd and 5th shocks (lidocaine 1 mg/kg is an alternative). Reference: Van de Voorde P et al. European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021: Paediatric Life Support. **Resuscitation** 2021;161:327–87 (unchanged in principle in ERC Guidelines 2025: Paediatric Life Support, **Resuscitation** 2025).

questions.stem: Regarding paediatric resuscitation formulae and equipment selection:
options: Length-based tapes or tools are preferred to age-based formulae for estimating weight when the weight is unknown.
For a cuffed tracheal tube in a child over 2 years, internal diameter (mm) ≈ age/4 + 4.
Oral tracheal tube insertion depth (cm at the lips) is approximately age/2 + 12.
The initial energy for synchronised cardioversion of unstable SVT is 4 J/kg.
questions.expl: ERC PLS recommends length-based methods (or parental estimate/known weight) over age formulae, which perform poorly at extremes of body habitus. Cuffed tubes are preferred: ID ≈ age/4 + 3.5 (age/4 + 4 is the uncuffed formula). Oral depth ≈ age/2 + 12 cm (nasal ≈ age/2 + 15), confirmed by capnography and imaging. Synchronised cardioversion starts at 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg; 4 J/kg is the defibrillation dose. Reference: Van de Voorde P et al. European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021: Paediatric Life Support. **Resuscitation** 2021;161:327–87.

title: Case-style practice · general · General medicine for the intensivist

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome (urine protein 9 g/day, albumin 18 g/L) is admitted to ICU. Regarding complications of nephrotic syndrome:
options: Membranous nephropathy carries a particularly high risk of renal vein thrombosis.
Loss of immunoglobulin increases susceptibility to infections such as pneumococcal peritonitis and cellulitis.
Total serum calcium is typically reduced.
Serum cholesterol is typically reduced.
questions.expl: A – VTE risk rises steeply when albumin falls below ~20–25 g/L (urinary loss of antithrombin, increased hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and factors V/VIII); membranous nephropathy has the highest risk, and prophylactic anticoagulation is considered. B – urinary loss of IgG and complement factors. C – hypoalbuminaemia lowers total calcium (and vitamin D-binding protein is lost); ionised calcium may be normal or low. D – hyperlipidaemia results from increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis and reduced catabolism. Reference: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases. **Kidney Int** 2021;100(4S):S1–S276; Kerlin BA, Ayoob R, Smoyer WE. Epidemiology and pathophysiology of nephrotic syndrome-associated thromboembolic disease. **Clin J Am Soc Nephrol** 2012;7:513–520.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old university student has fever, exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. After a course of amoxicillin he developed a widespread maculopapular rash. ALT is 210 U/L and the blood film shows atypical lymphocytes. He is able to swallow fluids and has no stridor. Each of the following is appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Confirming the diagnosis with a heterophile antibody test or EBV serology (VCA IgM)
Advising avoidance of contact sports for at least 3–4 weeks
Explaining that the rash does not necessarily indicate true penicillin allergy
Prescribing routine oral aciclovir to shorten the illness
Considering corticosteroids if tonsillar enlargement threatens the airway
questions.expl: This is infectious mononucleosis (EBV). Heterophile antibody (Monospot) or EBV-specific serology confirms it (A). Splenic rupture risk is highest in the first 3–4 weeks (B). The aminopenicillin rash in EBV is usually not IgE-mediated and does not mandate lifelong penicillin avoidance (C). Corticosteroids are reserved for complications such as impending airway obstruction, haemolytic anaemia or severe thrombocytopenia (E). Antivirals (aciclovir, valaciclovir) reduce viral shedding but have no proven clinical benefit and are not recommended routinely (D). Reference: Dunmire SK, Verghese PS, Balfour HH Jr. Primary Epstein–Barr virus infection. **J Clin Virol** 2018;102:84–92; Luzuriaga K, Sullivan JL. Infectious mononucleosis. **N Engl J Med** 2010;362:1993–2000.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman presents with an acutely hot, swollen knee and fever. Regarding the diagnosis of septic arthritis:
options: A synovial white cell count > 50 000/µL strongly suggests septic arthritis, but lower counts do not exclude it.
The presence of crystals in the aspirate excludes septic arthritis.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the most common cause in older adults.
Blood cultures are rarely positive and need not be taken.
questions.expl: A – higher counts increase likelihood (LR rises with > 50 000 and > 100 000/µL), but sensitivity is limited, especially in immunosuppression or prosthetic joints. B – crystal arthropathy and infection can coexist. C – S. aureus is the commonest pathogen in adults; gonococcal arthritis affects younger sexually active adults. D – blood cultures are positive in about half of cases and should be taken before antibiotics, together with synovial Gram stain and culture (Gram stain is negative in a substantial proportion). Reference: Margaretten ME, et al. Does this adult patient have septic arthritis? **JAMA** 2007;297:1478–1488; Mathews CJ, et al. Bacterial septic arthritis in adults. **Lancet** 2010;375:846–855.
